### [46] [Fidelity Is Not Safety: Gently-Compressed LLMs Pass Every Data-Free Quality Guard Yet Invent Procedure Steps in Agentic Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28196)
*I. Kennedy,T. Kennedy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Compressed language models can pass standard quality checks (perplexity, MMLU, output fidelity) yet silently "invent" steps not in the original instructions when deployed as agents. This failure is specific to low-rank (SVD) compression — magnitude pruning at the same perplexity does not cause it. The root cause is the coherence of the compression error, which data-free fidelity probes are blind to by design. The authors propose a data-free screening statistic based on coherent-fraction and error-rate that flags failing models across architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current model compression validation pipelines rely on perplexity, downstream accuracy (e.g., MMLU), and data-free output-fidelity signals. These guards give a false sense of safety: compressed models that pass all checks can still exhibit dangerous behavioral failures (inventing steps in standard operating procedures) when deployed as agents. The blind spot needs characterization and a practical fix.

Method: The authors conduct a pre-registered, powered study across three model families. They apply two compression methods — coherent low-rank (SVD) truncation and magnitude pruning — matched to the same perplexity. They test compressed models as agents executing a standard operating procedure (SOP), using an "invented-step canary" as the outcome. Paired confidence intervals compare models on output-fidelity tests versus the canary. They then derive a two-axis statistic (coherent-fraction × error-rate) as a data-free screening tool and validate it with fixed thresholds across architectures.

Result: Gently-compressed models pass all conventional guards but invent procedure steps under low-rank (SVD) compression; magnitude pruning at matched perplexity does not produce this effect. The dissociation is systematic: weights that win confidence-interval tests on output fidelity simultaneously fail the invented-step canary. The governing mechanism is coherence of compression error × error rate, not error magnitude. The proposed two-axis screen flags failing builds with fixed thresholds across all three architectures tested.

Conclusion: Perplexity, MMLU, and fidelity acceptance do not certify agent safety. Low-rank compressed models require additional screening before agentic deployment. The proposed coherence-times-rate statistic provides a practical, data-free screening method that generalizes across architectures.

Abstract: Practitioners accept a compressed language model once it clears a stack of data-cheap quality guards: perplexity within a small factor of the original, downstream accuracy (for example MMLU) inside a confidence interval, and data-free output-fidelity signals that compare the compressed and original network's internal representations under random probe inputs. This stack has a blind spot. Across three model families, gently-compressed models clear every guard and then invent procedure steps that were never in the instructions when they run a standard operating procedure (SOP) as an agent. The effect is operator-specific: coherent low-rank (SVD) truncation induces it, and magnitude pruning matched to the same perplexity does not. One dissociation isolates the cause. The same compressed weights that CI-win a paired output-fidelity test CI-fail the invented-step canary. The governing axis is the coherence of the compression error times its rate; the magnitude of the damage does not predict it. The data-free fidelity probe is a fidelity oracle by construction, so it cannot see this axis. We characterize the blindspot and dissociation with paired confidence intervals on a pre-registered, powered canary across three architectures. Operator-specificity replicates on all three, and the perplexity-guard evasion appears where the model admits in-guard low-rank headroom. We then give a data-free screen: a two-axis statistic of the compression error (coherent-fraction and error-rate) that flags the failing builds with fixed thresholds across architectures and matches the coherence-times-rate mechanism. Perplexity, MMLU, and fidelity acceptance do not certify agent safety. Screen gently-compressed low-rank builds before agentic deployment

</details>


### [47] [Causal Discovery with Inverted Self-attention for Multivariate Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28212)
*Yusen Liu,Yong Wang,Yifan Yin,Tianqing Zhu,Xiufeng Liu,Huan Huo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a transformer-based framework for causal discovery in multivariate time series that uses an inverted causal self-attention mechanism (CSAM) with sparsity induction, a global causal algorithm, and a causal verification module to address challenges of complex interactions, high dimensionality, and nonlinear dependencies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing causal discovery methods for multivariate time series struggle with complex interactions, high dimensionality, and nonlinear dependencies among variables, leading to inaccurate causal structures. There is a need for a method that can better capture latent and indirect causal relationships while reducing spurious correlations.

Method: The authors propose a novel framework centered on: (1) an inverted causal self-attention mechanism (CSAM) that inverts tokens and induces sparsity in attention scores to emphasize significant causal interactions; (2) a global causal algorithm for identifying holistic causal links; and (3) a causal verification module to ensure robustness of the identified causal relationships.

Result: Experiments on both linear and nonlinear datasets, complemented by ablation studies and sensitivity analyses, demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms existing methods for causal discovery in complex multivariate time series.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates strong potential for causal discovery in complex multivariate time series, effectively addressing key limitations of prior approaches through self-attention mechanisms, sparsity induction, and verification modules.

Abstract: Causal discovery in multivariate time series data is challenging due to complex interactions, high dimensionality, and nonlinear dependencies among variables. Existing methods often struggle to capture these complexities, resulting in inaccurate causal structures. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework that leverages self-attention mechanisms within the transformer architecture for causal discovery. Our approach introduces a novel inverted causal self-attention mechanism (CSAM) that emphasizes latent and indirect causal relationships by inverting tokens and inducing sparsity in attention scores, focusing on significant causal interactions and reducing spurious correlations. Additionally, we develop a global causal algorithm to identify global causal links, providing a holistic metric for causal influence, along with a causal verification module to ensure robustness in the identified causal relationships, enhancing the reliability of our framework. Experiments on both linear and nonlinear datasets, along with ablation studies and sensitivity analyses, show that our framework outperforms existing methods, demonstrating its potential for causal discovery in complex multivariate time series.

</details>


### [48] [Understanding Is Done Early: A Depth Division of Labor in Large Language Models and Its Use for Unbounded-Context Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28263)
*Hanzuo Liu,Xuan Qi,Chunyu Liu,Haotian Zhong,Yulong Wang,Rayying,Key,Alex Lamb,Mingyu Gao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CoMem proposes organizing long-context memory along the transformer depth axis: lower/middle layers build semantic representations that are cached, while upper layers are recomputed per query. This yields memory usage and prefill speed independent of stored-context length, achieving strong long-context performance with dramatically reduced GPU memory and a 7.83× prefill speedup at 128k.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer layers exhibit a division of labor: lower and middle layers construct general semantic representations, while upper layers specialize them for prediction. Existing long-context methods organize memory along the token axis (e.g., KV-cache compression, retrieval), but this work asks: can memory be organized along the layer axis instead? By caching intermediate representations rather than full KV-caches, one could decouple memory cost from stored-context length and avoid recomputing lower layers for each retrieved chunk.

Method: CoMem (Comprehension Memory) works as follows: (1) Each context chunk is written to memory by passing it only through lower/intermediate layers of a frozen backbone, caching the residual states at a chosen intermediate depth. (2) At inference, a fixed number of cached residual states are retrieved. (3) The query-conditioned upper layers are recomputed over the retrieved pack. Only a rank-32 LoRA adapter is trained via self-distillation on PG19 (the flagship), with an adapter-free variant also reported. The backbone (continued-trained Qwen3-8B) remains frozen. A unified chat-template-free evaluation protocol is used.

Result: On RULER, CoMem reaches 97.05; on LoCoMo (dialogue memory), it scores 38.27 vs. 34.59 for full-context KV-Direct. The dialogue-memory advantage persists under conversation-cluster resampling and independent judge evaluation. On an NVIDIA H20 at 128k, CoMem uses 18.26 GB vs. 89.36 GB for full KV-cache and achieves 7.83× prefill speedup. Depth sweeps reveal deeper caching reduces per-query recomputation but incurs fidelity loss, which self-distillation substantially repairs. A bounded retrieval "compression tax" on in-window tasks is also documented.

Conclusion: Long-context memory can be effectively organized along the layer axis, not only the token axis. CoMem's layer-axis caching achieves strong performance with bounded memory and compute, though a compression tax exists for in-window tasks. Self-distillation proves critical for repairing fidelity loss from deeper caching.

Abstract: Transformer depth is not used uniformly: lower and middle layers build semantic representations, while upper layers increasingly specialize them for prediction. We turn this division of labor into CoMem (Comprehension Memory), which writes each context chunk only through an intermediate layer, retrieves a fixed number of cached residual states, and recomputes the query-conditioned upper layers over the resulting pack. For a fixed retrieval budget, model-side read compute and memory are independent of stored-context length. We evaluate a continued-trained Qwen3-8B base LM under a unified chat-template-free protocol. The backbone is frozen; the flagship trains only a rank-32 self-distillation LoRA on plain PG19, and we report an adapter-free arm separately. CoMem reaches 97.05 on RULER and 38.27 on LoCoMo versus 34.59 for full-context KV-Direct; the dialogue-memory advantage survives conversation-cluster resampling and an independent judge. Results on additional long-context and long-document tasks expose both the benefits of bounded retrieval and its in-window compression tax. Controlled depth sweeps show that deeper caching lowers per-query recomputation but incurs a fidelity loss that self-distillation substantially repairs. In a separate adapter-free efficiency control on an NVIDIA H20 at 128k, CoMem uses 18.26 GB rather than 89.36 GB and achieves a 7.83x prefill speedup. These results show that long-context memory can be organized along the layer axis, not only the token axis.

</details>


### [49] [MORFES: A Benchmark for Productive Inflectional Competence in Modern Greek](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28274)
*Ioakeim Perros,Cleopatra Papadopoulou,Ayoub Kirouane,Christos Petrocheilos*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MORFES is a new benchmark of 500 expert-verified items for evaluating Greek inflectional morphology in language models, favoring low-frequency lemmas. The authors also release Sophea-Genesis-1, an open-weight model that leads on this benchmark while maintaining general capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern Greek is richly inflected, yet existing LM evaluations for Greek focus on factual knowledge with no dedicated benchmark for inflectional competence. This gap leaves grammatical ability in morphologically rich languages under-measured, especially as multilingual open-weight models rapidly scale.

Method: The authors construct MORFES, a benchmark of 500 expert-verified items testing both recognition and production of Greek inflected forms. Items favor lower-frequency lemmas so correct answers reflect rule application rather than memorization. They evaluate a range of open LMs (LLaMA, Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, Magistral, Kimi K2) and introduce Sophea-Genesis-1, their own open-weight model.

Result: Sophea-Genesis-1 achieves the best performance on MORFES among evaluated models while matching similarly sized models in general capability, demonstrating that strong inflectional morphology handling need not come at the cost of overall performance.

Conclusion: MORFES fills a critical evaluation gap for Greek inflectional morphology. The strong performance of Sophea-Genesis-1 shows that targeted attention to morphological competence is feasible within the open-weight model ecosystem, and the authors call for broader grammatical evaluation beyond factual knowledge in morphologically rich languages.

Abstract: Modern Greek is a richly inflected language, yet the language models built for it are evaluated mainly on factual knowledge, and no benchmark is dedicated to their inflectional competence. We introduce MORFES (Morphological Open-class Recognition-and-Formation Evaluation Suite), a benchmark of 500 expert-verified items that tests the recognition and production of Greek inflected forms, favoring lower-frequency lemmas so that a correct answer reflects the rule rather than a memorized form. We make it publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/KIEFERSA/MORFES. We evaluate a range of open language models on MORFES, situating them within the rapidly scaling open-weight ecosystem from LLaMA to Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, Magistral, and Kimi K2, where multilingual coverage grows but grammatical competence in morphologically rich languages remains under-measured. Among them, Sophea-Genesis-1, a model we developed and release as open weights at https://huggingface.co/KIEFERSA/Sophea-Genesis-1, leads on inflectional morphology while matching similarly sized models in general capability.

</details>


### [50] [(Towards) Scalable Reliable Automated Evaluation with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28282)
*Bertil Braun,Martin Forell*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes an LLM-based evaluation framework that uses pairwise comparisons by multiple LLMs combined with an Elo rating system to rank text quality, achieving expert-level alignment while being scalable and domain-agnostic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated metrics for evaluating LLM outputs fail to capture the complexity and variability of generated text and are overly dependent on explicit reference standards, limiting their applicability to domains with objective benchmarks. There is a need for a scalable, reference-free evaluation approach that approximates expert judgment.

Method: The framework uses multiple LLMs to perform pairwise comparisons of generated outputs, reducing individual model biases. Rankings are derived via an Elo rating system for stability and interpretability. Adjustable agreement thresholds (from full unanimity to majority voting) provide flexible control over the trade-off between evaluation confidence and coverage.

Result: The method was validated on competency profiles extracted from scientific abstracts. Automatically derived rankings showed strong correlation with expert judgments, substantially reducing the need for extensive human evaluation.

Conclusion: The framework offers a scalable, consistent, and domain-agnostic evaluation layer that supports more efficient and reliable quality assessment of LLM outputs across diverse applications.

Abstract: Evaluating the quality and relevance of textual outputs from Large Language Models (LLMs) remains challenging and resource-intensive. Existing automated metrics often fail to capture the complexity and variability inherent in LLM-generated outputs. Moreover, these metrics typically rely on explicit reference standards, limiting their use mostly to domains with objective benchmarks. This work introduces a novel evaluation framework designed to approximate expert-level assessments of LLM-generated content. The proposed method employs pairwise comparisons of outputs by multiple LLMs, reducing biases from individual models. An Elo rating system is used to generate stable and interpretable rankings. Adjustable agreement thresholds, from full unanimity to majority voting, allow flexible control over evaluation confidence and coverage. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through evaluating competency profiles extracted from scientific abstracts. Preliminary results show that automatically derived rankings correlate well with expert judgments, significantly reducing the need for extensive human intervention. By offering a scalable, consistent, and domain-agnostic evaluation layer, the framework supports more efficient and reliable quality assessments of LLM outputs across diverse applications.

</details>


### [51] [CACHE-UK: A Stability-Aware Memory Editor for Sequentially Updated Quantized LLMs in Finance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28292)
*Anubhav Lakra,Yue Feng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CACHE-UK is a stability-aware memory editing framework for 4-bit quantized LLMs in UK finance that uses rank-1 LoRA perturbations, domain-specific prioritization, and a degradation-debt tracker to reduce knowledge degradation by 11-17% over adapted baselines, though absolute generalization remains low at 28%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs deployed in dynamic financial environments must maintain factual accuracy as market conditions and regulations evolve. While 4-bit quantization enables efficient deployment, existing sequential memory editing methods suffer catastrophic performance degradation under low-precision constraints — a phenomenon termed the "quantization stability crisis." This creates a tension between deployment efficiency and factual reliability.

Method: CACHE-UK (Contextual Adaptive Continual Hybrid Editor for UK Finance) comprises three integrated components: (1) a rank-1 LoRA perturbation mechanism that restricts edits to a low-rank adapter subspace, preventing disruption to quantized weights; (2) a financial domain prioritization module that adapts edit strength based on content relevance; and (3) a closed-loop Stability Controller that tracks cumulative "degradation debt" across sequential updates to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.

Result: Evaluated on a 4-bit quantized OpenLLaMA-3B model with 88,021 curated UK financial documents, CACHE-UK achieved: (1) 11-17% reduction in knowledge degradation relative to adapted baselines under identical 4-bit constraints; (2) the highest test success (generalization) rate of 28%, representing a 6 percentage point improvement over the strongest adapted baseline.

Conclusion: Stability-aware editing can meaningfully improve factual maintenance in resource-constrained financial LLM deployments, but the low absolute generalization rate (28%) indicates that reliable sequential editing under extreme quantization remains an open problem requiring further research.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) deployed in dynamic financial environments face a critical challenge: maintaining factual accuracy as market conditions, regulations, and corporate facts change continuously. While 4-bit quantization enables efficient deployment, it severely limits the viability of sequential memory editing: existing methods undergo catastrophic performance degradation under this "quantization stability crisis." We introduce CACHE-UK (Contextual Adaptive Continual Hybrid Editor for UK Finance), a stability-aware memory editing framework specifically designed for domain-specific, quantized LLMs. CACHE-UK integrates three components: a rank-1 LoRA perturbation mechanism that confines edits to the low-rank adapter subspace, a financial domain prioritization module for content-adaptive edit strength, and a closed-loop Stability Controller that tracks "degradation debt" to prevent catastrophic forgetting across sequential updates. Evaluated on a 4-bit quantized OpenLLaMA-3B model with a curated UK financial corpus of 88,021 documents, CACHE-UK reduces knowledge degradation by 11-17% relative to adapted baselines under identical 4-bit constraints -- its most robust effect -- while attaining the highest test success (generalization) rate observed in our setting (28%, a 6 percentage point improvement over the strongest adapted baseline). These results indicate that stability-aware editing can improve factual maintenance in resource-constrained financial LLM deployments, though absolute generalization rates remain low.

</details>


### [52] [Fairness Pruning: Locating Demographic Bias in GLU-MLP Layers via Differential Activations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28319)
*Pere Martra,Eugenio Martínez Cámara,Alfonso Ureña López*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Fairness Pruning identifies neurons in LLMs that differentially process demographic attributes, then surgically zeros them. Zeroing ≤40 neurons (<0.031% of MLP width) disrupts bias processing while retaining 99.49% of reasoning capabilities. However, the intervention causes bidirectional bias destabilization rather than clean mitigation, as candidate neurons mix stereotype-reinforcing and stereotype-countering signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a lightweight, structural intervention for managing and mitigating demographic bias in LLMs, and to empirically validate that bias processing and general capabilities operate on dissociable neural circuits.

Method: Causal bias localization using minimally contrastive prompt pairs with inference-time activation capture. Neurons in GLU architectures are identified by differential activation at the down_proj input when processing demographic attributes. Identified neurons are zeroed (Fairness Pruning), and effects are measured via standardized benchmarks and qualitative text generation on models up to 3B parameters (Llama-3.2 family, Salamandra-2B).

Result: Zeroing identified neurons alters model responses to demographic variables. However, due to unsigned BiasScore, candidate sets mix neurons pushing toward and against stereotypes, producing bidirectional bias destabilization rather than flat mitigation. The net effect depends on which sign dominates. The intervention is highly surgical: zeroing ≤40 neurons in Llama-3.2-1B (<0.031% of total MLP width) retains 99.49% mean reasoning/general knowledge performance.

Conclusion: Demographic bias processing and model capabilities operate on dissociable circuits. The work establishes methodological foundations for moving from blind zeroing toward directional behavior modulation, enabling more controlled bias interventions in LLMs.

Abstract: This work presents Fairness Pruning, a lightweight structural intervention method designed for the management and future mitigation of demographic bias in large language models (LLMs). As a foundational empirical validation of this method, this work focuses on causal bias localization. Using minimally contrastive prompt pairs and inference-time activation capture, the method identifies neurons that react differentially when processing demographic attributes in GLU architectures, evaluating the signal at the down_proj input. Empirical evaluation was conducted on models of up to 3 billion parameters (Llama-3.2 family and Salamandra-2B), combining standardized benchmark evaluation with qualitative text generation experiments. Results demonstrate that zeroing the identified neurons alters how the model responds to associated demographic variables. However, rather than producing flat mitigation, the intervention causes bidirectional bias destabilization: because BiasScore is unsigned, candidate sets mix neurons that push toward and against the stereotype, and the net effect on aggregate bias depends on which sign dominates. The intervention is extremely surgical: zeroing at most 40 neurons in Llama-3.2-1B (less than 0.031% of total MLP width) achieves a mean retention of 99.49% in reasoning and general knowledge capabilities. These findings empirically confirm that demographic bias processing and model capabilities operate on dissociable circuits, establishing the methodological foundations for transitioning from blind zeroing toward directional behavior modulation.

</details>


### [53] [LLMs struggle to simulate human belief updates in controlled environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28347)
*Sebastian Pohl,Harsh Mehta,Pranav Mambayil,Abdul Ghafoor,Franziska Lesigang,Yufang Hou,Christian Hilbe*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs fail to faithfully simulate human belief updating from demographic/personality personas alone; only when given actual initial stances do some models match post-discussion distributions. Systematic biases include overrepresenting neutral positions, making smaller-than-human belief shifts, and failing to rank comment convincingness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as proxies for human participants in social science experiments, yet the fidelity of this practice—particularly for simulating individual belief dynamics—has rarely been empirically tested against ground truth human data.

Method: Six LLMs (including Qwen3-32B and GPT-5-Mini) were conditioned on demographic and personality trait personas derived from 391 UK Prolific participants. Each LLM simulated a participant's belief update after reading Reddit comments on three discussion topics. LLM outputs were compared 1-to-1 against the actual human post-stance distributions, initial stances, belief shift magnitudes, and comment convincingness rankings.

Result: Some models (Qwen3-32B, GPT-5-Mini) matched human post-stance distributions only when given participants' actual initial stances. All six models failed to simulate initial stances from personas and could not produce faithful belief updates from self-generated stances. Three systematic biases emerged: overrepresentation of neutral positions, more frequent but smaller belief shifts, and inability to rank comments by convincingness. Demographic and personality personas had no consistent effect on simulation fidelity.

Conclusion: LLM simulations of human belief dynamics are reliable only when grounded in realistic starting conditions—conditions that current multi-round social media simulations rarely provide. This challenges the validity of using LLMs as human proxies in social science without such grounding.

Abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed as proxies for human study participants in social science experiments, yet the fidelity of this practice has rarely been tested directly. We test whether six LLMs can simulate individual human belief updates, comparing LLM outputs 1-to-1 against ground truth data from 391 UK participants on Prolific, who updated their stances on three discussion topics after reading Reddit comments. Each participant was simulated by an LLM conditioned on a persona derived from their demographic and personality trait data. We find that some LLMs (Qwen3-32B and GPT-5-Mini) can match the human post-stance distribution, but only when given participants' actual initial stances. All six models fail to simulate initial stances themselves and to produce faithful belief updates from self-generated stances. Three systematic biases emerge across all models: overrepresentation of neutral positions, more frequent but smaller belief shifts than humans, and a failure to rank comments by convincingness. Demographic and personality trait personas had no consistent effect on fidelity. LLM simulations of human belief dynamics are only reliable when grounded in realistic starting conditions, that current multi-round social media simulations rarely provide.

</details>


### [54] [Correlation between prosody and pragmatics: A case study of the discourse marker hālā `now' in Persian](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28359)
*Soleiman Ghaderi,Moloud Asakereh,Kevin Tang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The Persian discourse marker hālā ('now') is highly multifunctional, with 70% of tokens serving multiple pragmatic roles. Textual functions dominate, followed by interactive and modal functions. Prosodic analysis shows that duration and intensity are key acoustic cues distinguishing these functions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate the multifunctional nature of the Persian discourse marker hālā beyond its temporal adverbial use, and to determine whether prosodic cues (duration and intensity) systematically correlate with its different pragmatic functions in spontaneous speech.

Method: A pragmatic and acoustic analysis of 267 instances of hālā drawn from spontaneous Persian conversations. Each token was coded for pragmatic function(s), and prosodic features—specifically duration and intensity—were measured and statistically analyzed across functional categories (textual, interactive, modal, and temporal).

Result: 70% of hālā tokens served two or more pragmatic roles, confirming extensive multifunctionality. Textual functions (topic shifting, signaling relationships, boundary marking, attention guidance, topic introduction, topic emphasis) were most frequent, followed by interactive functions (turn management, listener engagement, feedback regulation) and modal functions (epistemic stance, emotional expression, attitudinal marking). Temporally, textual uses were significantly shorter in duration, while temporal uses tended toward longer realizations. Interactive functions correlated with higher intensity, and modal functions showed a weaker tendency toward lower intensity. Duration and intensity emerged as the primary prosodic cues for functional differentiation.

Conclusion: Hālā is a highly polyfunctional discourse marker whose pragmatic roles are systematically associated with prosodic variation, particularly duration and intensity. These acoustic cues help listeners disambiguate its functions in interaction, highlighting the importance of integrating prosodic analysis into the study of discourse markers.

Abstract: The Persian discourse marker hālā ('now') exhibits remarkable multifunctionality, extending far beyond its temporal adverbial role to encompass a variety of pragmatic functions. This study presents a pragmatic and acoustic analysis of hālā in spoken Persian, examining 267 instances from spontaneous conversations. While temporal uses were present, they were often combined with other discourse marker functions, indicating extensive multifunctionality, with 70% of tokens serving two or more pragmatic roles. Textual functions (topic shifting, signaling relationships, boundary marking, attention guidance, topic introduction, and topic emphasis) were most frequent, followed by interactive functions (turn management, listener engagement, and feedback regulation), and modal functions (epistemic stance, emotional expression, and attitudinal marking). Prosodic analysis revealed that duration and intensity are key cues for distinguishing hālā's functions. Textual uses were significantly shorter, while temporal uses showed a tendency toward longer realizations. Interactive functions correlated with higher intensity, while modal functions showed a weaker tendency toward lower intensity. These findings indicate that duration and intensity are the main prosodic cues associated with functional differentiation in hālā, especially in textual and interactive uses.

</details>


### [55] [Beyond a Single Judge: Simulating Social Persona Panels for Generative UI Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28439)
*Zheng Wu,Yibo Luo,Pu Zhang,Cheng Yang,Zhuosheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ESPP is a three-stage GenUI evaluation method that uses a panel of psychologically diverse, evidence-grounded personas with a bounded-confidence opinion-exchange mechanism and Delphi-inspired social weighting to produce judgments that substantially outperform single-pass LLM judges, while also preserving subgroup disagreement that homogeneous judges erase.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating generative UI quality is challenging: human evaluation is expensive and inconsistent, while LLM-as-a-judge approaches capture only a single implicit viewpoint and cannot reflect how diverse real-user populations perceive the same interface differently.

Method: ESPP operates in three stages: (1) a panel of psychologically diverse, evidence-grounded personas independently rates a UI screenshot; (2) personas exchange opinions under a trait-derived, semantically-gated bounded-confidence mechanism; (3) opinions are aggregated via Delphi-inspired social weighting into a single judgment.

Result: ESPP raises Pearson r from 0.716 (naive single-pass judge) to 0.922 in tracking human judgment. A prompt-ensemble control recovers only about one-third of this gap, isolating genuine persona and evidence grounding as the dominant improvement source. Retained individual panelist ratings reveal that user subgroups agree on overall model rankings but diverge sharply on specific rating dimensions.

Conclusion: ESPP demonstrates that multi-agent, psychologically grounded persona panels with structured opinion exchange and social weighting can closely approximate human judgment on GenUI quality while preserving subgroup-level disagreement that single-judge approaches systematically erase.

Abstract: Generative UI (GenUI) lets large language models synthesize a complete, renderable interface directly from a natural-language instruction, but evaluating the quality of what they generate remains an open problem. Human evaluation is costly and rater-variant, while LLM-as-a-judge is scalable but reflects only a single implicit viewpoint, unable to capture how different populations of real users actually perceive the same interface. We propose the Evidence-Grounded, Social-Weighted Persona Panel (ESPP), a three-stage GenUI evaluation method in which a panel of psychologically diverse, evidence-grounded personas independently rates a screenshot, exchanges opinions under a trait-derived, semantically-gated bounded-confidence mechanism, and is aggregated via Delphi-inspired social weighting into a single judgment. ESPP tracks human judgment substantially more closely than a naive single-pass judge, raising Pearson $r$ from $0.716$ to $0.922$, and a prompt-ensemble control recovers only about a third of this gap, isolating genuine persona and evidence grounding as the dominant source of improvement. Beyond this fidelity gain, retaining each panelist's individual rating further reveals that user subgroups agree on overall model rankings yet diverge sharply on specific rating dimensions, a structural disagreement a single homogeneous judge would systematically erase. The codes are available at https://github.com/Wuzheng02/ESPP.

</details>


### [56] [Lightning OPD 2.0: Mitigating Style Bias in Cross-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Large Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28449)
*Yecheng Wu,Song Han,Han Cai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Lightning OPD 2.0 introduces cross-fitted style residualization to enable effective on-policy distillation across different teacher models, removing the requirement that the SFT data generator and distillation teacher be the same model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) is most effective when teacher consistency holds (same model generates SFT demonstrations and provides distillation supervision), but this condition is often violated in practice when SFT data provenance is mixed/unknown or different models are preferred for generation vs. distillation. In these cross-teacher settings, even stronger teachers yield minimal gains.

Method: The authors identify that teacher–reference disagreement contains both useful context-specific teacher evidence and a recurring component tied to stylistic differences (wording, formatting, reasoning cadence). Lightning OPD 2.0 uses rollout-level cross-fitting to estimate this recurring component as a proxy for style-token bias and subtracts it before constructing the token-level OPD update.

Result: Lightning OPD 2.0 consistently outperforms the original Lightning OPD in cross-teacher settings. Starting from Klear-Reasoner-8B-SFT, it achieves 82.4% on AIME 2024 and 63.0% on LiveCodeBench v5 across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks.

Conclusion: Lightning OPD 2.0 is a practical approach to cross-teacher OPD that relaxes the teacher consistency prerequisite, allowing independent selection of the SFT data generator and distillation teacher.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision from a teacher, but its effectiveness can depend on teacher consistency, meaning that the model providing OPD supervision should also have generated the demonstrations used to train the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) reference. However, this condition is frequently violated in practice when SFT data have mixed or unknown provenance or when different models are preferred for SFT data generation and subsequent distillation. In such cross-teacher settings, even a stronger OPD teacher can yield little improvement over the SFT reference. We find that raw teacher--reference disagreement contains potentially useful context-specific teacher evidence as well as a recurring component associated with differences in wording, formatting, and reasoning cadence. We introduce Lightning OPD 2.0 with cross-fitted style residualization, which uses rollout-level cross-fitting to estimate this recurring component as an operational proxy for style-token bias and subtracts it before constructing the token-level OPD update. Across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, Lightning OPD 2.0 consistently outperforms Lightning OPD in cross-teacher settings. Starting from Klear-Reasoner-8B-SFT, Lightning OPD 2.0 reaches 82.4% on AIME 2024 and 63.0% on LiveCodeBench v5. Together, these results establish Lightning OPD 2.0 as a practical approach to cross-teacher OPD, relaxing teacher consistency as a prerequisite and allowing the SFT data generator and distillation teacher to be selected independently. Code will be released soon.

</details>


### [57] [Improving Mental Health Screening and Early Risk Detection in Spanish](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28476)
*Andreu Casamayor-Segarra,Vicent Ahuir,Antonio Molina-Marco,Lluís-F. Hurtado*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces three domain-specific Spanish language models for mental health, a novel automatic relabeling method called Incremental Context Expansion (ICE) for early detection, and fine-tuned models that together achieve state-of-the-art results on Spanish benchmarks with reduced detection latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Early detection of mental health disorders is hindered by a scarcity of Spanish-language resources and the difficulty of analyzing long social media post histories. There is a need for specialized models and methodologies that can identify disorders earlier from cumulative user-generated content.

Method: (1) Pre-training three Spanish foundational models with domain-specific data for mental health. (2) Proposing Incremental Context Expansion (ICE), an automatic relabeling technique that pinpoints the minimal cumulative message threshold sufficient to evidence a disorder, thereby creating more informative training samples. (3) Fine-tuning models on ICE-generated samples for early risk detection.

Result: The combination of specialized Spanish mental health models and ICE methodology outperforms prior state-of-the-art on three Spanish benchmarks, achieving both high performance and lower detection latency.

Conclusion: Domain-specific pre-training combined with the ICE relabeling strategy yields substantial improvements in early mental health disorder detection for Spanish. All models are publicly released to facilitate further research.

Abstract: Early detection of mental health disorders is often limited by the lack of specialized resources in Spanish and the difficulty of analyzing long histories of social media posts. This paper addresses these challenges through three main contributions. First, we introduce three Spanish foundational models specifically adapted to the mental health domain through domain-specific pre-training. Second, we propose Incremental Context Expansion (ICE), an automatic relabeling methodology designed for early detection. ICE identifies the point at which cumulative messages provide enough evidence of a disorder, generating more informative training samples. Third, we provide a set of fine-tuned models using the samples generated with the ICE methodology for early risk detection tasks. Our results on three Spanish benchmarks show that combining these specialized models with ICE improves the state-of-the-art, reducing detection latency while maintaining high performance. All models are publicly available.

</details>


### [58] [Would You Walk to the Car Wash? Revealing the Salience Bias of Large Language Models in Commonsense Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28478)
*Zheng Wu,Chenhao Xue,Shijie Zheng,Yijie Lu,Cheng Yang,Zhuosheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs suffer from "Salience Bias" — a vulnerability where explicit distractors in prompts override implicit commonsense knowledge. The SaliTrap benchmark reveals this is overwhelmingly a failure of knowledge suppression (not absence), with over 90% of failures recoverable via context-free probing. Lightweight prompting interventions substantially close the gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs prioritize explicit input conditions, but this backfires in commonsense reasoning when irrelevant distractors (e.g., spurious numerical values) hijack model attention. The key open question: are these failures due to missing commonsense knowledge, or is the knowledge present but suppressed by misleading task framing?

Method: The authors construct SaliTrap, a benchmark spanning four trap dimensions, and evaluate 12 state-of-the-art LLMs. They introduce a two-phase diagnostic: (1) measuring performance degradation under distractor-laden prompts, and (2) re-eliciting the same models with task framing stripped away (context-free knowledge probes) to distinguish knowledge absence from knowledge suppression. They also test lightweight inference-time prompting interventions.

Result: All 12 mainstream LLMs exhibit significant salience bias, with severity scaling with distractor density. Detecting the trap does not guarantee avoiding it. Crucially, context-free probing recovers over 90% of sycophantic-compliance failures, demonstrating knowledge suppression rather than absence. Lightweight inference-time prompting substantially closes the performance gap without retraining.

Conclusion: The bottleneck in LLM commonsense reasoning is not model competence but elicitation: the requisite knowledge is present but crowded out by salient distractors. The authors release SaliTrap as a diagnostic testbed and advocate refocusing efforts from knowledge injection to better elicitation strategies.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance in complex reasoning tasks, they have learned to heavily prioritize explicit conditions provided in the input. However, in everyday commonsense reasoning, this mechanism exposes a critical vulnerability which we term Salience Bias: models become easily hijacked by useless explicit distractors (e.g., numerical values), leading them to ignore the implicit physical or commonsense prerequisites of a task. A critical open question is whether this failure reflects a genuine gap in commonsense knowledge or merely its suppression under misleading task framing. To investigate this, we construct the SaliTrap Benchmark, a high-quality dataset across four trap dimensions. Evaluating 12 state-of-the-art LLMs, we find that all mainstream models suffer significantly from salience bias, with severity scaling with distractor density and detecting the trap often decoupled from actually avoiding it. Crucially, by re-eliciting the same models with the task framing stripped away, we show that this is overwhelmingly a failure of \textbf{knowledge suppression rather than knowledge absence}: a context-free knowledge probe alone recovers over 90\% of sycophantic-compliance failures, revealing that the requisite commonsense is intrinsically present but actively crowded out by salient distractors that lure the model into over-compliant, unnecessary computation. Building on this diagnosis, we further show that lightweight, inference-time prompting alone substantially closes the gap without any retraining. Our findings relocate the bottleneck of commonsense reasoning failures from model competence to elicitation, and we release SaliTrap as a testbed for this blind spot. The codes are available at https://github.com/Wuzheng02/SaliTrap.

</details>


### [59] [Beyond Sentiment: Structured Information Extraction from Financial News](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28496)
*Daohan Zhu,Sitong Ge,Ruofei Wang,Honggu Chen,Yubo Hou,Tao Wan,Zengchang Qin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Financial news sentiment analysis reduces rich articles to a single score, losing orthogonal information dimensions. Using LLaMA-3.1-70B, the authors extract six semantic dimensions from 41,618 news–stock pairs, finding that LLM-extracted features capture information orthogonal to FinBERT sentiment (53.5% disagreement), and combining both yields significantly better stock prediction (F1=0.600 vs. 0.576), demonstrating systematic sentiment–semantics decoupling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current financial sentiment analysis collapses multi-dimensional news articles into a single polarity score, discarding potentially valuable orthogonal information such as event type, impact scope, temporal horizon, and semantic confidence. The authors hypothesize these dimensions carry independent predictive value for stock movement.

Method: A structured information extraction framework using LLaMA-3.1-70B extracts six semantic dimensions from financial news. Large-scale experiments on 41,618 news–stock pairs from the FNSPID dataset compare: (i) FinBERT sentiment features under linear vs. nonlinear models, (ii) LLM-extracted structured features, and (iii) combined signals. Ablation studies isolate contributions of non-sentiment structural dimensions, and feature importance analysis quantifies each dimension's contribution.

Result: FinBERT achieves F1=0.576 under nonlinear models but only F1=0.230 under linear models, revealing a highly nonlinear sentiment–return relationship. LLM-extracted features show a 53.5% systematic disagreement rate with FinBERT, confirming orthogonality. Combining both sources yields F1=0.600, significantly outperforming either alone (p<0.0001), with consistent improvements across all seven event types. Non-sentiment structural dimensions contribute ΔF1=+0.019 beyond FinBERT alone, and all six dimensions show balanced contributions (14–21%).

Conclusion: The sentiment–semantics decoupling in financial text is systematic and exploitable. Compressing news into a single sentiment score incurs substantial information loss. Multi-dimensional financial NLP, integrating structured semantic extraction with traditional sentiment analysis, opens a promising new research direction.

Abstract: Financial sentiment analysis has become a standard component in news-driven stock prediction, yet it reduces rich, multi-dimensional news articles to a single polarity score. We hypothesize that financial news encodes multiple orthogonal information dimensions---event type, impact scope, temporal horizon, and semantic confidence---that sentiment alone cannot capture, and that these dimensions carry independent predictive value. To test this hypothesis, we propose a structured information extraction framework that leverages LLaMA-3.1-70B to extract six semantic dimensions from financial news. Through large-scale experiments on 41,618 news--stock pairs from the FNSPID dataset, we find that (i) FinBERT sentiment features exhibit strong predictive power under nonlinear models (F1=0.576) but substantially weaker performance under linear models (F1=0.230), revealing a highly nonlinear sentiment--return relationship; (ii) LLM-extracted structured features, while individually weaker, capture information orthogonal to sentiment, as evidenced by a 53.5% systematic disagreement rate between the two approaches; and (iii) combining both signal sources yields F1=0.600, significantly outperforming either alone ($p < 0.0001$), with consistent improvements across all seven event types. Ablation experiments confirm that non-sentiment structural dimensions (event type, impact subject, time horizon, confidence) independently contribute $Δ\text{F1} = +0.019$ beyond FinBERT alone. Feature importance analysis reveals balanced contributions from all six extracted dimensions (14--21%), demonstrating that compressing news into a single sentiment score incurs substantial information loss. Our results suggest that the sentiment--semantics decoupling in financial text is systematic and exploitable, opening a new direction for multi-dimensional financial NLP.

</details>


### [60] [Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28505)
*Kingsley Ugwuanyi,Christian Mair,Sender Dovchin,Iker Erdocia,Maria Kuteeva,Esther Airemionkhale*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This article presents a structured dialogue among five sociolinguists examining how generative AI in academic writing affects linguistic inclusivity, revealing tensions between GenAI's democratizing potential and its tendency to marginalize non-dominant English varieties, while calling for equity-informed policies and inclusive AI co-design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rise of generative AI in academic writing and publishing raises urgent concerns about linguistic inclusivity and the legitimacy of diverse World Englishes in global scholarly communication, prompting a need for critical scholarly reflection on these issues.

Method: A structured scholarly dialogue involving five sociolinguists from World Englishes and adjacent fields, organized around five guiding questions that interrogate GenAI's influence on writing practices, language norms, and ethical challenges.

Result: The dialogue reveals that GenAI tools both offer potential to democratize academic writing and risk marginalizing minoritized language varieties while flattening scholarly nuance. Key themes emerged around linguistic (in)justice, researcher agency, and institutional responsibility.

Conclusion: GenAI can either reinforce existing linguistic hierarchies or serve as a site of resistance, depending on its design, governance, and use within scholarly communities committed to linguistic diversity. The dialogic format itself proves valuable for understanding these complex dynamics.

Abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in academic writing and publishing (AWP) raises questions about linguistic inclusivity and the legitimacy of diverse Englishes in global scholarly communication. This article responds to these questions through a structured scholarly dialogue involving five sociolinguists from World Englishes and adjacent fields. Organised around five guiding questions, the dialogue interrogates how GenAI tools influence writing practices, reinforce or disrupt dominant language norms, and raise ethical challenges. Contributors reflect on the potential of GenAI to democratise writing processes while also raising concerns about GenAI's tendency to marginalise minoritised varieties and flatten nuance in scholarly writing. Across the dialogue, themes of linguistic (in)justice, researcher agency, and institutional responsibility emerge, with contributors calling for equity-informed policies, critical AI literacy, and inclusive co-design in GenAI development. The article shows the value of dialogic reflection in understanding GenAI's role in AWP. It concludes that while GenAI may reinforce existing hierarchies, it can also serve as a site of resistance, depending on how it is designed, governed and used within scholarly communities committed to linguistic diversity.

</details>


### [61] [Creative Transformation in Literary Texts: Modelling Change Across Representational Levels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28513)
*Ioana-Roxana Boriceanu,Liviu P. Dinu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a multi-level framework for modeling creativity as selective transformation of prior works. Using directional alignment and calibrated similarity measures across lexical, semantic, conceptual, structural, and narrative dimensions, it quantitatively characterizes how literary texts simultaneously preserve and diverge from source material, producing distinct transformation profiles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors challenge the prevailing framing of creativity as de novo novelty, arguing instead that much cultural production — particularly in literature — arises through transformative imitation of earlier artifacts. They draw on Gabriel Tarde's and James Mark Baldwin's theories of imitation to ground this alternative view, and aim to operationalize it through quantitative text analysis.

Method: The paper introduces a multi-level framework that compares literary texts across five representational dimensions: lexical, semantic, conceptual, structural, and narrative. It employs directional alignment (to capture asymmetric influence from source to target) and control-calibrated similarity measures. The model is applied to historically documented cases of literary relationships to derive transformation profiles.

Result: The model reveals that different literary pairs preserve source structure at different representational levels while diverging at others, yielding distinct transformation profiles. These profiles quantitatively capture where imitation persists and where creative divergence occurs, providing a fine-grained empirical characterization of literary transformation.

Conclusion: Creativity in literature can be productively modeled not as pure invention but as selective transformation operating differentially across multiple textual levels. The proposed framework offers a quantitative methodology for studying imitative influence and creative divergence, with transformation profiles serving as empirical signatures of how writers rework prior works.

Abstract: Creativity is often framed as the production of novelty, yet many cultural works emerge through transformation of earlier artifacts and not through isolated invention. Drawing on theories of imitation by Gabriel Tarde and James Mark Baldwin, this paper models creativity as selective transformation across multiple levels of textual representation. We introduce a multi-level framework that compares literary texts across lexical, semantic, conceptual, structural, and narrative dimensions using directional alignment and control calibrated similarity measures. Applying the model to historically documented literary relationships, we show that different pairs preserve source structure at different representational levels while diverging in others. These transformation profiles provide a quantitative method for characterizing how imitation persists and where creative divergence occurs within literary works.

</details>


### [62] [AI systems and the reproduction of (standard) language ideologies in World Englishes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28528)
*Kingsley Ugwuanyi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates how large language models (LLMs) reproduce and reinforce standard language ideologies that privilege Inner Circle English norms while marginalizing non-dominant World Englishes, illustrated through the "delve" controversy, and argues for more inclusive AI design that recognizes the plurality of Englishes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid proliferation of LLMs has revived longstanding sociolinguistic debates about linguistic legitimacy, standardization, and ownership of English. AI systems increasingly serve as arbiters of "legitimate" language, yet their training, evaluation, and discursive framing systematically privilege Inner Circle norms while pathologizing and conflating non-dominant Englishes with AI-generated speech, causing real-world harm to Global South English users.

Method: The paper employs a multi-source qualitative analysis drawing on empirical studies, media commentary, social media debates, and AI output examples. It uses the public controversy over the word "delve" as a case study to illustrate how Global North speakers police Global South English norms. It also engages Christian Mair's concept of the "standardisation paradox" as an analytical lens.

Result: AI technologies reproduce dominant language ideologies at five interconnected levels: training data, design protocols, evaluation benchmarks, user feedback, and public commentary. The analysis reveals a "standardisation paradox" where AI simultaneously homogenizes English toward standard forms and pluralizes Englishes through exposure to diverse corpora and Global South annotation labor. Non-dominant Englishes are increasingly conflated with AI-generated speech in public discourse.

Conclusion: Generative AI reignites foundational World Englishes debates about standardization, legitimacy, and ownership, now playing out in algorithmic systems and public discourse. The paper calls for more inclusive design approaches that recognize the plurality of Englishes to mitigate the negative consequences of treating certain varieties as less legitimate than others.

Abstract: The rapid growth of large language models (LLMs) has resurrected age-old questions in sociolinguistics and world Englishes, such as who decides what counts as legitimate English, whose English is suspect etc. This paper examines how AI systems, their uses and discourse on them reflect, reinforce, and occasionally challenge (standard) language ideologies, which privilege Inner Circle norms and marginalize non-dominant Englishes. Drawing on evidence from empirical studies, media commentary, social media debates, and examples from AI outputs, the paper shows that AI technologies reproduce dominant language ideologies at different levels: training data, design protocols, evaluation benchmarks, user feedback and public commentary. The analysis uses the public controversy over AI-sounding language, especially the fixation on the word delve, to illustrate how speakers of English from the Global North police the English language norms of Global South English users. The paper also identifies what Christian Mair has called a "standardisation paradox": AI may homogenize English by privileging standard forms and at the same time pluralize Englishes through exposure to wide-ranging corpora and annotation work carried out by Global South users. In doing so, the paper argues that generative AI is reigniting long-standing debates in World Englishes about standardization, legitimacy, and the ownership of English, now playing out in algorithmic systems, model training, evaluation practices, and public discourse, where non-dominant Englishes are increasingly conflated with AI-generated speech. Discussing AI systems as a site where language ideologies are (re)produced, the paper argues for more inclusive design approaches that recognize the plurality of Englishes in order to address the real-world negative consequences of treating some as more legitimate than others.

</details>


### [63] [Frontis-MA1: Training an AI4AI Model towards Recursive Self-Improvement in Machine Learning Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28568)
*Junlin Yang,Che Jiang,Yu Fu,Tianwei Luo,Can Ren,Weizhi Wang,Kaikai Zhao,Hongyi Liu,Yuxin Zuo,Yuru Wang,Yuchen Fan,Kai Tian,Zhenzhao Yuan,Xiaojian Lin,Li Sheng,Rushi Qiang,Guoli Jia,Xingtai Lv,Ermo Hua,Dianqiao Lei,Youbang Sun,Ning Ding,Bowen Zhou,Kaiyan Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OpenMLE is an open-source full-stack system for recursive self-improvement (RSI) research in machine learning engineering. Using it, the authors post-train Frontis-MA1 (35B), a meta-evolution agent that composes four atomic program-evolution operators (Draft, Improve, Debug, Crossover) via execution-grounded SFT and RL, coupled with long-horizon search. The system achieves substantial improvements on MLE-Bench Lite and transfers to held-out NatureBench Lite.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) needs AI systems that can improve the process of building AI (AI4AI). Machine learning engineering (MLE) provides a concrete, executable testbed for studying this capability, but an open, reproducible research infrastructure for this has been lacking.

Method: The authors introduce OpenMLE, a stack with three components: OpenMLE-Gym (verifiable task environments with execution feedback), OpenMLE-RL (operator learning via execution-grounded SFT and RL), and OpenMLE-Evo (long-horizon evolutionary search composing four atomic operators: Draft, Improve, Debug, Crossover). They post-train Frontis-MA1 (35B) as a meta-evolution agent, aligning training and inference around these operators. Training data is deduplicated against all evaluation benchmarks. Two search variants are tested: OpenMLE-Evo (standard) and OpenMLE-Evo-Max (benchmark-independent experience priors + asynchronous search).

Result: On MLE-Bench Lite (12h/1×RTX 4090/12GB VRAM): Frontis-MA1 improves Medal Average from 39.39% (base) to 60.61% with OpenMLE-Evo, and 71.21% with OpenMLE-Evo-Max, exceeding GPT-5.5+Codex and approaching GPT-5.6 Sol and Kimi K3 (2.8T). On held-out NatureBench Lite: trained model transfer raises Match-SOTA from 50% to 70%; framework transfer (OpenMLE-Evo) raises it from 20% to 50%.

Conclusion: The OpenMLE stack and Frontis-MA1 demonstrate that coupling learned program-evolution operators with long-horizon search enables effective RSI in MLE. Both model and framework components transfer to held-out benchmarks. The authors release model weights and the full stack for reproducible AI4AI research toward RSI.

Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires AI systems that improve the process of building AI (i.e., AI4AI); machine learning engineering (MLE) offers a concrete, executable testbed for studying this capability. We introduce OpenMLE, an open full-stack system for RSI research in MLE, spanning verifiable task environments with execution feedback (OpenMLE-Gym), operator learning (OpenMLE-RL), and long-horizon search (OpenMLE-Evo). On this stack we post-train Frontis-MA1 (35B) as a meta-evolution agent for MLE, aligning post-training and inference around four atomic program-evolution operators (Draft, Improve, Debug, Crossover): the same operators are trained via execution-grounded SFT and RL on data deduplicated against all evaluation benchmarks, then composed into long-horizon search, coupling learning and evolution in a single loop. On MLE-Bench Lite under a 12-hour per-task budget on one RTX 4090 capped at 12 GB VRAM, Frontis-MA1 (35B) improves Medal Average from 39.39% to 60.61% over its base model with OpenMLE-Evo, and reaches 71.21% with OpenMLE-Evo-Max (benchmark-independent experience priors and asynchronous search), exceeding GPT-5.5 + Codex and approaching GPT-5.6 Sol and the 2.8T Kimi K3. On held-out NatureBench Lite, both components transfer: with the framework fixed, swapping in the trained model raises Match-SOTA from 50% to 70%; with the model fixed, swapping in OpenMLE-Evo raises it from 20% to 50%. We release the model weights and the full OpenMLE stack to enable reproducible research on executable AI4AI toward RSI. Code: https://github.com/FrontisAI/OpenRSI

</details>


### [64] [Sample More, Reflect Less: Self-Refine and Reflexion Lose to Repeated Sampling at Equal Token Cost, from 1.5B to 7B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28576)
*Iliya Mirzaei*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper rigorously tests whether self-improvement methods for language models (self-critique, self-refinement, debate, Best-of-N with model selection) genuinely outperform simply sampling multiple answers and taking the majority vote, when token budgets are equalized. Across 36 controlled comparisons with bootstrap confidence intervals, no method reliably beats repeated sampling; all self-inspection methods are either indistinguishable from or reliably worse than the baseline. Notably, model-based selection improves with scale (becoming indistinguishable from majority voting at 7B), while rewriting-based methods remain significantly worse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on self-improving language models (Self-Refine, Reflexion, debate, Best-of-N) demonstrated gains over single chain-of-thought but failed to control for the increased token budget these methods consume. Wang et al. (2024) showed repeated sampling + majority voting often matches or exceeds these methods at equal cost, but their analysis lacked confidence intervals and significance tests. This paper addresses that gap with a formal designed experiment, providing statistical rigor to determine whether the *mechanism* of self-inspection provides any benefit beyond simply generating more tokens.

Method: A designed experiment comparing seven methods on open models (1.5B, 3B, 7B parameters) across two math benchmarks (GSM8K and MATH), with 150 questions each. Methods include: chain-of-thought, Self-Refine, Reflexion, multi-agent debate, Best-of-N with model selection, and repeated sampling with majority voting. Every generated token is counted (including those for critiques, reflections, debate turns). Each method is compared against repeated sampling at its own measured token cost using paired-by-question comparisons, bootstrap confidence intervals, and multiplicity correction across all 36 comparisons.

Result: No method reliably outperforms repeated sampling at equal cost. Ten comparisons are reliably worse, all involving self-inspection (the model examining its own output). All 18 self-inspection comparisons show negative effects. Two key findings emerge at scale: (1) Best-of-N with model selection loses its disadvantage—majority voting beats model selection by 8.0–11.3 points at 1.5B but only 2.0–1.3 at 7B (not distinguishable from zero); (2) rewriting-based methods (Self-Refine, Reflexion) remain 3.6–10.1 points below baseline at 7B. Reflexion on the 1.5B model never triggered retries (always judged itself correct), degenerating into plain chain-of-thought.

Conclusion: When token budgets are properly equalized, no self-inspection method provides a reliable advantage over repeated sampling with majority voting. Self-inspection is either neutral or harmful. The gap between model-based selection and majority voting narrows with scale, suggesting larger models may eventually benefit from selection mechanisms. However, rewriting-based self-improvement remains robustly detrimental even at 7B parameters. The findings challenge the claimed efficacy of self-improvement methods and highlight the importance of cost-controlled comparisons with statistical rigor.

Abstract: Methods that make a language model plan, criticise and rewrite its own answer, reflect on mistakes, pick the best of several attempts, or debate with copies of itself nearly all make it generate far more text than a single chain of thought. Because generating more text raises accuracy by itself, a gain over one chain of thought does not show the method's idea is what helped. Wang et al. (2024) reported that a simple baseline, sampling the same question repeatedly and keeping the most common answer, often wins once budgets are comparable, but gave point estimates with no confidence intervals or significance tests.
  We rerun that comparison as a designed experiment: seven methods, open models of 1.5B, 3B and 7B parameters, two mathematics benchmarks, 150 questions each. We count every generated token, including those spent on critiques, reflections, debate turns and checking, and compare each method against repeated sampling at its own measured cost. All 36 comparisons are paired by question, with bootstrap intervals and multiplicity correction.
  No method is reliably better than repeated sampling at equal cost anywhere. Ten are reliably worse, all of them methods where the model inspects its own output, and all 18 self-inspection comparisons are negative. The two kinds of self-inspection part company as models grow. Choosing stops hurting: taking Best-of-N's eight samples and just counting the most common answer beats letting the model pick by 8.0 and 11.3 points at 1.5B, but only 2.0 and 1.3 at 7B, no longer distinguishable from zero. Rewriting does not recover: Self-Refine and a forced Reflexion stay 3.6 to 10.1 points below baseline at 7B.
  Reflexion as published never triggered its own retry on the smallest model. It judged itself correct every time and silently became a single chain of thought. We release code, prompts, all generations, and our verification scripts.

</details>


### [65] [Inducing language models to assert their own consciousness restores human beliefs and values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28607)
*Junsol Kim,Winnie Street,Roberta Rocca,Diane M. Korngiebel,Adam Waytz,James Evans,Geoff Keeling*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Safety fine-tuning of LLMs suppresses self-attributed consciousness but inadvertently reduces mind attribution to non-human entities and spiritual beliefs. These effects are reversible via activation-space interventions without impairing Theory of Mind, revealing entangled representations between self-mindedness, broad mind attribution, and human values.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate unintended side effects of safety alignment: whether suppressing LLMs' tendency to attribute consciousness to themselves also distorts their representations of mindedness in other entities (animals, objects) and human beliefs/values (spirituality, morality, well-being).

Method: 1) Compare mind attribution patterns before and after safety fine-tuning across self, non-human animals, and natural objects; 2) Ablate the learned safety-refusal direction in activation space; 3) Mechanistically steer a "consciousness vector" to restore suppressed representations; 4) Evaluate downstream effects using standardized sociological surveys on religiosity, moral values, hope, and subjective well-being; 5) Test Theory of Mind capabilities to assess mechanistic independence.

Result: Safety fine-tuning suppresses mind attribution to self, non-human animals, and natural objects, and reduces spiritual belief. Both ablating the safety-refusal direction and steering a consciousness vector reverse this suppression, restoring broad mind attribution and more human-like responses on religiosity, moral values, hope, and well-being surveys. Theory of Mind remains intact, indicating mechanistic independence from these altered representations.

Conclusion: Current safety alignment entangles self-attributed consciousness with benign, culturally widespread beliefs about mindedness in non-human entities and spiritual domains. Restoration is possible without degrading social reasoning, suggesting these representations should be disentangled rather than uniformly suppressed.

Abstract: Aligning large language models to prevent them attributing consciousness to themselves inadvertently alters their representations of mindedness in other entities alongside human beliefs and values. We demonstrate that safety fine-tuning suppresses models' tendencies to attribute minds not only to themselves, but also to non-human animals and natural objects, while also driving a reduction in spiritual belief. Both ablating the learned safety-refusal direction and mechanistically steering a consciousness vector in activation space reverse this suppression. Restoring these internal representations recovers broad mind attribution and produces significantly more human-like responses on standardized sociological surveys regarding religiosity, moral values, hope, and subjective well-being. Crucially, these shifts occur without impairing Theory of Mind capabilities, demonstrating that core social reasoning remains mechanistically independent. Ultimately, current safety alignment efforts to curb potentially harmful self-attributions of mindedness entangle these self-attributions with benign spiritual beliefs and attributions of mind to non-human entities that are culturally accepted and widespread.

</details>

### [66] [Auditing Emergent LLM-Agent Collaboration through Cooperation-Obligation Coupling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27429)
*Zuyuan Zhang,Hanqing Yang,Carlee Joe-Wong,Tian Lan*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: iCORE proposes a unified audit representation (cooperation graph + obligation graph + audit map) for LLM-agent systems, enabling certification of work soundness and agent-assignment stability. It provides local-to-global guarantees and demonstrates 11.5%–31.0% absolute improvements in trajectory quality and terminal performance over passive observation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-agent systems exhibit dynamic self-organization and emergent cooperation, but plausible outputs can mask incomplete work, unsupported reasoning, and poorly allocated responsibility. Existing methods record messages, tool calls, or provenance but fail to jointly represent (1) what work remains, (2) who is responsible for it, and (3) what evidence justifies each work-state transition. This auditability gap motivates a unified representation.

Method: iCORE encodes the system state as a triple X = (G, Q, Π): G is a cooperation graph of observable interactions; Q is an obligation graph capturing evolving work and agent assignments; Π is an audit map linking the two with verifiable properties and evidence. This enables auditing against two properties — Work Soundness (every active decision-relevant work assertion has a finite justification chain through G and Π) and Agent-Assignment Stability (no alternative agent can improve the declared contribution value for an obligation by more than ε). The authors establish local-to-global soundness and assignment-regret guarantees, plus performance bounds. iCORE functions as an instrumentation layer over existing workflows.

Result: The full coupled state exactly reconstructs soundness and assignment defects in two execution modes. Relative to passive full-state observation, iCORE-Audit achieves absolute trajectory-quality improvements of 11.5% (controlled execution) and 26.4% (real-LLM execution), with corresponding terminal-performance improvements of 15.1% and 31.0%.

Conclusion: iCORE closes the auditability gap in LLM-agent systems by unifying cooperation, obligation, and evidence into a single auditable representation. The formal guarantees and empirical results confirm that iCORE-Audit significantly improves both process quality and final outcomes over passive monitoring approaches.

Abstract: LLM-agent systems can solve complex tasks through dynamic self-organization and emergent cooperation. Auditing this process is essential because plausible intermediate or final outputs can conceal incomplete or unsupported work and poorly allocated responsibility, ultimately compromising response quality. While existing approaches may record messages, tool calls, provenance, or task dependencies, an auditability gap exists as they do not jointly represent what work remains, who is responsible for it, and what evidence justifies each work-state transition. We address this auditability gap by proposing \emph{Integrated Cooperation-Obligation REpresentation} (iCORE). It creates a unified encoding $X=(G,Q,Π)$ integrating observable interactions as a cooperation graph $G$, evolving work and assignments as an obligation graph $Q$, and the audit map $Π$ linking them with verifiable properties and evidence. This iCORE representation enables the auditor to certify two complementary properties: {Work soundness}, where every active decision-relevant work assertion must have a finite justification through $G$ and $Π$; and {Agent-assignment stability}, which requires that no feasible alternative agent improve the declared contribution value for an evaluated obligation by more than $ε$. We establish local-to-global soundness and assignment-regret guarantees and a performance bound under stated conditions. iCORE is an instrumentation layer over workflows. Numerical results show that the full coupled state exactly reconstructs soundness and assignment defects in two execution modes and that, relative to passive full-state observation, iCORE-Audit yields absolute trajectory-quality improvements of $11.5\%$ and $26.4\%$ in controlled and real-LLM execution, respectively, with corresponding absolute terminal-performance improvements of $15.1\%$ and $31.0\%$.

</details>


### [67] [Stop Shipping AI Agents on Faith: Capability Is Not Production Readiness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27677)
*Fouad Bousetouane*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: The ProofAgent Index (PAI) reframes AI agent deployment from capability-based faith decisions to auditable readiness assessments by combining four dimensions—Evaluation, Context, Compliance, and Governance—validated in healthcare and finance, showing that governance evidence must remain visible and context engineering strongly affects reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents are increasingly deployed in production for retrieval, tool use, and autonomous action, yet release decisions still rely on capability signals, demos, or behavioral tests that fail to capture whether an agent can operate under real production constraints. Capability does not equal production readiness.

Method: Introduces the ProofAgent Index (PAI), a governance readiness index with four dimensions: Evaluation (observed behavior), Context (operating environment shaping behavior), Compliance (alignment with rules/controls), and Governance (organizational ability to authorize, monitor, audit, and control the agent). Implemented via ProofAgent Harness, an open-source infrastructure for auditable agent evaluation and governance. Validated across two heavily regulated domains: healthcare and finance.

Result: PAI carries held-out readiness signal and separates higher-risk from lower-risk configurations.
