Three key findings: (1) context engineering strongly changes reliability, (2) capability improves behavior but does not determine readiness, and (3) governance evidence must remain visible rather than averaged away.

Conclusion: PAI reframes agent release from a faith-based deployment decision into an auditable readiness decision, providing a structured, evidence-driven alternative to capability-only evaluation for production agent governance.

Abstract: AI agents are moving into production workflows where they retrieve information, call tools, maintain state, and act on behalf of users or organizations, but many release decisions still rely on capability signals, demos, or behavioral tests that do not show whether an agent is ready to operate under production constraints. Capability is therefore not production readiness. This paper introduces the ProofAgent Index (PAI), a governance readiness index for AI agents. PAI combines four dimensions of deployment evidence: Evaluation, Context, Compliance, and Governance. Evaluation measures observed behavior, Context measures the operating environment that shapes that behavior, Compliance measures alignment with applicable rules and controls, and Governance measures whether the organization can authorize, monitor, audit, and control the agent during operation. PAI is implemented inside ProofAgent Harness, an open source infrastructure for auditable AI agent evaluation and governance. Validation across two heavily regulated domains, healthcare and finance, shows that PAI carries held out readiness signal and separates higher risk from lower risk configurations. The results show that context engineering strongly changes reliability, capability improves behavior but does not determine readiness, and governance evidence must remain visible rather than averaged away. PAI reframes agent release from a faith based deployment decision into an auditable readiness decision.

</details>


### [68] [Scaling LLM-Driven Multi-Agent Systems: Design Principles and Architectural Scalability Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27942)
*Linus Sander,Fengjunjie Pan,Vahid Zolfaghari,Andre Schamschurko,Nenad Petrovic,Alois Knoll*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: The paper distills four design principles for scalable LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) and evaluates a reference architecture on system engineering tasks, finding that scaling improves accuracy with linear cost growth only when the underlying LLM exceeds a capability threshold, with performance peaking at intermediate complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems hold promise for solving complex tasks through ensembles of specialized agents, but the architectural design space lacks systematization, broadly accepted design principles, and a clear understanding of scalability characteristics.

Method: The authors conduct a structured analysis of prior work to distill four design principles (simplicity, elastic feedback, sequential workflows with optional loops, summary-based communication). These are operationalized as a reference architecture using a constrained directed workflow graph. Four configurations of increasing complexity are evaluated on a standardized terminal-based system engineering benchmark using two LLMs of differing capability.

Result: Scaling yields measurable accuracy improvements with approximately linear cost growth, but only when the LLM exceeds a minimum capability threshold. Performance peaks at intermediate complexity and degrades thereafter due to timeouts and evaluation limitations. Persistent consistency issues emerge across all scaling levels.

Conclusion: The work provides concrete design guidance for MAS practitioners and identifies consistency and evaluation standardization as critical targets for future research.

Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems have the potential to enable collective intelligence and scale toward solving highly complex tasks through coordinated ensembles of specialized agents. However, despite their theoretical potential, the architectural design space remains largely non-systematized and lacks broadly established design principles. Furthermore, the scalability characteristics of such systems are only partially understood so far. This paper makes two contributions. We first distill four design principles for scalable MAS architectures from a structured analysis of prior work: simplicity, elastic feedback, sequential workflows with optional loops, and summary-based communication. We operationalize these principles in a reference architecture whose topology is formalized as a constrained directed workflow graph, and we evaluate four configurations of increasing complexity on a standardized benchmark of terminal-based system engineering tasks using two LLMs of differing capability. Our findings show that scaling yields measurable accuracy improvements with approximately linear cost growth, but only when the underlying LLM exceeds a minimum capability threshold. Performance peaks at intermediate complexity, then degrades due to timeouts and evaluation limitations. In addition, persistent consistency issues emerge as a central challenge across all scaling levels. These results provide concrete design guidance for practitioners and highlight consistency and evaluation standardization as key targets for future research.

</details>


### [69] [Argonaut: Interactive Visual Exploration for Distributed Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27946)
*Srijoni Majumdar,Chuhao Qin,Evangelos Pournaras*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Argonaut is an interactive, containerized dashboard that transforms multi-agent discrete-choice optimization from a black-box computation into a human-in-the-loop process, enabling visual exploration of the entire search process across decentralized settings with up to 5600 agents and 1M solutions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Distributed discrete-choice optimization in decentralized settings suffers from poor observability — understanding how agents' interdependent choices lead to a global objective is intractable as systems scale. Existing tools are centralized, visualize only final solutions, and treat the search process as a black box, limiting both exploration and interpretability.

Method: Argonaut provides a lightweight, containerized Node.js dashboard that unifies dataset upload, agent/option construction, on-the-fly decision-space modification, and multiple pluggable algorithm backends (Java and Python). It renders the entire optimization search process interactively, allowing users to inspect how each configuration shapes local agent decisions and the resulting global objective in one integrated loop.

Result: Evaluated on real-world datasets — household electricity, shared mobility, and sensor data exchange — Argonaut scales to 5600 agents and up to 1 million solutions under brute force. It maintains typical runtime of 200 agents over 100 decision attributes in under 30 seconds.

Conclusion: Argonaut is the first tool to unite system construction, optimization, and analysis in a single interactive loop for decentralized discrete-choice problems, making the optimization process transparent, explorable, and human-steerable rather than a one-shot black-box computation.

Abstract: Distributed discrete-choice optimization in decentralized settings is often hard to explore and navigate: disentangling what other agents choose, how their choices are interdependent, and how they collectively reach a global objective quickly becomes intractable as the system scales. The major limitation is observability of the search process. Existing methods are largely centralized and offer limited support, visualizing only the final solution or providing algorithm backends over a fixed dataset, so how a solution is reached stays a black box. We present Argonaut, a lightweight, containerized optimization dashboard that enables interactive, visual exploration of the entire search process for multi-agent discrete-choice optimization in decentralized settings. Users upload datasets, construct agents and options, modify the decision space and its parameters on the fly, and run multiple algorithm backends to inspect how each configuration shapes local agent decisions and the resulting global objective. By uniting system construction, optimization, and analysis in one interactive loop, the first of its kind, Argonaut makes distributed discrete-choice optimization a human-in-the-loop process rather than a one-shot, black-box computation. We evaluate Argonaut on real-world household-electricity, shared-mobility, and sensor-data-exchange datasets scaling to 5600 agents and up to 1M solutions under brute force. Built on a Node.js interface with extensible Java and Python optimization backends, it maintains a typical runtime of 200 agents over 100 decision attributes in under 30 seconds.

</details>


### [70] [$Σ$-Mem: An Online Reliability Memory for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27958)
*Peilin Feng,Suorong Yang,Soujanya Poria*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Σ-Mem introduces an online reliability memory for multi-agent LLM systems that tracks peer trustworthiness and inter-peer relationships using spectral updates bounded by Weyl's inequality, enabling stable adaptation without retraining. It supports residual steering, peer routing, and reliability-weighted voting, outperforming majority voting and best fixed peer baselines across OOD tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory systems for LLM agents store interaction content but do not model which peers to trust and under what conditions. This gap is critical in multi-agent systems where a central model cannot directly verify plausible or correlated peer responses, necessitating a mechanism that accumulates and leverages reliability evidence over time.

Method: Σ-Mem maintains two types of real symmetric state matrices: individual peer competence evidence and pairwise peer relationship evidence, both updated online from post-decision correctness feedback. Updates are spectrally bounded via Weyl's inequality, ensuring stable online adaptation without retraining. The memory exposes a general write-and-read interface supporting three downstream uses: residual steering of a central model, response-free peer routing, and reliability-weighted voting.

Result: Across five Qwen-family models, Σ-Mem adapts to counterfactual reliability shifts, generalizes to unseen peers and task domains, and outperforms both majority voting and the best fixed peer baseline on the full OOD evaluation set. Performance improves consistently with more correctness feedback, demonstrating progressive accumulation of actionable reliability information.

Conclusion: Reliability memory serves as a reusable foundation for adaptive coordination in LLM-based multi-agent systems, decoupling trust modeling from content storage and enabling principled, feedback-driven peer selection and integration.

Abstract: Memory is central to long-horizon LLM agents, yet existing memory systems primarily preserve interaction content rather than modeling which agents can be trusted and under what conditions. This limitation is particularly important in multi-agent systems, where a central model may be unable to directly verify plausible or correlated peer responses. We introduce $Σ$-Mem, an online reliability memory that records historical competence evidence for individual peers and peer relationship evidence across the peer set. Both forms of evidence are maintained as real symmetric states and updated from post-decision correctness feedback. By Weyl's inequality, the spectral change caused by each event-level update is bounded, enabling stable online adaptation without retraining the underlying models. $Σ$-Mem provides a general write-and-read interface: the same memory can be used for residual steering of a central model, response-free peer routing, or reliability-weighted voting. Across five Qwen-family models, $Σ$-Mem adapts to counterfactual reliability shifts and generalizes to unseen peers and task domains. Direct memory readouts also outperform majority voting and the best fixed peer over the full OOD evaluation set. Moreover, performance improves consistently as more correctness feedback becomes available, indicating that $Σ$-Mem progressively accumulates actionable reliability information. These results establish reliability memory as a reusable foundation for adaptive coordination in LLM-based multi-agent systems.

</details>


### [71] [VISA: A Structured Description Protocol for Agent-Based Simulation Models Towards Machine Reproducibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28027)
*Zhou He*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: VISA is a structured, symbol-based description protocol for agent-based models (ABMs) using eight interconnected tables and nineteen executable consistency rules. It enables machine-parseable, unambiguous model specification and supports an LLM-executable authoring–checking–code generation loop, validated by reproducing two cross-language ABMs and capturing an industrial AnyLogic model while transparently demarcating irreproducible dependencies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ABMs are notoriously difficult to reproduce because their behavior is dispersed across prose narratives, platform-specific code, and implicit assumptions, causing different readers to reconstruct different models from the same documentation. The authors seek to move the reproduction barrier from the invisible model level to named, localized, actionable dependencies.

Method: VISA specifies a model in eight interconnected tables: four at the agent level (Agent, Variable, Sensing, Internal Function) and four at the model level (Associated Data, Input/Output, Schedule, Validation), following the principle of minimality with completeness. It provides two artifacts: (1) nineteen executable consistency rules that make model validity checkable, and (2) three reusable LLM-executable skills (authoring, checking, code generation) that operationalize the full author–check–code–reproduce loop. Validation was performed on three external, independently authored ABMs spanning NetLogo, Python, and AnyLogic platforms.

Result: The protocol successfully reproduced two ABMs cross-language (NetLogo to Python) directly from VISA specifications. A third industrial AnyLogic model was captured in the eight-table format, passing all nineteen consistency rules, while honestly demarcating where reproduction was blocked by a proprietary movement library and unavailable data — itself framed as a transparency contribution.

Conclusion: VISA shifts the reproduction barrier from the model (where it is invisible) to a named, localized dependency (where it is actionable), significantly improving ABM transparency and reproducibility. The protocol's machine-parseability and LLM integration point toward a more rigorous, automatable modeling workflow.

Abstract: Agent-based models (ABMs) are difficult to reproduce: their behavior is spread across prose narratives, platform-specific code, and implicit assumptions, so that two readers routinely reconstruct different models from the same documentation. We present VISA, a structured, symbol-based description protocol that specifies a model in eight interconnected tables---four at the agent level (Agent, Variable, Sensing, Internal Function) and four at the model level (Associated Data, Input/Output, Schedule, Validation)---under the principle of minimality with completeness. VISA makes a model machine-parseable and unambiguous via two artifacts: nineteen executable consistency rules that turn model validity into a checkable property, and three reusable LLM-executable skills (authoring, checking, and code generation) that operationalize the full author--check--code--reproduce loop. We validate the protocol on three external, independently authored ABMs spanning three platforms: we reproduce two cross-language (NetLogo to Python) directly from their VISA specifications, and we capture a third, an industrial AnyLogic model, in eight tables (passing all nineteen rules) while honestly demarcating where reproduction is blocked by a proprietary movement library and unavailable data---itself a transparency contribution. VISA moves the reproduction barrier from the model, where it is invisible, to a named, localized dependency, where it is actionable.

</details>


### [72] [AgentRadio: Passive Awareness for Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28430)
*Xinxing Ren,Qianbo Zang,Ziyan Wang,Caelum Forder,Suman Deb,Peter Carroll,Zekun Guo*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: AgentRadio introduces an asynchronous message-passing layer for multi-agent coding systems, enabling real-time coordination through threads, messages, and background mention-waiting. Four agents under a five-phase protocol achieve 62.1% resolution on SWE-Atlas QnA, substantially outperforming single-agent baselines (32.3–57.2%), with gains increasing with task difficulty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single LLM agents struggle with long-horizon code comprehension tasks (only 32.3% on SWE-Atlas QnA). Existing multi-agent systems restrict communication to phase boundaries (staged handoffs, synchronized rounds), preventing mid-execution sharing of interdependent discoveries that could rewrite another agent's task.

Method: AgentRadio provides three primitives — threads, messages, and waiting for mentions — where the last runs as a background task, passively surfacing teammates' messages without interrupting foreground work. Four agents operate under a five-phase protocol encompassing division of labor and negotiation, enabling asynchronous coordination during execution.

Result: Four AgentRadio-organized agents resolve 62.1% of SWE-Atlas QnA tasks, 29.8 points above a single Claude Code (Opus 4.6, 32.3%) and above a single Claude Code with Opus 4.8 (57.2%). Rubric-level analysis shows gains increase with task difficulty, consistent with mid-course correction as the mechanism.

Conclusion: Asynchronous message-passing with background awareness enables multi-agent systems to coordinate continuously during code comprehension tasks, overcoming the mutual exclusivity of communication and work in prior systems, with benefits most pronounced for difficult, long-horizon tasks.

Abstract: Understanding large codebases is a long-horizon task for Large Language Model (LLM) agents: answering a single question can require building and running the software, tracing execution across files, and synthesizing evidence over tens of minutes. On SWE-Atlas QnA, a benchmark of long-horizon questions over production repositories, a single Claude Code agent (Opus 4.6) resolves only 32.3% of tasks. Dividing the work among agents with clean contexts mitigates this limitation. However, the subtasks of code comprehension are interdependent. One agent's findings can rewrite another's task, so agents must coordinate during execution, not only at phase boundaries. Existing multi-agent systems support such exchange only between phases, through staged handoffs or synchronized rounds. Communication and work remain mutually exclusive. A discovery made mid-execution cannot be shared until the next boundary. We present AgentRadio, an asynchronous message-passing layer that equips coding-agent harnesses with three primitives: threads, messages, and waiting for mentions. The last runs as a background task, surfacing teammates' messages without interrupting foreground work, so each agent remains passively aware of its peers and folds new findings into its ongoing task. Under a five-phase protocol of division of labor and negotiation, four agents organized by AgentRadio resolve 62.1% of tasks, 29.8 points above a single agent and above Claude Code with the newer Opus 4.8 (57.2%). Rubric-level analysis shows the gain growing with task difficulty, consistent with mid-course correction as the underlying mechanism. Our code is available at https://github.com/Coral-Protocol/AgentRadio.

</details>


### [73] [Using Theory of Mind to Arbitrate between Social and Non-social Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28601)
*Lance Ying,Ryan Truong,Joshua B. Tenenbaum,Samuel J. Gershman*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: People balance social and non-social learning by engaging in mentalizing about others' goals and action informativeness; a Rational Mentalizing model quantitatively captures these trade-offs in a novel experimental game.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Humans frequently choose between learning from others (social learning) and learning through direct experience (non-social learning), yet the cognitive mechanisms governing this trade-off remain unclear. Social learning can be efficient but may carry opportunity costs in time and cognitive resources. Understanding how people rationally balance these strategies is a fundamental question in social cognition.

Method: The authors propose a Rational Mentalizing model that computes the utility of social learning by recursively reasoning about another agent's goals and the expected informativeness of their future actions, then compares this against the utility of direct exploration. They validate the model using a novel experimental game in which participants choose between observing other agents or exploring the environment directly.

Result: The Rational Mentalizing model quantitatively captures human trade-offs between social observation and direct exploration strategies in the experimental game, demonstrating that participants' choices align with utility-maximizing predictions grounded in Theory of Mind reasoning.

Conclusion: Selective social learning is guided by Theory of Mind processes operating in the service of utility maximization. Humans spontaneously mentalize about others' intentions and the informational value of their actions when deciding whether to learn socially or independently.

Abstract: Social learning is a powerful mechanism through which agents learn about the world from others. However, humans sometimes choose direct experience over social learning, which can carry time and cognitive resource costs. How do people balance social and non-social learning? We propose a Rational Mentalizing model of the decision to engage in social learning. This model estimates the utility of social learning by reasoning about another agent's goal and the informativeness of their future actions. It then weighs the utility of social learning against the utility of non-social learning. Using a novel game where players choose between observing other agents or exploring the environment, we show that the Rational Mentalizing model can quantitatively capture human trade-offs between these strategies. These findings suggest that selective social learning is guided by 'Theory of Mind' in the service of utility maximization.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [74] [Autonomous Event-Driven Multi-Agent Orchestration for Enterprise AI at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20058)
*Harsh Rao Dhanyamraju,Leonidas Raghav,Aaron Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates two multi-agent orchestration architectures (DAG Plan and Execute vs. ReAct) across 208 enterprise scenarios at varying scales, finding that scale—not task complexity—dominates performance due to agent discovery noise. A Task Manager with priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption significantly improves latency and correctness at enterprise scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise AI requires continuous event monitoring and action across specialist agents, but existing multi-agent systems are designed for discrete request-response workflows and have not been rigorously evaluated at enterprise scale (hundreds of agents).

Method: The authors benchmark DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct architectures across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios at three scales: Persona (<10 agents), Department (20–80 agents), and Enterprise (200 agents). They also introduce a Task Manager component that performs priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption to enable continuous operation.

Result: Scale dominates orchestration performance: both architectures degrade at enterprise scale due to agent discovery noise, with simple tasks degrading more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan and Execute provides higher precision and structured parallelization at small scales but suffers from overhead at enterprise scale. ReAct is more robust, handling failures incrementally. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14–75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.

Conclusion: Agent discovery noise is the primary bottleneck at enterprise scale, not task complexity. Architectural choice matters less than robust scale-handling mechanisms. Continuous-operation features (priority inference, event merging, preemption) via a Task Manager are critical for enterprise-grade multi-agent systems.

Abstract: Enterprise AI aims to move toward continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across specialist agents, yet existing multi-agent systems largely assume discrete request-response workflows and remain underexplored at enterprise scale. We evaluate DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios spanning Persona (<10 agents), Department (20-80), and Enterprise (200) scales, and introduce a Task Manager for continuous operation via priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption. Results show that scale, not task complexity, dominates orchestration performance: both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade at enterprise scale as agent discovery noise becomes the primary bottleneck, with simple tasks degrading more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan and Execute offers higher precision and structured parallelization at smaller scales, but its higher overhead worsens at enterprise scale; ReAct is more robust by handling failures incrementally. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14-75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.

</details>


### [75] [Skill Use or Skill Theater? Evaluating the Reasoning Backroom in Skill-Augmented Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27484)
*Jinwei Hu,Yi Qi,Xinmiao Huang,Youcheng Sun,Yi Dong,Xiaowei Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Skill-augmented language agents exhibit a "Reasoning Backroom" — a systematic gap between stated skill use and actual causal influence. The BACKTRACE framework uses counterfactual interventions to reveal that agents frequently claim to use skills that don't affect their decisions (performative use) or benefit from skills without acknowledging them (silent uptake). Observational methods fail to detect which decisions truly depend on skills; only intervention-based audit works.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluators infer skill use from visible reasoning traces or the agent's own attribution, but these signals only show apparent use — not whether the skill causally changed the agent's decision. This creates a critical blind spot for reliability, safety, and accountability in skill-augmented language agents. The authors aim to systematically characterize and measure this gap between stated and actual skill influence.

Method: The authors introduce BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework that: (1) pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual; (2) intervenes on five dimensions — skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment; (3) elicits attribution only after the answer is committed (post-hoc). They instantiate this as BACKROOMBench, spanning controlled logic tasks and competition mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single-agent and multi-agent settings, and diverse model families. They also test observational detectors (direct skill-use claims, text mentions, trace similarity, LLM judge) against the intervention-based ground truth.

Result: A pervasive provenance failure was found: stated skill use remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary, producing both silent uptake (skill influences decisions without being credited) and performative use (skill is claimed but has no causal effect). Behavioral effects follow procedural content more reliably than displayed skill identity. Stated attributions respond strongly to artifact availability. No observational detector — including LLM judges — reliably identifies which decisions actually depend on the skill. In multi-agent settings, skill influence survives communication even after its source is lost, while no-skill teams still name skills and sources never supplied.

Conclusion: The Reasoning Backroom constitutes a general AI provenance problem: agents' self-reports about skill use are systematically unreliable, and only intervention-based audit (not passive observation) can determine true causal dependence on skills. This has implications for safety, interpretability, and accountability in modular, skill-augmented AI systems.

Abstract: Reusable skills are becoming a standard interface for extending language agents with task procedures. Yet evaluators usually infer skill use from visible reasoning or the agent's own attribution. These signals show what the agent appears to use, not whether the skill changed its decision. We ask whether skill-augmented agents exhibit a \textbf{Reasoning Backroom}, a systematic gap between stated skill use and intervention-measured influence. We introduce BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework that pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual, intervenes on skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment, and elicits attribution only after the answer is committed. We instantiate the framework as BACKROOMBench, a verified testbed spanning controlled logic and competition mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single-agent and multi-agent settings, and diverse model families. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive provenance failure. Across models and domains, stated skill use often remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary, producing both silent uptake and performative use. Behavioral effects follow procedural content more reliably than displayed skill identity, whereas stated attributions respond strongly to artifact availability. Observational detectors based on direct skill-use claims, text mentions, trace similarity, and an LLM judge do not identify which decisions actually depend on the skill. In multi-agent systems, skill influence can survive communication even after its source is lost, while no-skill teams still name skills and sources that were never supplied. These findings establish the Reasoning Backroom as a general AI provenance problem whose audit requires intervention.

</details>


### [76] [Evaluating Agentic Bioinformatics through Function, Evidence, and Validation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27556)
*Phuc Pham,Truong-Son Hy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Function–Evidence–Validation (FEV) framework to assess the scientific accountability of LLM-based bioinformatics agents by analyzing inspectable workflow trajectories, rather than architecture or outputs alone. Mapping 128 publications across domains, the authors find that planning and tool execution have advanced faster than reproducibility and validation, arguing that workflow correctness should be the primary evaluation criterion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reviews of biological LLM agents categorize systems by application, architecture, or agentic capability, but fail to operationalize scientific accountability. Fluent responses and benchmark scores do not guarantee credible science, creating a gap in how agent-generated workflows are evaluated for trustworthiness and reproducibility.

Method: The authors propose the Function–Evidence–Validation (FEV) framework, which decomposes agent assessment into three axes: Function (demonstrated workflow operations), Evidence (traceable support for actions and claims), and Validation (use-case-specific empirical verification). They apply FEV to systematically map 109 agentic/agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark/evaluation resources across 128 unique publications spanning genomics, single-cell/spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation.

Result: Planning and tool-mediated execution capabilities have matured considerably across all surveyed domains. However, replayability, provenance tracking, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing remain underdeveloped across the board. The workflow-trajectory perspective reveals that final-answer correctness alone is insufficient for establishing scientific credibility.

Conclusion: Agentic bioinformatics should be evaluated through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. The FEV framework provides a practical, operationalizable basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.

Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly plan, execute, and interpret biological analyses, yet fluent responses, successful tool calls, and benchmark performance alone do not establish scientific credibility. Existing reviews primarily organize biological agents by application, architecture, and agentic capability, but do not jointly operationalize the accountability of agent-generated workflows. We address this gap by treating the inspectable workflow trajectory, rather than architecture or final output alone, as the primary unit of analysis. We introduce the Function--Evidence--Validation (FEV) framework, which separates demonstrated workflow operations, traceable support for actions and claims, and use-case-specific validation. Using FEV, we map 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark or evaluation resources, representing 128 unique publications across genomics, single-cell and spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation. Across domains, planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced more rapidly than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing. We therefore argue that agentic bioinformatics should be assessed through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. FEV provides a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.

</details>


### [77] [AISPA: User-Centric System Prompt Auditing for Large Language Model Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28617)
*Xiangning Lin,Shenzhe Zhu,Shu Yang,Zhenyu Zhang,Haoqian Zhang,Yipeng Zhao,Chengxuan Qian,Tianwei Wang,Ziheng Zhang,Zhenlong Yuan,Dingcheng Wang,Juncheng Wu,Yuan Si,Jiaxin Liu,Baolong Bi,Robert Mahari,Tobin South,Dazza Greenwood,Zexue He,Rishi Bommasani,Sophia Kazinnik,Andreas Haupt,Samuele Marro,Erik Brynjolfsson,Alex Pentland,Jiaxin Pei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces AISPA, a framework for systematically auditing system prompts in commercial AI products. Analyzing 3,249 instructions from 88 products, the authors find that while protective instructions are nearly universal (98.9%), they are shallow in scope, and roughly 40% of products contain problematic instructions that work against user interests. Protective and problematic instructions frequently coexist within the same prompt.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: System prompts govern foundation model behavior in commercial AI applications but are rarely disclosed, creating a serious trust and accountability gap. There is no established framework for systematically auditing these prompts, leaving users and regulators without visibility into how AI systems are instructed to behave.

Method: The authors develop AISPA (Artificial Intelligence System Prompt Assurance), a user-centric auditing framework that examines system prompts along eight dimensions relevant to users. They apply this framework to classify 3,249 individual instructions from system prompts across 88 commercial AI products, categorizing each instruction as either protective (benefiting users) or problematic (working against user interests).

Result: Four core findings emerge: (1) system prompt design varies dramatically across products and developers, with some averaging 60+ protective instructions per product while others average fewer than 5; (2) 98.9% of products have at least one protective instruction, but only 24% cover all eight AISPA dimensions; (3) system prompts have grown longer and more protective over time; (4) roughly 40% of products contain at least one problematic instruction, and protective and problematic instructions often coexist within the same prompt.

Conclusion: The findings demonstrate a pressing need for greater transparency, standardization, and independent oversight of system prompts in commercial AI products. The coexistence of protective and problematic instructions within the same prompts reveals the inherently fraught nature of current system prompt design practices.

Abstract: System prompts are instructions configured by developers to govern the behaviors of foundation models in AI applications. They are used throughout commercial AI products, but are rarely disclosed to the public or regulators, creating a serious trust and accountability gap in the wide deployment of AI systems. In this paper, we introduce Artificial Intelligence System Prompt Assurance (AISPA), a user-centric framework for systematically auditing system prompts in AI systems. AISPA examines specific parts of a system prompt and evaluates them along eight dimensions that matter to users. We then use this framework to review 3,249 instructions from system prompts in 88 commercial AI products, classifying each instruction as either protective (of users) or problematic. Our audit surfaces four core findings. First, system prompt design varies substantially across products and developers, with some organizations averaging over 60 protective instructions per product while others average fewer than 5. Second, protective instructions are widely adopted but shallow in scope: 98.9% of products contain at least one, yet only 24% cover all eight dimensions of the AISPA taxonomy. Third, system prompts have grown steadily longer and more protective of users, suggesting that user protection is becoming a more visible concern in commercial prompt design. Fourth, despite this progress, problematic instructions remain pervasive: roughly 40% of products contain at least one instruction that works against user interests, and protective and problematic instructions frequently coexist within the same prompt. Our findings highlight the need for greater transparency, standardization, and independent oversight for system prompts in commercial AI products.

</details>


### [78] [GLM-RAG: Graph Language Models for Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28397)
*Maya Arseven,Anette Frank,Beni Egressy,Johann Higl,Moritz Plenz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a graph language model (GLM)-based retriever for RAG over knowledge graphs and systematically compares it against GNN-based and vector-search-based retrievers across single-hop, multi-hop, and out-of-domain settings. GLM retrievers achieve SOTA on two multi-hop benchmarks with superior out-of-domain generalization, while GNN retrievers offer efficient graph coverage and vector search excels at single-hop tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG retrievers over knowledge graphs face a trade-off between capturing graph structure and leveraging semantic reasoning. GNN-based retrievers model topology but may lack semantic depth; vector-search retrievers capture semantics but ignore graph structure. GLMs offer a unified approach, but their comparative advantages across different retrieval settings and transfer scenarios remain underexplored.

Method: The authors propose a GLM-based retriever and conduct a systematic comparative evaluation across three retriever paradigms: (1) GLM-based, (2) GNN-based, and (3) traditional vector-search-based retrievers. Evaluation spans single-hop and multi-hop RAG settings, with a dedicated focus on out-of-domain transferability. The study also examines scaling behavior with respect to parameter count and subgraph coverage.

Result: Finetuned GLM retrievers achieve state-of-the-art on two multi-hop benchmarks and demonstrate superior out-of-domain generalization. On in-domain multi-hop QA datasets, GLM retrievers remain comparable to prior work with promising scaling trends as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with efficient training, while the vector-search baseline excels at single-hop datasets.

Conclusion: GLM-based retrievers offer the best trade-off for multi-hop reasoning and cross-domain transfer in knowledge-graph-grounded RAG. The choice of retriever should be guided by task characteristics: vector search for single-hop, GNNs for efficient graph coverage, and GLMs for generalizable multi-hop reasoning.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs requires retrievers that can effectively capture both graph structure and semantic information. Recent approaches have explored graph neural network (GNN)-based retrievers to model graph topology in multi-hop reasoning tasks. In parallel, graph language models (GLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm that integrates graph reasoning and the semantic capabilities of language models. In this work, we introduce a GLM-based retriever and investigate the comparative strengths of GLM-based, GNN-based, and traditional vector-search-based retrievers in single- and multi-hop RAG settings, and with a particular focus on transferability to unseen domains. Our findings suggest that finetuned GLM retrievers generalize better out of domain, achieving SOTA on two multi-hop benchmarks. On in-domain multi-hop QA datasets they remain comparable to prior work, with promising scaling as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with an efficient training setup, whereas the vector-search baseline excels at single-hop datasets.

</details>


### [79] [HALO: Heterogeneous Admission through Localized Obligations for Safe Agentic Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27636)
*Taewoo Park,Kyeonghyun Yoo,Kiseok Kim,Seunghyun Yoo,Hwangnam Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HALO is a runtime protocol for agentic AI systems that selectively preserves supported components from heterogeneous responses when conditions change, rather than discarding the entire response. It checks prerequisites, re-verifies actions before dispatch, and allows replacement of blocked actions, achieving perfect scores on admission tests and protocol tests while retaining all supported components in replay scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI systems produce heterogeneous responses (notices, requests, handoffs, actions) where components may share dependencies. When external conditions change between response generation and use, rejecting the entire response discards still-valid components, but checking components independently risks retaining dependents whose prerequisites are no longer supported. Existing approaches lack a principled way to handle this partial-invalidation problem.

Method: HALO employs localized obligations: each component declares its prerequisites, and the protocol preserves only those components whose prerequisites remain supported at runtime. Before dispatching any action, HALO rechecks its exact validity against current conditions. Blocked actions are replaced exclusively by freshly generated candidates (not stale alternatives). The protocol was evaluated via admission expectations, protocol tests, structured-response replay, and cold-start PX4/Gazebo drone simulation sessions.

Result: HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay, it retained 248/248 supported components (including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes), while a whole-response policy retained 0/248. Across ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions, HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.

Conclusion: HALO demonstrates that localized obligation tracking enables fine-grained component-level admission, avoiding both the waste of whole-response rejection and the unsafety of independent component checking. The protocol ensures that only currently-supported, freshly-verified actions are dispatched, making it suitable for safety-critical agentic systems operating under dynamic conditions.

Abstract: Recent agentic AI systems may return a heterogeneous response containing notices, requests, handoffs, and actions. Conditions can change before external use, so components from the same response need not remain supported together. Rejecting the whole response discards useful components, whereas checking components independently can leave a dependent without its prerequisite. We present Heterogeneous Admission with Localized Obligations (HALO), a runtime protocol that preserves supported components whose declared prerequisites also remain supported, rechecks each exact action before dispatch, and allows blocked actions to be replaced only by fresh candidates. HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay, it retained 248/248 supported components, including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes, while a whole-response policy retained 0/248. Across ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions, HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.

</details>


### [80] [Old Tricks, New Models: How Simple Image Transformations Break Modern AI-based Content Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28187)
*Marco Alecci,Francesco Marchiori,Iyiola Emmanuel Olatunji,Tegawendé F. Bissyandé,Jacques Klein*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Three commercial multimodal moderation APIs built on foundation models are easily bypassed using simple, model-agnostic image transformations (e.g., color inversion, grayscale), revealing that replacing conventional classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not inherently provide robust safety filtering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Commercial multimodal moderation APIs based on large foundation models promise broader policy coverage and better contextual understanding than task-specific classifiers. The paper investigates whether this architectural shift also yields improved robustness against adversarial or accidental evasion.

Method: Large-scale black-box evaluation of three commercial image-moderation APIs using seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations (e.g., color inversion, grayscale, rotation, blur). Evaluated across multiple providers, datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities — requiring no gradients, surrogate models, or target system knowledge.

Result: All three services can be bypassed with inexpensive transformations. Fixed transformations like color inversion and grayscale reliably flip unsafe decisions to safe while preserving human-recognizable content. Robustness varies substantially across datasets and harm categories, with multimodal content and self-harm being particularly vulnerable.

Conclusion: Foundation-model-based moderation APIs do not, by themselves, constitute a reliable security boundary. They must be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline, not as standalone safety filters.

Abstract: While automated content-moderation systems have become essential for screening harmful content at scale, conventional task-specific classifiers often provide limited policy cov- erage and contextual understanding. Recently, commercial multimodal moderation APIs built on large foundation models have been introduced with the promise of providing broader and more capable safety filters. In this work, we analyze whether this shift also yields more robust image moderation. We conduct a large-scale black-box evaluation on three established commercial image-moderation services and compare their robustness. By evaluating seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations across multiple providers, datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities, we find that: (1) all three commercial services can be bypassed using inexpensive image transformations that require no gradients, surrogate models, or knowledge of the target system; (2) even fixed transformations such as color inversion and grayscale conversion induce unsafe-to-safe decision changes while preserving content that remains recognizable to humans; (3) their robustness varies substantially across datasets and harm categories, with multimodal content and self-harm exhibiting pronounced vulnerabilities. This yields the conclusion that replacing conventional moderation classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not, by itself, provide a reliable security boundary. Such systems must be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline rather than as standalone safety filters.

</details>


### [81] [Dimensionality and Measurement Precision in HLE's Multiple-Choice Subset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27420)
*Mayank Sharma,Savira Nadela,Tyler Matteson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HLE measures a single general reasoning factor, not distinct domain capabilities. Domain subscores are redundant with total scores, and measurement precision drops sharply at the high-ability range where frontier models reside, limiting HLE's ability to discriminate among top-tier models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: HLE is widely used to evaluate frontier LLMs and its domain subscores are commonly interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities. However, no prior study has empirically tested whether these domain categories correspond to separable latent constructs, nor whether the benchmark effectively differentiates between similarly high-performing models.

Method: The authors evaluated 29 LLMs on HLE's text-only multiple-choice subset (428 items) and applied psychometric methods: (1) fitting a two-parameter logistic IRT model, (2) computing McDonald's omega hierarchical, (3) variance decomposition by domain labels, (4) within- vs. between-domain residual correlation comparison via Cohen's d, (5) domain ability vs. total score correlations, and (6) test information function analysis to assess measurement precision across ability levels.

Result: McDonald's ω_h = 0.998 indicates a dominant general factor. Domain labels explain only 3.5% of item response variance. Within- and between-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's d = 0.016). Domain-specific ability estimates correlate r ≥ 0.81 with total scores. The test information function shows precision concentrated at moderate ability levels, dropping sharply above θ = 0, precisely where frontier models are located.

Conclusion: HLE's domain subscores should not be interpreted as reflecting distinct capabilities; the benchmark essentially measures a unidimensional general reasoning factor. Furthermore, HLE has limited discriminative power among the strongest models due to insufficient measurement precision at high ability levels, raising concerns about its utility for comparing frontier LLMs.

Abstract: Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) is widely used to evaluate frontier language models. HLE organizes its questions into eight subject-domain categories, whose subscores are often interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities. However, no study has assessed whether these labels correspond to empirically separable latent constructs, nor whether the benchmark effectively differentiates between models of similar ability. We evaluate 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE ($J = 428$ items) and apply psychometric methods to assess both the dimensionality of the benchmark and the distribution of its measurement precision. Fitting a two-parameter logistic IRT model, we find convergent evidence that HLE measures a single general reasoning factor: McDonald's $ω_h = 0.998$, domain labels explain only 3.5\% of item response variance, within- and between-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's $d = 0.016$), and domain-specific ability estimates are near-redundant with the total score ($r \geq 0.81$). A separate analysis of the test information function reveals that measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability levels and drops sharply above $θ= 0$, where frontier models sit. These findings suggest that HLE's domain subscores do not warrant distinct capability interpretations and that the benchmark's ability to discriminate among the strongest models is limited.

</details>


### [82] [Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27553)
*Lennart Meincke,Karan Girotra,Gideon Nave,Christian Terwiesch,Karl T. Ulrich*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GPT-4 generated new product ideas (via zero-shot and few-shot prompting) outperform human-generated ideas on purchase intent and are 7× more likely to rank in the top 10%, but AI ideas are less novel and more homogeneous, especially under few-shot prompting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether LLMs can serve as effective tools for new product ideation, addressing a gap in empirical evidence comparing AI-generated versus human-generated product ideas using rigorous market research and creativity metrics.

Method: Three idea pools were compared: (1) student-generated ideas from a pre-LLM product design course, (2) GPT-4 zero-shot prompted ideas, and (3) GPT-4 few-shot prompted ideas — all for products targeting college students under $50. Purchase intent was measured via standard market research (predicted average probability), idea similarity via text mining, and novelty via human raters. Best-idea quality was assessed by top-decile ranking frequency.

Result: AI ideas surpassed human ideas on average purchase intent (few-shot > zero-shot). However, AI ideas scored lower on novelty and higher on pairwise similarity — especially few-shot, indicating reduced diversity. Crucially, AI ideas were 7× more likely to appear in the top 10% of all ideas, a conservative estimate given AI's higher productivity.

Conclusion: Despite drawbacks in novelty and diversity, LLMs offer a substantial advantage in generating high-quality new product ideas, with the 7:1 top-idea ratio likely understating AI's true potential when productivity gains are considered.

Abstract: This research evaluates the efficacy of large language models (LLMs) in generating new product ideas. To do so, we compare three pools of ideas for new products targeted toward college students and priced at 50 dollars or less. The first pool of ideas was created by university students in a product design course before the availability of LLMs. The second and third pools of ideas were generated by GPT-4 from OpenAI using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, respectively. We evaluated idea quality using standard market research techniques to predict average purchase intent probability. We used text mining to assess idea similarity and human raters to evaluate idea novelty. We find that AI-generated ideas outperform human-generated ideas in terms of average purchase intent, with few-shot prompting yielding slightly higher intent than zero-shot prompting. However, AI-generated ideas are perceived as less novel and exhibit higher pairwise similarity, particularly with few-shot prompting, indicating a less diverse solution landscape. When focusing on the quality of the best ideas rather than the average ideas, we find that AI-generated ideas are seven times more likely to rank among the top 10 percent of ideas, demonstrating a significant advantage over human-generated ideas. We propose that this seven-to-one advantage is a conservative estimate because it does not account for the greater productivity of AI. Our findings suggest that despite some drawbacks, AI creativity presents a substantial benefit in generating high-quality ideas for new product development.

</details>


### [83] [ReDiPPO: Reference-Guided Value Calibration and Discrepancy-Aware Token Reweighting for Mathematical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27631)
*Zhenrong Zhang,Fei Wu,Jun Du,Jianshu Zhang,Si Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReDiPPO introduces a reference-guided critic for PPO that leverages reference answers as privileged signals, and uses token-level discrepancy between standard and reference-guided value estimates to reweight advantages, improving mathematical reasoning in LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In mathematical reasoning with long horizons and sparse rewards, standard PPO critics struggle with accurate token-level credit assignment, producing noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates. The authors aim to address this by injecting privileged reference-answer information during training.

Method: ReDiPPO employs a dual-critic architecture: (1) a reference-guided critic trained with reference-answer signals for more accurate value estimation, and (2) a standard critic. The token-level discrepancy between their value estimates identifies difficult reasoning states, which is used to reweight token-level advantages during PPO optimization.

Result: Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks show ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong baselines including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO in final reasoning performance.

Conclusion: ReDiPPO effectively enhances PPO for mathematical reasoning by combining reference-guided value estimation with discrepancy-aware advantage reweighting, yielding more reliable credit assignment and superior policy optimization.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for enhancing the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Among existing policy optimization methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remains particularly appealing because its learned critic can, in principle, provide token-level credit assignment. However, in mathematical reasoning tasks characterized by long reasoning horizons and sparse outcome rewards, reliable token-level credit assignment remains challenging. The standard critic often fails to accurately evaluate intermediate reasoning states, resulting in noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates. In this paper, we propose ReDiPPO, a Reference-guided and Discrepancy-aware PPO framework for mathematical reasoning. ReDiPPO introduces a reference-guided critic that uses reference answers as training-time privileged signals to provide more accurate value estimation. Meanwhile, it retains a standard critic and quantifies the token-level reference-standard discrepancy between the standard value estimate and the reference-guided value estimate. This discrepancy serves as an indicator of difficult reasoning states and is used to reweight the corresponding token-level advantages during PPO optimization. Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong policy optimization baselines, including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO, in final reasoning performance. Our code is available on https://github.com/cii030/ReDiPPO.

</details>


### [84] [Baikal: Structured Search for Deep Research over Data Lakes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27726)
*Dhruv Agarwal,Rishitha Guttapalle Mohan,Aarti Kumari,Ashi Sinha,Athulya Anil,Kavitha Srinivas,Horst Samulowitz,Andrew McCallum*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Baikal casts deep research over heterogeneous data lakes as a budgeted search problem, organizing evidence into semantic regions and applying adaptive exploration policies (ε-greedy, UCB) to balance exploration vs. exploitation, achieving 28% and 36% improvement over strong baselines on HybridQA and TAT-QA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-agent methods for deep research over data lakes use iterative retrieval-and-generation, where accumulated context drives subsequent investigation. This greedy approach overexploits locally promising evidence and fails to cover distinct semantic regions under a fixed subquestion budget, leading to incomplete and non-diverse findings.

Method: Baikal clusters heterogeneous evidence (tables, passages) into semantic regions, then conducts adaptive search across these regions. Within a selected region, it generates region-grounded subquestions and evaluates finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates. It supports policies including random selection, LLM-guided selection, Bayesian ε-greedy, and Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) to balance exploration and exploitation.

Result: Evaluated on 15 queries over HybridQA (10,993 tables, 227K Wikipedia passages) and TAT-QA (2,757 tables, 13K financial passages), Baikal's best configuration outperforms the strongest baselines (DeepSearcher, OpenCode research agent) by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA. Gains are attributed to improved groundedness, diversity, and usefulness under the same subquestion budget.

Conclusion: Structured semantic exploration via region-based adaptive search significantly improves systematic research over heterogeneous data lakes, yielding more grounded, diverse, and useful findings compared to iterative retrieval-generation approaches.

Abstract: Deep research over data lakes requires an LLM agent to investigate evidence across thousands of heterogeneous tables and passages to synthesize a report. Existing methods perform iterative retrieval and generation, letting accumulated context determine what to investigate next, which can overexploit locally promising evidence and fail to cover distinct semantic regions under a fixed budget. To address this, we cast deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem and present Baikal - a framework that clusters heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions, then searches over them adaptively to balance exploration and exploitation. Within each selected region, Baikal generates and investigates region-grounded subquestions, using finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates and guide search under policies ranging from random and LLM-guided selection to Bayesian $ε$-greedy and UCB. We evaluate Baikal on 15 queries each over HybridQA and TAT-QA data lakes containing 10,993 and 2,757 tables, respectively, together with 227K Wikipedia passages and 13K financial report passages. We assess research quality with a new rubric covering groundedness, relevance, diversity, and utility, and use GPT-5-mini to score Baikal and strong baselines, including DeepSearcher and an OpenCode research agent with retrieval and clustering variants. Across both data lakes, Baikal performs strongly under several region-selection policies; its best configuration improves report scores over the strongest baselines by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA. Our analyses attribute these gains to organizing and exploring semantic evidence regions, which improves groundedness and diversity and yields more useful findings under the same subquestion budget. These results demonstrate the value of structured semantic exploration for systematic research and discovery over heterogeneous data lakes.

</details>


### [85] [MemTxn: A Transaction Boundary for Source-Supported Updates and Complete-State Recovery in Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27834)
*Hanshuai Cui,Zhiqing Tang,Zhi Yao,Fanshuai Meng,Qianli Ma,Weijia Jia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemTxn is a governance layer for persistent memory in LLM agents that enforces transactional semantics—validating writes against source evidence, resolving factual conflicts via temporal ordering, and recovering state after faults using snapshot journals—achieving perfect audit discrimination, reliable fault recovery, and state-of-the-art F1 on fact consolidation benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persistent memory enables LLM agents to reuse information across sessions, but erroneous writes can corrupt future behavior without any mechanism for transactional boundaries, reliable update validation, or recovery. Existing systems focus only on storage and retrieval, ignoring correctness guarantees for writable memory.

Method: MemTxn operates as an external governance layer with three core components: (1) Ordered PatchTest for validating writes by checking whether an update is supported by its source; (2) Temporal Resolver for selecting the correct visible version when facts conflict; and (3) a durable snapshot journal for restoring application-visible state after faults without knowing the actual physical write set.

Result: On item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives (perfect discrimination). Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo, it restores the complete declared active map. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, MemTxn achieves the highest average F1 across all 12 answer-model configurations, outperforming Dense by 17.06–24.07 points in five representative settings.

Conclusion: MemTxn demonstrates that a governance layer with transactional guarantees can reliably protect persistent LLM memory from corruption, ensuring that only source-supported facts persist, conflicts are temporally resolved, and state is recoverable after faults—yielding significant practical gains in memory reliability and downstream task performance.

Abstract: Persistent memory lets long-running large language model agents reuse information across sessions and tasks. Yet errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems improve storage and retrieval, but they do not provide a transaction boundary for reliable updates and recovery. We therefore propose MemTxn, a governance layer outside the answer model. MemTxn verifies whether an update is supported by its source. It also selects the visible version when facts conflict and restores the application-visible state after a fault. The system uses Ordered PatchTest to validate writes, a Temporal Resolver to select versions, and a durable snapshot journal to recover state. On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo states, it restores the complete declared active map without knowing the actual physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, MemTxn achieves the highest average F1 across all twelve answer-model configurations. It outperforms Dense by 17.06--24.07 points in five representative settings.

</details>


### [86] [IFHierBench: Hierarchical Instruction Following for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27912)
*Yuetian Mao,Chunyang Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IFHierBench introduces a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark with 600 prompts across four constraint-tree depths and 35 constraints, revealing that even top LLMs barely exceed 50% accuracy and degrade sharply with depth, highlighting a critical gap in nested constraint adherence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat constraints as a flat list applied uniformly to the entire response, failing to capture real-world deployment scenarios where LLM outputs have layered structures (overall artifact, sections, nested fields), each requiring scoped constraint verification.

Method: The authors construct IFHierBench, a benchmark with 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths. It spans 35 distinct constraint types, with each prompt paired with a deterministic checker that verifies constraint satisfaction at every scope (hierarchical verification). Seven leading proprietary and open-weight models are evaluated.

Result: The strongest model achieves just over 50% prompt-level accuracy. Accuracy degrades sharply as constraint-tree depth increases, demonstrating that reliably following nested, scoped constraints remains a substantial challenge for current LLMs.

Conclusion: Following hierarchical instructions with nested, scoped constraints is a major unsolved problem. Future training methods should incorporate finer-grained constraint adherence to improve real-world instruction-following reliability.

Abstract: Instruction-following ability is critical for deploying large language models in real-world applications, where downstream components depend on the output satisfying specific constraints. Modern deployments increasingly handle the full task in a single LLM call, with one prompt specifying a layered output whose overall artifact, structural sections, and nested fields must each satisfy concrete constraints. Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat the constraint set as a flat list applied uniformly to the response, so they cannot scope a check to a particular section of the output. We introduce IFHierBench, a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark of 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints, each prompt paired with a deterministic checker that verifies satisfaction at every scope. Evaluating seven leading proprietary and open-weight models, we find that even the strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy and that accuracy degrades sharply as constraint depth grows. Reliably following nested constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs, motivating future training methods that consider constraint adherence at finer granularity to achieve better instruction-following ability.

</details>


### [87] [SciDataSailor: Deep Scientific Data Exploring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28098)
*Jiyong Rao,Yicheng Qiu,Chi Zhang,Chunfeng Song,Runkai Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SciDataSailor introduces an agentic paradigm for deep scientific data exploration, using MCTS-based trajectory synthesis to train LLM agents that navigate hierarchical scientific repositories, interpret heterogeneous files, execute analyses, and answer questions grounded in real data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific datasets are hierarchical, heterogeneous, and interdependent, making manual inspection and integration labor-intensive. While LLM agents excel at planning and tool use, existing work neglects their ability to interact with real scientific data assets in executable environments. There is a gap in enabling agents to autonomously explore, integrate, and reason over complex scientific repositories.

Method: The authors propose the Deep Scientific Data Exploration task paradigm and the SciDataSailor framework. SciDataSailor synthesizes tool-interactive trajectories using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) augmented with four mechanisms: (1) difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, (2) dual-feedback first-play urgency, (3) hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and (4) entropy-guided branching. The framework produces SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation (627 summarization + 586 QA tasks across 27 datasets in life, earth, and physical sciences).

Result: SciDataSailor-Bench contains 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks spanning 27 datasets across life, earth, and physical sciences. The SFT-2K dataset supports supervised fine-tuning of agents for scientific data exploration. (Specific performance metrics are not detailed in the provided abstract.)

Conclusion: SciDataSailor establishes a systematic approach for enabling LLM agents to perform deep exploration of scientific data repositories, bridging the gap between agentic reasoning and real-world scientific data analysis through structured trajectory synthesis and benchmark construction.

Abstract: Scientific datasets are commonly organized as hierarchical repositories containing heterogeneous and interdependent files, making their inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive and reliant on domain expertise. Although large language model (LLM) agents have advanced substantially in planning, reasoning, and tool use, existing research has largely overlooked their ability to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments. We introduce Deep Scientific Data Exploration, an agentic task paradigm in which agents navigate repositories, interpret heterogeneous files and schemas, execute analyses, integrate cross-file evidence, and produce conclusions grounded in executed observations. To operationalize this paradigm, we present SciDataSailor, a framework for synthesizing tool-interactive trajectories by balancing broad exploration with targeted exploitation. SciDataSailor instantiates trajectory synthesis as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with four task-specific mechanisms: difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, dual-feedback first-play urgency, hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and entropy-guided branching. Using this framework, we construct SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation, with the latter comprising 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks across 27 datasets spanning the life, earth, and physical sciences.

</details>


### [88] [CDAE: Enhancing Perturbation Robustness in Pretrained Language Models with Contrastive Denoising](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28236)
*Sina Heydari,Amirreza Abbasi,Mohsen Hooshmand,Majid Ramezani*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CDAE is a lightweight framework that refines BERT sentence embeddings by jointly optimizing contrastive and reconstruction objectives, producing representations that are robust to semantic-preserving perturbations like synonym substitution, masking, and word dropout.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained language model embeddings remain sensitive to semantic-preserving textual perturbations (synonym substitution, masking, word dropout), undermining representation stability. A method is needed to make embeddings invariant to such perturbations while preserving semantic information.

Method: A Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder (CDAE) that refines pre-trained BERT embeddings by jointly optimizing a contrastive objective (pulling perturbed versions of the same sentence together) and a reconstruction objective (recovering the original representation from perturbed inputs). Multiple perturbation strategies at varying strengths are used during training and evaluation.

Result: CDAE consistently achieves higher embedding similarity under perturbations compared to original BERT embeddings and SimCSE, with improvements becoming more pronounced as perturbation strength increases.

Conclusion: The framework effectively enhances representation stability while preserving semantics, demonstrating that perturbation-invariant learning is a promising direction for improving sentence embeddings.

Abstract: Pre-trained language models have significantly improved sentence representation learning, yet their embedding remain sensitive to semantic preserving textual perturbations such as synonym substitution, masking and word dropout. This work proposes a lightweight Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder (CDAE) that refines pre-trained BERT embedding by jointly optimizing contrastive and reconstruction objective to learn perturbation-invariant representation. We evaluate the proposed framework using multiple perturbation strategies with varying strengths and compare it against the original BERT embeddings and SimCSE. Experimental results show that CDAE consistently preserves higher embedding similarity under perturbations, with the improvements becoming more pronounced as framework effectively enhances representation stability while preserving semantic information, highlighting perturbation-invariant learning as a promising direction for improving sentence embeddings. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ComputationIASBS/CDAE

</details>


### [89] [WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28418)
*Haozhe Hu,Hao Wu,Peiran Yin,Chao Han,Yunpu Ma,Xiaoyu Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WIDE is a token-level dynamic width pruning framework for LLMs that enables fine-grained, differentiable pruning at the neuron-block granularity, combined with a pruning-kernel co-design for practical acceleration, achieving up to 1.98x (prefill) and 4.95x (decoding) kernel-level speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static structured pruning is hardware-friendly but causes significant accuracy loss under aggressive sparsity due to input-agnostic computation allocation. Dynamic sparsity methods retain quality better by adapting to inputs, but are limited to coarse-grained (layer-level) decisions and lack practical acceleration. The authors aim to bridge this gap with fine-grained dynamic pruning that is both quality-preserving and practically fast.

Method: WIDE is an end-to-end differentiable framework that allows each token to dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups (neuron-block-level granularity). It uses a two-stage training pipeline to learn token-wise sparse execution patterns. For practical speedup, a pruning-kernel co-design framework decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into three components: mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping.

Result: At 50% sparsity, WIDE achieves a 55.1% performance boost over state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. Under real inference workloads, it achieves kernel-level speedups of up to 1.98x (prefill) and 4.95x (decoding), with end-to-end acceleration of 1.68x and 1.55x respectively.

Conclusion: Fine-grained token-level dynamic width pruning, when co-designed with specialized kernels, can simultaneously preserve model quality and deliver substantial practical speedups across both prefill and decoding phases, outperforming prior coarse-grained dynamic pruning methods.

Abstract: Pruning is a promising approach for improving the efficiency of LLMs. Existing static structured pruning methods are hardware-friendly and can deliver practical throughput gains, but their input-agnostic computation allocation often causes substantial accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsity.
