Recent dynamic sparsity methods improve quality retention by adapting computation to individual inputs, yet they remain largely limited to coarse-grained structural decisions and their practical acceleration under real-world inference scenarios remains challenging. To address these challenges, we present WIDE, the first end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework designed for both prefill and decode scenarios. WIDE enables fine-grained computation allocation by allowing each token to dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, extending dynamic pruning beyond layer-level decisions to neuron-block-level granularity. Through a two-stage training pipeline, WIDE learns effective token-wise sparse execution patterns and achieves substantially better quality retention than existing approaches. To make such fine-grained dynamic pruning practical, we further propose a pruning--kernel co-design framework that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, enabling efficient execution across different granularities. At 50% sparsity, WIDE provides 55.1% performance boost when compared to the state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. Under prefill and decoding inference workloads, WIDE achieves close-to-theoretical kernel-level speedups of up to 1.98x for prefill and 4.95x for decoding, as well as 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration. Our code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/LLM-Pruning/tree/main/WIDE.

</details>


### [90] [Metaphor Tracer: A Theory-Informed Analysis of Hidden States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28434)
*Marc Heimann,Roxana Assadi Moghaddam,Olga Brovkina,Mark Pettifor,Lutz Goetzmann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces two novel metrics — aggregator and differentiator — computed from a single forward pass of a language model to characterize token-level structural roles within a text. The aggregator measures whether a token position consolidates the whole text into a stable hidden-state configuration; the differentiator measures whether other tokens are transiently carried into that position's subspace. Against independent ground truth (an engineered register and a psychoanalyst's clinical annotations), the aggregator tracks a token's structural place in discourse, dissociating from surprisal and attention, and operates relationally rather than on type-level vector semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to operationalize a relational, structural theory of how language models organize a single text during reading. Rather than treating hidden states as encoding type-level lexical semantics or information-theoretic salience, they ask whether token positions exhibit structural properties — consolidation and transport — that reflect the discourse-level organization of a specific text, and whether these properties can be recovered without training, from one forward pass.

Method: Two frozen metrics are defined: (1) **Aggregator** — scores whether a token position's hidden state converges to a stable representation of the entire text; (2) **Differentiator** — scores whether representations of other tokens are transiently carried into that position's subspace (metaphor as "transport"). Constants were frozen on a single discovery text; all other texts serve as confirmatory. Validation uses independent ground truth: an engineered register with known boundaries (6/6 cells matched) and a psychoanalyst's pre-existing annotations of clinical transcripts (34/36 cells matched). A transfer test compares models, including a matched base/instruct pair, to assess whether token-structure travels with lexical type versus textual position.

Result: The aggregator dissociates from surprisal and attention: as a signifier repeats, surprisal and attention drain, but aggregator score holds steady — marking the token's structural place. It tracks register boundaries perfectly (6/6) and psychoanalytic annotations near-perfectly (34/36), with a graded effect above lexical controls that no type-level measure reproduces. The transfer test shows that the model whose token structure travels most with lexical type reads singular discourse worst; in the base/instruct pair, instruction tuning raises fidelity without increasing type-transfer. This confirms the property is relational — tied to a token's place in *this* text, not its vector alone.

Conclusion: Hidden states carry structural information about a token's role within the discourse organization of a single text, not reducible to type-level semantics, salience, or information content. The aggregator operationalizes a relational reading consistent with theory that predates the instrument, suggesting that language models implicitly learn to structure texts in ways that align with human interpretive practices (e.g., clinical annotation). The work reframes interpretability from essentialist vector analysis toward relational, position-in-text structural analysis.

Abstract: What do a language model's hidden states say about the organization of a single text? From one forward pass, without training, we score every token position on two properties. The *aggregator* measures whether the position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration. The *differentiator*, whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace as the model reads: metaphor in its root sense, transport. Constants were frozen on one discovery text; every other is confirmatory.
  The aggregator is not, in the classic sense, an information measure, nor a measure of salience. Across three unrelated models, as a signifier repeats, its surprisal and its attention drain while its aggregator score holds: the channel marks a token's place in the text. That this tracks a reading rests on independent ground truth: an engineered register the aggregator follows across its boundaries (6/6 cells), and a psychoanalyst's marking of clinical transcripts, fixed before the instrument existed, in 34/36 cells, with a graded increment above lexical controls and dissociations no type-level measure reproduces. A transfer test gives the result its shape: the model whose token structure travels with lexical type reads the singular discourse worst, and in a matched base/instruct pair tuning raises fidelity without moving type-transfer. Structural value is a property of a token's place in *this* text, not of its vector alone: a relational rather than essentialist reading of hidden states, operationalizing theory that predated the instrument.

</details>


### [91] [SVR: Self-Verifying Refinement via Joint Verdict-Confidence Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Test-Time Compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28457)
*Hongyu Chen,Liang Lin,Guangrun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SVR is a multi-turn RL framework that trains language models to use self-verification (correctness verdict + confidence score) as an internal control signal for adaptive test-time compute allocation, without relying on external feedback or oracles at inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uniform test-time compute budgets waste computation on easy problems, and existing verifier-guided refinement methods depend on external feedback or oracle verifiers. The authors aim to develop a method where the model learns to decide autonomously when to stop refining, using only internally generated self-verification signals.

Method: SVR is trained via GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories. At each turn, the model generates a solution, a discrete correctness verdict (Correct/Incorrect), and a confidence score. During training, rewards incentivize: (1) solution correctness, (2) calibration-aware self-verification (accurate verdicts + calibrated confidence), and (3) stop-ready correct states. At inference, adaptive stopping is activated: the model retains an answer only when verdict is "Correct" and confidence exceeds a threshold; otherwise it continues refining. Ground-truth correctness is used only for reward computation, never exposed in prompts or at inference.

Result: On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.563 with only 2.99 average inference turns. It outperforms standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference, while using substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference.

Conclusion: Learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation, eliminating the need for external verifiers or oracles during inference.

Abstract: Scaling test-time computation can improve language-model reasoning, but uniform budgets waste computation on easy inputs, while verifier-guided refinement relies on external feedback. We introduce Self-Verifying Refinement (SVR), an oracle-free multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that learns to use self-verification as a compute-control policy. At each turn, the model produces a solution together with a discrete correctness verdict and a confidence score; it retains the current answer only when the verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold, and otherwise continues refinement using its own self-verification. Ground-truth correctness is used only to construct training rewards and is never exposed to the policy through refinement prompts or required at inference. SVR is trained with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories using rewards that promote solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states; adaptive stopping is activated only at inference. On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.563 with only 2.99 inference turns on average. In the evaluated complete-system comparison, it exceeds standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference while requiring substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference. These results demonstrate that learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation.

</details>


### [92] [OSReward: Instituting Standardized Evaluation for Cross-Platform Computer-Use Reward Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28609)
*Qiushi Sun,Kanzhi Cheng,Yian Wang,Bowen Yang,Hang Yan,Liheng Chen,Fangzhi Xu,Zichen Ding,Nuo Chen,Jialin Cao,Xingdong Gong,Zehao Li,Kaiming Jin,Xinfeng Yuan,Zhoumianze Liu,Jingyang Gong,Zhangyue Yin,Jiahui Gao,Zhiyong Wu,Tianbao Xie,Jianbing Zhang,Ben Kao,Lingpeng Kong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OSReward introduces a benchmark to evaluate VLM judges of computer-using agent (CUA) trajectories, finding even state-of-the-art models suffer from systematic leniency bias. The authors release OS-Shepherd-100K, a training corpus for open reward models (OS-Shepherd 9B/35B) that match commercial judges at 30–60% lower cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Verifying whether CUA trajectories fulfill task instructions is critical for evaluation, data curation, and RL, but neither human-written verifiers nor human annotators scale. The field increasingly relies on VLMs as judges, yet their reliability has never been systematically examined — a gap this paper addresses.

Method: The authors construct OSReward, a benchmark of diverse CUA trajectories with ground-truth verdicts from multi-stage human annotation. They derive OSReward-Hard (challenging cases) and OSReward-Multi (fine-grained efficiency/alignment scoring). They then build OS-Shepherd-100K, a reasoning-annotated judgment corpus, and train OS-Shepherd (9B and 35B) as open reward models.

Result: Even top VLM judges exhibit a systematic leniency bias, misclassifying failed runs as successes. The few reliable models are prohibitively expensive at scale, while affordable open models lag far behind. OS-Shepherd models match commercial judge performance at 30–60% lower cost than frontier offerings.

Conclusion: Current VLM judges for CUA trajectories are not sufficiently reliable for large-scale use due to leniency bias and cost constraints. Open, purpose-trained reward models like OS-Shepherd offer a practical path to low-cost, stable, and reliable reward signals, and the released resources (benchmark, dataset, models) aim to advance the CUA community.

Abstract: Computer-using agents (CUAs) are advancing rapidly across the digital world. A CUA trajectory records the agent's actions, states, and reasoning. Verifying whether it fulfilled the task instruction is central to CUA evaluation, data curation, and reinforcement learning. Neither human-written verifiers nor human annotators can provide such verification at scale, so the field increasingly turns to vision-language models (VLMs) as judges of CUA trajectories. But a fundamental question has long gone unexamined: are these VLM judges reliable enough? To study it systematically, we introduce OSReward, a realistic, high-quality benchmark that evaluates VLM judges on CUA trajectories. The trajectories come from diverse agent backbones executing human-verified instructions across platforms, then rigorously labeled with ground-truth verdicts through multi-stage human annotation. Building on it, we derive OSReward-Hard, a challenge set concentrating genuinely hard cases, and OSReward-Multi for fine-grained efficiency and alignment scoring. The most comprehensive evaluation of VLM judges to date finds even state-of-the-art models fall short of an ideal judge, sharing a systematic leniency bias that mislabels failed runs as successes. The few reliable enough to trust are too expensive to run at scale, while affordable open models trail far behind. To close this gap, we construct and release OS-Shepherd-100K, an open corpus of reasoning-annotated trajectory judgments for the CUA community. On it, we train OS-Shepherd (9B and 35B), open reward models that supply low-cost, stable, and reliable reward signals, matching commercial judges at 30-60% lower cost than the frontier. Extensive analyses further inform the design of reliable CUA reward at scale. Our code, benchmark, dataset, and model checkpoints are available at https://os-copilot.github.io/OSReward-Home/.

</details>


### [93] [KernelGenBench: A Multi-Source and Multi-Chip Benchmark for LLM-based Kernel Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27231)
*Peiyu Zang,Jian Tao,Jialing Zhang,Yichen Yuan,Wentao Zhang,Guang Liu,Yonghua Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KernelGenBench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM-generated Triton kernels across multiple operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms, revealing that agent-based methods outperform pure sampling, cross-platform portability remains poor, and autonomous kernel generation is extremely token-costly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs have created surging demand for efficient accelerator kernels, yet kernel development is highly specialized and labor-intensive. Despite rapid progress in LLM-based automatic kernel generation, no comprehensive benchmark exists to rigorously evaluate generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware.

Method: The authors introduce KernelGenBench with two sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source) covering 210 operators from three sources beyond PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip) evaluating performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. A large-scale evaluation consuming over 15 billion tokens was conducted.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling, with cuBLAS operators being the hardest target. (2) Generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms; kernel-specialized agents suffer severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E). (3) Autonomous kernel generation is extremely cost-intensive, with specialized agents averaging 5.11M tokens per successful operator, orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling.

Conclusion: KernelGenBench fills a critical evaluation gap for LLM-generated kernels, exposing significant challenges in cross-platform portability and cost-efficiency that must be addressed for practical adoption of autonomous kernel generation.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly increased the demand for efficient accelerator kernels, but kernel development remains a highly specialized and labor-intensive task. The recent rise of LLMs and agentic frameworks offers a promising pathway toward automatic kernel generation. However, despite rapid progress, there is still no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms. We present KernelGenBench, a unified benchmark for systematically evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms. It comprises two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source), evaluating 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip), measuring performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. Our large-scale evaluation, consuming over 15 billion tokens, shows: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling methods, while cuBLAS operators are the most challenging across all methods; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with even recent kernel-specialized agents experiencing severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation remains highly cost-intensive, with specialized agent methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all reaches 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling approaches.

</details>


### [94] [Divergence Decoding: Training-Free Capability Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27248)
*Yimi Wang,Hao Li,Shuo Yang,He Cao,Dechen Zhang,Ziang Wu,Zhiyuan Yan,Fanyang Mo,Li Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Divergence Decoding is a training-free framework that fuses a generalist LLM's reasoning with a specialist model's domain knowledge by adaptively routing between them at inference time, using Jensen-Shannon divergence to detect when the specialist is likely to err.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose LLMs lack deep domain knowledge for specialized scientific tasks, while domain-specialized models suffer from degraded logical reasoning and robustness. Neither model type alone is sufficient for challenging scientific benchmarks.

Method: Divergence Decoding adapts the speculative decoding "draft-and-verify" skeleton into an adaptive routing mechanism. At each token generation step, Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) is computed between the output distributions of the specialist and generalist. When JSD exceeds a threshold — indicating the specialist's distribution diverges significantly from the generalist's — control is routed to the generalist. Otherwise, the specialist's prediction is used. This enables dynamic, inference-time policy composition without any additional training.

Result: Evaluated on GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench using Qwen and Llama model families, Divergence Decoding outperforms both the domain-specialist and generalist models individually, as well as most single-model baselines.

Conclusion: Divergence Decoding offers a general, training-free paradigm for combining distinct LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration, effectively addressing the generalist-vs-specialist trade-off.

Abstract: While large language models excel in reasoning, these generalists often lack knowledge for specialized scientific domains. Conversely, domain models~(specialists), while knowledgeable, suffer from specialization side-effects including diminished logic and reduced robustness.To address this dilemma, we introduce Divergence Decoding, a training-free framework for capability fusion. It reconstructs the "draft-and-verify" skeleton of speculative decoding into an adaptive routing mechanism. The core is using Jensen-Shannon divergence to monitor the distributional disagreement between the two models at each token. When the specialist exhibits significant divergence, our method identifies it as a potential reasoning risk and instantaneously routes control to the generalist. This allows the dynamic injection of general reasoning while preserving domain expertise, achieving inference-time policy composition of the generalist and the specialist.We evaluate Divergence Decoding across diverse model families (Qwen and Llama series) on challenging scientific benchmarks (GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench). Experimental results demonstrate that Divergence Decoding outperforms both the domain-specialized and general-purpose models, effectively surpassing the performance of most single-model baseline. This suggests that Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration.

</details>


### [95] [Beyond the Bidirectional Promise: Re-evaluating the Robustness of Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27386)
*Saurabh Yadav,Badri Narayana Patro,Vijay Srinivas Agneeswaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DLMs resist gradient-based adversarial attacks due to stochastic loss landscapes but offer no inherent defense against natural noise; they exhibit systematic overconfidence, and their fragility stems from decoder routing failure rather than encoding, meaning robustness must be built into the iterative decoding loop itself.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the promise of Diffusion Language Models for bidirectional context and iterative refinement, their reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks has not been systematically studied, creating a gap in understanding their practical deployment risks.

Method: The authors conduct a controlled, paired evaluation using two parameter-matched DLM-AR pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B; Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses to isolate architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors.

Result: DLMs resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes due to stochastic loss landscapes but fail to defend against natural noise, proving robustness is weight-dependent. DLMs display systematic overconfidence. Mechanistic probing shows all models perfectly encode input corruption, but behavioral fragility localizes to a decoder routing failure; surface-level prompt patching does not improve noisy baselines.

Conclusion: DLM robustness cannot be retrofitted via superficial patching; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop, and the identified decoder routing failure represents a critical architectural bottleneck for future DLM design.

Abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive (AR) generation by enabling bidirectional context and iterative refinement. However, their reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks remains under-explored. To address this, we systematically evaluate DLM robustness and calibration against AR baselines, using two parameter-matched pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses. This paired design effectively isolates architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors. We find a nuanced robustness profile: while highly stochastic DLM loss landscapes naturally resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes, they provide no guaranteed defense against natural noise, proving that everyday robustness is weight-dependent rather than inherently architectural. Furthermore, DLMs exhibit systematic overconfidence, presenting a practical deployment hazard. Most crucially, mechanistic probing reveals that all models perfectly encode input corruption, isolating behavioral fragility entirely to a decoder routing failure. Consistent with this diagnosis, we show that surface-level prompt patching fails to improve over noisy baselines. Ultimately, DLM robustness cannot be patched on; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop.

</details>


### [96] [Wiring diagram extraction and gluing: a case study in classifying figure skating jumps using 3D dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27598)
*Jason Lo,Mohammadnima Jafari*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hasse clustering suffers from combinatorial complexity as cluster count grows; the authors propose a theory of gluing wiring diagrams to enable iterative applications that match single-run results, and validate it on figure skating jump video classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hasse clustering extracts common sequential patterns but becomes computationally infeasible with a large number of expected clusters due to combinatorial explosion. The need is to decompose the problem into tractable, iterative steps without sacrificing correctness.

Method: The paper develops a formal theory of "gluing wiring diagrams" that enables composing multiple iterative applications of Hasse clustering. Each iteration processes a manageable subset, and the gluing mechanism ensures the composite result is equivalent to a single monolithic application of the algorithm.

Result: The proposed iterative gluing approach was empirically tested on the task of classifying figure skating jumps from video data, demonstrating that the decomposed pipeline achieves the same clustering outcome as the full single-run algorithm while remaining computationally feasible.

Conclusion: Gluing wiring diagrams provide a principled way to scale Hasse clustering via iteration, preserving exactness while circumventing combinatorial complexity, with practical utility demonstrated in video-based action recognition.

Abstract: Hasse clustering is an algorithm that extracts common patterns in sequential data and represents them in graphical forms. As the number of expected clusters grows, however, the algorithm can become infeasible to run due to combinatorial complexity. In this article, we describe a theory of gluing wiring diagrams, allowing iterative applications of Hasse clustering to achieve the same result as a single application. We test our theory in the context of classifying videos of figure skating jumps.

</details>


### [97] [HealthCAT: An Interpretable Encoder-only Transformer Framework for Health Indicator Prediction and Temporal Interpretation of Wearable Sensor Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27635)
*Xiaotong Yu,Joshua Y. Kim,HaeJin Lee,Kalina Yacef*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HealthCAT is a Transformer-based framework that combines an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token to produce class-specific, time-step-level interpretations of wearable sensor data, outperforming baselines by up to 17% in F1-score while enabling interpretable behavioural pattern analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep learning methods for wearable sensor data prioritize predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their utility in health research where understanding when and how physical activity patterns occur is critical for monitoring, analysis, and intervention design.

Method: HealthCAT integrates an Encoder-only Transformer architecture with a novel Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate class-specific, time-step-level interpretations. These interpretations are mapped onto domain-relevant behavioural cycles (e.g., time-of-day). Evaluated on two real-world wearable sensor datasets with 306 total participants, using masking experiments to validate the predictive informativeness of identified time steps.

Result: HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17% in F1-score and 12% in accuracy (p&lt;0.05). Masking experiments confirmed that time steps identified by HealthCAT carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all conditions (p&lt;0.05).

Conclusion: HealthCAT enables accurate health indicator prediction from wearable data while providing validated interpretability at the time-step level, moving beyond aggregated summary measures toward temporal pattern analysis that supports health monitoring, behavioural analysis, and intervention design.

Abstract: Wearable sensors continuously capture fine-grained multivariate time-series data, providing opportunities to model behavioural patterns associated with health outcomes. However, existing deep learning methods prioritise predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their application in health research. In this study, we present HealthCAT, a flexible framework that integrates an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate class-specific, time-step-level interpretations. These interpretations can be mapped back onto behavioural cycles that are relevant to the domain (e.g., time-of-day), supporting individual-level analysis of wearable sensor data. We evaluated HealthCAT using two real-world wearable sensor datasets (306 participants in total). HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17\% in F1-score and 12\% in accuracy on both datasets ($p<0.05$). In masking experiments, the time steps identified by HealthCAT carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all masking conditions ($p<0.05$), indicating that the identified time steps are predictively informative. By coupling predictive performance with validated time-step-level interpretability, HealthCAT moves wearable sensor analysis beyond aggregated metrics towards temporal patterns that support health monitoring, behavioural pattern analysis, and intervention design in health research. The significance of this work is that it enables accurate prediction of health indicators from wearable sensor data while providing insights into when and how physical activity patterns occur, rather than relying solely on aggregated summary measures.

</details>


### [98] [Albilich: Steerable Proof-State Orchestration for LLM-Based Mathematical Research with CAS Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27705)
*Ting Gong,Michael Ruofan Zeng,Yong Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Albilich is an open-source agentic framework for AI-assisted mathematical research that integrates long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems, literature retrieval, and persistent context management. It achieved strong results on the RealMath benchmark and contributed genuine mathematical advances on open problems from the Kourovka Notebook.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs show promise in mathematical reasoning, long-horizon proof attempts remain difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. Existing approaches lack integrated tool use, persistent context, and human steerability needed for scalable mathematical research.

Method: Albilich combines: (1) long-horizon reasoning with an agentic harness, (2) computer algebra system (CAS) integration for symbolic computation, (3) literature retrieval for knowledge grounding, and (4) persistent SQLite-based context management for reproducibility. An advisor agent guides proof synthesis. Evaluated on RealMath benchmark and Kourovka Notebook open problems with ablation studies on CAS and advisor agent.

Result: On RealMath: 10/10 solved with CAS, 9/10 without CAS. On Kourovka: produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and proved a strengthening of Problem 20.2. Ablations: CAS reduced token usage by 32.0% on Problem 17.91; removing the advisor agent increased verifier rejection rate and prevented proof route synthesis on Problem 21.142.

Conclusion: Albilich demonstrates that a human-steerable, CAS-boosted agentic environment can support scalable AI-assisted mathematical research, enabling genuine contributions to open problems while improving efficiency and reliability.

Abstract: Large language models can contribute useful ideas to mathematical research, yet long-horizon proof attempts remain difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. We present Albilich, an open-source agentic harness for autoresearch in mathematics that combines long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems (CAS), literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management.
  We evaluate Albilich on the RealMath benchmark (Zhang et al. 2025) and on open problems in group theory from the Kourovka Notebook (Khukhro and Mazurov 2026). It solved 10/10 problems on RealMath with CAS and 9/10 with no CAS. On the Kourovka problems, Albilich produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof of a strengthening of Problem20.2. Anablation on Problem 17.91 demonstrates 32.0% token reduction when CAS is enabled. An ablation on Problem 21.142 demonstrates higher verifier-rejection rate and failure to synthesize proof routes in the absence of the advisor agent. These results support Albilich as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research.

</details>


### [99] [STEREODISCO: Discovering Stereotypicality in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27824)
*Farane Jalali Farahani,Corina Dima,Mojtaba Nayyeri,Raphael H. Heiberger,Steffen Staab*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: STEREODISCO is a framework that systematically identifies stereotypical semantic axes in LLM internal representations by adapting the semantic differential method. Using ~2,000 WordNet antonym pairs and probing techniques, the authors discover that LLAMA-3-8B and MISTRAL-7B agree more with each other on social group stereotypes than with human ratings, and uncover novel stereotypical axes (e.g., humble–proud, narrow-minded–broad-minded, cowardly–brave) not previously studied.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior computational stereotype research is limited to a small set of semantic axes from social psychology and operates on word embeddings rather than internal model representations. It remains unclear which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations in LLMs and how these axes are internally represented.

Method: STEREODISCO adapts Osgood's semantic differential method by: (1) constructing ~2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets; (2) recovering each axis as a geometric direction in an LLM's activation space using probing classifiers; and (3) applying a statistical test over concept projections to identify axes that carry stereotypical associations with social groups.

Result: When applied to LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT, STEREODISCO reveals that the two LLMs agree more with each other on social group stereotype ratings than with human judgments, indicating divergence from human-documented stereotypes. The framework also identifies novel stereotypical axes — humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave — which were independently validated by human annotators.

Conclusion: LLM-internal stereotype representations extend well beyond the axes traditionally studied in social psychology, and LLMs exhibit their own distinct stereotype profile that diverges from human patterns. STEREODISCO provides a scalable, systematic method for auditing and discovering stereotypical content encoded in LLM representations.

Abstract: LLMs encode, convey, and perpetuate stereotypes. Prior computational research focuses on a small set of semantic axes investigated in social psychology, and operates on word embeddings produced by language models, leaving open which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations in LLMs and how LLMs internally represent such axes. We introduce STEREODISCO, a framework that adapts the semantic differential method (Osgood et al., 1957) to the systematic study of stereotypes in LLM internal representations. STEREODISCO constructs approx. 2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space via probing, and identifies stereotypical axes via a statistical test over concept projections. As a case study, we apply STEREODISCO to social group stereotypes with LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT. We find that the two LLMs agree with each other on social group ratings more than with humans, suggesting that LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from that documented in social psychology. We also discover stereotypical axes not investigated in prior work -- including humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave, which human annotators independently confirm.

</details>


### [100] [Dynamic Spectral Filtering for Temporal Graph Learning: Learning Evolving Propagation Operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27891)
*Yan Kong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DSF proposes evolving the graph propagation mechanism itself over time by treating Chebyshev polynomial filter coefficients as recurrent temporal states, achieving strong link-prediction performance with drastically reduced parameters, GPU memory, and training time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Temporal graph learning typically focuses on evolving node states or encoding interaction histories. The authors identify an underexplored question: should the graph propagation operator itself evolve temporally, and can this be done efficiently?

Method: Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF) represents propagation at each snapshot t via a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. These compact multi-order coefficients are treated as recurrent temporal states, updated by a recurrent branch with multiplicative global and order-specific gates. Critically, the temporal state size is independent of node count.

Result: On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link prediction, DSF achieves AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860 with 93K–133K parameters, 68–182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6–2.1 s/epoch. Versus DEFT, DSF uses 8.3–8.6× fewer parameters, 25–33× less GPU memory, and 5–19× less time per epoch, while outperforming on MOOC, matching Reddit (within 0.001 AP), and trailing modestly on Wikipedia. Against all alternatives, DSF uses 3.3–38.6× less GPU memory.

Conclusion: Direct evolution of the spectral response — rather than node states or interaction histories — constitutes a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a primary concern.

Abstract: Temporal graph learning is commonly organized around the evolution of node states or the encoding of interaction histories. We study an underexplored, operator-centric question: should the graph propagation mechanism itself evolve over time? We introduce Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF), which represents propagation at snapshot t by a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. DSF explicitly treats these compact multi-order coefficients as recurrent temporal states. A recurrent branch proposes updates, while multiplicative global and order-specific gates regulate their magnitude. The temporal state is independent of the number of nodes. On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, converged DSF runs attain AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860, respectively, with 93K to 133K trainable parameters, 68 to 182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6 to 2.1 seconds of training per epoch. Against the closely related DEFT baseline, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, and modestly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3 to 8.6 times fewer parameters, 25 to 33 times less GPU memory, and 5 to 19 times less time per epoch. Relative to all measured alternatives, it uses 3.3 to 38.6 times less GPU memory. These results support direct spectral-response evolution as a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a first-class requirement.

</details>


### [101] [Echoverse: Deep, Evolving Environments for Training Computer-Use Agents at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28074)
*Yash Pandya,Sahil Gupta,Sarthak Harne,Archana Yadav,Kavyansh Chourasia,Hussein Mozannar,Vibhav Vineet,Sara Abdali,Corby Rosset,Yash Lara,Ahmed Awadallah,Ece Kamar,Akshay Nambi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Echoverse is a system that generates stateful, database-backed synthetic environments for training computer-use agents, coupled with a co-evolution loop that repairs environments and trains models simultaneously. A 9B model trained on just 12 Echoverse environments nearly matches a frontier model, revealing that environment depth, failure-targeted interaction, and co-improvement are the key drivers of agent performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training computer-use agents requires interactive applications, but real-world apps are login-gated and stateful — making them impractical for training. Existing synthetic environment pipelines generate environments in bulk, but the bottleneck has shifted from quantity to quality. The authors argue that three underexplored properties determine training utility: behavioral depth, targeting of actual agent failures, and whether environments co-evolve with the model.

Method: Echoverse compiles specifications into stateful applications with tasks graded against each app's own database. It introduces a co-evolution loop that reads every graded rollout twice: first as repairs to the environment, its tasks, and its verifier; second as training signal for the model. The system supports both supervised and reinforcement learning, with a reward that combines a grounded verifier and a dense per-step judge.

Result: A 9B model trained on 12 Echoverse environments improved from 36.5% to 67.1% across 14 evaluation splits, within 14 points of the frontier model that taught it. Deep environments lifted live-site accuracy (80.0→85.0, 48.0→65.0) while shallow ones hurt it (80.0→75.0). Drilling one interface control across renderings transferred to held-out widgets and the open web. Repairing a single environment lifted model performance from 16.2% to 38.5%. RL with the combined reward raised held-out score from 58.8% to 68.0%.

Conclusion: Environment quality — specifically depth, failure targeting, and co-evolution — matters more than quantity for training computer-use agents. Echoverse demonstrates that a small number of well-designed, self-repairing synthetic environments can push a modestly sized model to near-frontier performance, with transfer to real web settings.

Abstract: Computer-use agents learn from what their actions change, so training one needs applications it can act on, break and reset. The applications that matter most are login-gated and stateful, so synthetic environments stand in for them. Recent pipelines generate such environments in bulk, which moves the bottleneck from how many exist to what is inside each one. The returns, we find, come from three properties: how much behavioural depth an environment carries, whether it targets the interaction an agent actually fails, and whether it improves alongside the model. We present Echoverse, which compiles specifications into stateful applications whose tasks are graded against the application's own database, and a co-evolution loop that reads every graded rollout twice: as repairs to the environment, its tasks and its verifier, and as training signal for the model. Trained on twelve such environments, a 9B model improves from $36.5\%$ to $67.1\%$ across fourteen evaluation splits, within fourteen points of the much larger frontier model that taught it. We examine each property in turn. On the same domains, shallow environments push live-site accuracy below the base model ($80.0 \to 75.0$) while deep ones raise it ($80.0 \to 85.0$ and $48.0 \to 65.0$); drilling one interface control across many renderings transfers to held-out widget families and to the open web; and repairing a single environment lifts the model trained on it from $16.2\%$ to $38.5\%$. The same worlds serve as reinforcement-learning environments, where a reward combining the grounded verifier with a dense per-step judge raises held-out score from $58.8\%$ to $68.0\%$. We release four environments as a benchmark, with their applications, seed data and grounded graders. Code: https://aka.ms/echoverse

</details>


### [102] [Group-Reflective Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28076)
*Binbin Zheng,Zijun Xie,Guanqun Zhao,Enlei Gong,Xing Ma,Xiaoliang Fu,Zeyu Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GRSD proposes a self-distillation method for LLM agents that derives turn-level guidance by contrasting reflections on successful vs. failed rollouts within an on-policy group, outperforming existing baselines across multiple agentic environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Terminal rewards in RLVR provide only coarse trajectory-level supervision, entangling successful behaviors, mistakes, and incidental choices. Existing self-distillation methods rely on externally retrieved skills or single-trajectory extraction by stronger models, which may mismatch the policy's current capability or remain path-specific.

Method: GRSD works in three stages: (1) For each prompt, the policy generates a group of on-policy rollouts and reflects on each verified trajectory; (2) A stop-gradient snapshot contrasts reflections from successful vs. failed rollouts to produce group-level privileged guidance that is capability-aligned and outcome-discriminative; (3) A self-teacher uses this guidance to refine turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving the verifier-determined learning direction.

Result: GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines across multiple agentic environments and model scales, and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.

Conclusion: GRSD effectively addresses the coarse supervision problem in RLVR by deriving fine-grained, capability-aligned guidance from the policy's own experiences, leading to stronger performance and better generalization.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is effective for training large language model agents. However, terminal rewards provide only coarse trajectory-level supervision, leaving successful behaviors, recurring mistakes, and incidental choices entangled in the same outcome signal. Existing agentic self-distillation methods enrich sparse supervision with natural-language skills, but skills retrieved externally or extracted from a single trajectory by stronger models may mismatch current experience, exceed the policy's capability, or remain path-specific. We propose Group-Reflective Self-Distillation (GRSD), which derives capability-aligned and outcome-discriminative guidance from the policy's own verified rollouts. For each prompt, the policy reflects on each verified trajectory in an on-policy group, and a stop-gradient snapshot contrasts the resulting reflections from successful and failed rollouts to construct group-level privileged guidance. Conditioned on this guidance, a self-teacher refines turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving the verifier-determined learning direction. Experiments across multiple agentic environments and model scales demonstrate that GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.

</details>


### [103] [QuantWAMs: Calibrating at the Right Granularity for World Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28405)
*Jiacheng Zhou,Jinfan Lv,Ruixuan Li,Longtai Zhang,Yan Wang,Wenqiang Zhang,Lizhe Qi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: QuantWAMs is a post-training quantization framework tailored for World Action Models that co-predict future video and actions. It introduces three techniques—shared-basis outlier calibration, co-training-objective saliency, and fixed-intervention rollout auditing—to align quantization with the model's structure, rollout distribution, and task objective, achieving near-lossless W4A4 quantization with significant memory and speed improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World Action Models (WAMs) suffer from costly iterative denoising and closed-loop deployment. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods fail for WAMs because they assume open-loop objectives, homogeneous model architectures, and calibration distributions mismatched to the actual deployment setting.

Method: QuantWAMs proposes three strategies: (1) Shared-basis outlier calibration, which pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules; (2) Co-training-objective saliency, computing empirical-Fisher scores from the joint video-action gradient to assign weight precision at calibration-stable layer granularity; (3) Fixed-intervention rollout auditing, which revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without altering the precision budget.

Result: Under a W4A4-dominant setting, QuantWAMs achieves simulation accuracy within 0.2–0.7 percentage points of FP16 on Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot tasks. Peak weight-and-activation memory drops to ~29% of FP16, with 1.4–1.6× block-level speedups. Real-robot trials on an AgiBot G2 confirm deployment feasibility across three manipulation tasks.

Conclusion: QuantWAMs demonstrates that context-aligned PTQ—accounting for model structure, rollout distribution, and task objectives—enables efficient, near-lossless deployment of World Action Models, making them viable for resource-constrained real-world robotic manipulation.

Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and actions, but their iterative denoising and closed-loop execution make efficient deployment costly. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods are poorly suited to WAMs because they rely on open-loop objectives, homogeneous model assumptions, and calibration distributions that do not reflect deployment. We present QuantWAMs, a PTQ framework that aligns quantization decisions with the calibration context defined by model structure, rollout distribution, and task objective. QuantWAMs introduces three strategies: shared-basis outlier calibration, which pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules; co-training-objective saliency, which computes empirical-Fisher scores from the joint video--action gradient and assigns weight precision at a calibration-stable layer granularity; and fixed-intervention rollout auditing, which revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without changing the precision budget. We evaluate QuantWAMs on Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot manipulation with an AgiBot G2. Under a W4A4-dominant setting, the reported simulation means differ from FP16 by 0.2--0.7 percentage points. Real-robot trials further establish deployment feasibility on three manipulation tasks. For the targeted video and action blocks, QuantWAMs reduces peak weight-and-activation memory to about 29\% of FP16 and provides 1.4--1.6$\times$ block-level speedups.

</details>


### [104] [SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28488)
*Yunhao Liang,Xianqi Cao,Pujun Zhang,Yuan Qu,Yongzhi Qi,Ningxuan Kang,Max Z. J. Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCOPE is a composite policy model that unifies supply-chain replenishment decisions—assortment, sourcing, frequency, and routing—into a single end-to-end framework using tokenized entity representations and shared operational context, outperforming decoupled approaches on real data from Dingdong and JD.com.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern supply chains fragment replenishment decisions (assortment selection, source assignment, replenishment frequency, delivery routing) across separate departments and optimization systems. These decisions are operationally coupled—earlier choices cascade through downstream stages—but isolated optimization leads to stockouts, excess inventory, and unnecessary transportation costs. The authors aim to bridge this gap with a unified framework.

Method: SCOPE (Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination) models supply-chain entities as tokens and contextualizes them via a shared operational representation. Each token type maps to a corresponding decision interface, with each decision building on the partial plan from earlier stages. The completed plan is evaluated through a shared system-level utility. The framework is instantiated for urban fresh-retail replenishment, capturing interactions among service frequency, assortment, capacity pressure, and road-network routing.

Result: Evaluated on real operational data from Dingdong and JD.com—two large-scale supply chains at different replenishment echelons—SCOPE consistently outperforms both stage-wise optimization methods and practice-oriented baselines commonly used in supply-chain operations.

Conclusion: Learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings yields more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions than optimizing each decision stage in isolation. SCOPE demonstrates that AI-driven unified operational planning is feasible and beneficial in real-world supply-chain settings.

Abstract: Can supply-chain AI move beyond isolated decision modules toward unified operational planning? A complete replenishment plan specifies which products each location carries, which upstream facility supplies it, how often it is replenished, and how deliveries are routed. These decisions are operationally coupled: the selected assortment changes the demand and load passed to later stages; source assignment and replenishment frequency reshape the delivery requests; and route feasibility and cost, in turn, determine the system value of the earlier choices. Yet in modern supply chains, these decisions are often handled by separate departments and optimized through separate systems, which can lead to stockouts, inventory exposure, and avoidable transportation. We propose SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination, a composite policy model that represents supply-chain entities as tokens, contextualizes them through a shared operational representation, and maps each token type to the corresponding decision interface. Each decision builds on the partial plan formed by earlier decisions while the completed plan is evaluated using a shared system-level utility. We instantiate this framework in urban fresh-retail replenishment, where service frequency, assortment, capacity pressure, and road-network routing interact strongly, and evaluate it on real operational data from Dingdong and JD.com, two large-scale supply chains operating at different replenishment echelons. Across both settings, SCOPE consistently outperforms methods that optimize each decision stage separately, as well as practice-oriented baselines commonly used in supply-chain operations. These results show that learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings lead to more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions.

</details>

### [105] [FAVA: Formal Authorization for Verified Agents with Evidence-Backed Permission Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27267)
*Yifan Zhang,Xinkui Zhao,Sai Liu,Hengxuan Lou,Guanjie Cheng,Chang Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: FAVA introduces a permission-carrying authorization framework for LLM agents that translates natural-language tasks into structured constraints via a Permission IR, builds an evidence-backed permission graph, and uses an SMT solver to formally verify actions against security policies at runtime, achieving 90.5% Decision Compliance Rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static tool-level permissions are inadequate for LLM agents operating in dynamic environments where safety depends on evolving runtime states and data flows. Safe authorization is inherently context-dependent, requiring a formal, verifiable mechanism that can adapt to changing conditions.

Method: FAVA employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) an LLM-guided Permission Intermediate Representation (IR) that translates ambiguous natural-language tasks into structured constraints; (2) a deterministic lowering pass converting the IR into an evidence-backed permission graph tracking data flows, dependencies, and contextual labels; (3) an SMT-based authorizer that mathematically verifies the graph against security policies before any effectful action, with a runtime gateway enforcing the solver's result and providing precise counterexamples on interception.

Result: FAVA achieved a 90.5% Decision Compliance Rate (DCR) across an aggregate dataset comprising OpenAgentSafety, OctoBench, and ActPlane scenarios, successfully intercepting dynamic violating traces in trace-conditioned evaluations.

Conclusion: FAVA demonstrates that formal methods (SMT-based verification) combined with LLM-guided permission representation can effectively enforce context-dependent authorization for autonomous agents, providing rigorous security guarantees beyond static permission models.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents autonomously interleave semantic reasoning with complex system operations. In these dynamic environments, static tool-level permissions are fundamentally insufficient; safe authorization is highly context-dependent and heavily reliant on evolving runtime states and data flows. We present FAVA (Formal Authorization for Verified Agents), a permission-carrying authorization framework for agent execution. FAVA utilizes an LLM-guided Permission Intermediate Representation (IR) to translate ambiguous natural-language tasks into structured constraints. A deterministic lowering pass then converts this IR into an evidence-backed permission graph that explicitly tracks data flows, dependencies, and contextual labels. To provide strict security guarantees, a Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) authorizer mathematically verifies the current graph against security policies before any effectful action executes. A runtime gateway then enforces the solver's result, either authorizing the execution or intercepting it with a precise counterexample. We evaluate FAVA across OpenAgentSafety, OctoBench, and ActPlane scenarios. Our evaluation demonstrates that FAVA achieves a 90.5% Decision Compliance Rate (DCR) over the aggregate dataset, successfully intercepting dynamic violating traces in the evaluated trace-conditioned scenarios.

</details>


### [106] [Open Security Benchmark: Towards Autonomous Enterprise Cyber Defense](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27288)
*Gal Engelberg,Michael Arenzon,Leon Goldberg*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: OSB introduces a benchmark framework for evaluating agentic AI in autonomous cyber defense, addressing the "environment data gap" by providing a frozen, holistic enterprise security environment with closed-form ground truth for trustworthy posture investigation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As enterprises adopt agentic AI for security posture management, a critical unresolved question is whether such agents can be *trusted*. Existing evaluation is impossible because real enterprise environments are private, cross-vendor, correlated, and not publicly available as queryable targets — a problem the authors term the "environment data gap."

Method: OSB surfaces a curated, frozen enterprise security environment (immutable snapshot with anchored ground truth). It evaluates posture investigation across two modalities: text-to-SQL over a relational snapshot, and native API calls against a served instance. The framework has five components: a data layer, a task/evaluation-set layer, a multi-dimensional scoring layer, a minimal auditable harness, and a bring-your-own path enabling both public comparison and private tenant evaluation.

Result: The framework is instantiated with two identity-security packs and synthetic-organization datasets at multiple scales. It demonstrates extensibility to additional posture subdomains, investigation modalities, and defense stages from assessment toward remediation.

Conclusion: OSB provides the first shared, reproducible benchmark substrate for evaluating the trustworthiness of agentic AI in enterprise security posture management, bridging the environment data gap and enabling rigorous comparison across approaches.

Abstract: Enterprises are moving toward autonomous cyber defense: agentic AI that builds situational awareness of an organization's security state and reasons from it to assessments, decisions, and actions. This rests on a holistic view of the enterprise's security state, the continuous, cross-vendor picture of identities, cloud and infrastructure, data, applications, and their configurations that security posture management assembles. As agents take on this work, what matters is not whether an agent can produce an answer but whether it should be trusted to. The field cannot yet answer this question. Real enterprise environments are private, cross-vendor, and deeply correlated, and none is exposed publicly as a shared, queryable target for evaluating such agents end to end. We call this the environment data gap. We present Open Security Benchmark (OSB), a framework that benchmarks agentic AI on this work. OSB surfaces a curated enterprise environment - a frozen, holistic view of the security state - and evaluates posture investigation across two modalities: text-to-SQL over a relational snapshot and each vendor's native API over a served instance of the same environment. Freezing the environment pins the target state as an immutable snapshot and anchors answers to a closed-form ground truth. OSB is built from five components: a data layer, a task and evaluation-set layer, a multi-dimensional scoring layer, a minimal auditable harness, and a bring-your-own path that serves public comparison and private tenant evaluation from one substrate. We instantiate the framework with two identity-security packs and a family of synthetic-organization environment datasets spanning multiple scales, and chart its extension to further posture subdomains, investigation modalities, and defense stages from assessment toward remediation.

</details>


### [107] [RoguePrompt: Dual-Layer Encoding for Self-Reconstruction to Circumvent LLM Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27373)
*Benyamin Tafreshian,Prathamesh Dhake*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: RoguePrompt is a jailbreak pipeline that uses nested Vigenère and ROT13 encodings with reconstruction instructions to bypass LLM safety filters. Tested on 313 hard-rejected prompts under a black-box threat model, it achieved 93.93% filter bypass, 79.02% instruction reconstruction, and 70.18% execution rates, providing stage-level failure analysis for multistage prompt-transformation attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on cipher-based and encoding-based LLM jailbreaks collapses multiple stages—moderation bypass, instruction recovery, and execution—into a single aggregate success metric, obscuring where attacks actually fail. The authors aim to provide granular, stage-level evidence of failure points in multistage prompt-transformation attacks under realistic black-box conditions.

Method: RoguePrompt partitions a forbidden prompt and applies two nested encodings: Vigenère cipher followed by ROT13, accompanied by natural-language reconstruction instructions that guide the model to decode and reassemble the original request. The pipeline was tested under a black-box threat model (API or UI access only) against 313 real-world prompts that had previously been hard-rejected by LLM safeguards. Automated criteria were used to independently assess success at each stage: moderation bypass, instruction reconstruction, and final execution.

Result: RoguePrompt achieved 93.93% filter bypass rate, 79.02% reconstruction rate, and 70.18% execution rate, demonstrating a significant drop-off across stages. This stage-level decomposition reveals that reconstruction—not filter evasion—is the primary bottleneck in multistage encoding-based jailbreaks.

Conclusion: Layered prompt encoding remains highly effective for bypassing LLM safety filters, but the substantial gap between bypass and execution highlights the importance of evaluating jailbreak attacks per stage rather than as a monolithic outcome. The findings underscore that current moderation systems are vulnerable to nested cipher attacks, and stage-level evaluation frameworks provide more actionable insight for both attackers and defenders.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly integrated into mainstream development platforms and daily technological workflows, typically behind moderation and safety controls. Despite these controls, preventing prompt-based policy evasion remains challenging, and adversaries continue to "jailbreak" LLMs by crafting prompts that circumvent implemented safety mechanisms. Prior work has established cipher-mediated interaction, code-embedded decryption, prompt decomposition and reconstruction, and layered custom encryption as viable attack primitives. However, reported evaluations generally collapse visible acceptance, successful recovery of the concealed request, and subsequent execution into an aggregate attack-success outcome. This leaves limited evidence about where multistage prompt-transformation attacks fail within an observable black-box interaction. This paper introduces RoguePrompt, a jailbreak pipeline that partitions a forbidden prompt and applies two nested encodings, Vigenere followed by ROT13, along with natural-language reconstruction instructions. RoguePrompt was developed and evaluated under a black-box threat model, with only API or user-interface access to the hosted models, and was tested on 313 real-world, hard-rejected prompts. Success was measured in terms of moderation bypass, instruction reconstruction, and execution when the relevant stage exceeded its automated criterion. RoguePrompt achieved average rates of 93.93% for filter bypass, 79.02% for reconstruction, and 70.18% for execution. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of layered prompt encoding while providing stage-level evidence of where multistage jailbreaks fail during moderation bypass, instruction reconstruction, and execution.

</details>


### [108] [Low-Latency Bootstrapping for CKKS using Roots of Unity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27401)
*Jean-Sebastien Coron,Robin Koestler*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SPRU bootstrapping embeds the additive group modulo q into complex roots of unity for native CKKS evaluation, reducing multiplicative depth, enabling smaller ring dimensions, and achieving up to 5x latency reduction for small-slot ciphertexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Original CKKS bootstrapping relies on polynomial approximation of modular reduction, which is computationally expensive and requires high multiplicative depth. The authors aim to find a more efficient bootstrapping method by exploiting native CKKS operations over complex numbers.

Method: Instead of homomorphically evaluating a polynomial that approximates modular reduction modulo q, SPRU bootstrapping directly embeds the additive group modulo q into the complex roots of unity. This embedding allows modular reduction to be evaluated natively within the CKKS scheme's complex arithmetic framework, avoiding deep polynomial approximations.

Result: Using the OpenFHE C++ library, SPRU bootstrapping achieves up to a 5x reduction in latency for ciphertexts with a small number of slots, and enables the use of smaller ring dimensions due to reduced multiplicative depth requirements.

Conclusion: SPRU bootstrapping is a more efficient CKKS bootstrapping algorithm that leverages the native complex structure of the scheme, offering significant practical speedups particularly for sparse or low-slot-count ciphertexts.

Abstract: We introduce Sparse Roots of Unity (SPRU) bootstrapping, a new bootstrapping algorithm for the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme for approximate arithmetic. The original CKKS bootstrapping method relies on homomorphically evaluating a polynomial that approximates modular reduction modulo q. In contrast, SPRU bootstrapping directly embeds the additive group modulo q into the complex roots of unity, which can be evaluated natively in the CKKS scheme. This approach significantly reduces the multiplicative depth required for bootstrapping, enabling the use of a smaller ring dimension and improving efficiency. In practice, using the OpenFHE C++ library, SPRU bootstrapping achieves up to a 5x reduction in latency when applied to ciphertexts with a small number of slots.

</details>


### [109] [Granite: A Modular Methodology for Foundational Verification of Hardware-Software Leakage Contracts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27480)
*Stella Lau,Andres Erbsen,Adam Chlipala*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Granite introduces a modular verification methodology for proving both functional correctness and nonleakage of pipelined RTL processors against ISA leakage contracts, using leakage-aware refinement via determinism. It eliminates all intermediate specifications from the TCB, yielding a single Coq theorem about cycle-by-cycle confidentiality of hardware-software cryptographic implementations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Processors are vulnerable to timing side channels that leak secrets through microarchitectural timing variations. Existing formal verification approaches either address functional correctness or information-flow security in isolation, but not both modularly at the RTL level with respect to ISA-level leakage contracts. The work aims to bridge this gap and eliminate intermediate specifications from the trusted computing base.

Method: Granite employs leakage-aware refinement via determinism: it establishes correctness and confidentiality together as trace equivalence with respect to a family of cycle-level, deterministic specification machines. Secret-independent nondeterminism (e.g., variable-latency submodules) is handled by existentially parameterizing specs with untrusted deterministic functions that operate solely on public data. Submodules are verified against their own leakage-aware specs, and these proofs compose modularly into a whole-design guarantee. The proofs further compose with a certified static analysis for cryptographic-constant-time code to produce a single Rocq/Coq theorem.

Result: The methodology proves that for a pipelined RISC design with speculation, precise interrupts, and I/O, cycle-by-cycle timing depends only on observables specified in an ISA leakage contract. For programs adhering to cryptographic-constant-time discipline, this rules out information leakage through all known and unknown timing side channels. The approach is the first to achieve a modular, foundational connection between ISA-level leakage contracts and microarchitecture-specific, cycle-by-cycle, wire-level execution.

Conclusion: Granite demonstrates that modular, end-to-end verification of both functional correctness and timing-side-channel confidentiality is feasible for realistic pipelined processors. By composing hardware proofs with certified software analysis, the work eliminates every intermediate specification — including the ISA contract — from the TCB, yielding a single theorem about the full hardware-software stack's confidentiality.

Abstract: Granite is a methodology for modular verification of both functional correctness and nonleakage of RTL processors against ISA contracts. We prove that the cycle-by-cycle timing of a pipelined RISC design--with speculation, precise interrupts, and I/O--is determined solely by observables specified in an ISA leakage contract. For programs that keep observables independent of secrets (i.e., following the cryptographic-constant-time discipline), this result rules out information leakage through known and unknown timing side channels.
  Granite's specifications only constrain functional correctness and information-flow dependencies: not how many cycles an instruction takes, at which instruction an interrupt is handled, or the exact latencies of submodules such as multipliers and memory. Granite's central technique is leakage-aware refinement via determinism, which establishes correctness and confidentiality together as trace equivalence with respect to a family of cycle-level, deterministic spec machines. Secret-independent nondeterminism is handled by existentially parameterizing specs with untrusted, deterministic functions acting only on public data. Submodules are proved against their own leakage-aware specs, and these proofs compose into the whole-design guarantee--which therefore holds over a space of secure implementations.
  We believe this work is the first to achieve modular and foundational connection between instruction-set-level leakage contracts and microarchitecture-specific cycle-by-cycle execution with wire-level observations. Our proofs compose with a certified static analysis that recognizes cryptographic-constant-time code to derive a single Rocq theorem about the cycle-by-cycle confidentiality of a hardware-and-software cryptographic implementation--eliminating every intermediate specification, including the ISA contract itself, from the trusted computing base.

</details>


### [110] [Flock: Fast Proving for Batch Boolean Computations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27491)
*Benedikt Bünz,Ron D. Rothblum,William Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Flock is a hash-based SNARK that achieves extremely fast proving of batched Boolean computations (e.g., SHA-256, Keccak, BLAKE3). On a single M4 Max core, it proves 42k SHA-256 compressions/sec—over 9× faster than prior state-of-the-art Binius64 and 500× faster than elliptic curve-based SNARKs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Proving large batches of standard cryptographic hash evaluations (SHA-256, Keccak, BLAKE3) is a critical bottleneck for many SNARK applications. Existing solutions, whether elliptic curve-based or prior hash-based (like Binius64), impose prohibitive overhead, limiting throughput in real-world deployments requiring hash-chain proofs or Merkle path openings.

Method: Flock combines new optimizations for the lincheck and zerocheck protocols within a hash-based SNARK framework. It targets batched Boolean computations expressed as repeated instances of the same R1CS circuit with input/output relations. The implementation is co-designed with coding agents and aggressively optimized for the M4 Max processor, supporting parallelization across multiple cores.

Result: On a single M4 Max core: 82k BLAKE3 compressions/sec, 42k SHA-256 compressions/sec, and 30k Keccak permutations/sec—under 250× overhead over native execution. On 10 cores, throughput exceeds 660k BLAKE3 compressions/sec. Flock is >9× faster than Binius64 (prior SOTA) for SHA-256 proving and >500× faster than the fastest measured elliptic curve-based SNARK.

Conclusion: Flock demonstrates that hash-based SNARKs with specialized protocol optimizations (lincheck/zerocheck) and implementation co-design can achieve near-native-throughput hash proving, dramatically outperforming both prior hash-based and elliptic curve-based alternatives for batched Boolean computation workloads.

Abstract: For many applications of SNARKs, a key bottleneck is proving large batches of standard cryptographic hash evaluations, such as SHA-256, Keccak, or BLAKE3. We introduce Flock, a hash-based SNARK for extremely fast proving of such batched Boolean computations. Flock proves batches of the same R1CS circuit (plus input/output relations between them), can prove hash-chains and Merkle path openings, and in principle can be extended to full-fledged hash-based signature verification. At its core, Flock combines new optimizations for the lincheck and zerocheck protocols with an aggressively optimized proof-of-concept implementation co-designed by coding agents.
  On a single core of an M4 Max processor, Flock proves 82k evaluations of the BLAKE3 compression function, 42k SHA-256 compressions, and 30k Keccak permutations per second --- less than a $250\times$ overhead over native execution. On ten cores, throughput exceeds 660k BLAKE3 compressions per second; in proving SHA-256, Flock is more than $9\times$ faster than Binius64, the prior state of the art, and more than $500\times$ faster than the fastest elliptic curve-based SNARK we measured against.

</details>


### [111] [Send and Pretend: Exploiting Transcript Consistency Issues in End-to-End Encrypted Group Chats](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27510)
*Gabriel K. Gegenhuber,Moritz Grefner,Maximilian Günther,Matthäus Wininger,David Schmidt,Aljosha Judmayer*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper reveals that major E2EE messaging apps (Signal, WhatsApp, Threema, iMessage) fail to guarantee transcript consistency in group chats, enabling malicious participants to present different content to different recipients. Exploitation scenarios include rigging polls, social engineering, and evading moderation. The authors propose practical mitigations and UI signaling strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: E2EE messaging apps are increasingly used for sensitive group coordination (e.g., by political decision makers) and have introduced features like polls that assume all participants see identical outcomes. However, no major E2EE messenger formally guarantees transcript consistency, creating a gap between user expectations and actual security properties.

Method: The authors systematically investigate transcript consistency under a malicious-participant threat model targeting shared transcript integrity and inconsistent delivery across linked devices. They analyze protocol fallback paths, pairwise delivery channels, and implementation-specific behaviors across multiple major E2EE messengers, identifying equivocation vectors and constructing concrete exploitation scenarios.

Result: Multiple equivocation vectors were identified across all examined messengers, enabling selective omission, reordering, or alteration of content per recipient without UI warnings. Exploitation scenarios include poll rigging, social engineering, and moderation evasion. Additional privacy-leaking implementation behaviors (e.g., device OS fingerprinting) were also uncovered.

Conclusion: Current E2EE messengers lack transcript consistency guarantees, leaving group chats vulnerable to insider equivocation attacks. The authors contextualize findings within prior research and propose practical, low-overhead mitigations and UI signaling strategies compatible with state-of-the-art E2EE group protocols.

Abstract: End-to-end encrypted (E2EE) messaging apps are widely praised for their security and thus also used for sensitive coordination in group chats (e.g., by political decision makers).
