After Threema and WhatsApp, also Signal and iMessage have recently introduced polls to aid agreement processes in groups. This implicitly sets the expectation that all participants see the same outcome and thus have the same view of the conversation. This property is commonly referred to as transcript consistency (TC). In this work, we demonstrate that today's major E2EE messengers do not guarantee any form of TC for group chats, allowing a malicious group member to selectively omit, reorder, or present altered content to different recipients without triggering warnings in their user interface. We systematically investigate the extent of the problem under a malicious-participant threat model that targets the integrity of the shared transcript, or inconsistent delivery across a user's linked devices. We identify multiple equivocation vectors that range from protocol fallback paths to deliberate use of pairwise delivery channels within groups. We demonstrate concrete exploitation scenarios such as social engineering, evading moderation, and, in particular, rigging polls. Beyond these cross-service design issues, we also uncover implementation-specific behaviors with privacy implications (e.g., device OS fingerprinting). Finally, we contextualize our findings within prior transcript-consistency research and outline practical low-overhead mitigations and UI signaling strategies that can be integrated into state-of-the-art E2EE group protocols.

</details>


### [112] [ThreatForest: Multi-Agent Attack Tree Generation with Pluggable TTP Framework Mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27528)
*Cristian Leo,Anton Dykyi,Danny Cortegaca,Daniel Begimher,Prakash Jha*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: ThreatForest is a multi-agent system that automates threat modeling from source code by generating TTP-mapped attack trees with mitigations. Evaluated across 7 domains, it achieves 0.63-0.68 quality scores on threat statements, attack trees, and mitigations, but only 0.29 on TTP mapping due to an embedding encoder bottleneck — not the multi-agent architecture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual threat modeling for cloud-native architectures is slow and requires scarce security expertise. Existing approaches lack end-to-end automation from code to structured, framework-mapped threat artifacts with evidence-based mitigations, creating a need for scalable, automated threat analysis pipelines.

Method: ThreatForest implements a multi-stage agent pipeline: repository analysis → context refinement → threat generation → parallel attack-tree construction with TTP mapping and mitigation synthesis → report generation. It is orchestrated as a directed graph with deterministic verification gates, bounded retries, and three human-in-the-loop validation points. A domain-specific sentence-transformer performs TTP mapping via cosine similarity against pluggable frameworks (MITRE ATT&CK, CAPEC, cloud-specific matrices). Evaluation uses a sixteen-dimension rubric scored by independent LLM raters with adversarial verification and expert review.

Result: Panel-measured quality reaches 0.63–0.68 (0–1 scale) for threat statements, attack trees, and mitigations across seven application domains. TTP mapping scores only 0.29 — a gap stable across all domains. A controlled single-call baseline on the same model more than doubles mapping defensibility, confirming the embedding encoder as the dominant accuracy bottleneck rather than the multi-agent architecture.

Conclusion: ThreatForest demonstrates the first end-to-end system converting code repositories into TTP-mapped attack trees with evidence-based mitigations across multiple adversary frameworks. The embedding stage is the binding constraint on accuracy, not the multi-agent design. The system provides a reusable benchmarking framework for future threat modeling automation research.

Abstract: Threat modeling is essential for secure software development, yet manual analysis of cloud-native architectures is slow and demands scarce security expertise. We present ThreatForest, a multi-agent system that generates structured attack trees from source code repositories, maps attack steps to adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) from a pluggable set of frameworks (MITRE ATT&CK, CAPEC, and cloud-specific threat matrices), and synthesizes actionable mitigations. ThreatForest decomposes threat modeling into a multi-stage agent pipeline -- repository analysis, context refinement, threat generation, parallel attack-tree construction with TTP mapping and mitigation synthesis, and report generation -- orchestrated as a directed graph with deterministic verification gates, bounded retries, and three human-in-the-loop validation points. A domain-specific sentence-transformer maps each attack step to candidate techniques by cosine similarity; we show empirically that this embedding stage, not the surrounding pipeline, is the dominant accuracy bottleneck. We evaluate ThreatForest across seven application domains on a sixteen-dimension rubric, scored by a panel of independent LLM raters with an adversarial verification pass and expert review. Panel-measured quality reaches 0.63-0.68 (on a 0-1 scale) for threat statements, attack trees, and mitigations, but only 0.29 for embedding-only TTP mapping -- a gap stable across all seven domains that isolates the binding constraint. A controlled single-call baseline on the same model more than doubles mapping defensibility, pinning the limitation on the embedding encoder rather than the multi-agent design. To our knowledge, ThreatForest is the first end-to-end system that turns a code repository into TTP-mapped attack trees with evidence-based mitigations across adversary frameworks, with a reusable framework for benchmarking such systems.

</details>


### [113] [AnchorMark: Robust Diffusion Watermarking via Latent-Space Rotation Synchrony](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27551)
*Yuqi Qian,Yun Cao,Haocheng Fu,Haochen Zhao,Hong Zhang,Meineng Zhu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: AnchorMark is a training-free, inversion-based watermarking method that exploits a newly discovered "Rotation Synchrony" property—where image-domain and latent-space rotations share the same angle—to embed a synchronization anchor enabling robust rotation correction, significantly improving bit accuracy under rotation and compound attacks with minimal image quality degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing inversion-based watermarking methods are vulnerable to compound lossy post-processing, especially rotation, which disrupts the spatial correspondence needed for latent-space decoding. A robust solution is needed that can handle rotation without sacrificing visual fidelity or requiring additional training.

Method: The authors introduce AnchorMark, which leverages the "Rotation Synchrony" property: rotations applied in the image domain correspond to rotations of the same angle in the recovered initial latent. AnchorMark embeds a synchronization anchor in the central region of the initial latent; during extraction, this anchor allows accurate estimation and correction of the rotation angle before watermark decoding.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that AnchorMark substantially improves bit accuracy under both pure rotation and combined lossy post-processing attacks, while incurring only limited impact on image quality.

Conclusion: AnchorMark effectively addresses the vulnerability of inversion-based watermarking to rotation attacks by exploiting the Rotation Synchrony property, offering a training-free, robust solution that maintains high visual fidelity.

Abstract: Inversion-based watermarking embeds watermark payloads directly into the generative process, avoiding a separate post-hoc image-domain embedding stage while preserving the native visual fidelity of synthesized images. However, existing methods remain vulnerable to compound lossy post-processing, particularly when rotation is involved, as it disrupts the spatial correspondence required for latent-space decoding. To overcome this limitation, we introduce AnchorMark, a training-free, robust inversion-based watermarking. We uncover a latent-space property termed Rotation Synchrony: image-domain rotations and their counterparts in the recovered initial latent share the same angle. Building on this property, AnchorMark embeds a synchronization anchor in the central region of the initial latent, enabling accurate estimation and correction of the rotation angle during extraction. Experiments show that AnchorMark substantially improves bit accuracy under rotation and combined attacks, with limited impact on image quality.

</details>


### [114] [Revisiting the Adversarial Robustness of Graph-Based Traffic Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27604)
*Qingzhao Zhang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Conventional graph-based traffic forecasting robustness research relies on unrealistic threat models (norm-bounded, untargeted attacks). This paper introduces a practical targeted adversary—limited model knowledge, few-sensor manipulation, localized link/route attacks causing plausible congestion—and reframes defense as a physics-informed detection problem. The proposed detector-hardened forecaster outperforms adversarial training across 13 of 15 model–dataset settings, especially against held-out attacks, with minimal clean-data degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior robustness evaluations in graph-based traffic forecasting assume unrealistic threat models (full model access, unbounded perturbations, untargeted objectives). Real-world attackers have limited knowledge, access to few sensors, and localized goals (e.g., misleading estimated arrival times or causing unnecessary rerouting on specific routes). Existing defenses, particularly adversarial training tuned for norm-bounded attacks, fail against structurally different, physics-aware attacks that mimic genuine congestion. This gap motivates both a re-examination of threat modeling and a new defense paradigm.

Method: The authors propose a targeted, physics-aware adversarial attack constrained by limited model knowledge and sparse sensor manipulation, designed to induce localized congestion-like effects on specific links/routes while leaving broader network metrics largely unchanged. For defense, they reframe robustness as a detection problem: a learned physics-informed detector inspects inputs and produces a signal fed as an additional input feature to a hardened forecaster. The forecaster is kept fixed while the detector is trained against adaptive attacks. Evaluation spans multiple model architectures and benchmark datasets.

Result: The physics-aware targeted attack multiplies error on targeted links several-fold while network-wide error remains nearly unchanged, confirming stealth. Adversarial training (tuned for norm-bounded perturbations) provides negligible defense against this attack. The proposed detection–mitigation defense improves over adversarial training in 13 of 15 model–dataset combinations, with the largest margin on a held-out (unseen) attack, and incurs near-zero cost on clean data.

Conclusion: Security evaluations of AI-based traffic forecasting must incorporate application-specific constraints—limited model access, sparse sensor manipulation, and localized, physics-consistent objectives—to yield meaningful robustness assessments. Detection-based mitigation, leveraging physics-informed signals, offers a more effective defense paradigm than standard adversarial training when attacks deviate from norm-bounded assumptions.

Abstract: Traffic forecasting by graph-based AI is a critical component of intelligent transportation systems, motivating security research on robustness to malicious sensor readings. We argue that prior robustness evaluations are largely shaped by unrealistic threat models and untargeted objectives, so both attacks and defenses must be revisited. We study a practical adversary with limited model knowledge and the ability to monitor and manipulate only a few road sensors. More importantly, practical attacks can be localized to specific links or routes, causing incorrect estimated arrival times or unnecessary rerouting while leaving the broader network largely unaffected. This targeted setting remains underexplored, and defenses such as adversarial training do not transfer well from the norm-bounded attacks they train on to structurally different, physics-aware attacks that mimic genuine congestion. We therefore reframe robustness as a detection problem, introducing a learned physics-informed detector whose output is fed to a hardened forecaster as an input feature and trained against adaptive attacks with the forecaster fixed. We evaluate across a variety of model architectures and benchmarks. The physics-aware attack multiplies target-link error several-fold while the network-wide error barely moves, and adversarial training, tuned to norm-bounded perturbations, barely dents it. Our detection--mitigation defense improves even on adversarial training hardened against the physics-aware attack itself, on $13$ of $15$ model--dataset settings and by the widest margin on a held-out attack, at near-zero clean cost. The results emphasize the need to examine abstracted AI adversarial attacks under application-specific constraints to assess their true security impacts.

</details>


### [115] [Strategy Phasing of Cyber Attacks on Digital Substations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27661)
*Akila Herath,Chen-Ching Liu,Junho Hong,Kuchan Park*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SubCASP uses Hidden Markov Models fused with IDS logs to infer current and next attack phases and reconstruct attack paths in IEC 61850 digital substations, demonstrating robustness under varying IDS observability and missing data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing IDSs for IEC 61850 substations flag isolated symptoms but lack contextual understanding of the multi-phase attack strategy, hindering effective mitigation deployment. There is a need to infer the broader attack phase and attack path from IDS alerts.

Method: The paper proposes SubCASP, an HMM-based method that fuses IDS data logs. Attack phases are defined via ATT&amp;CK-based threat modeling. The HMM infers the current attack phase, predicts the next phase, and reconstructs the retrospective attack path. Training and evaluation use a reproducible attack-graph dataset, with tests across varying IDS observability levels and missing log scenarios.

Result: Test results demonstrate the robustness of the SubCASP model under various IDS observability levels and scenarios with missing IDS data logs.

Conclusion: SubCASP provides a context-aware, phase-level view of cyber attacks in IEC 61850 substations, enabling more informed and timely mitigation responses by fusing IDS logs within an HMM framework grounded in ATT&amp;CK threat modeling.

Abstract: Digital substations that comply with IEC 61850 have improved the operational efficiency of modern power systems. However, adversaries can abuse IEC 61850 communication to manipulate circuit breaker operations in substations, which can result in severe system impacts. These cyber attacks are crafted based on broader multi-phase strategies. The existing intrusion detection systems (IDSs) often flag only isolated symptoms. Thus, there is a lack of context in the attack phase to support the deployment of mitigation measures. This paper proposes Substation Cyber Attack Strategy Phasing (SubCASP), a Hidden Markov Model(HMM)- based method that fuses IDS data logs to infer the current attack phase, next attack phase, and retrospective attack path. The attack phases are derived from an ATT&CK-based threat modeling. The SubCASP model is trained and evaluated on a reproducible attack-graph dataset. Test results are presented to demonstrate the robustness of SubCASP for various IDS observability levels and missing IDS data logs scenarios.

</details>


### [116] [Distributed Point Functions and Function Secret Sharing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27696)
*Elette Boyle,Niv Gilboa,Yuval Ishai,Peter Scholl*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A survey of distributed point functions (DPFs) — a cryptographic primitive for compressed secret sharing of point functions — covering definitions, constructions, applications, and the generalization to function secret sharing (FSS).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DPFs offer a lightweight, communication-efficient way to secretly share weight-1 vectors, enabling numerous privacy-preserving protocols. The paper aims to provide a comprehensive survey of this fundamental primitive and its broader generalization.

Method: This is a survey article that reviews existing definitions, constructions, and applications of DPFs, and discusses the extension from DPFs to function secret sharing (FSS) schemes that support richer function classes.

Result: The survey catalogs how DPFs enable applications such as private information retrieval (PIR), anonymous messaging, secure computation with preprocessing, and pseudorandom correlation generators (PCGs). It also highlights that efficient FSS schemes extend these applications to more general function classes.

Conclusion: DPFs are a versatile, lightweight cryptographic building block with broad practical impact. Generalizing DPFs to FSS further amplifies their applicability across secure computation and privacy-preserving systems.

Abstract: A distributed point function (DPF) is a cryptographic primitive that enables compressed additive sharing of a secret weight-1 vector (equivalently, a point function) across two or more parties. The appealing lightweight structure of DPF constructions has enabled a wide range of applications. These include private information retrieval, anonymous messaging, secure computation with preprocessing, and pseudorandom correlation generators for expanding small correlated seeds into large pseudorandom instances of cryptographic correlations.
  In this article, we survey definitions, constructions, and applications of DPFs. We also discuss the extension of DPF to function secret sharing (FSS), which generalizes point functions to support richer function classes. Efficient FSS schemes yield a similar generalization for most of the applications of DPFs.

</details>


### [117] [CHARGE: Leveraging CWE Hierarchies for Hardware Security SystemVerilog Assertion Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27776)
*Xiao Tan,Cynthia Sturton*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: CHARGE is an automated framework that uses CWEs and LLMs to generate security properties for unverified RTL modules without trusted specs. It detects 27/42 known bugs across Hack@DAC benchmarks, with 89% of generated SVAs running in formal verification and 92.2% being non-vacuous. It also found a previously unknown bug.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual generation of security properties for hardware RTL modules is labor-intensive and requires trusted design specifications. There is a need for automated, specification-free property generation to scale hardware security verification, especially for detecting bugs in unverified third-party IP.

Method: CHARGE identifies security-critical assets in unverified RTL by reasoning over the hierarchical structure of CWE entries using LLMs (GPT-4.1). It infers expected security behaviors from identified assets and CWE semantics, then automatically generates SystemVerilog Assertions (SVAs) capturing these security properties—all without relying on a trusted design specification.

Result: Evaluated on Hack@DAC18/19/21 open-source SoCs: CHARGE detects 27 of 42 known bugs. On OpenPiton (Hack@DAC21), 89% of generated SVAs run in Cadence JasperGold FPV, 92.2% are non-vacuous. CHARGE correctly writes properties for three bugs where manually written properties were incorrect, and discovers a previously unidentified bug in OpenPiton.

Conclusion: CHARGE demonstrates that LLM-driven reasoning over CWE hierarchies can effectively automate security property generation for unverified RTL, matching or exceeding manual property quality while reducing engineering effort and eliminating dependence on trusted specifications.

Abstract: This paper presents CHARGE, an automated framework for generating security properties for unverified RTL modules using CWEs and large language models (LLMs). The hallmark is a reasoning process that leverages the hierarchical nature of CWE entries to improve accuracy when identifying security-critical assets in unverified RTL modules. As a result, the approach can infer expected security behaviors and generate properties from identified assets and CWE semantics, avoiding the need for trusted design specifications and reducing manual engineering effort. We evaluate the framework on the Hack@DAC18, 19, and 21 open source SoC designs using OpenAI's GPT-4.1. CHARGE detects 27 of 42 known bugs in these designs. For Hack@DAC21 OpenPiton SoC, 89% of the generated SVAs run in Cadence JasperGold FPV, and 92.2% are non-vacuous. We compare to an open-source, manually written set of properties for these designs and find that CHARGE correctly writes properties for three bugs in which the manually written properties were incorrect. In addition, CHARGE-generated properties identify a new bug in the Hack@DAC21 OpenPiton SoC that was not previously identified.

</details>


### [118] [Adaptive Security at the Edge for 6G-Enabled Healthcare IoT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27858)
*Ijaz Ahmad,Ijaz Ahmad,Erkki Harjula*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: NANOEDGEGUARD is a kernel-plane rate controller for healthcare IoT edge gateways that uses in-kernel traffic-control hooks to enforce multi-tier rate policies, reducing alarm latency and excess burst traffic compared to user-space or no-enforcement baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Healthcare IoT edge gateways must simultaneously handle routine telemetry and rare, time-critical alarms. Even short traffic bursts can inflate worst-case delay and interfere with urgent messages, yet existing solutions (static firewall rules, user-space control loops) lack the speed, adaptability, and auditability needed for this domain.

Method: NANOEDGEGUARD is a kernel-plane closed-loop controller that monitors per-source traffic intensity and enforces a multi-tier rate policy via in-kernel traffic-control hooks. It prioritizes fast actuation, explicit recovery through hysteresis, and records policy transitions for auditability. Evaluation uses a Raspberry Pi gateway with an MQTT broker and two ESP32 endpoints generating vitals, alarms, and timed bursts.

Result: Compared to a user-space firewall baseline, adaptive kernel-plane rate control reduces 99th-percentile alarm RTT by 13.3% while maintaining no-enforcement-level RTT. It also reduces excess admitted burst traffic by 46% compared to no enforcement.

Conclusion: Adaptive, auditable enforcement at the edge gateway improves resilience for healthcare IoT and can be extended toward on-demand policy deployment in future edge intelligence systems.

Abstract: Healthcare IoT services increasingly rely on edge gateways to relay routine telemetry and deliver rare but timecritical alarms. Even short traffic bursts can inflate worstcase delay and interfere with urgent messages. We present NANOEDGEGUARD, a kernel-plane closed-loop controller that observes per-source traffic intensity at the edge and enforces an auditable, multi-tier rate policy using in-kernel traffic-control hooks. Unlike static firewall rules or user-space control loops, our design prioritizes fast actuation and explicit recovery through hysteresis, and it records policy transitions for auditability. Using a Raspberry Pi gateway hosting an MQTT broker and two ESP32 endpoints generating vitals, alarms, and a timed burst, we show that adaptive kernel-plane rate control reduces the 99th-percentile alarm RTT by 13.3% compared to a user-space firewall baseline while maintaining no-enforcement-level RTT, and it reduces excess admitted burst traffic by 46% compared to no enforcement. These early results indicate that adaptive, auditable enforcement at the gateway can improve resilience for healthcare IoT, and it can be extended toward on-demand policy deployment in future edge intelligence.

</details>


### [119] [Don't Trust the AI Ecosystem: Analyzing Privacy Leakage in Compromised Open-Source Components](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27886)
*Jin-Seong Kim,Han-Ju Lee,Seok-Won Hong,Takeshi Takahashi,Chansu Han,Tomohiro Morikawa,Seok-Hwan Choi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: GradLock is a training-time injection attack that embeds private data directly into model parameters using stateless deterministic indexing and dynamic gradient locking, enabling near-lossless, instant extraction of private data from the final model without requiring access to the training environment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing model inversion attacks are post-training methods limited by the target model's generalization bottleneck, recovering only generic features rather than specific identities on high-dimensional data. The authors aim to overcome this by injecting data during training within a compromised supply chain, achieving pixel-perfect reconstruction.

Method: GradLock operates in two phases: (1) **Stateless deterministic indexing** establishes isolated data vaults within model parameters, mapping private data to specific parameter subsets without maintaining state. (2) **Dynamic gradient locking** prevents payload degradation during optimization by locking the gradients of vault parameters, ensuring injected data survives training. Extraction requires only the final model and the deterministic index, with no training environment access needed.

Result: On MNIST, Imagenette, and CelebA, GradLock achieves near-lossless reconstruction (SSIM ~1.0) and instant extraction under 1 second. It demonstrates superior robustness against quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning compared to prior training-time injection methods. A user study shows 93.3% of participants failed to detect the malicious logic.

Conclusion: GradLock exposes a critical blind spot in AI supply chain security: training-time data injection can be both highly effective and stealthy, surviving standard deployment optimizations while remaining undetectable to most practitioners.

Abstract: Existing model inversion (MI) attacks predominantly rely on post-training optimization to recover private data from model outputs. However, these methods are fundamentally constrained by the target model's generalization bottleneck, often yielding generic features rather than specific identities, particularly on high-dimensional datasets. In this paper, we introduce GradLock, a novel training-time injection attack that stealthily injects sensitive training data directly into the model parameters. Operating within a compromised supply chain context, GradLock leverages stateless deterministic indexing to establish isolated data vaults and employs dynamic gradient locking to prevent payload degradation during the optimization process. This mechanism allows the adversary to extract pixel-perfect data from the final model without retaining access to the training environment. Extensive experiments on MNIST, Imagenette, and CelebA demonstrate that GradLock achieves near-lossless reconstruction (SSIM ~ 1.0) and instant extraction (< 1.0s). Compared to existing training-time injection methods, our approach exhibits superior robustness against standard deployment optimizations, including quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning. Furthermore, a user deployment study reveals that 93.3% of participants failed to detect the malicious logic, highlighting a severe blind spot in the security of modern AI supply chains.

</details>


### [120] [Benign on Label, Malicious by Design: Clean-Label Dormant-to-Activated Backdoor via Machine Unlearning with Removable Camouflage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27936)
*Dongdong Zhao,Can Li,Xiang Yao,Fan He,Qihang Ge,Baogang Song*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a clean-label backdoor attack where the backdoor remains dormant after training and only activates after specific training samples are unlearned, achieving low pre-unlearning attack success rates and high post-unlearning activation through a dual-generator bilevel optimization framework that coordinates persistent latent associations with removable suppression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing backdoor attacks are effective immediately after implantation, risking exposure before exploitation. Unlearning-activated dormant backdoors aim to mitigate this by staying inactive post-training and activating only after data unlearning. However, current methods fail to simultaneously achieve low pre-unlearning attack success rates and strong post-unlearning activation under clean-label constraints and realistic unlearning requests.

Method: The authors propose a clean-label unlearning-activated backdoor framework using dual-generator learning, formulated as a bilevel optimization problem. The framework alternately learns: (1) sample-specific triggers that establish a latent trigger-to-target association, and (2) label-consistent camouflage samples that provide removable suppression. When a small subset of camouflage samples is unlearned, suppression is lifted and the dormant backdoor activates.

Result: Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-10 demonstrate that the proposed method achieves lower pre-unlearning attack success rates and stronger post-unlearning activation across multiple unlearning algorithms compared to representative backdoor baselines.

Conclusion: Reliable dormancy-to-activation transitions can be achieved by coordinating a persistent latent association with removable suppression under clean-label and realistic deletion constraints.

Abstract: Existing backdoor attacks often become effective immediately after backdoor implantation and may therefore be exposed before exploitation. Machine unlearning activated dormant backdoors mitigate such behavioral exposure by remaining inactive after training and becoming effective only after selected training records are unlearned. However, existing methods struggle to simultaneously achieve a low pre-unlearning attack success rate and strong post-unlearning activation under clean-label constraints and realistic unlearning requests. Achieving this transition requires jointly establishing a persistent latent association and a removable suppressive influence. To address this challenge, we propose a clean-label unlearning-activated backdoor framework based on dual-generator learning and formulate it as a bilevel optimization problem: By simulating latent backdoor establishment and machine unlearning, the framework alternately learns sample-specific triggers that establish a latent trigger-to-target association and label-consistent camouflage samples that provide removable suppression. Once a small subset of camouflage samples is unlearned, the suppression is lifted and the dormant backdoor is activated. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-10 show that our method maintains lower pre-unlearning attack success rates while achieving stronger post-unlearning activation across multiple unlearning algorithms than representative backdoor baselines. These results demonstrate that reliable dormancy-to-activation transitions can be achieved by coordinating a persistent latent association with removable suppression under clean-label and realistic deletion constraints.

</details>


### [121] [Safeguards Based on Copyable Context Cannot Provide Reliable Safety for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27951)
*Pingyu Wu,Lingyao Zhu,Weiming Zhang,Nenghai Yu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper identifies a fundamental limitation in LLM safeguards: since the same answer can serve both legitimate and malicious purposes, and attackers can mimic benign users, a provable worst-case floor on attacker assistance exists whenever evidence of downstream use is copyable. This yields a "safety trilemma" — Useful Capability, Reliable Safety, and Open Access cannot simultaneously hold. Trusted credentials providing hard-to-copy information about actual use can break this floor under specific conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM safeguards decide whether to respond before observing how the answer will ultimately be used. For dual-use tasks — where identical information aids both authorized professionals and attackers — this creates a fundamental vulnerability: attackers can imitate benign requests and interaction histories, making it impossible to reliably distinguish good from bad actors based solely on copyable evidence.

Method: The authors formalize the problem by separating "capability" (what the model can do) from "evidence" (observable information about downstream use). They derive the exact worst-case lower bound on attacker assistance when evidence is copyable, proving the safety trilemma. They then analyze how trusted credentials — hard-to-copy signals (e.g., verified institutional affiliation) that predict actual downstream use — can complement existing safeguards. They identify the stronger condition required to eliminate the attacker assistance floor and validate their analysis through dual-use evaluations, adaptive attacks, and deployed trusted-access program data.

Result: The analysis proves a safety trilemma: Useful Capability, Reliable Safety, and Open Access cannot coexist. When evidence is copyable, there exists an inescapable worst-case floor on how much assistance an attacker can extract. However, trusted credentials that provide hard-to-copy, use-predictive information can, under a specific stronger condition, eliminate this floor entirely. Empirical results from dual-use evaluations, adaptive attack simulations, and real-world trusted-access deployments corroborate the practical significance of these theoretical conditions.

Conclusion: Reliable safety for dual-use LLM capabilities cannot be achieved under open access with copyable evidence alone — a fundamental trilemma constrains all such systems. Incorporating hard-to-copy trusted credentials that credibly predict downstream use offers a principled path to breaking the attacker assistance floor, but only when a stronger condition (beyond mere credential verification) is satisfied, pointing to concrete design requirements for safer deployment of powerful AI systems.

Abstract: Large language model safeguards decide whether to answer before seeing how an answer will be used. This creates a basic problem for dual-use tasks: the same answer can help an authorized professional or an attacker, while an attacker can imitate a benign request and interaction history. We separate the capability released by the model from the evidence available about downstream use. When that evidence is copyable, we derive the exact worst-case floor on attacker assistance while preserving useful answers. The result yields a safety trilemma: Useful Capability, Reliable Safety, and Open Access cannot coexist. We then show how a trusted credential can complement existing safeguards by adding hard-to-copy information that predicts actual downstream use, and identify the stronger condition needed to eliminate the floor. Evidence from dual-use evaluations, adaptive attacks, and deployed trusted-access programs supports the practical relevance of these conditions.

</details>


### [122] [Driving up Inference Energy on SNNs: Per-Sample and Universal Sponge Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27990)
*Spyridon Raptis,Haralampos-G. Stratigopoulos*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are vulnerable to "sponge attacks" that inflate energy consumption by increasing spike activity. The authors introduce both per-sample and the first universal sponge attack for native event-based SNN inputs, demonstrating 1.5-2.6× and 1.09-1.24× SynOp inflation respectively across three neuromorphic datasets, with estimated energy overheads up to 13.24 mJ on Loihi-1.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SNNs are increasingly deployed in always-on, battery-powered edge systems due to their energy-efficient sparse binary spike communication. However, this efficiency advantage creates a novel attack surface: adversaries can craft inputs that deliberately maximize spike activity and synaptic operations (SynOps), draining battery life while maintaining correct outputs — thereby evading correctness-based monitoring. Prior work on SNN efficiency attacks is limited to per-sample optimization in rate-coded settings, leaving native event-based inputs and universal (reusable) perturbations unexplored.

Method: The authors study two attack models on native event-based SNN inputs. (1) A per-sample sponge attack using gradient-based optimization to craft adversarial binary spike trains for each input, maximizing SynOps while preserving predicted class. (2) The first universal sponge attack: a fixed binary perturbation mask computed offline and applied via XOR to all subsequent inputs, requiring no per-sample optimization. Experiments span three datasets (NMNIST, SHD, IBM DVS Gesture) and three SNN models. Energy impact is estimated by mapping SynOp counts to Loihi-1 neuromorphic hardware energy consumption.

Result: The per-sample attack achieves 1.5-2.6× SynOp inflation while preserving correct classification on ≥98% of samples. The universal attack yields 1.09-1.24× SynOp inflation across all datasets — weaker but more deployable. Estimated per-inference energy overheads on Loihi-1 range from 14 μJ to 13.24 mJ, demonstrating that even universal perturbations can accumulate into significant battery drain in continuously operating edge deployments.

Conclusion: Native event-based SNNs are practically vulnerable to input-space efficiency attacks. Reusable universal perturbations pose a realistic threat to battery-powered edge deployments, as their modest per-inference overhead accumulates into meaningful energy drain over continuous operation. This exposes a security blind spot in correctness-only monitoring for neuromorphic systems.

Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) communicate through sparse binary spike events rather than dense activations, enabling energy-efficient inference on neuromorphic hardware and motivating their use in always-on, battery-powered edge systems. We show that this same efficiency advantage creates a distinct security risk: sponge attacks can increase inference-time spike activity and synaptic workload, inflating energy consumption while remaining difficult to detect through correctness-based monitoring alone. Prior input-space efficiency attacks on SNNs have focused on per-sample optimization, primarily in rate-coded settings. We extend this threat to native event-based binary inputs and study two attack models. First, we develop a per-sample sponge attack that crafts a custom adversarial spike train for each input via gradient-based optimization. This attack increases per-inference SynOps by 1.5-2.6x on three SNN models for the NMNIST, SHD, and IBM DVS Gesture datasets, while preserving the predicted class on at least 98% of evaluated samples. Second, to the best of our knowledge, we introduce the first universal sponge attack for native event-based SNN inputs: a fixed binary perturbation computed offline and applied via XOR to all subsequent inputs. Although weaker, it still inflates SynOps by 1.09-1.24x across all three datasets and represents a more realistic deployment threat because it requires no per-input optimization. Mapping SynOp inflation to estimated Loihi-1 energy yields per-inference overheads from 14 $μ$J to 13.24 mJ. These results show that native event-based SNNs are vulnerable to practical input-space efficiency attacks, and that reusable universal perturbations can accumulate into meaningful battery drain in continuously deployed edge systems.

</details>


### [123] [Temporal Poisoning: Clean-Label Backdoors via Event Redistribution in SNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28075)
*Roberto Riaño,Gorka Abad,Stjepan Picek,Aitor Urbieta*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper introduces the first clean-label backdoor attack on Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) using neuromorphic event data. Unlike prior dirty-label attacks, the proposed method applies a temporal transformation only to target-class samples—preserving event counts exactly—making clean and poisoned samples indistinguishable after temporal aggregation. The attack achieves perfect ASR (1.00) across multiple datasets and architectures, while exposing that rate-collapsed defenses are blind to this threat and feature-space defenses only partially effective. A model-free detector based on per-step event mass can detect the transformations, delineating the attack's stealth boundary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing backdoor attacks on SNNs rely on dirty-label poisoning (relabeling triggered samples), which is less realistic than clean-label attacks where labels remain correct. The authors aim to demonstrate that SNNs are vulnerable to clean-label temporal backdoors that exploit the temporal dynamics unique to spiking models—a threat vector unexplored in prior work. They also seek to evaluate whether existing backdoor defenses, especially those that collapse the temporal dimension, can detect such attacks.

Method: The attack applies a fixed temporal timestamp transformation exclusively to training streams of the target class, leaving their original labels intact. Critically, the transformation preserves the per-pixel, per-polarity event count exactly, so temporally aggregated representations (rate-coded views) are identical for clean and triggered samples—only the sequential spike timing differs. The attack is evaluated on three neuromorphic datasets (N-MNIST, DVS Gesture, CIFAR10-DVS) against convolutional (SERT, VGG-based) and transformer-based (Spike-driven Transformer) SNN victims. Ablations study poison budget and trigger shape. Defenses tested include STRIP, Neural Cleanse, spectral signatures, and a proposed model-free detector based on per-step event mass.

Result: The clean-label temporal backdoor achieves an Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 1.00 in its strongest configurations across all three datasets and both convolutional and transformer architectures. Rate-collapsed defenses (those that aggregate events into frames before inspection) are blind to the attack by construction, since clean and poisoned samples are statistically identical in the rate domain. Feature-space defenses (e.g., spectral signatures) detect the poison only in selected settings. The proposed per-step event mass detector successfully identifies the temporal transformations, highlighting both the insufficiency of rate-based defenses and the limits of the attack's stealth.

Conclusion: This is the first clean-label backdoor attack demonstrated on SNNs with neuromorphic event data, revealing a fundamental vulnerability in the temporal processing pipeline of spiking models. The findings underscore that security for neuromorphic systems must account for the temporal dimension explicitly—rate-collapsed defenses are structurally inadequate. The event-mass detector shows that temporal artifacts are detectable, but the attack's near-perfect ASR before detection implies a need for robust, temporally-aware defense mechanisms in SNN deployments.

Abstract: Backdoor attacks on Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have primarily assumed dirty-label poisoning, in which triggered training samples are relabeled to an attacker-selected class. We study clean-label temporal poisoning, where a fixed timestamp transformation is applied only to the target-class training streams, leaving their labels unchanged. The transformation preserves the per-pixel, per-polarity event count exactly, making clean and triggered samples identical after temporal aggregation while altering the sequence processed by the SNN. Across three neuromorphic datasets and both convolutional and transformer-based victims, the attack reaches an ASR of 1.00 in the strongest configurations. We analyze the attack through poison-budget and trigger-shape ablations and evaluate established backdoor defenses adapted to spiking models. Defenses that collapse the time axis before inspection are blind by construction, while feature-space methods detect the poison only in selected settings. Our model-free detector, based on per-step event mass, detects the evaluated temporal transformations, demonstrating both the limitation of rate-collapsed defenses and the boundary of the attack's stealth. To our knowledge, this is the first clean-label backdoor attack evaluated on SNNs and neuromorphic event data.

</details>


### [124] [Checking Information Flow in Cloud-based IoT Access Control Policies (Extended Version)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28088)
*Lorenzo Ceragioli,Letterio Galletta,Edoardo Lunati*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper presents IOT:POKER, a tool that formally models AWS IoT Core access control policies and uses SMT solving to detect unwanted information flow between IoT devices with different trust levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing access control verification in IoT cloud platforms (like AWS IoT Core) checks permissions in isolation, which is insufficient when devices have heterogeneous trust levels or are compartmentalized. Unwanted information flow between devices in different trust domains can lead to security vulnerabilities that go undetected by standard permission analysis.

Method: The authors formally model AWS IoT Core components (devices, topics, rules, policies) and define an information flow graph capturing permitted inter-device communication. They build a finite, symbolic representation of this graph and leverage an SMT solver to verify (or disprove) whether information can flow between designated devices. The approach is implemented in the IOT:POKER tool.

Result: The tool was evaluated on a realistic smart-home scenario and multiple real-world AWS IoT policies, demonstrating its ability to identify unwanted information flows that isolated permission checks would miss.

Conclusion: Information flow analysis of IoT access control policies reveals security vulnerabilities invisible to permission-by-permission auditing. Automated formal verification with SMT solvers provides a practical means to enforce compartmentalization and trust boundaries in IoT cloud platforms.

Abstract: Many cloud providers for IoT technologies offer access control mechanisms whose proper configuration is critical for security. However, verifying permissions in isolation is insufficient in a setting where devices have different levels of trust or are compartmentalised in various subsystems. This work analyses IoT access control policies to identify potential security vulnerabilities from unwanted information flow between devices. To this end, we formally model AWS IoT Core's components and define an information flow graph to capture the communication among devices permitted by the access control policies. We build a finite representation of the graph by leveraging an SMT solver, thus enabling the verification of information flow between devices. We implement our approach in a tool called IOT:POKER, and assess it on a realistic scenario and several real-world policies.

</details>


### [125] [Agent Harness Distillation: Inference-Time Harness Extraction and Exploitation in Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28147)
*Yu Cui,Wuli Yang,Yirui Shi,Junhao Xia,Hui Jiang,Lei Gao,Chenfu Bao*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper introduces Agent Harness Distillation (AHD), a framework that extracts inference-time harnesses from autonomous multi-agent systems (AMAS) via black-box interactions, revealing significant intellectual property leakage risks. A two-stage distillation process infers and refines harness behavior, and the authors propose a deception-based defense to mitigate extraction while preserving agent utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AMAS increasingly depend on inference-time harnesses that are costly to engineer and constitute valuable IP. While IP leakage has been studied in static multi-agent systems, it is unclear whether similar risks extend to AMAS where harness behavior emerges dynamically during inference. This gap motivates a systematic investigation of harness extraction as a novel security threat.

Method: AHD formalizes harness extraction as a security problem with an evaluation framework. It operates in two stages: (1) pre-distillation — inferring harness behaviors from target agent responses to construct an initial harness; (2) post-distillation — iterative refinement of the initial harness to align with the target agent's behavioral patterns. All extraction occurs through black-box interactions. A deception-based defense is also proposed to counter extraction.

Result: Experiments conducted on real-world AMAS across multiple backbone LLMs demonstrate that AHD effectively extracts inference-time harness capabilities, confirming substantial IP leakage risks. The proposed deception-based defense reduces extraction effectiveness while maintaining the protected agent's utility.

Conclusion: The paper uncovers a previously underexplored security threat to AMAS: the extractability of inference-time harnesses via black-box distillation. This highlights the need for defenses in dynamically orchestrated LLM-based agent systems and opens a new direction in agent security research.

Abstract: Autonomous multi-agent systems (AMAS) built on large language models (LLMs), such as Hermes, increasingly rely on inference-time harnesses to coordinate reasoning and action. Constructing these harnesses requires substantial engineering effort and computational resources, as they are iteratively optimized over a combinatorial search space while co-evolving with the underlying LLM. Inference-time harnesses therefore constitute valuable intellectual property (IP). Although prior work has investigated IP leakage in static multi-agent systems with pre-configured architectures, it remains unclear whether similar risks arise in AMAS, where harness behavior emerges dynamically during inference. To address this gap, we introduce Agent Harness Distillation (AHD), a framework for studying the security risks arising from inference-time harness extraction in AMAS. We formalize harness extraction as a new security problem and develop an evaluation framework for quantifying such risks. AHD extracts inference-time harness capabilities from a target agent through black-box interactions and consists of two stages. In the pre-distillation stage, AHD infers inference-time harness behaviors from the responses of the target agent and constructs an initial harness. In the post-distillation stage, AHD iteratively refines the initial harness to align with the behavioral patterns of the target agent. Experiments on real-world AMAS across multiple backbone LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of AHD and reveal substantial IP leakage risks. We further propose a deception-based defense that reduces harness extraction effectiveness while preserving the utility of the protected agent. Our findings uncover a previously underexplored security threat to AMAS.

</details>


### [126] [Piggybacking on Perception: Stealthy Concurrent Audio Prompt Injections against Multimodal LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28165)
*Mingxiao Liu,Yitong Li,Haoren Zhao,Yaoxiang Bian,Jianan Ma,Jian Zhang,Jialuo Chen,Xinhao Deng,Zhen Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper investigates concurrent audio prompt injection attacks on LLM-driven multimodal agents, where malicious audio instructions are imperceptibly embedded in environmental noise to hijack agent behavior. The authors construct the first comprehensive benchmark (AudioAgentSecurity), evaluate 11 state-of-the-art agents achieving 69.10% ASR against Gemini 3 Pro, and propose CADV, a defense based on source separation and consistency analysis that achieves over 90% detection success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-driven multimodal agents increasingly rely on continuous audio interaction, but audio inputs inevitably contain uncontrolled environmental noise. This creates a critical yet under-explored attack surface where malicious audio can be injected concurrently with user speech, distinct from traditional acoustic attacks on voice devices. No prior work systematically studies or benchmarks this threat.

Method: The authors propose two novel attack techniques: (1) instruction augmentation — embedding malicious instructions into environmental noise that "piggyback" onto legitimate user speech, and (2) scenario concealment — camouflaging attack intent within contextually plausible background sounds. For evaluation, they construct AudioAgentSecurity, the first benchmark with 8 real-world task scenarios and 10 attack patterns. For defense, they introduce Cascaded Audio Decoupling and Verification (CADV), which combines acoustic source separation to isolate candidate instruction signals with cross-modal consistency analysis to detect anomalous injected instructions, providing more robust detection than prompt-level defenses.

Result: The proposed attack methods achieve an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 69.10% against Gemini 3 Pro across 11 evaluated state-of-the-art agents. The CADV defense mechanism achieves over 90% detection success across diverse attack vectors. Real-world experiments on the Doubao AI Smartphone with human volunteers confirm both high attack stealth/efficacy and reliable defense mitigation in dynamic scenarios.

Conclusion: Concurrent audio prompt injection poses a significant real-world threat to multimodal LLM agents, as demonstrated by high ASR against production systems like Gemini 3 Pro. The CADV defense, leveraging source separation and cross-modal consistency, effectively mitigates these attacks. This work establishes the first systematic framework for understanding and defending against audio-based prompt injection in autonomous agent systems.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-driven multimodal agents are increasingly deployed to execute autonomous tasks via continuous audio interaction. While this paradigm enhances interaction naturalness, it introduces a critical yet under-explored attack surface, as audio inputs inevitably contain environmental noise beyond user control. In this paper, we investigate concurrent audio prompt injection attacks targeting multimodal agents. Distinct from traditional acoustic attacks on voice devices, we propose novel techniques for instruction augmentation and scenario concealment. These methods allow malicious audio instructions to imperceptibly "piggyback" onto user speech, thereby hijacking agents to execute malicious actions. To systematically quantify this threat, we construct AudioAgentSecurity, the first comprehensive benchmark for audio instruction injection attacks, encompassing 8 real-world task scenarios and 10 distinct attack patterns. We evaluate 11 state-of-the-art agents, including Gemini 3 Pro and GPT-4o-audio. Notably, our methods achieve an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 69.10\% against the advanced Gemini 3 Pro. To counter this threat, we further introduce Cascaded Audio Decoupling and Verification (CADV), a defense mechanism based on source separation and consistency analysis. Compared with existing prompt-level defenses, CADV leverages acoustic source separation and cross-modal consistency analysis to detect audio instruction injections more robustly, achieving over 90\% detection success across diverse attack vectors. Finally, real-world experiments with human volunteers on Doubao AI Smartphone in diverse dynamic real-world scenarios confirm the attacks' high stealth and efficacy, while demonstrating that our defense reliably mitigates these vulnerabilities.

</details>


### [127] [Secure Aggregation for Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning on Clinical EEG Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28191)
*Pouya Rajabi,Mohsen Toorani*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A privacy-preserving federated learning framework for clinical EEG data that uses masking-based secure aggregation, supporting both semi-honest and malicious settings, implemented in Flower and evaluated on TUH EEG data, demonstrating feasibility with varying computational and communication overhead trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard federated learning for clinical EEG data still leaks privacy through individual model updates. Stronger protection is needed that hides individual contributions from the aggregation server while remaining compatible with practical cross-silo healthcare training.

Method: A masking-based secure aggregation framework integrating graph-based communication, threshold secret sharing, dropout-resilient aggregation, local update clipping, an optional Bloom filter-based privacy-preserving record-linkage module, and auxiliary-notary verifiability. Implemented in Flower and evaluated under semi-honest, malicious, and auxiliary-notary aggregation variants on TUH EEG data.

Result: All secure variants successfully hide individual updates from the server. The semi-honest variant incurs the lowest overhead. Malicious-setting safeguards and lightweight consistency checks introduce additional computation, communication, and round-duration costs but provide stronger consistency, integrity, and verification.

Conclusion: Masking-based secure aggregation is a viable privacy mechanism for federated EEG training, with a clear trade-off: semi-honest security offers efficiency, while malicious and notary-based variants provide stronger integrity guarantees at higher cost.

Abstract: Federated learning enables multiple institutions to train shared models without exchanging raw clinical EEG data, but it does not fully prevent privacy leakage from individual model updates. This paper presents a privacy-preserving federated learning framework for clinical EEG data using masking-based secure aggregation as the core protection mechanism. The framework combines graph-based communication, threshold secret sharing, dropout-resilient aggregation, local update clipping, an optional Bloom filter-based privacy-preserving record-linkage initialization module, and auxiliary-notary-based verifiability. It supports both semi-honest and malicious aggregation settings and is implemented using the Flower federated learning framework. The secure-aggregation variants are evaluated in a simulated cross-silo healthcare setting using TUH EEG-derived data under different client configurations. Under the stated assumptions, the secure variants hide individual updates from the aggregation server. The results show that these variants remain compatible with federated model training, although malicious-setting safeguards and lightweight consistency-checking mechanisms introduce additional computation, communication, and round-duration overhead. The semi-honest variant provides the lowest overhead among the secure configurations, while malicious and auxiliary-notary variants offer stronger consistency, integrity, and lightweight verification support at higher cost.

</details>


### [128] [Security of World-Model-Based Embodied AI: A Lifecycle of Threats, Defenses, and Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28226)
*Fazhong Liu,Zhuoyan Chen,Haozhen Tan,Yan Meng,Guoxing Chen,Haojin Zhu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A survey examining security threats to world models in embodied AI across their entire lifecycle, from data construction to deployment, revealing how classical attacks take on new forms and proposing a taxonomy of threats, evaluation protocols, and defense strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models provide embodied AI with predictive capabilities for planning beyond reactive control, but this predictive layer introduces a new security boundary. Compromises can propagate from data, sensors, prompts, or feedback into physical actions. Existing security analyses treat world models as isolated components, missing lifecycle-wide vulnerabilities.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic survey tracing threats across the full world-model lifecycle: data construction, representation learning, state grounding, imagination, trajectory evaluation, execution, and long-term adaptation (memory and tools). They map classical attack families (poisoning, backdoors, adversarial examples, sensor spoofing, prompt injection, trajectory manipulation, supply-chain attacks) onto world-model-specific security properties and propose a lifecycle taxonomy with evaluation protocols and defense structuring.

Result: The survey reveals that familiar attacks take on distinct meanings when targeting world states, learned dynamics, affordance estimates, or safety costs. It identifies a key duality: world models can serve as runtime safety shields but generate predictive safety illusions when compromised or over-trusted. The work produces a lifecycle taxonomy mapping attacks to security properties, outlines evaluation protocols for safety failures, and structures defenses across provenance, robust grounding, uncertainty-aware prediction, trajectory gating, feedback auditing, and deployment assurance.

Conclusion: World-model security must be addressed as a lifecycle-spanning concern rather than a component-level one. Defenses require a multi-layered approach spanning data provenance, robust state grounding, uncertainty quantification, trajectory validation, feedback auditing, and deployment-time assurance to prevent predictive safety illusions from translating into physical harm.

Abstract: World models give embodied AI a predictive core: they compress observations into states, simulate action-conditioned futures, and enable planning beyond reactive control. This predictive layer, however, opens a new security boundary-compromise can propagate from data, sensors, prompts, or feedback into physical action. Rather than treating world models as an isolated component, this survey traces threats across their entire lifecycle-from data construction and representation learning, through state grounding and imagination, to trajectory evaluation, execution, and long-term adaptation via memory and tools. We show that familiar attack families: poisoning, backdoors, adversarial examples, sensor spoofing, prompt injection, trajectory manipulation, and supply-chain attacks take on distinct meanings when they corrupt world states, learned dynamics, affordance estimates, or safety costs. We also highlight a duality: world models can serve as runtime safety shields, yet when compromised or over-trusted they generate predictive safety illusions. The survey offers a lifecycle taxonomy, maps existing attacks to world-model security properties, outlines evaluation protocols for safety failures, and structures defenses across provenance, robust grounding, uncertainty-aware prediction, trajectory gating, feedback auditing, and deployment assurance.

</details>


### [129] [Implementing Homomorphic Encryption-Based Logic Locking in System-on-Chip Designs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28542)
*Ye Ziyang,Makoto Ikeda*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A logic locking scheme using binary Ring-LWE is implemented on a RISC-V SoC, securing privilege switching without exposing locking parameters, with ~6% hardware overhead and 2.6 µs unlock latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional logic locking methods require exposing raw locking parameters to users, creating a fundamental security vulnerability. The authors aim to eliminate this exposure by leveraging post-quantum cryptographic primitives (binary Ring-LWE) to protect critical logic paths without revealing sensitive locking parameters.

Method: The authors design and implement a logic locking scheme based on the binary Ring Learning With Errors (Ring-LWE) algorithm, integrated into a RISC-V System-on-Chip. The locking mechanism targets critical logic paths involved in the privilege switching process (user mode ↔ supervisor mode transitions). Unlike conventional methods, the scheme does not require distributing raw locking parameters to end users, as the Ring-LWE-based protocol inherently conceals them during the unlock challenge-response exchange.

Result: The locking module consumes 3,519 LUTs and 2,645 Registers, yielding an overall overhead of 6.0% (LUTs) and 6.9% (Registers) relative to the baseline RISC-V SoC. The unlock process takes approximately 2.6 µs, introducing moderate performance overhead that primarily impacts system-level operations (e.g., context switches, privilege transitions) while leaving user-level computational efficiency largely unaffected.

Conclusion: The proposed binary Ring-LWE-based logic locking scheme successfully protects critical privilege-switching paths in a RISC-V SoC without exposing raw locking parameters, achieving a favorable security-hardware overhead trade-off with only ~6–7% resource increase and minimal user-level performance degradation.

Abstract: This study presents a logic locking scheme based on the binary Ring Learning With Errors algorithm, implemented in a RISC-V System-on-Chip design. Unlike traditional logic locking methods that require providing users with raw locking parameters, the proposed approach secures critical logic paths in the privilege switching process without exposing these sensitive parameters. The implemented locking module itself consumes 3519 Look-Up Tables and 2645 Registers, leading to an overall overhead of 6.0% in Look-Up Tables and 6.9% in Registers compared to the baseline system. The unlock process requires about 2.6 us, introducing moderate performance impact, primarily affecting system-level operations while preserving user-level computational efficiency.

</details>


### [130] [Formalization of security](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28551)
*Gilles Barthe*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This chapter surveys the use of proof assistants for validating security properties across system security, language-based security, secure compilation, and cryptography, emphasizing their role in certification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Beyond functional verification, proof assistants serve dual purposes: (1) validating that designs and implementations satisfy security properties, and (2) supporting formal certification processes, which demand rigorous, machine-checkable evidence.

Method: The chapter adopts a survey-based approach, reviewing and synthesizing applications of proof assistants across four domains: system security, language-based security, secure compilation, and cryptography. It examines how proof assistants are leveraged for formal specification, mechanized verification, and construction of foundational security guarantees.

Result: The survey demonstrates that proof assistants have been successfully applied across all four domains, enabling mechanized proofs of security properties that were previously only argued informally. It highlights key case studies, tools, and frameworks within each domain.

Conclusion: Proof assistants are increasingly indispensable for high-assurance security verification and certification. Their application across diverse security domains shows growing maturity, though challenges remain in scalability, automation, and usability for non-experts.

Abstract: Proof assistants are often used to validate that designs and implementations meet their expected security properties. A further motivation for using proof assistants is to support certification. This chapter focuses on their applications to system security, language-based security, secure compilation, and cryptography.

</details>
