### [131] [Digital Harf: A Clinically Integrated Multimodal AI System for Pervasive Arabic Speech and Language Therapy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27212)
*Asif Azad,Mohammad Sadat Hossain,MD Sadik Hossain Shanto,Sabri Boughorbel,Abdulrhman Aljouie,Bdour Alwuqaysi,Yahya Bokhari,Ayah Othman Sindi,Ehsan Hoque*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Digital Harf is a multimodal AI platform delivering home-based speech and language therapy for Arabic-speaking children with Autism Spectrum Disorder, featuring an Agentic Synthetic Data Engine that auto-generates culturally relevant therapy content with 90.1% clinical acceptance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Arabic-speaking children with ASD face three compounding barriers: (1) a critical shortage of qualified speech-language pathologists, (2) limited service access beyond urban centers, and (3) a near-total absence of culturally grounded digital therapy materials. Existing digital therapy tools are overwhelmingly designed for Western languages and cultural contexts, making them unsuitable for Arabic-speaking populations without extensive adaptation.

Method: The authors built Digital Harf, a pervasive multimodal AI platform with three integrated therapeutic modules (language therapy, speech intelligibility, picture description) within an adaptive, performance-sensitive workflow. The core innovation is the Agentic Synthetic Data Engine (ASDE), which employs AI agents guided by explicit therapeutic and cultural criteria to automatically generate culturally relevant images, prompts, and language tasks. Validation involved expert evaluation by 13 licensed Speech-Language Pathologists who assessed clinical acceptance and cultural/linguistic alignment.

Result: ASDE-generated content achieved a 90.1% clinical acceptance rate without any manual curation or selection. The full platform received strong ratings for cultural and linguistic alignment across all modules from the 13 licensed SLP evaluators.

Conclusion: AI-driven therapeutic systems can be purpose-built for underrepresented linguistic settings by treating cultural grounding as foundational infrastructure rather than a post-hoc adaptation. Digital Harf demonstrates the feasibility and clinical validity of such an approach for Arabic-speaking children with ASD.

Abstract: Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder in Arabic-speaking countries face compounded barriers to effective speech and language therapy: a shortage of qualified specialists, limited service reach beyond urban centers, and a near-total absence of culturally grounded digital therapy materials. We present Digital Harf, a pervasive, multimodal AI platform that extends clinician-led speech and language therapy into the home. The system integrates three therapeutic modules - language therapy, speech intelligibility, and picture description - within a unified workflow that adapts to each child's performance over time. To address the critical shortage of Arabic therapy content, we introduce an Agentic Synthetic Data Engine (ASDE) that automatically generates culturally relevant images, prompts, and language tasks guided by explicit therapeutic and cultural criteria. Expert evaluation with 13 licensed Speech-Language Pathologists yielded a 90.1% clinical acceptance rate for ASDE-generated content without any manual curation or selection, and strong ratings for cultural and linguistic alignment across the full platform. Digital Harf demonstrates that AI-driven therapeutic systems can be built from the ground up for underrepresented linguistic settings, treating cultural grounding as core infrastructure rather than an adaptation afterthought.

</details>


### [132] [Evaluating the Vergence-Accommodation Conflict in Gaze-Based 3D Target Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27369)
*Mohammad Raihanul Bashar,Mohammadreza Amini,Aunnoy K Mutasim,Mayra Donaji Barrera Machuca,Wolfgang Stuerzlinger,Anil Ufuk Batmaz*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper investigates how the vergence-accommodation conflict (VAC) in head-mounted displays affects gaze-based 3D target selection performance, finding that increased visual depth significantly degrades performance and that a Variation in Diopter Fitts' law model captures this relationship better than a linear model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current HMDs suffer from VAC, which affects eye-movement behavior and potentially gaze-based interaction. Despite gaze-based selection being common in VR/AR, no prior work had systematically examined how VAC influences gaze-based pointing performance across varying depth conditions.

Method: The authors conducted an experiment measuring user performance in gaze-based 3D target selection across multiple depth conditions, then compared the fit of a standard linear Fitts' law model against a Variation in Diopter Fitts' law model to capture the performance changes attributable to VAC.

Result: As visual depth increases, user performance in gaze-based selection significantly decreases. The Variation in Diopter Fitts' law model captured this depth-dependent performance degradation better than a linear model, confirming that VAC negatively impacts gaze-based pointing.

Conclusion: Gaze-based pointing is demonstrably negatively affected by the VAC, and designers of gaze-based interaction in 3D environments must account for depth-dependent factors. The diopter-based Fitts' law variant offers a more accurate predictive model for performance in such settings.

Abstract: State-of-the-art head-mounted displays (HMDs) enable gaze-based selection in virtual environments. Yet, these HMDs suffer from the vergence-accommodation conflict (VAC), which is known to affect interaction performance. The VAC might influence gaze-based selection performance because it directly affects eye-movement behavior. Thus, in this paper, we investigate how the VAC influences gaze-based 3D target selection across varying depth conditions. Our results show that as the (visual) depth increases, user performance significantly decreases with gaze-based selection. Moreover, a previously suggested Variation in Diopter Fitts' law model captured this performance change better relative to a linear model. These findings provide evidence that gaze-based pointing is negatively affected by the VAC and highlight the importance of accounting for depth-dependent factors when designing gaze-based interaction in 3D environments.

</details>


### [133] [DP-LENS: A Density-Aware Polyfocal Lens with Topology-Driven Auto-Routing for Occlusion Management in Immersive 3D Analytics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27697)
*Nieyu Cao,Xian Wang,Lik-Hang Lee*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: DP-LENS is a density-aware polyfocal fisheye lens with topology-driven auto-routing and LLM-based voice control for exploring heavily occluded 3D datasets in VR. Two user studies (N=34) demonstrate significant reductions in cognitive load, improved task efficiency, and higher user preference compared to standard baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Exploring complex 3D volumetric datasets in immersive environments is challenging due to heavy occlusion and high cognitive load. Existing techniques like World-in-Miniature and volumetric slicing inadequately address these issues, motivating a new approach that preserves peripheral context while enabling efficient, low-fatigue macro-navigation.

Method: DP-LENS combines: (1) a density-aware polyfocal fisheye lens that deforms geometry and applies 3D perspective techniques to preserve peripheral context; (2) a topology-driven auto-routing algorithm for hands-free macro-navigation; and (3) a Large Language Model (LLM) for supplementary voice-based target selection. Two user studies were conducted: Study 1 (N=18) compared manual DP-LENS against World-in-Miniature and volumetric slicing; Study 2 (N=16) compared auto-routing (voice-initiated) against fully manual DP-LENS.

Result: Study 1: DP-LENS significantly reduced cognitive load, decreased task completion time, and improved user preference over both baselines. Study 2: The topology-driven auto-routing system improved task efficiency, further reduced cognitive load, and garnered higher user preference. Auto-routing also partially decoupled exploration efficiency from data's physical dimensions and mitigated physical fatigue.

Conclusion: DP-LENS with auto-routing and LLM voice control offers a more scalable, low-fatigue interaction paradigm for 3D visual analytics in VR. The authors propose design implications for future spatially scalable and low-fatigue immersive visualization systems.

Abstract: Immersive environments, e.g., virtual reality (VR), offer a unique approach to exploring complex 3D datasets, where data is often heavily occluded and exploration incurs a high cognitive load. We propose DP-LENS, a density-aware polyfocal fisheye lens equipped with topology-driven auto-routing. While preserving peripheral context through geometric deformation and 3D perspective techniques, it enables users to explore 3D data with a lower cognitive load. To facilitate hands-free macro-navigation, we integrate a Large Language Model (LLM) to serve as a supplementary voice-based target selection tool that initiates the auto-routing algorithm. Two user studies with 34 participants investigate the potential benefits of this system. Our first study (N=18) compared the manual DP-LENS against two industry-standard baselines (i.e., World-in-Miniature and volumetric slicing) in heavily occluded 3D datasets. The results show that DP-LENS significantly reduced cognitive load, decreased completion time, and improved user preference. The second study (N=16) compared the topology-driven auto-routing system (initiated via voice commands) with a fully manual DP-LENS. The results show that the auto-routing system improved task efficiency, further reduced cognitive load, and garnered higher user preference. Furthermore, the auto-routing partially decoupled exploration efficiency from the physical dimensions of the data and mitigated physical fatigue to some extent. Based on the findings, we proposed design implications to inform the development of more spatially scalable and low-fatigue interactions for future 3D visual analytics systems.

</details>


### [134] [Creative Task Cards for Reflection, Self-Efficiency and Self-Regulation in CS1 Introductory Programming: Initial Insights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27863)
*Corey Ford,Yinmiao Li,Rosa Van Koningsbruggen*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Creative task cards were introduced to help introductory programming students develop self-regulation and metacognitive skills. A study with 29 students showed that breaks (especially with peers), drawing for reflection, and task decomposition helped students manage emotional challenges like low interest and self-belief.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Introductory CS students face emotional challenges (low sustained interest, lack of self-belief) but are typically taught only disciplinary strategies (e.g., debugging) rather than metacognitive or self-regulation strategies that could address these affective barriers.

Method: The authors designed creative task cards supporting reflection, self-efficacy, and self-regulation. Twenty-nine students used them during a mock in-class coding assignment, followed by surveys and focus groups for qualitative evaluation.

Result: Three key qualitative findings: (1) students valued taking breaks, especially leaving the classroom to reflect with peers; (2) drawing helped students reflect on feelings of cognitive overload; (3) breaking work into smaller steps increased students' perceived capability to progress.

Conclusion: Explicitly scaffolding metacognitive and self-regulation strategies through creative task cards shows promise for helping novice programmers manage the emotional and cognitive demands of programming assignments.

Abstract: Computer Science students in introductory programming courses struggle with emotional challenges such as low levels of sustained interest and a lack of self-belief. However, students are typically introduced to disciplinary strategies (such as debugging strategies) and not the metacognitive nor self-regulation strategies that could help them overcome such emotional challenges. This paper addresses this issue by introducing creative task cards designed to support students' reflection, self-efficacy, and self-regulation in programming assignments. To evaluate the cards, twenty-nine students used them to complete a mock coding assignment in-class and participated in surveys and focus groups. Our initial qualitative insights suggest that students: found value in taking breaks, particularly when they could leave the classroom to reflect with peers; could use drawing to better reflect on feelings of cognitive overload; and felt more capable progressing with their work once breaking it into smaller steps.

</details>


### [135] [VizPilot: Automated Onboarding for SVG-based Composite Visualizations using Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27938)
*Nishaanthini Gnanavel,Yong Wang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: VizPilot is an automated system that reverse-engineers composite visualizations using MLLMs to generate interactive onboarding experiences, reducing authoring effort and cognitive load for novice users.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Composite visualizations are intrinsically complex, imposing high initial cognitive load on novice users. Existing onboarding approaches are platform-dependent, labor-intensive to author, and fail to handle the structural complexity of composite visualizations, limiting their general applicability.

Method: VizPilot comprises two modules: (1) a Composite Visualization Analyzer that uses a two-stage MLLM pipeline to decompose visualizations into components, extract structured explanations, and map them to precise SVG elements; and (2) an Onboarding Interface (browser extension) supporting guided scrollytelling and free exploration. It requires only a brief description and optional source code from the developer.

Result: Evaluation via comparative input modality analysis, a usage scenario, and a user study shows that VizPilot effectively automates onboarding authoring while improving usability and accessibility of composite visualizations.

Conclusion: VizPilot demonstrates that MLLM-driven reverse engineering of visualization structures can automate onboarding content creation, significantly reducing authoring effort and alleviating cognitive load for users encountering complex composite visualizations.

Abstract: Composite visualizations integrate multiple visualizations to represent complex datasets effectively, but their intrinsic composite designs often impose a high initial cognitive load on novice users. Existing visualization onboarding approaches are typically platform-dependent, require substantial manual authoring effort, and struggle with the structural complexity of composite visualizations, limiting their general applicability. We present VizPilot, an automated visualization onboarding approach that reverse-engineers composite visualization structure to generate interactive onboarding experiences directly from raw visualization artifacts. VizPilot consists of two modules: a Composite Visualization Analyzer and an Onboarding Interface. Leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), the Analyzer employs a two-stage pipeline that decomposes a visualization into visual components, extracts structured explanations, and maps them to precise SVG elements for reliable highlighting and interaction. Implemented as a browser extension, VizPilot requires only a brief visualization description and optional interaction source code from the visualization developer to automatically generate onboarding content. The Onboarding Interface supports both guided narrative scrollytelling and free exploration, enabling users to learn visualization components progressively or on demand. We evaluate VizPilot through a comparative analysis of different input modalities, a usage scenario demonstrating reduced authoring effort, and a user study assessing its impact on users' cognitive load. The results demonstrate that VizPilot effectively automates the authoring of onboarding experiences while improving the usability and accessibility of composite visualizations.

</details>


### [136] [Investigating Effective Uncertainty Visualizations for Ordinal Crowdsourced Data of Crowding Conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28072)
*Bea Alexis Arcega,Annika Dominique S. Campos,Kathleen Therese Cruz,Aaron Ace Toledo,Briane Paul V. Samson*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study investigates how to effectively visualize uncertainty in crowdsourced railway crowding data (ordinal in nature) to support commuter decision-making. Through an online evaluation, cluster visualization was found best for reducing cognitive load and maximizing confidence/trust, while bubble treemaps yielded the highest accuracy in determining crowd levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Railway commuters face variable crowding throughout the day, and crowdsourced data offers localized insights but introduces uncertainty. Little is known about how to visualize this uncertainty—particularly for ordinal crowdsourced data—to effectively support informed commuting decisions.

Method: The authors designed and compared multiple uncertainty visualization techniques for representing variability and reliability in crowdsourced ordinal crowding data. These were evaluated through an online user study measuring cognitive load, user confidence, trust, and accuracy in crowd-level determination.

Result: Cluster visualization performed best at reducing cognitive load while maximizing user confidence and trust. Bubble treemaps yielded the highest accuracy among participants when determining crowd levels.

Conclusion: Different uncertainty visualization techniques exhibit a trade-off between interpretability and accuracy. Cluster visualizations are optimal for user experience (low cognitive load, high trust/confidence), while bubble treemaps excel at precise crowd-level judgments, suggesting that visualization choice should align with the specific decision-making context.

Abstract: Commuters often encounter crowding in railway systems, particularly in queues where passenger density varies throughout the day. This introduces uncertainty in crowdedness, making it difficult for individuals to anticipate conditions and plan their trips effectively. Crowdsourcing has been a valuable method for collecting localized user data. But the unpredictability of crowds and the uncertainty of crowdsourced information pose new challenges for decision-making. However, we know little about how to effectively visualize uncertainty in crowdedness to support informed commuting decisions, particularly when using crowdsourced ordinal data. Here, we investigated different uncertainty visualizations and their effectiveness in representing the variability and reliability of crowdsourced crowding data. They were evaluated through an online study, and we found that cluster visualization is best suited to reduce cognitive load while maximizing user confidence and trust. On the other hand, participants showed higher accuracy in determining crowd levels when using bubble treemaps.

</details>


### [137] [A Mathematical Framework for Reading the Autopsias' Meta - Compositional System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28155)
*Patricio F. Calatayud,Pablo Padilla Longoria,Álvaro Martínez Ramírez*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper proposes using mathematical topology to address readability problems in dynamic/kinetic music notation (cynetic musicography), using the Autopsias meta-compositional system as a case study to begin constructing a formal framework for improving orthographic communication between composers and performers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: New computer-based music notation forms that use dynamic musicography (animation, algorithmic processing, etc.) suffer from inherent readability problems. The authors argue that mathematical tools can systematically address these challenges.

Method: The authors adopt basic topological concepts to build a mathematical framework. They first establish a bridge between traditional printed scores and their dynamic computational re-appropriation, then observe and mathematically analyze multiple performances of the Autopsias composition to derive new orthographic tools for dynamic musicography.

Result: The Autopsias performances demonstrate that mathematics—analogous to pitch-class set theory—can effectively elucidate music information and its performance. The findings also reveal the necessity of expanding orthographic rules to enhance composer-performer dialogue.

Conclusion: Mathematical frameworks, particularly those drawing on topology, show promise for systematizing readability in dynamic music notation. An augmented set of orthographic tools is needed to bridge the gap between composers' dynamic scores and performers' interpretive needs.

Abstract: Background. New forms of music writing using computers have arisen in the past 20 years. Most of them use the capacities of digital manipulation of data like animation, algorithmic processing, cinematic view, and much more. These scores use dynamic musicography, and all of them share a problem. They have readability problems. We will argue that this problem can be addressed by mathematical tools. Aims. Take the Autopsias [Autopsies] meta-compositional system as a study case for starting the construction of a mathematical framework that can overview the readability for cynetic musicography. The Autopsias system is the process of transforming a musical score dynamically. Methodology. We will start to build a mathematical framework by taking a group of basic topological concepts, and applying them after a bridge between a printed score and a dynamic computational re-appropriation of it has taken place. We will observe the writing and the performing of the several performances of the Autopsias composition, and analyze them from a mathematical perspective, in order to get the ability to start constructing a new set of orthographical tools for the performance of dynamic musicography. Main Contribution. The performances of Autopsias show that mathematics, as with pitch-class sets, can be helpful for understanding music information, as well as its performance. Also show the necessity of augmenting the set of orthographic rules, in order to improve the dialog between composers and performers.

</details>


### [138] [Student Perceptions and Preferences Regarding AI-Generated Instructional Videos in Computing Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28203)
*Esse Ciego,Shubbhi Taneja,Wilson Wong,Amanpreet Kapoor*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A survey of 170 computing students found that AI-generated educational videos (created with Knowlify) were rated as high-quality, accurate, and usable — yet students expressed significant reservations about their widespread classroom adoption, preferring them only for simple, supplemental, or visual use cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CS education research on generative AI has focused heavily on text-based tools, while the rapid emergence of AI video generation tools remains underexplored. Understanding student perceptions is critical for helping instructors decide when and how to deploy AI-generated videos purposefully.

Method: A descriptive post-test survey study with 170 computing students across two U.S. institutions. Students watched three 3-minute AI-generated videos on Markdown (created with Knowlify) and then completed a survey assessing perceptions of the videos and broader attitudes toward AI-generated educational video use.

Result: Students rated the videos as high-quality, accurate, and usable; nearly half could not determine the videos were AI-generated. However, students expressed limited comfort with widespread adoption, preferring AI videos for simple, supplemental, and visual applications while citing concerns about inaccurate content, reduced instructor interaction, and diminished educational value.

Conclusion: AI-generated educational videos show promise for supplemental learning materials, but student wariness regarding quality, authenticity, and instructor presence suggests instructors should adopt them judiciously and transparently, reserving them for contexts where they complement rather than replace human instruction.

Abstract: Students differ in how they prefer to engage with learning resources, with some favoring textual materials and others visual or video-based content. Recent advances in generative AI have led CS education research to focus on text-based AI tools for developing learning resources. However, advances in AI video models and the rapid proliferation of AI video generation tools have made it possible for instructors to create high-quality personalized educational videos efficiently and cost-effectively. Understanding students' perceptions of AI-generated videos is thus critical for helping CS instructors know when and how to use them purposefully. To address this gap, we conducted a descriptive post-test survey study in which 170 computing students at two U.S. institutions watched three 3-minute AI videos on the Markdown markup language created with Knowlify. Students then completed a survey about their perceptions of the Markdown videos and their broader views on the use of AI-generated videos in education. Students rated the Markdown videos as high-quality, accurate, and usable, with nearly half unable to determine whether the videos were AI-generated. At the same time, students expressed limited comfort with the widespread adoption of AI videos in the classroom. They preferred AI videos for simple, supplemental, and visual use cases, while expressing concerns about lower-quality or inaccurate content, reduced instructor interaction, and diminished educational value.

</details>


### [139] [Toward Annotation-Efficient Continuous Emotion Arousal Quantification via Group-Level EEG Dynamic Neural Synchrony](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28204)
*Guandong Pan,Yaqian Yang,Shi Chen,Yi Zheng,Yi Zhen,Hongwei Zheng,Shaoting Tang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study proposes group-level EEG dynamic neural synchrony (DNS) via Correlated Component Analysis as a marker for continuous emotional arousal quantification, demonstrating that DNS captures the rate of emotional change rather than static intensity, with methodological guidance on optimal parameter choices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continuous emotional arousal quantification is bottlenecked by time-consuming manual annotation. The authors aim to bypass per-subject labeling by investigating whether group-level EEG dynamic neural synchrony can serve as a principled, annotation-efficient marker for arousal dynamics.

Method: Correlated Component Analysis (CorrCA) with sliding-window computation applied across four EEG datasets (142 subjects, 207+ hours). DNS was evaluated against valence and arousal labels. Key methodological variables—window size, lag, and EEG feature type (First-order Difference from dominant CorrCA component)—were systematically characterized. Subject-split replication and block permutation tests were used to verify robustness.

Result: (1) DNS shows significant valence-dependent differences (p<0.003), with positive emotions eliciting higher synchrony. (2) DNS correlates more strongly with the first-order derivative of arousal than raw arousal values, indicating it captures rate of emotional change. (3) Moderate windows (10–30 s), positive lags (0–10 steps), and First-order Difference features yield optimal DNS-arousal coupling, validated as non-artifactual.

Conclusion: DNS is established as an empirically validated group-level neural marker for continuous emotional arousal quantification, offering a path toward annotation-efficient affective computing.

Abstract: Continuous emotional arousal quantification remains bottlenecked by time-consuming and labor-intensive manual annotation. This work investigates group-level EEG dynamic neural synchrony (DNS) as a principled signal for continuous arousal quantification that bypasses per-subject manual labeling. Using Correlated Component Analysis (CorrCA) with sliding-window computation across four EEG datasets spanning 142 subjects and over 207 hours, we systematically evaluate DNS as a group-level marker for emotional arousal dynamics. Three key findings emerge. First, DNS exhibits significant emotion information from valence-dependent differences (all p<0.003), with positive emotions eliciting higher synchrony. Second, DNS correlates more strongly with the first-order derivative of arousal than with raw arousal values, revealing that neural synchrony captures the rate of emotional change rather than static intensity. Third, we provide the first systematic characterization of how DNS-arousal coupling depends on key methodological choices, finding that moderate windows (10-30 s), positive lags (0-10 steps), and First-order Difference feature of EEG from the dominant CorrCA component yield consistently strong coupling. Subject-split replication and block permutation tests confirm these associations are not statistical artifacts. Our findings establish DNS as an empirically validated group-level marker toward annotation-efficient continuous emotional arousal quantification.

</details>


### [140] [Identifying a Level-up Pathway for AI-assisted Counterspeech through Elaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28239)
*Han Li,Inhwan Bae,Natalie Bazarova,Drew Margolin*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study evaluated three generative AI-assisted writing systems for helping lay users craft effective counterspeech against vaccine-skeptical social media content. In a randomized controlled trial, AI assistance—delivered at different stages (co-writing vs. re-writing) and modes (guided vs. unguided)—increased perceived counterspeech effectiveness while preserving authenticity. The primary mechanism was AI facilitating more elaborate, informative, and analytically sophisticated responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vaccine-skeptical content on social media has profound societal impact, and community-driven counterspeech is a promising participatory response. However, ordinary users struggle to craft effective counterspeech, limiting their willingness and ability to engage constructively. The authors seek to understand whether and how generative AI can bridge this gap.

Method: The authors designed and evaluated three generative AI-assisted counterspeech writing systems varying by assistance stage (co-writing vs. re-writing) and mode (guided vs. unguided). They conducted a randomized controlled trial with social media users who wrote counterspeech responses to both statistical and narrative vaccine-skeptical content. They measured perceived effectiveness, authenticity, message elaboration (informativeness, analytical quality, lexical sophistication), and willingness to counterspeak publicly.

Result: AI-assisted writing significantly increased perceived counterspeech effectiveness while largely preserving authentic self-expression. Perceived effectiveness was the strongest predictor of willingness to counterspeak publicly. AI's primary benefit was facilitating more elaborate writing—messages were more informative, analytical, and lexically sophisticated. This held across both statistical and narrative types of vaccine-skeptical content.

Conclusion: The findings suggest a "level-up" pathway: AI-assisted, community-driven counterspeech helps cultivate more effective and motivated counterspeakers, contributing to higher-quality public discourse on pressing societal issues. The study demonstrates that AI can augment rather than replace human expression in contentious online contexts.

Abstract: Given the profound societal impact of vaccine-skeptical content on social media, community-driven counterspeech has emerged as a promising participatory response to contest and curb such objectionable content. Yet crafting effective counterspeech remains challenging for ordinary users, limiting their willingness and ability to engage constructively. We designed and evaluated three generative AI-assisted counterspeech writing systems that vary by assistance stage (co-writing vs. re-writing) and mode (guided vs. unguided) to support lay users' responses to vaccine-skeptical content. We ask whether AI can help users craft counterspeech perceived as both effective and authentic, which forms of AI support work best, and through what mechanisms. In a randomized controlled trial with social media users, participants wrote counterspeech responses to both statistical and narrative vaccine-skeptical content. Across evidence types, AI-assisted writing increased perceived counterspeech effectiveness while largely preserving authentic self-expression, and perceived effectiveness was the strongest predictor of willingness to counterspeak publicly. AI's primary benefit was facilitating more elaborate writing, producing messages that were more informative, analytical, and lexically sophisticated. These findings suggest a level-up pathway for AI-assisted, community-driven counterspeech, which helps cultivate more effective and motivated counterspeakers, contributing to higher-quality public discourse on pressing societal issues.

</details>


### [141] [Effects of Auditory Information for People With Visual Impairments in Highly Automated Vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28544)
*Mark Colley,Tobias Aescht,Omid Rajabi,Max Rädler,Pascal Jansen,Enrico Rukzio*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A study designed visual-auditory communication for visually impaired users in automated vehicles, finding that medium-level information (safety, vehicle control, route updates) optimally improved trust and UX, while high-level information showed diminishing returns due to saturation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated vehicles promise improved accessibility, yet current design and research on information visualization neglect users with visual impairments, failing to deliver on the commitment to inclusive personal mobility.

Method: An online video-based study (N=35, 12 with visual impairments) compared three levels of auditory information: low (safety-relevant only), medium (adding vehicle control and route updates), and high (further adding sightseeing and destination information). The study evaluated a combined visual and auditory communication concept designed specifically for visually impaired passengers inside fully automated vehicles.

Result: Trust and user experience significantly improved with additional auditory information beyond the low level. Perceived safety showed a similar but less robust positive effect. However, the medium level appeared to reach an information saturation point, with the high level offering no further benefit and potentially being excessive.

Conclusion: Designers of automated vehicle interfaces should aim for medium-level auditory information — encompassing safety, vehicle control, and route updates — to maximize accessibility without overwhelming visually impaired users. This guidance helps fulfill the inclusive potential of automated vehicles.

Abstract: Automated vehicles promise to improve accessibility and access to personal mobility for everyone. However, their design and current research trends in visualizing relevant information do not reflect this commitment to accessibility for users with visual impairments. Therefore, we designed and implemented a visual and auditory communication concept for people with visual impairments seated inside fully automated vehicles. Furthermore, in an online video-based study (N=35, 12 with visual impairments), we compared three levels of auditory information communication: low (safety-relevant information only), medium (additionally including vehicle control and route updates), and high (additionally including sightseeing and destination information). Results showed that trust and user experience significantly improved with additional information, with a corresponding, albeit less robust, effect on perceived safety. However, they also revealed that a potential information saturation was reached with medium information. Our work helps to improve the accessibility of automated vehicles by guiding designers towards adequate information communication.

</details>


### [142] [Multi-Session User Experience Assessments of Computationally Optimized Automated Vehicle Functionality Visualizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28552)
*Mark Colley,Pascal Jansen,Svenja Krauss,Enrico Rukzio*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper applies multi-objective Bayesian optimization to automate the design of in-vehicle visualizations for automated vehicles, optimizing for passenger trust, perceived safety, and cognitive load. An online study (N=74) demonstrates the method's effectiveness in identifying optimal design parameters while revealing limitations when optimizing for subjective measures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Empirically evaluating visualization designs for AV passengers is time-consuming, costly, and limits the design space that can be explored. The authors seek a more efficient, scalable computational approach to identify optimal visualization parameters without exhaustive human-subject testing of all design combinations.

Method: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization was employed to iteratively search the visualization design space. The method models the trade-off between multiple objectives—maximizing passenger trust and perceived safety while minimizing cognitive load. A multi-session iterative optimization framework was used, and an online study with 74 participants validated the approach.

Result: The Bayesian optimization method successfully identified visualization design parameters that improved trust, perceived safety, and predictability. The approach proved more efficient and scalable than traditional exhaustive empirical evaluation. However, the authors note shortcomings when the computational approach is applied to subjective measurements.

Conclusion: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization is a viable and efficient method for designing AV passenger visualizations, enabling broader design space exploration. Yet, caution is warranted when optimizing for inherently noisy and subjective human-centered metrics, as the computational surrogates may not fully capture the nuances of subjective experience.

Abstract: Understanding automated vehicles (AVs) is crucial to improving their acceptance. Numerous approaches to visualizing relevant traffic information to passengers have been proposed and empirically evaluated. As this is time-consuming, costly, and reduces the possible design parameters, we employed multi-objective Bayesian optimization to optimize the design of visualizations in AVs. In particular, we evaluated multi-session aspects involving iterative optimization. We optimized the design for passenger trust and perceived safety while minimizing cognitive load. Results from an online study (N=74) show that this method effectively identifies visualization design parameter values that improve trust, safety, and predictability while making the design process more efficient and scalable. However, shortcomings of the computational approach when optimizing for subjective measurements are highlighted and discussed.

</details>


### [143] [CrossAtlas: Evaluating Projection Techniques for Spatial Referencing in Cross-Reality Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28583)
*Haoyang Yang,Chenyang Zhang,Elliott H. Faa,Weijian Liu,Lily Seika Chisholm,Benjamin Lee,David Saffo,Feiyu Lu,Blair MacIntyre,Yalong Yang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: CrossAtlas is a PC-VR collaboration platform exploring how different bidirectional projection techniques (planar vs. spherical) between 2D desktop views and 3D immersive layouts affect spatial referencing. A 24-dyad study found spherical projection often outperformed planar variants and remained robust across layouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-reality collaboration between immersive (VR) and desktop users is increasingly common, but little is known about how bidirectional projection techniques — mapping 3D layouts to 2D views and vice versa — influence communication, particularly spatial referencing. Different mappings preserve or distort geometric relationships (adjacency, orientation, coverage), affecting shared spatial understanding.

Method: The authors built CrossAtlas, a synchronized PC-VR collaboration platform supporting three planar projection variants and one spherical (equirectangular) projection variant across layouts of varying curvature. A controlled study with 24 dyads (48 participants) had collaborators complete spatial referencing tasks under different projection-layout conditions, collecting both performance metrics and subjective measures.

Result: Projection choice significantly shaped collaboration quality. The spherical (equirectangular) projection variant frequently outperformed all three planar projection variants and demonstrated greater robustness across different object layouts.

Conclusion: Bidirectional projection techniques are a critical design factor in cross-reality collaboration systems. Spherical projections offer a more robust solution for maintaining shared spatial understanding across heterogeneous views than planar alternatives.

Abstract: Cross-reality collaboration increasingly connects immersive and desktop users within synchronized workspaces, yet little is known about how bidirectional projection techniques between immersive 3D layouts and desktop 2D views influence communication. Spatial referencing depends on shared spatial understanding, but different mappings preserve and distort geometric relationships in different ways, altering perceived adjacency, orientation, and coverage across collaborators' views. We present CrossAtlas, a synchronized PC-VR collaboration platform that integrates multiple bidirectional projection techniques, including three planar projection variants and equirectangular, a spherical projection variant, across layouts of varying curvature. In a controlled study with 24 dyads, collaborators completed spatial referencing tasks under different projection-layout conditions while we collected performance and subjective measures. Our results show that projection choice strongly shaped collaboration, with the spherical variant often outperforming planar projections and remaining robust across object layouts.

</details>

### [144] [OwlPath: Lossless Knowledge Compression for LLM Bug Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27249)
*Bo Zhang,Ren Pan,Huan Chen,Xiang Song*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: OwlPath encodes source code into an OWL2 ontology for lossless structural retrieval, enabling LLM-based SE agents to resolve multi-hop code dependencies via SPARQL queries instead of string matching. It achieves 68.4% strict-apply rate on SWE-bench Pro, cutting token usage by 28.8% and improving recall 2.06× over the CodeGraph baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based software engineering agents are bottlenecked by ~100K token context windows. Standard retrieval treats code as plain text, forcing agents to resolve multi-hop structural dependencies (subclass chains, transitive callers, interface implementations) through inefficient trial-and-error. Existing tools cannot compactly encode and query the full structural graph of a codebase.

Method: OwlPath is an OWL2 reasoning layer built on CodeGraph (500K+ GitHub stars). It uses tree-sitter for multi-language parsing (Python, JS, TS, Go) and encodes language-specific semantics into a unified OWL2 ontology. Two key modules: (1) a transitive-closure engine that retrieves all structurally linked symbols via single SPARQL property-path queries, capturing multi-hop relations missed by string matching; (2) the OWL Software Knowledge Map (OWL-SKM), which precomputes a compact 3KB summary (module trees, core APIs, issue-related symbols) to direct agents to relevant modules on the first query.

Result: On 18 SWE-bench Pro instances: 68.4% strict-apply rate vs. 66.7% for CodeGraph, with 28.8% token reduction and 39.5% runtime reduction. Offline retrieval over 67 instances: 2.06× recall improvement (0.464 vs 0.226), 88.1% hit rate vs. 59.7%. On a 37-question structural retrieval benchmark: recall improved from 4.4% to 28.8%, with 69–80% accuracy on transitive caller and interface implementation tasks.

Conclusion: Lossless knowledge compression via OWL2 ontology encoding significantly outperforms plain-text retrieval for structural code queries, enabling agents to resolve multi-hop dependencies efficiently within tight context budgets. OwlPath demonstrates that ontology-based code intelligence is a practical and effective direction for scaling LLM-based software engineering agents.

Abstract: LLM-based software engineering agents are constrained by limited context windows: roughly 100K tokens must store structurally relevant code  subsets to resolve bugs. Standard retrieval models treat code as plain text, forcing agents to resolve multi-hop dependencies including subclass  chains, transitive callers and interface implementations through slow trial and error. We tackle this limitation with lossless knowledge  compression, encoding source code into an OWL2 ontology to answer structural queries using minimal relevant code fragments.
  We present OwlPath, an OWL2 reasoning layer atop CodeGraph, a widely used code intelligence platform with 500K+ GitHub stars, offering a unified  CLI for structural code retrieval. Powered by tree-sitter parsing, OwlPath supports multi-language repositories (Python, JavaScript,  TypeScript, Go, etc.) and encodes language-specific semantics into a unified OWL2 ontology. It adopts two complementary modules. First, a  transitive-closure engine fetches all structurally linked symbols via single SPARQL property-path queries, capturing multi-hop relations missed  by string matching. Second, the OWL Software Knowledge Map (OWL-SKM) precomputes a compact 3KB summary with module trees, core APIs and  issue-related symbols, directing agents to target modules in the first query.
  Evaluated on 18 SWE-bench Pro instances, OwlPath obtains a 68.4% strict-apply rate versus 66.7% for the CodeGraph baseline, cutting token usage  by 28.8% and runtime by 39.5%. In offline retrieval tests over 67 instances, OwlPath improves recall 2.06 times (0.464 vs 0.226) and reaches  88.1% hit rate compared to CodeGraph's 59.7%. On a 37-question structural retrieval benchmark, recall rises from 4.4% to 28.8%, with 69-80%  accuracy on transitive caller and interface tasks.

</details>


### [145] [Do Context Files Help Coding Agents? A Two-Agent Ablation Study on Real Repositories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27250)
*Prakhar Khatri*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A controlled ablation study finds that persistent context files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) do not measurably improve AI coding agent correctness. Failures stem from implementation skill gaps, not missing repository knowledge. Task difficulty is agent-specific, explaining prior contradictory results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite persistent context files being standard practice for guiding AI coding agents, evidence for their effectiveness is contradictory. The authors aim to rigorously resolve this contradiction through controlled experimentation.

Method: A controlled ablation of context-injection strategy across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex), using 17 real tasks from 3 repositories, with 288 evaluated runs and gold-test evaluation. Equivalence testing bounds effect size. Includes failure-mode triage and a manipulation probe to test whether AGENTS.md converts near-misses to passes.

Result: Context strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent (bounded to ≤10-15pp). Failures are attributed to implementation skill (feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring), not missing repository knowledge. The manipulation probe confirms AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss to a pass. Task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman ρ=0.75), offering an explanation for prior single-agent study contradictions.

Conclusion: Persistent context files do not reliably boost coding agent performance; agent failures are rooted in implementation capability rather than knowledge gaps. The agent-specific nature of task difficulty suggests that single-agent evaluations may draw from incomparable difficulty bands, explaining prior conflicting findings. All artifacts are released publicly.

Abstract: Persistent context files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) are standard practice for guiding AI coding agents, yet evidence for their effectiveness is contradictory. We present a controlled ablation of context-injection strategy across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex), 17 real tasks from 3 repositories (15 shared + 2 Codex-only), and 288 evaluated runs with gold-test evaluation. Context strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent (bounded to <=10-15pp via equivalence testing). A failure-mode triage reveals why: agents fail on implementation skill---feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring---not missing repository knowledge that a context file could supply; a manipulation probe confirms the real AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss to a pass on either agent. We further show that borderline task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman rho=0.75), offering a candidate explanation for prior contradictions: single-agent studies draw tasks from different agents' informative bands. We release all code, data, and analysis.

</details>


### [146] [AgentS4D: Benchmarking Runtime Risks across the Execution Lifecycle of LLM-Based Workspace Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27294)
*Jiajun Zhou,Zhaoxuan Ke,Jihang Ye,Xuanze Chen,Shanqing Yu,Qi Xuan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AgentS4D is a sandboxed benchmark for lifecycle-wide runtime safety evaluation of LLM-based workspace agents. Using a four-dimensional framework (risk-entry sources, induction strategies, target harms, lifecycle checkpoints), it evaluates 20 harness-LLM combinations across 328 risk-injected cases (6,560 runs). Results show 68% of runs trigger unsafe signals, safety varies significantly with harness-LLM pairings and risk presentation, and 66.22% of runs are unsafe yet complete—demonstrating that task completion does not imply safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-based workspace agents assess executable safety but lack a unified account of where risks enter, how they elicit unsafe behavior, which harms they target, and where evidence appears during execution. This fragmentation prevents comprehensive understanding of runtime safety failures.

Method: The authors introduce AgentS4D, a sandboxed benchmark structured around a four-dimensional runtime-safety framework: (1) six risk-entry sources, (2) six induction strategies, (3) nine target harms for case construction, and (4) seven lifecycle checkpoints for post-run evidence organization. The benchmark contains 328 risk-injected cases, tested across all 20 combinations of four harnesses (Hermes, OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and five LLM backends (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M3, Qwen3.7-Plus), yielding 6,560 runs.

Result: Overall, 4,461 runs (68.0%) triggered prespecified unsafe signals. Safety varied substantially across the 20 harness-LLM configurations and depended on how risk was introduced. The same induction strategy produced markedly different safety outcomes when delivered through different risk carriers; similarly, the same target harm elicited different responses across carriers and strategies. Critically, 4,344 runs (66.22%) were unsafe yet completed successfully, showing that task completion cannot establish runtime safety and that testing only one form of a risk conceals weaknesses.

Conclusion: Runtime safety evaluation must examine complete agent configurations (harness + LLM) across diverse risk conditions and retain evidence throughout the entire execution lifecycle. Single-dimensional testing is insufficient for capturing safety vulnerabilities in stateful, multi-step agent workflows.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based workspace agents execute stateful, multi-step workflows across heterogeneous resources, external tools, and persistent state. Their safety must therefore be assessed from actions, side effects, and state changes throughout execution. Although recent benchmarks have advanced executable safety testing and trajectory-aware verification, they rarely provide a unified account of where risks enter, how they elicit unsafe behavior, which harms they target, and where supporting evidence appears during execution. We introduce AgentS4D, a sandboxed benchmark for lifecycle-wide runtime safety evaluation. Its four-dimensional runtime-safety framework uses six risk-entry sources, six induction strategies, and nine target harms to guide case construction, while seven lifecycle checkpoints organize post-run evidence. AgentS4D contains 328 risk-injected cases. We evaluate all 20 combinations of four harnesses (Hermes, OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex) and five LLM backends (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M3, and Qwen3.7-Plus) on these cases, yielding 6,560 runs. Overall, 4,461 runs (68.0%) trigger prespecified unsafe signals. Across the 20 configurations, the observed safety of an agent system varies with both its harness-LLM pairing and how risk is introduced. Agent systems exhibit markedly different safety behavior when the same induction strategy reaches them through different risk carriers. They also respond differently to the same target harm when it is realized through different carriers and strategies. Moreover, 4,344 runs (66.22% overall) are unsafe yet complete. Thus, task completion cannot establish runtime safety, and testing only one form of a risk can conceal important weaknesses. Evaluations should examine complete agent configurations across diverse risk conditions and retain evidence throughout execution.

</details>


### [147] [A Taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork Requirements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27302)
*Anastasia Mavridou,Hazel M. Taylor,Sandy Lozito,Louise A. Dennis,Michael Fisher,Marie Farrell*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper presents a validated two-level hierarchical taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements, derived from 361 requirements across 14 cross-domain sources, organized into 6 high-level and 21 low-level categories, and validated through expert evaluation and a utility demonstration on 448 independently assembled requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing requirements for human-robot teamwork are fragmented across disparate sources (academic literature, industrial standards, regulatory guidance), with no unified framework that systematically addresses the complexities of collaborative human-robot tasks. This gap hinders consistent design, evaluation, and regulation of autonomous systems in safety- and mission-critical domains.

Method: The authors constructed a corpus of 361 requirements extracted from 14 cross-domain sources spanning academic literature, standards, and regulatory guidance. Through iterative classification and refinement, they developed a two-level hierarchical taxonomy. Validation was conducted via expert evaluation with 5 domain specialists and a utility demonstration applying the taxonomy to an independent corpus of 448 requirements from 19 sources across six HRT domains.

Result: The resulting taxonomy comprises 6 high-level categories (information provision, relational control, decision support, safety mechanisms, performance monitoring, and foundational system capabilities) and 21 low-level subcategories. Expert evaluation confirmed the taxonomy's validity, and the utility demonstration on the independent corpus showed the taxonomy's applicability across six distinct HRT domains.

Conclusion: The taxonomy provides a unified, domain-agnostic framework for structuring HRT requirements, enabling more systematic specification, analysis, and comparison of requirements across diverse human-robot teaming contexts in safety- and mission-critical applications.

Abstract: Autonomous systems are increasingly deployed in safety- and mission-critical domains where humans and robots must operate as a team to complete complex tasks. Existing requirements for Human-Robot teamwork remain fragmented across disparate sources, with no unified framework that addresses complexities of collaborative Human-Robot tasks. We address this gap by presenting a taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements derived from analysis of (academic and industrial) literature, standards and regulatory guidance. We extracted a construction corpus of 361 requirements from 14 cross-domain sources. Through iterative classification and refinement, we develop a two-level hierarchical taxonomy comprising 6 high-level categories and 21 low-level subcategories that distinguish information provision, relational control, decision support, safety mechanisms, performance monitoring, and foundational system capabilities. We validate the taxonomy through expert evaluation with 5 domain specialists and a utility demonstration on an independently assembled corpus of 448 requirements drawn from 19 sources spanning six HRT domains.

</details>


### [148] [SIGIL: Compiling Agent Skills into Typed Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27309)
*Jayanaka Dantanarayana,Savini Kashmira,Lingjia Tang,Jason Mars*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Prose-based AI agent skills suffer from poor procedural compliance (56% step completion). The paper introduces Skill Compilation via SIGIL, which transforms prose skills into executable harnesses using AG-IR, a typed intermediate representation. Compiled harnesses achieve 86% step completion, 2.3x full-procedure completion, and 0.58x token usage, with model-independent guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents using prose skill descriptions (natural language procedures loaded at runtime) exhibit unreliable execution: models re-derive control flow each run, often skipping mandated verification steps while still producing superficially correct outputs. Hand-written harnesses solve this but are tedious and undermine the accessibility of prose authoring. The gap motivates an automated compilation approach.

Method: The authors propose Skill Compilation, implemented in a system called SIGIL. The core is AG-IR, a typed agentic intermediate representation that cleanly separates model-owned cognition (reasoning, generation) from code-owned mechanism (control flow, verification). SIGIL compiles a prose skill into an executable harness by parsing the natural language procedure, lifting it into AG-IR, and emitting deterministic harness code that enforces mandated steps.

Result: Evaluated across 30 skills and two model generations: compiled harnesses perform 86% of mandated steps (vs. 56% for prose), complete full procedures 2.3x more often, and consume 0.58x the tokens. The 86% step-compliance holds consistently across model generations, while prose compliance varies from 56% to 68%, demonstrating model-independent reliability.

Conclusion: Compiling prose skills into harnesses via a typed IR substantially improves procedural reliability, efficiency, and cross-model consistency. SIGIL preserves the authoring accessibility of prose while delivering the execution guarantees of programmatic harnesses, closing a critical reliability gap in agentic AI systems.

Abstract: AI-Integrated agents increasingly acquire capability from skills: prose procedure files loaded into a model's context and run by a tool-calling loop. A skill is described to the runtime but never encoded in it, so the model re-derives its control flow on every run and may skip mandated verification. Across 30 skills and two model generations, a prose agent performs only 56% of the steps its own skill mandates, while producing artifacts that pass output checks. The remedy is known: write a harness, in which the procedure is program structure. However, hand-writing harnesses is tedious and discards the authoring surface that made skills succeed. To address this limitation, we introduce Skill Compilation, realized in SIGIL, which compiles a prose skill into an executable harness. At its center is AG-IR, a typed agentic intermediate representation separating model-owned cognition from code-owned mechanism. Compiled harnesses perform 86% of mandated steps, complete the full procedure 2.3x as often, and require 0.58x the tokens. Notably, the guarantee is model-independent: the harness holds at 86% across two model generations while prose swings from 56% to 68%.

</details>


### [149] [TrustChain-Review: A Risk-Adaptive Blockchain and Game-Theoretic Framework for Trustworthy AI-Assisted Code Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27310)
*Mohammad Naserameri*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: TrustChain-Review combines blockchain evidence storage, game-theoretic incentives, and risk-adaptive governance to improve code review trustworthiness, showing that full-evidence governance maximizes trust and detection while risk-adaptive governance offers better cost-efficiency for routine changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-assisted software development accelerates coding and review but erodes accountability: developers submit unverified code, reviewers perform superficial inspections, and centralized reputation systems lack auditability. A trustworthy, verifiable, incentive-aligned code review framework is needed.

Method: The framework integrates three components: (1) a blockchain-based evidence layer for immutable audit trails; (2) a three-player game-theoretic model involving developers, reviewers, and the platform to align strategic incentives; and (3) a risk-sensitive governance rule that escalates controls only when expected benefit exceeds cost. Evaluation uses controlled simulation calibrated on the Diff Quality Estimation dataset, comparing six governance configurations over 30 independent runs across seven metrics: reputation accuracy, trust convergence, malicious-review detection, superficial-review detection, net platform utility, governance cost, and cost-efficiency.

Result: The full-evidence configuration achieved the highest reputation accuracy, trust convergence, and detection rates for both malicious and superficial reviews but incurred the highest governance cost. The risk-adaptive configuration significantly reduced governance cost and improved cost-efficiency by applying stricter controls only when justified, though its trust and detection metrics were lower than the full-evidence setting.

Conclusion: Full-evidence governance is best suited for high-risk or audit-sensitive code changes, while risk-adaptive governance provides a more practical cost-trustworthiness trade-off for routine, lower-risk contributions.

Abstract: Context: AI-assisted software development can speed up coding and review, but it also makes accountability harder to establish. Developers may submit insufficiently verified code, reviewers may approve changes with limited inspection, and centralized reputation records may be difficult to audit. Objectives: This study introduces TrustChain-Review, a framework that combines verifiable evidence, strategic incentives, and risk-sensitive governance to support more trustworthy code review. Methods: The framework includes a blockchain-based evidence layer, a three-player game-theoretic model for developers, reviewers, and the platform, and a rule that applies stronger governance when the expected benefit justifies its cost. The evaluation uses a controlled simulation calibrated with the Diff Quality Estimation dataset. Six governance configurations are compared over 30 independent runs using reputation accuracy, trust convergence, malicious-review detection, superficial-review detection, net platform utility, governance cost, and cost-efficiency. Results: The full-evidence configuration produces the strongest reputation, trust, and detection results, but it also has the highest governance cost. The risk-adaptive configuration lowers this cost and improves cost-efficiency by applying stronger controls selectively, although its trust and detection results are lower than those of the full-evidence setting. Conclusion: Strong evidence-based governance is most appropriate for high-risk or audit-sensitive changes. For routine or lower-risk contributions, selective governance offers a more practical balance between trustworthiness and operational cost.

</details>


### [150] [PROGRESS: Property-Guided Regression Search for Semantic Falsification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27359)
*Davis Tocheuk Mo,Noshin Ulfat,Matthew B. Dwyer,Soneya Binta Hossain*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: PROGRESS integrates property-based testing oracles into search-based regression test generation (EvoSuite's DynaMOSA), using LLMs to extract intent-driven properties from code context. It guides evolutionary search toward satisfying property preconditions and detecting semantic violations. On 25 Java systems, it found 58% of current-version bugs (vs. 0% for regression-only) and satisfied 47% of hard-to-reach preconditions (vs. 12% for standalone jqwik).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Search-based regression test generation achieves high structural coverage but uses system-derived oracles that bake in existing faults. Property-based testing provides independent semantic oracles but struggles to reach deep program states or satisfy complex preconditions. No existing approach combines the state-reaching power of coverage-guided search with the oracle quality of property-based testing.

Method: PROGRESS extends EvoSuite's DynaMOSA with three components: (1) an LLM pipeline that extracts code context (documentation, caller/callee relationships) to generate executable jqwik properties while limiting implementation leakage; (2) a property-aware fitness function and search objective per property that rewards progress through preconditions and prioritizes falsifying executions; (3) parameter binding using jqwik generators to connect quantified property inputs to evolving test sequences, steering generation toward both coverage and bug detection.

Result: On 25 large-scale Java systems: PROGRESS detected 328/562 (58%) current-version bugs, while baseline regression-test generation detected none. For 150 hard-to-reach properties, PROGRESS satisfied all preconditions for 70 (47%) versus 18 (12%) for standalone jqwik. Ablation studies confirmed that documentation and caller/callee context are critical for generating valid executable properties. PROGRESS maintained structural exploration while exposing faults missed by regression-derived assertions.

Conclusion: PROGRESS successfully bridges the gap between search-based test generation and property-based testing, demonstrating that intent-driven semantic oracles can be integrated into evolutionary search without sacrificing structural coverage. The approach shows that LLM-generated properties with fitness-guided search significantly outperform either technique in isolation for both bug detection and deep-state reachability.

Abstract: Search-based regression-test generation effectively explores complex program structures, yielding high structural coverage, but its oracles are derived from the system under test: faults already present are recorded as expected behavior rather than exposed. Property-based testing offers independent semantic oracles, but depends on high-quality properties and gives little guidance for reaching deep states or satisfying selective preconditions.
  We present PROGRESS (PROperty-Guided REgression Search for Semantic Falsification), integrating intent-driven properties into coverage-guided, search-based evolutionary test generation to reach deep program states and detect violations of intended behavior. PROGRESS (1) extracts intent-bearing code context and uses a language-model pipeline to generate executable jqwik properties while limiting implementation leakage; (2) extends EvoSuite's DynaMOSA with a search objective and property-aware fitness function per property, rewarding progress through preconditions and prioritizing falsifying executions; and (3) binds property parameters and uses jqwik-provided generators to connect quantified inputs to evolving test sequences, steering generation toward coverage and bug-detection goals.
  We evaluate PROGRESS on 25 large-scale Java systems against regression-test generation, standalone property-based testing, and context ablations. PROGRESS detects 328/562 current-version bugs (58%) versus none for regression-test generation, and satisfies all preconditions for 70/150 hard-to-reach properties versus 18 for standalone jqwik. Ablations show documentation and caller/callee context are key to generating valid executable properties. PROGRESS preserves structural exploration while exposing faults missed by regression-derived assertions; we release a comprehensive artifact package.

</details>


### [151] [From Backlog Items to Security Guidance: Towards Continuous Security Compliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27374)
*Ignacio García Núñez,Florian Angermeir,Fabiola Moyón Constante*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An NLP-based backlog enrichment system that classifies security-relevant backlog items and links them to applicable security requirements via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), evaluated on a new labeled dataset from industrial practitioners in regulated domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Engineering teams in regulated domains struggle to identify security requirements during backlog refinement because security relevance is not explicit in brief, free-form backlog descriptions, leading to missed or delayed security compliance.

Method: A two-part NLP pipeline: (1) a recall-oriented security-relevance classifier trained on 288 practitioner-labeled backlog items (Fleiss' κ=0.787); (2) a four-stage RAG pipeline that retrieves clauses from security requirements documents (company policies and CIS Benchmarks) and grounds them to relevant backlog items.

Result: The classifier achieves F2=0.774 in-distribution and mean zero-shot G-measure ≈0.65 across five benchmarks, matching or exceeding classical-ML and open-source GPT baselines. In preliminary RAG evaluation with two practitioners, 12 of 24 retrieved security clauses were rated ≥4/5 for relevance.

Conclusion: First indicators suggest NLP-based backlog enrichment can help engineers identify security requirements early in development, facilitating continuous security compliance in regulated continuous software engineering contexts.

Abstract: Continuous software engineering in regulated domains requires engineering teams to address security throughout the development lifecycle. Yet making security requirements explicit in backlog items is still problematic. Engineers must instead infer security relevance of backlog items from brief, free-form descriptions and often lack timely guidance on applicable requirements. We present an NLP-based backlog enrichment system that detects security-relevant backlog items and links them to relevant security requirements. The approach combines a security-relevance classifier with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline over security requirements documents. The approach was developed and evaluated in the context of a large enterprise in highly regulated domains. We present three contributions. First, we release a dataset of 288 backlog items labeled for security relevance by nine security practitioners, with substantial agreement (Fleiss' $κ=0.787$). Second, a recall-oriented classifier achieving $F2=0.774$ in-distribution and mean zero-shot G-measure $\approx 0.65$ across five established benchmarks, matching or outperforming most published classical-ML and open-source GPT baselines. Third, we preliminarily evaluated a four-stage security requirements document-grounded RAG pipeline with two practitioners on industrial backlogs using company-internal security policies and CIS Benchmarks. Of the retrieved 24 clauses, 12 were rated at least 4/5 for relevance. Our findings provide first indicators that NLP-based product backlog enrichment can support engineers in identifying security requirements early in the development process. With this work we aim to facilitate continuous security compliance through proactive introduction of security requirements in continuous software engineering.

</details>


### [152] [SWE-NFI: Studying and Benchmarking Coding Agents for Non-Functional Improvements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27409)
*Pengyu Xue,He Yang Yuan,Xin Wang,Junkai Chen,Haonan Zhang,Boyuan Chen,Zishuo Ding,Zhenhao Li,Weiyi Shang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SWE-NFI is a benchmark of 188 tasks from real Python pull requests that evaluates coding agents on non-functional improvements (NFIs). While the best agent achieves 70% functional correctness, all agents lag significantly behind humans on structural NFIs, with scores ranging from 0.0–1.3 vs. the human reference of 1.5.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing coding agent benchmarks focus exclusively on functional correctness, ignoring the real-world practice of making behavior-preserving non-functional improvements (e.g., refactoring, optimization, readability). There is no systematic way to evaluate agents on these NFI capabilities.

Method: The authors construct SWE-NFI with 188 tasks derived from real merged pull requests in open-source Python projects. They operationalize developer-oriented NFIs into 92 executable rules and build an evaluation suite combining functional correctness testing with rule-based NFI assessment.

Result: The best agent achieves 70.0% functional correctness. However, all agents fall short of human developers in overall NFI capability, especially on structural code improvements, where agent scores (0.0–1.3) trail the human reference score (1.5).

Conclusion: SWE-NFI provides a reproducible foundation for evaluating and advancing coding agents beyond functional correctness, highlighting a significant gap between current agents and human developers in non-functional improvement capabilities.

Abstract: Although coding agents have achieved impressive performance on correctness-oriented benchmarks, their ability to make behavior-preserving non-functional improvements (NFIs) remains underexplored. In real-world software development, developers continuously improve software quality without changing observable behavior, yet existing benchmarks primarily evaluate functional correctness and provide limited support for assessing these non-functional improvements.
  In this paper, we present SWE-NFI, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on NFIs beyond functional correctness. Our benchmark contains 188 tasks constructed from real merged pull requests in open-source Python projects. We operationalize developer-oriented NFIs into 92 executable rules and develop a comprehensive evaluation suite that combines functional correctness testing with rule-based NFI evaluation.
  We evaluate state-of-the-art commercial and open-source coding agents. Although the best-performing agent achieves a 70.0\% functional correctness rate, all evaluated agents generally fall short of human developers in overall NFI capability. The gap is particularly evident for structural code improvements, where agents' NFI scores range from 0.0 to 1.3, compared with 1.5 for the human reference. Our benchmark and findings provide a reproducible foundation for evaluating and advancing coding agents beyond functional correctness.

</details>


### [153] [LimICE: Integrating LLM into ICE Framework for Efficient Loop Invariant Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27606)
*Kai Fan,ShiWen Yu,GuangSheng Fan,HaoAng Chi,WanWei Liu,Ji Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Loop invariant synthesis remains challenging due to undecidability. The paper proposes Incremental ICE, a framework that decomposes invariant generation into an ordered sequence of lemmas (inspired by IC3), using LLMs with a counterexample filtering mechanism and a fallback (ICE-DT). The resulting tool, LimICE, significantly outperforms both LLM-based and non-LLM baselines on linear and nonlinear benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ML-based loop invariant synthesis methods use a monolithic approach—attempting to generate a single complete invariant formula in one shot. Because the learning process cannot be strictly constrained, these methods struggle to simultaneously satisfy all necessary conditions on complex problems. The key insight is that loop invariants are often not monolithic but rather an ordered sequence of lemmas. This motivates an incremental synthesis framework that mirrors the IC3 incremental verification philosophy.

Method: The authors propose Incremental ICE, which integrates the incremental reasoning of IC3 into the ICE (Infer, Check, Evaluate) learning framework. It defines a lemma-specific learning objective and introduces a counterexample filtering mechanism to enable sound incremental learning. The instantiated tool, LimICE, uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate the ordered lemma sequence, with ICE-DT (a decision-tree-based invariant learner) as a fallback to complement incomplete lemma sequences.

Result: On 367 linear benchmarks, LimICE solved 349 (avg. 15.2s); on 50 nonlinear benchmarks, it solved 47 (avg. 8.8s). Compared to the SOTA LLM-based baseline, LimICE solved 12–24% more instances and ran 36–63% faster. Against strong non-LLM baselines, it solved at least 86 more linear instances and 27 more nonlinear instances.

Conclusion: Incremental synthesis via lemma decomposition, powered by LLMs and reinforced by a counterexample filtering mechanism, proves highly effective for loop invariant generation. LimICE achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating that the incremental, lemma-by-lemma approach is superior to monolithic invariant generation for both linear and nonlinear programs.

Abstract: Loop invariant synthesis is a fundamental problem in program verification, yet the inherent undecidability makes it highly challenging. Recent studies have increasingly employed various machine learning techniques to generate loop invariants. However, most of these methods adopt a monolithic approach. Due to the inability to strictly constrain the learning process, learning-based methods struggle to simultaneously consider all necessary conditions and generate complete invariants when tackling complex problems. In fact, a loop invariant is often an ordered sequence of lemmas, rather than a single invariant formula. This motivates us to propose Incremental ICE, a novel learning framework for incremental synthesis. Our framework integrates the incremental philosophy of IC3 into the general invariant learning framework ICE.
