By defining a lemma-specific learning objective and introducing a counterexample filtering mechanism, we can achieve sound incremental learning. Under this framework, we instantiate a loop invariant synthesis tool, LimICE, which leverages LLMs to generate the ordered sequence of lemmas and incorporates ICE-DT as a fallback mechanism to complement the lemma sequence. Experiments on 367 linear benchmarks and 50 nonlinear benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. LimICE solves 349 (out of 367) linear problems on an average of 15.2 seconds and 47 (out of 50) nonlinear problems on an average of 8.8 seconds. Compared to the state-of-the-art LLM-based baseline, our approach solves 12-24% more instances while running 36-63% faster across linear and nonlinear benchmarks. LimICE also consistently outperforms strong non-LLM baselines and solves at least 86 and 27 additional instances on the linear and nonlinear benchmarks, respectively.

</details>


### [154] [Not as Sweet by Another Name: An Empirical Study of Format Robustness in LLM Document Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27648)
*Xiaoyu Zhang,Xianyun Cheng,Tianlin Li,Yuwei Zheng,Yue Yang,Yang Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates the format robustness of LLM-driven document workflows, revealing that simply changing document formats (e.g., CSV, PDF) can cause accuracy drops up to 53.63% and decision drifts in over 41% of cases. The authors propose a format-aware metamorphic testing framework, conduct a large-scale empirical study (48,000 executions), and offer lightweight mitigation strategies that recover up to 44.21% of format-induced errors without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM systems are increasingly used in document-centric end-to-end workflows where the same semantic content can be delivered in different file formats. Existing testing research focuses narrowly on single-prompt robustness, leaving unaddressed whether these systems maintain consistent behavior across document format variations—a critical gap given real-world deployment in high-stakes scenarios.

Method: The authors propose a format-aware metamorphic testing framework with three metamorphic relations to evaluate format robustness. They conduct a large-scale empirical study covering 4 representative LLM workflows, 4 real-world tasks, and 4 document formats, totaling 48,000 workflow executions. They also design lightweight mitigation strategies from the user's perspective that require no model retraining.

Result: Format variation poses a systematic threat: accuracy drops by up to 53.63% and decision drifts occur in over 41% of instances merely from switching document formats. The proposed mitigation strategies recover up to 44.21% of format-induced decision drift without retraining.

Conclusion: Document format is not a neutral wrapper but a critical factor affecting LLM system reliability. The findings call for dedicated testing frameworks and safeguards when deploying document-centric LLM workflows in high-stakes real-world settings.

Abstract: LLM-driven software systems are rapidly evolving from plain-text conversations to document-centric end-to-end workflows, where the same semantic content can be delivered in diverse document formats (e.g., CSV) through file upload interfaces. Yet existing testing work focuses on the robustness and reliability of models and systems whose input is a single prompt string, leaving a critical question unanswered: Can these document workflows maintain robust behaviors when the same content arrives in a different document format? To fill the gap, in this paper, we propose a format-aware metamorphic testing framework with three metamorphic relations to comprehensively evaluate the format robustness of end-to-end LLM document workflows. Based on this framework, we conduct a large-scale empirical study spanning four representative LLM workflows, four real-world tasks, and four document formats, comprising a total of 48,000 workflow executions. Our findings reveal that format variation poses a systematic and serious threat. Merely switching formats can cause accuracy to drop by up to 53.63% and trigger decision drifts in over 41% of instances. We further design lightweight mitigation strategies from the users' perspective that recover up to 44.21% of format-induced decision drift without model retraining. Our study demonstrates that document format is not a neutral wrapper but a critical factor affecting the reliability of LLM software systems, calling for corresponding testing and safeguards in the deployment in real-world high-stakes scenarios.

</details>


### [155] [Can Large Language Models Resolve Real Java Merge Conflicts? An Evaluation with a Calibrated LLM-as-Judge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27674)
*Bowen Shen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents an LLM-based merge conflict resolver evaluated with a calibrated LLM-as-judge metric. The LLM solver (a generate-validate-retry agent using only inference-time signals) matches developer resolutions on ~55% of true conflicts, outperforming traditional tools (AutoMerge, 36.7%) by 18-22 points — gains driven by coverage, not accuracy. The G-Eval judge achieves 100% precision at 64.6% recall against human labels. Results also show structural correctness must not be delegated to an LLM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Merge conflicts are a persistent cost in collaborative development. Traditional structured/semi-structured merge tools frequently abstain when heuristics fail, leaving conflicts unresolved. LLMs can generate candidate resolutions for nearly any conflict, but evaluating resolution quality at scale is difficult because human desirability judgments don't scale. The paper addresses both problems — resolution generation and scalable evaluation — simultaneously.

Method: The authors build an LLM solver as a generate-validate-retry agent that uses only inference-time signals: conflict markers, a Java parser, and duplicate-declaration checks — crucially never seeing the developer's ground-truth answer. For evaluation, they introduce a two-metric suite: (1) a developer-match LLM-as-judge (G-Eval metric) calibrated against ConflictBench's human labels, and (2) a deterministic structural-validity check that uses no LLM. The judge is meta-evaluated on 292 human-labeled cases.

Result: The G-Eval judge achieves 100% precision (zero false accepts) at 64.6% recall, making every acceptance trustworthy and downstream rates conservative lower bounds. Under this judge, LLM solvers match the developer's resolution on ~55% of true conflicts. In coverage-fair comparison, LLMs (55-59%) beat AutoMerge (36.7%) by 18-22 points; the advantage comes from coverage (LLMs abstain on 0%, tools on 20-90%). Critically, the LLM judge accepted 4 of 5 resolutions that failed the deterministic structural check, demonstrating LLMs cannot be trusted for structural correctness.

Conclusion: LLM-based merge conflict resolution offers a significant coverage advantage over traditional tools, matching developer intent in a majority of cases. The calibrated LLM-as-judge provides trustworthy, conservative evaluation at scale. However, structural validity must be enforced deterministically — LLM judges are unreliable for syntactic correctness. The two-metric approach (LLM judge + deterministic check) proves both practical and rigorous.

Abstract: Merge conflicts are a recurring cost of collaborative software development, and the traditional structured and semi-structured merge tools that address them frequently abstain: when their heuristics do not apply, they leave the conflict unresolved. Large language models (LLMs) can instead produce a candidate resolution for almost any conflict, but measuring whether those resolutions are actually good at scale is hard, because obtaining human desirability judgments for every model output does not scale. We study both problems together on real Java merge conflicts from ConflictBench. We first build an LLM solver as a generate-validate-retry agent that uses only inference-time signals (conflict markers, a Java parser, and duplicate-declaration checks) and never sees the developer's answer. We then evaluate its resolutions with a two-metric suite: (1) a developer-match LLM-as-judge implemented as a G-Eval metric and, crucially, calibrated against ConflictBench's human labels before use, and (2) a deterministic structural-validity check that uses no LLM. On a meta-evaluation of 292 human-labeled cases, the judge reaches 100% precision (zero false accepts) at 64.6% recall, so every acceptance is trustworthy and every downstream rate is a conservative lower bound. Under this validated judge, LLM solvers match the developer's own resolution on about 55% of true conflicts (conservative floor), and under a coverage-fair comparison the LLMs (55-59%) beat the strongest traditional tool (AutoMerge, 36.7%) by roughly 18-22 points; the edge comes almost entirely from coverage, not raw accuracy, since the tools abstain on 20-90% of conflicts while the LLM under forced resolution abstains on none. Finally, the LLM judge accepted 4 of the 5 resolutions that fail the deterministic structural check, evidence that structural correctness must not be delegated to an LLM.

</details>


### [156] [A comparative analysis of automated techniques for security bug report identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27893)
*Muhammad Laiq*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A comparative analysis of automated techniques for identifying security-related bug reports, evaluating traditional ML, transformer models, and GPT-5.2. SetFit achieved the best F1-score (0.80), while GPT-5.2 performed poorly even with few-shot prompting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The literature on automated identification of security-related bug reports is fragmented: studies evaluate different techniques under incompatible experimental setups, making cross-study comparisons unreliable. This leaves researchers and practitioners without clear, evidence-based guidance on which approach to adopt.

Method: The authors conducted a comparative evaluation using benchmark datasets, testing seven techniques: Logistic Regression, SVM, Random Forest (traditional ML); BERT-base, RoBERTa (fine-tuned transformers); SetFit (few-shot sentence transformer framework); and GPT-5.2 (zero-shot and few-shot). Evaluation used F1-score across four datasets, including both within-project and cross-project transfer learning settings.

Result: SetFit achieved the best overall F1-score of 0.80, outperforming others on 3 of 4 datasets. RoBERTa was competitive and approached SetFit on some projects. Logistic Regression remained a strong baseline in certain contexts. GPT-5.2 performed poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings. Cross-project transfer learning helped data-limited projects but degraded performance when project-specific characteristics were strong.

Conclusion: SetFit offers the best balance of performance and practicality for security bug report identification. Traditional ML (especially Logistic Regression) should not be dismissed as a baseline. GPT-5.2 is not yet suitable for this task. Transfer learning is beneficial only when target-project data is scarce and source/target characteristics align.

Abstract: Timely identification of security-related bug reports is essential to minimize the window of vulnerabilities in software systems. Manually screening incoming bug reports to identify security-related issues is time-consuming, error-prone, and non-scalable for large-scale software systems. Thus, a variety of automatic techniques, including traditional machine learning (ML) techniques and large language models, have been proposed to facilitate this task. However, the literature remains fragmented. Most studies introduce or optimize a particular technique and evaluate it against a limited set of baselines, often under different experimental setups. As a result, it is difficult to compare their results and draw reliable conclusions about the effectiveness of existing approaches, leaving researchers and practitioners without clear guidance on which techniques are most suitable for the task.
  To address this gap, we conducted a comparative analysis of several promising automated techniques to identify security-related bug reports using benchmark datasets. We evaluated Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, OpenAI's GPT-5.2, BERT-base, RoBERTa, and SetFit (a state-of-the-art few-shot learning framework).
  Our results indicate that SetFit achieves the best overall performance, achieving an F1-score of 0.80 and outperforming other techniques on three of the four datasets. RoBERTa performs competitively and approaches SetFit in some projects, while traditional ML techniques, particularly Logistic Regression, remain a strong baseline in certain contexts. In contrast, GPT-5.2 performs poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings. In addition, cross-project experiments demonstrate that transfer learning can improve performance for projects with limited data, but may degrade results for projects with strong project-specific characteristics.

</details>


### [157] [The Case for Vibe Modeling: A Missing Step in AI-Based Trustworthy Software Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27923)
*Shalini Chakraborty,Michael Mittermaier,Judith Michael*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper introduces "vibe modeling" as a lightweight intermediate abstraction between natural language prompts and code generation in LLM-based software development, arguing that current practices over-emphasize direct code output at the expense of traceability and trust. A student survey study explores perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust, and the perceived usefulness of vibe modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI-assisted software development practices focus predominantly on direct code generation from natural language prompts, neglecting intermediate representations that preserve human intent and enable reasoning about system behavior. This creates significant challenges in understanding, validation, traceability, and trust of LLM-generated artifacts.

Method: The authors conducted a student survey study examining perceptions across multiple AI-assisted development scenarios, measuring variables including LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust, and the perceived usefulness of the proposed vibe modeling approach as an intermediate abstraction layer.

Result: Results are presented as preliminary and intended to inform future research directions; specific quantitative or qualitative findings are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: Vibe modeling is proposed as a promising direction for achieving more trustworthy and explainable AI-based software engineering, with the survey results serving as a foundation for future studies in this area.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate software artifacts from natural language prompts. While this enables rapid prototyping and lowers the barrier to software creation, it also introduces challenges related to understanding, validation, traceability, and trust. In this paper, we argue that current AI-based development practices focus too heavily on the direct generation of code and insufficiently on intermediate representations that preserve human intent and support reasoning about system behavior. We argue for vibe modeling as a lightweight intermediate abstraction between natural language interaction and code generation. To explore its potential, we present a student survey study that examines perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust and the perceived usefulness of vibe modeling across several AI-assisted development scenarios. Our results are intended to inform future studies for trustworthy and explainable AI-based software engineering via vibe modeling.

</details>


### [158] [Specification-Guided Synthesis of Deadlock-Free Communication Protocol Refinements with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27964)
*Yang Li,Ping Hou,Nobuko Yoshida*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Syntropy is a framework that combines multiparty session types (MPST) with LLMs to automatically synthesize correct protocol refinements, achieving 95.6–99.5% validity while preserving deadlock freedom guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Protocol refinement—safe substitution of protocols preserving correctness and compatibility—is critical in distributed systems to avoid deadlocks. LLMs excel at code generation but lack behavioral correctness guarantees, while MPST offers rigorous deadlock-freedom guarantees but provides limited automated support for constructing refinements. This paper bridges the gap.

Method: The authors propose Syntropy, a framework that integrates MPST formal specifications into the LLM generation pipeline by embedding refinement constraints directly into the synthesis process. This ensures any generated protocol variant provably satisfies deadlock freedom and compatibility with existing components.

Result: A comprehensive evaluation shows Syntropy achieves 95.6%–99.5% validity across multiple LLMs, maintains high syntactic correctness, and produces diverse, non-trivial protocol refinements.

Conclusion: Syntropy demonstrates that combining formal methods (MPST) with LLMs is a viable approach for automated, correct-by-construction protocol refinement synthesis, overcoming the individual limitations of each technique.

Abstract: Ensuring behavioural correctness in communication protocols is a central challenge in distributed software systems, as subtle inconsistencies can lead to deadlocks. In such settings, protocol refinement - the safe substitution of a protocol that preserves correctness and compatibility with other components - is essential. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and program synthesis, yet lack mechanisms to reliably produce outputs with correct behaviour. Formal specification approaches, such as multiparty session types (MPST), offer rigorous guarantees, including deadlock freedom, but provide limited support for automatically constructing protocol refinements. In this paper, we present Syntropy, a framework for synthesising protocol refinements guided by MPST specifications and LLMs. It incorporates refinement constraints directly into the generation process, ensuring the generated variants satisfy these guarantees. Our comprehensive evaluation indicates that Syntropy achieves 95.6%-99.5% validity while maintaining high syntactic correctness, and produces diverse, non-trivial refinements across multiple LLMs.

</details>


### [159] [Advancing Awkward Arrays for High-Performance CPU and GPU Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28145)
*Ianna Osborne,Manasvi Goyal*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Awkward Array now features a GPU backend with CUDA/CCCL implementations, optimized memory management, and segmented reduction algorithms for ragged arrays, preserving the Python API while significantly improving GPU throughput on nested, variable-length data common in high-energy physics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: HL-LHC analyses increasingly depend on accelerator hardware (GPUs), yet nested, variable-length data structures — core to high-energy physics — resist GPU acceleration due to indirect indexing, segmented operations, and irregular memory access patterns. Existing solutions lack efficient GPU support for such irregular workloads while maintaining a usable Python programming model.

Method: The authors developed a GPU backend for Awkward Array using CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CCCL (CUDA Core Compute Libraries). Key components include optimized memory management tailored for ragged data structures and segmented reduction algorithms. The architecture preserves the existing Python programming model and includes an automated validation framework. Benchmarks compare CPU, CuPy, and CUDA implementations.

Result: The GPU backend substantially improves throughput on irregular workloads compared to CPU and CuPy implementations, as demonstrated by benchmark results, while maintaining the same Python API surface.

Conclusion: Efficient GPU acceleration of nested, variable-length data is achievable through careful backend design leveraging CCCL, optimized memory management, and segmented reductions, without sacrificing the high-level Python programming model that Awkward Array users rely on.

Abstract: Awkward Array is a Python library for representing and processing nested, variable-length data that is widely used in high-energy physics. As HL-LHC analyses increasingly rely on accelerator hardware, efficient execution of irregular workloads has become essential. While dense numerical arrays map naturally to GPUs, nested and variable-length data structures remain significantly more difficult to accelerate because they require indirect indexing, segmented operations, and irregular memory access patterns. We present recent developments in the Awkward Array GPU backend, including CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CUDA Core Compute Libraries (CCCL), optimized memory management, and segmented reduction algorithms for ragged arrays. These developments preserve the existing Python programming model while substantially improving GPU throughput on irregular workloads. We describe the backend architecture, automated validation framework, and benchmark results comparing CPU, CuPy, and CUDA implementations.

</details>


### [160] [Integrating AI into Requirements Quality Learning in Software Engineering Education: A TPACK-Guided Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28176)
*Hansika Ekanayake Mudiyanselage,Rohan Jai Dharmaraj,Malik Abdul Sami,Zheying Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A TPACK-guided multi-agent AI tool was integrated into a master-level requirements engineering assignment. Students (N=100) used AI selectively for analysis rather than automation, showing improved understanding of concrete quality dimensions (value articulation, testability) but mixed results for negotiability. The study offers design guidance for responsible AI integration in RE education.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid adoption of generative AI in software engineering practice creates an urgent need for pedagogically sound approaches to integrating AI into SE education, particularly in conceptually intensive areas like requirements engineering where the risks of uncritical AI use are high.

Method: A mixed-methods design with 100 participants and 72 analyzed submissions. The study examined a TPACK-guided (Technological, Pedagogical, and Content Knowledge) structured assignment that incorporated a multi-agent AI tool into a master-level RE task on user story quality analysis. Both quantitative alignment measures and qualitative perceptions were assessed.

Result: Students used the AI tool selectively as analytical support rather than for automation. Alignment improvements were strongest for structurally concrete quality dimensions (value articulation, testability) but mixed for negotiability. Students reported conditional trust in AI outputs, engaged in active refinement, and developed increased awareness of quality criteria, though moderate usability challenges were noted.

Conclusion: TPACK-guided scaffolding can successfully align AI affordances with pedagogical goals and RE content, providing actionable design guidance for responsible AI integration in requirements engineering education without displacing critical human judgment.

Abstract: The rapid adoption of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in software engineering (SE) practice creates a need for pedagogically grounded approaches to AI integration in SE education, especially in conceptually intensive subjects such as requirements engineering (RE). This study examines a TPACK-guided integration of a multi-agent AI tool into a master-level RE assignment on requirements quality analysis. Using a mixed-methods design (N=100; 72 submissions analysed), we examine how structured assignment design shaped students' AI use, affected their understanding of user story quality criteria, and influenced their perceptions of AI's benefits and limitations. Results show that students used the AI tool selectively, mainly as support for analysis and evaluation rather than automation. Alignment improvements were most evident for structurally concrete requirements quality dimensions, such as value articulation and testability, while negotiability showed mixed effects. Students reported conditional trust, active refinement, and increased awareness of quality criteria, alongside moderate usability challenges. The findings show that TPACK-guided scaffolding can align AI affordances with pedagogical goals and RE content, offering design guidance for responsible AI integration in RE education.

</details>


### [161] [Agentic Metaverse Services: A New As-a-Service Paradigm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28242)
*Xiaofei Xu,Quan Z. Sheng,Zhongjie Wang,Boualem Benatallah,Xiao Wang,Ruipeng Han*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper introduces Agentic Metaverse Service (AMServ) and Meta-AaaS — a paradigm combining GenAI-powered agentic services with the metaverse, where agent abilities (perception, decision-making, execution, collaboration, content generation) are encapsulated as services for metaverse business processing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The shift from conversational chatbots to agentic AI, driven by GenAI breakthroughs, has created agentic services and Agent-as-a-Service (AaaS). However, these have not been systematically examined within the metaverse context, creating a need to formalize how agentic services can operate in and enhance metaverse ecosystems.

Method: The paper takes a conceptual/overview approach: it traces the evolution of agents and services under GenAI, articulates the roles and principles of agentic services in the metaverse, defines AMServ and Meta-AaaS (their forms, characteristics, and principles), provides application examples, and identifies future research directions.

Result: The paper formally defines AMServ as a new metaverse service form and Meta-AaaS as the realization approach. It presents the characteristics, principles, and typical application scenarios of both constructs, and maps out emerging tendencies and open research directions for the field.

Conclusion: AMServ and Meta-AaaS represent a significant opportunity for human society and the service industry in the AI era, poised to drive rapid development of emerging service industries by integrating agentic AI capabilities into metaverse environments.

Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reconstructing the digital virtual world, upgrading agents through enhancing their abilities in autonomous learning, multi-modal interaction, content generation, and collaborative decision-making. In particular, the shift from conversational chatbots to agentic AI, the most recent significant technical breakthrough of GenAI, has brought a new form of services, agentic services and Agent-as-a-Service (AaaS), in which the agent's abilities are encapsulated, such as perception, decision-making, execution, collaboration, and content generation, to provide the customized agent services to users. The metaverse is a virtual ecosystem for human life, work, creation, and entertainment, supported by the new generation of digital technologies. Through combining agentic services and the metaverse, an Agentic Metaverse Service, denoted as AMServ, is produced for metaverse business processing, as a new form of metaverse service. The AaaS in the metaverse environment, denoted as Meta-AaaS, as an approach to realize AMServ, has become a new paradigm of agentic services and service computing. This paper overviews the evolution and new features of agents and services empowered by GenAI, reveals the roles and principles of agentic services in the metaverse environment, presents the forms, characteristics, and principles of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS, discusses the typical application examples of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS, and finally points out the new tendencies and research directions of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS. The AMServ and the Meta-AaaS will bring great opportunities to human society and services in the AI era, and promote the rapid development of emerging service industries in the future.

</details>


### [162] [Agentic Method for Deterministic Validation of Legacy Code Migration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28271)
*Andras Ferenczi,Jordan Docherty,Mariya Bessonov,Matthew Findlay,Krishna Lingamneni*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper presents the "Locksmith Loop," an agentic test-synthesis method for migrating COBOL to Java. It uses an iterative loop of Witness Search to explore branches via input mocks and parity-preserving mutations, identifying "Locked Paragraphs" that block deeper exploration. Tested on three programs (430–4,114 LOC), the approach achieved near-complete coverage on two open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on a production-like program, with deterministic parity checks ensuring Java output matches COBOL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Migrating legacy COBOL programs to Java requires extensive testing, but this is complicated by a lack of test data and the difficulty of validating all corner cases. Existing approaches struggle with systematic coverage of program branches.

Method: The Locksmith Loop sets up dual runtime environments: COBOL source and generated Java, each instrumented with mocks and executed off-mainframe on commodity hardware. An iterative agentic loop performs Witness Search over input mocks to penetrate program branches, followed by parity-preserving mutations. When routing boundaries are encountered, an analyzer identifies Locked Paragraphs — conditions preventing deeper exploration — enabling targeted intervention.

Result: Across three COBOL-Java case studies (two open-source, one internal production-like; 430–4,114 SLOC), Locksmith consistently improved coverage beyond input-search plateaus, achieving near-complete coverage on the two open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on the internal production-like program. Generated Java matched the COBOL reference under deterministic parity checks in all accepted test cases.

Conclusion: The authors demonstrate a novel approach for validating agentic coding output using a deterministic oracle, showing that the Locksmith Loop can achieve high branch coverage and reliable parity between COBOL source and Java target in migration testing scenarios.

Abstract: Migration of legacy COBOL programs to Java requires extensive testing to ensure correct functionality. This effort is often complicated by the lack of test data and the difficulty of validating all corner cases. In this paper we propose a novel agentic test-synthesis method, the "Locksmith Loop," which is initiated by preparing two runtime environments: the COBOL source and the generated Java target are each instrumented with mocks and executed off-mainframe on commodity hardware, then an iterative agentic loop performs Witness Search over input mocks to penetrate program branches, followed by parity-preserving mutations. When routing boundaries are reached, an analyzer identifies a Locked Paragraph: a condition preventing deeper exploration. Across three COBOL-Java case studies, spanning two open-source programs and one internal production-like COBOL program and ranging from 430 to 4,114 source lines, Locksmith consistently improved coverage beyond input-search plateaus, reaching nearly complete coverage on the two open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on the internal production-like COBOL program. The generated Java matched the COBOL reference under deterministic parity checks in all accepted test cases. Through these findings we demonstrate, to the best of our knowledge, a novel approach for validating agentic coding output using a deterministic oracle.

</details>


### [163] [From Textual Requirements to Microservice Architectures - A Comprehensive Evaluation of LLM-Based Design Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28307)
*Danyllo Albuquerque,José Renan,Guillermo Rodríguez,Guillermo Rodríguez,Emanuel Dantas,Ademar França,Mirko Perkusich,Kyller Gorgônio,Angelo Perkusich*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study investigates whether OpenAI o3 can generate microservice architectures directly from natural-language requirements using zero-shot and few-shot prompting. Evaluated on two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic), few-shot prompting achieves near-perfect service identification (F1=0.97 vs. 0.79 ZS) and substantially improved communication recovery (F1=0.82 vs. 0.61 ZS). Expert assessment confirms few-shot outputs are more modular, coherent, and plausible, demonstrating LLM potential for requirements-driven architectural synthesis when guided by exemplars.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing microservice decomposition approaches are predominantly code-centric, limiting their applicability in early design stages where only textual requirements are available. Despite advances in LLMs, limited empirical evidence exists on their ability to synthesize complete microservice architectures—including service definitions and inter-service interactions—from natural-language requirements alone.

Method: A mixed-method study using OpenAI o3 under zero-shot (ZS) and few-shot (FS) prompting across two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic), with one execution per system/condition. Evaluation combines: (i) quantitative comparison with reference architectures using precision, recall, and F1-score for service identification and communication recovery; and (ii) a blinded expert assessment covering correctness, completeness, modularity, and plausibility, plus open feedback synthesis.

Result: Few-shot prompting dramatically outperforms zero-shot: service identification F1 improves from 0.79 (ZS) to 0.97 (FS). Communication recovery is harder—ZS produces dense architectures with high recall but low precision (F1=0.61), while FS reaches F1=0.82 with fewer unsupported dependencies. Expert evaluation corroborates these findings, with FS architectures rated as more modular, coherent, and plausible.

Conclusion: OpenAI o3 demonstrates clear potential for requirements-driven microservice architecture synthesis when guided by exemplar-based prompting. However, results are model- and context-specific (two small systems), not constituting model-independent proof. Broader validation across diverse systems and models is needed.

Abstract: Microservice architectures have become dominant for modernizing monolithic systems, yet identifying appropriate services remains challenging and largely manual. Existing decomposition approaches are predominantly code-centric, limiting applicability in early design stages where only textual requirements are available. Despite advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), limited empirical evidence exists on their ability to synthesize complete microservice architectures from natural-language requirements, including service definitions and inter-service interactions. This study investigates whether an LLM can bridge requirements engineering and architectural design, generating architectures solely from textual requirements and evaluating structural agreement and perceived quality of results. We conduct a mixed-method study using OpenAI o3 under zero-shot (ZS) and few-shot (FS) prompting across two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic), one execution per system/condition. Architectures are evaluated through (i) comparison with reference architectures using precision, recall, and F1-score for service identification and communication recovery, and (ii) a blinded expert assessment of correctness, completeness, modularity, and plausibility, plus open feedback synthesis. OpenAI o3 identifies services with higher agreement under FS prompting (F1 = 0.79 for ZS versus = 0.97 for FS). Communication recovery is more challenging: ZS produces dense architectures with high recall but low precision (F1 = 0.61), while FS improves agreement, reaching F1 = 0.82 and reducing unsupported dependencies. Expert evaluation corroborates these results, with FS architectures perceived as more modular, coherent, and plausible than ZS outputs. OpenAI o3 shows potential for requirements-driven synthesis when guided by exemplar prompting. Results are model- and context-specific from two small systems, not model-independent proof.

</details>


### [164] [Structural Validation of LLM-Generated Microservice Decompositions Using Source-Code Dependencies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28331)
*Daniel Silva,Renan Alves,Emanuel Dantas Filho,Ademar Sousa Neto,Mirko Perkusich,Danyllo Wagner Albuquerque,Kyller Gorgônio,Angelo Perkusich*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether LLM-generated microservice decompositions (using OpenAI o3) preserve source-code structural dependencies. An automated validation pipeline using static dependency analysis compares zero-shot and few-shot prompting on two benchmark systems, revealing that after controlling for mapping coverage, both strategies yield equivalent structural adherence (68%–83% TPD). The study cautions that without coverage normalization, apparent differences between prompting strategies may stem from methodological bias rather than true architectural quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs can produce semantically plausible microservice decompositions from textual requirements, no prior work has rigorously assessed whether these decompositions respect the actual structural dependencies encoded in source code. The authors aim to fill this gap and to determine whether prompting strategy (zero-shot vs. few-shot) meaningfully affects structural adherence.

Method: An automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis is applied to decompositions generated by OpenAI o3 for two systems (PetClinic and Bookstore). Two metrics are used: Total Preserved Dependencies (TPD) and Total Violated Dependencies (TVD). Zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies are compared, with a robustness analysis that normalizes for class-to-service mapping coverage to control for confounding effects.

Result: After normalization for mapping coverage, both prompting strategies produced equivalent structural adherence: TPD of 68.0% for PetClinic and 83.3% for Bookstore. Apparent differences between strategies before normalization were attributable to differences in mapping coverage rather than genuine architectural quality.

Conclusion: Structural evaluations of LLM-generated microservice decompositions must explicitly control for mapping coverage; otherwise, observed differences between prompting strategies may reflect methodological bias. The work establishes a baseline for structurally-aware, LLM-driven decomposition and advocates for coverage-normalized metrics in future evaluations.

Abstract: Decomposing monolithic systems into microservices is a key activity in software modernization. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate semantically plausible decompositions from textual requirements, it remains unclear whether these proposals preserve the structural dependencies implemented in the source code. This paper evaluates the structural adherence of microservice decompositions generated by OpenAI o3 for the PetClinic and Bookstore systems. We propose an automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis and compare zero-shot and few-shot prompting using dependency preservation (TPD) and dependency violation (TVD) metrics. A robustness analysis was conducted to control for differences in class-to-service mapping coverage. After normalization, both prompting strategies produced equivalent structural adherence, achieving TPD values of 68.0% (PetClinic) and 83.3% (Bookstore). The findings demonstrate that structural evaluations of LLM-generated decompositions should explicitly control for mapping coverage, as apparent differences between prompting strategies may otherwise reflect methodological bias rather than genuine architectural quality.

</details>


### [165] [Demystifying Solana Bots: From GitHub Blueprints to On-Chain Fingerprints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28424)
*Xiaoye Zheng,Yujing Chen,Minghao Wu,David Lo,Difan Xie,Daoyuan Wu,Xiaohu Yang,Zhiyuan Wan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A systematic empirical study analyzing Solana bots from both code (586 GitHub repositories) and on-chain data (200 bot addresses, 44M+ transactions), yielding a 15-category taxonomy across five domains, identifying a common five-stage operational pipeline, and revealing systematic variations in trading behaviors across platforms and assets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Solana's high throughput and low fees attract substantial bot activity — exceeding $250M in daily DEX trading volume — yet prior research lacks a systematic understanding of bot implementations and their on-chain footprints. This gap motivates a comprehensive dual-view empirical characterization.

Method: A large-scale empirical study combining two complementary perspectives: (1) qualitative and quantitative analysis of 586 open-source bot repositories mined from GitHub, and (2) on-chain analysis of 200 identified bot addresses on Solana encompassing over 44 million transactions, cross-referencing implementation patterns with observable execution behaviors.

Result: The study produces (1) a taxonomy of 15 bot categories organized into five domains (Trading Operations, MEV, On-chain Analytics, and others); (2) identification of a largely shared five-stage operational pipeline across diverse bot implementations; and (3) evidence of systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors tied to different trading platforms and asset types.

Conclusion: The findings establish a foundational understanding of Solana bot ecosystems, highlighting future research directions and offering actionable recommendations for building and operating bots on Solana responsibly.

Abstract: Solana is an emerging blockchain platform designed for high throughput and low transaction fees, making it inexpensive to submit transactions at scale and, consequently, increasing exposure to bot spamming and related financial exploitation. Solana bots are typically off-chain software systems that operate in a competitive on-chain execution environment by constructing and submitting transactions, and the bot-related transactions on the decentralized exchanges exceed 250 million dollars in daily trading volume in January 2026. Prior studies on Solana have examined system performance, smart-contract security, and specific on-chain phenomena. However, we still lack a systematic understanding of what Solana bots implement in practice and how these implementations manifest as observable on-chain execution fingerprints. To address this gap, we performed a large-scale empirical study of Solana bots from two complementary views: (i) 586 bot repositories collected from GitHub, and (ii) 200 bot addresses on Solana, with over 44 million on-chain transactions. Our study derives an implementation-grounded taxonomy of Solana bots comprising 15 categories grouped into five domains (e.g., Trading Operations, MEV, and On-chain Analytics), identifies a largely shared five-stage operational pipeline manifested in bot implementations, and uncovers systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors of Solana bots across diverse trading platforms and assets. Based on our findings, we highlight future research directions, and provide recommendations for building and operating bots on the Solana blockchain.

</details>


### [166] [Emerging Challenges in Threat Modeling for GenAI-Augmented Systems: A View from the Trenches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28431)
*Nicolás E. Díaz Ferreyra,Manish Mahesh Kumar,Nohemí Villarreal,Pankaj Pantel,Immo Brueggemann,Riccardo Scandariato*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An exploratory study evaluating three GenAI-aware threat modeling methods in an SME context reveals gaps in coverage for GenAI-specific risks, particularly supply chain and human-centered threats, and identifies practitioner-perceived usability and adoption challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional threat modeling methods like STRIDE are inadequate for capturing emerging risks specific to Generative AI systems. As GenAI becomes pervasive in software systems, there is an urgent need to assess whether existing GenAI-aware threat modeling methods are effective and practical for real-world industrial adoption, particularly in resource-constrained SME environments.

Method: The authors conducted a rapid literature review to identify and shortlist three GenAI-aware threat modeling techniques. These methods were then systematically applied to an industrial case study of a GenAI-augmented system within an SME setting. The study assessed both the types of threats identified by each method and practitioners' perceptions regarding usability, integration effort, and adoption barriers.

Result: The three methods produced notably different threat profiles, indicating inconsistent coverage. Critical gaps were found in GenAI-specific risk categories, especially software supply chain threats and human-centered security issues. Practitioners reported concerns about the effort required and challenges integrating these methods into existing SME development workflows.

Conclusion: Current GenAI-aware threat modeling methods show promise but remain incomplete and variably effective when applied in SME industrial settings. There is a clear need for more comprehensive, usable, and integration-friendly threat modeling approaches that address GenAI-specific risks — particularly supply chain and human-centric threats — tailored to the constraints of smaller organizations.

Abstract: Threat modeling remains a central task in secure software engineering, as it enables the identification of security issues from system architectures. As Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly pervasive across software systems, traditional threat modeling methods (e.g., STRIDE) are insufficient to assess emerging GenAI-specific risks. In this work, we present the first results from an exploratory assessment of GenAI-aware threat modeling methods in a Small and Medium Enterprise (SME) setting. For this, we conducted a rapid literature review to select relevant techniques and systematically applied three shortlisted methods to an industrial case study involving a GenAI-augmented system. The results highlight differences in the threats identified by each technique and reveal limited support for certain GenAI-specific risk categories, particularly those related to software supply chains and human-centered security issues. We further report practitioners' perceptions of the usability and integration of these methods in SME development workflows, including their perceived effort and adoption challenges.

</details>


### [167] [CoGate: Confidence-Gated Co-Decoding for Secure Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28529)
*Minghao Hu,Lannan Luo,Allen Roush,Phillip Howard*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CoGate introduces a confidence-gated decoding mechanism for secure code generation, where the influence of a security expert model during co-decoding is modulated based on its confidence level, preventing misleading guidance from out-of-distribution contexts and achieving up to 12.6% improvement on CWEval over existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing co-decoding approaches for secure code generation apply the security expert's guidance uniformly, without considering the expert's confidence. When the expert encounters unseen patterns or OOD contexts, its low-confidence guidance can mislead the generation process, producing insecure code despite the steering mechanism.

Method: CoGate (Confidence-Gated Co-Decoding) controls the expert model's influence during decoding based on its confidence score. At each decoding step, the expert's confidence is evaluated, and its guidance is gated — allowed through when confidence is high, suppressed when low — preventing unreliable steering from OOD or unfamiliar contexts.

Result: Evaluated across multiple LLM backends (CodeGen, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen-Coder, StarCoder) on HumanEval, security suite, and CWEval benchmarks, CoGate outperforms existing co-decoding methods (CoSec+), achieving up to a 12.6% improvement in Func-Sec@10 on CWEval.

Conclusion: Confidence-gating is an effective mechanism for improving the reliability of decoding-time steering for secure code generation, ensuring that only confident, trustworthy expert guidance influences the output and mitigating the risk of OOD-induced errors.

Abstract: Large language models are widely used for code generation, but they can also produce insecure programs due to patterns learned from their pretraining data. Decoding-time steering has become an important solution to this problem: a small expert model is combined with the target model at each step to generate more secure code, which is referred to as co-decoding. However, the acceptance rule for existing co-decoding approaches does not consider the expert model's confidence. When the security expert is unconfident due to unseen patterns or out-of-distribution (OOD) contexts, its guidance can therefore be misleading. To address the challenge, we propose CoGate, a confidence-gated co-decoding approach that controls the expert's influence on the co-decoding process based on its confidence. We implement our approach and evaluate it across multiple LLM backends (CodeGen, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen-Coder, StarCoder) on several code generation benchmarks (HumanEval, security suite, and CWEval). Our approach outperforms existing co-decoding methods (CoSec+) across multiple benchmarks, achieving up to a 12.6% gain of Func-Sec@10 on CWEval.

</details>


### [168] [PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28587)
*Manyi Wang,Junjielong Xu,Pinjia He*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SWE-bench benchmarks suffer from PR-Issue misalignment (13.6% in Verified subset across five patterns/eleven scenarios). The authors propose PAIChecker, a three-phase multi-agent system combining pattern identification, cross-agent label synthesis, and code-level validation to detect misalignment, achieving up to 92.12% binary accuracy on SWE-Gym and 91.67% on SWE-bench Multilingual.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SWE-bench-like benchmarks are widely used to evaluate LLMs' issue-resolution capabilities, but their construction relies on pairing PRs with linked issues via issue references in PR descriptions. In practice, these PR-Issue pairings are often misaligned due to the complexity of large repository maintenance, compromising benchmark reliability. No systematic study or automated detection method previously existed for this problem.

Method: PAIChecker is a multi-agent system with a three-phase design: (1) specific pattern identification to recognize five misalignment patterns across eleven fine-grained scenarios, (2) cross-agent label synthesis where multiple agents collaboratively produce consensus labels, and (3) code-level validation for progressively verified detection. The system is evaluated across four LLM backbones.

Result: Systematic analysis of SWE-bench Verified reveals 13.6% of instances exhibit misalignment. PAIChecker achieves the best performance across all four LLM backbones on both SWE-Gym (up to 92.12% binary accuracy) and SWE-bench Multilingual (up to 91.67% binary accuracy).

Conclusion: PR-Issue misalignment is a non-trivial problem in SWE-bench-like benchmarks. PAIChecker provides a reliable, scalable, and generalizable solution for detecting such misalignment, enabling more trustworthy benchmark construction in the future.

Abstract: SWE-bench-like benchmarks are widely used for evaluating LLM's issue resolution capability. They typically follow a common construction pipeline: each PR (Pull Request) is paired with its linked issue by extracting issue references from the PR description; the issue description is used as the problem statement, and the PR patch serves as the test oracle. However, due to the inherent complexity of developing and maintaining large repositories, such PR-Issue pairings are often misaligned in practice. In this work, we systematically study SWE-bench Verified instances, finding that 13.6% exhibit misalignment across five patterns in eleven fine-grained scenarios. To enable reliable and scalable construction of those benchmarks in the future, we propose PAIChecker, a multi-agent system for checking PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench-like benchmarks. Specifically, PAIChecker adopts a three-phase design that combines specific pattern identification, cross-agent label synthesis, and code-level validation, thereby enabling more accurate, generalizable, and progressively verified detection. Experiments on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual show that PAIchecker achieves the best performance across all four LLM backbones, reaching up to 92.12% and 91.67% binary accuracy, respectively.

</details>


### [169] [Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28591)
*Haomin Qi,Xingliang Wang,Xuanqi Gao,Baihui Sang,Xin Zhang,Minghua Ma,Pengfei Gao,Yu Kang,Qingwei Lin,Saravan Rajmohan,Dongmei Zhang,Qi Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Change2Task is a system that derives verified, executable coding tasks from merged pull requests by reconstructing task states on modern repository revisions. It achieves 79.6% task construction success across five task families and recovers 29.2% more verified tasks than a PR-based baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scaling coding agents requires a continuous supply of executable data for training, benchmarking, and evaluation. Manually creating tasks that couple realistic software states with specifications, tools, and verification is expensive and unsustainable. Repository history (merged PRs) contains rich, developer-authenticated evidence, but directly using historical commits fails because modern codebases have evolved. Change2Task bridges this gap by leveraging historical evidence to create tasks on current, healthy repository states.

Method: Change2Task operates in three stages: (1) Aligning historical evidence from merged PRs with the evolved modern codebase; (2) Reconstructing task states via one of three strategies — Patch Reversal (reverting the fix), Code Mapping (transplanting the change to modern code), or Agent Reconstruction (using an agent to recreate the state); (3) Validating the full lifecycle: from a healthy modern base → task state (with injected defect/missing feature) → restored state (post-fix). The system targets five task families: Bug Fix, Feature Addition, Test Generation, API Migration, and Security Repair.

Result: From 1,130 eligible source changes, Change2Task achieves 79.6% verified task construction success across all five task families. On a matched candidate set, it recovers 29.2% more verified tasks than a baseline that constructs tasks directly from pull requests. Historical and reconstructed cases exhibit up to 98.0% matched outcome agreement under agent evaluation. Reuse of modern bases reduces measured pipeline expenditure by 10.8%.

Conclusion: Change2Task demonstrates that repository history can be effectively mined to produce verified, executable coding tasks at scale. By grounding task construction in developer evidence and modern, maintained environments, the system addresses a critical bottleneck in coding agent research while improving efficiency through base reuse.

Abstract: Scaling coding agents requires a continuing supply of executable data for training, benchmarking, and continuous evaluation. Each task must couple a realistic software state with a specification, development tools, and reliable verification. To expand this supply, we present Change2Task, a system grounded in repository history that converts merged pull requests into verified tasks on healthy modern revisions of the same repository. It aligns historical evidence with evolved code, reconstructs task states through Patch Reversal, Code Mapping, or Agent Reconstruction, and validates the lifecycle from a healthy base to a task state and a restored state. By deriving multiple tasks grounded in developer evidence from maintained environments, Change2Task provides executable data for coding agent training and evaluation while reducing repeated environment setup, storage, and task construction effort. We evaluate the system through five common and widely adopted coding agent task families: Bug Fix, Feature Addition, Test Generation, Application Programming Interface Migration, and Security Repair. Starting from 1,130 source changes eligible for construction, Change2Task achieves 79.6% verified task construction success across these task families. On a matched candidate set, it recovers 29.2% more verified tasks than a construction baseline based on pull requests. Historical and reconstructed cases achieve up to 98.0% matched outcome agreement under agent evaluation, while reuse of modern bases reduces measured expenditure across the complete pipeline by 10.8%.

</details>

# cs.IR [[Back]](#toc)

### [170] [OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27475)
*Ziwei Li,Shuyao Li,Xufeng Cai,Xue Zou,Yiming Ma,Huiting Lu,Wujie Yan,Zhichen Zhao,Yang Lu,Zhe Wang,Rui Luo,Zhengyu Su,Dan Zhang,Ji Liu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: OneShot is an end-to-end retrieval framework that jointly learns indexing and ranking objectives, resolving the structural misalignment between ranking accuracy and indexing efficiency. Deployed at Instagram, it delivers 20% recall gains and 10x efficiency improvements through neural scoring beyond dot-product.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional retrieval systems suffer from a fundamental misalignment: ranking models optimize for prediction accuracy against user behavior, while indexing structures optimize for proximity-based fast search among billions of items. This structural dichotomy limits retrieval expressiveness, particularly constraining interaction modeling to dot-product bottlenecks despite scaling efforts.

Method: OneShot proposes an in-model index learning framework that natively co-optimizes index structure and ranking objectives in an end-to-end fashion. It replaces the conventional two-stage paradigm (separate indexing then ranking) with joint learning, and scales neural interaction modeling beyond the dot-product limitation for richer retrieval expressiveness.

Result: Fully deployed in Instagram's short-video recommendation system, OneShot achieved significant uplift in user daily sessions, engagement, and time-spent. Quantitatively, it delivered a 20% recall gain at operational ranking volume and a 10x efficiency improvement at equivalent recall levels.

Conclusion: By structurally aligning index learning with ranking objectives, OneShot effectively resolves a long-standing dichotomy in large-scale retrieval systems, demonstrating that joint optimization can simultaneously improve both effectiveness and efficiency in production-scale industrial recommendation.

Abstract: In modern recommendation systems, retrieval serves as a primary stage responsible for filtering billions of candidate items down to thousands prior to refined ranking. To make this massive search effective and efficient, the system relies on ranking accuracy and indexing efficiency. However, these two objectives are traditionally misaligned: while the former optimizes for the alignment between ranking predictions and user behavior, the latter optimizes for a structural grouping of item representations which enables fast search among billions of candidates. Thus, despite extensive efforts to scale up interaction modeling for retrieval, they remain fundamentally limited by the structural misalignment between the ranking objectives and the proximity-learned index. In this work, we address this long-standing dichotomy by proposing a new holistic retrieval framework, OneShot. It is an end-to-end, in-model index learning framework that natively aligns index learning with ranking objectives. Using this joint learning as a structural foundation, OneShot pushes the boundaries of retrieval expressiveness by scaling interaction modeling with neural scoring beyond the persistent dot-product bottleneck. OneShot is fully deployed in Instagram's industrial short-video recommendation system, driving significant wins in user daily sessions, engagement, and time-spent. Additionally, OneShot achieves a $20\%$ recall gain at the operational ranking volume and a 10x efficiency improvement at an equivalent recall level.

</details>


### [171] [Hierarchical Reranking for Scalable Financial RAG System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27523)
*Joohyun Lee,Sungwoo Hong*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Proposes Hierarchical Reranker, a RAG framework for financial document analysis that improves retrieval and generation through pre-retrieval optimization, two-stage ranking, and long-context management, achieving 0.7918 NDCG@20 and second place in the ACM-ICAIF '24 FinanceRAG Challenge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG systems struggle with hybrid text-table structures and the massive scale of financial documents (10-K filings, tabular disclosures, macroeconomic reports), which demand expert reasoning and extensive time.

Method: Three integrated innovations: (1) Pre-Retrieval Optimization via normalization, keyword expansion, and table transformation; (2) Hierarchical Reranker Architecture with two-stage ranking; (3) Long-Context Management using adaptive input partitioning and fusion under extensive contexts.

Result: Achieved NDCG@20 of 0.7918 across FinQA, FinanceBench, and ConvFinQA benchmarks with superior factual consistency. Secured second place in the ACM-ICAIF '24 FinanceRAG Challenge.

Conclusion: The framework presents a deployable, domain-optimized RAG pipeline that enhances accuracy and scalability of financial reasoning, enabling automated audit reporting and quantitative investment analysis. Code to be open-sourced on GitHub.

Abstract: Analyzing financial documents such as 10-K filings, tabular disclosures, and macroeconomic reports demands expert reasoning and extensive time. However, existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems often struggle to process hybrid text-table structures or the massive scale of financial documents. To address these challenges, we propose Hierarchical Reranker, a RAG framework designed to improve retrieval performance and generative reliability across large-scale financial datasets. The system integrates three key innovations: Pre-Retrieval Optimization, enhancing query clarity and search efficiency through normalization, keyword expansion, and table transformation; Hierarchical Reranker Architecture, improving retrieval precision through a two-stage ranking mechanism; and Long-Context Management, preserving reasoning accuracy through adaptive input partitioning and fusion under extensive contexts. Across multiple benchmarks, including FinQA, FinanceBench, and ConvFinQA, the proposed system achieved an NDCG@20 score of 0.7918 and demonstrated superior factual consistency. Its robustness was further validated by achieving second place in the ACM-ICAIF '24 FinanceRAG Challenge. This work presents a deployable, domain-optimized RAG pipeline that enhances both the accuracy and scalability of financial reasoning, paving the way for automated audit reporting and quantitative investment analysis. The source code will be made publicly available on GitHub upon acceptance.

</details>


### [172] [Heterogeneous Ranking in Industrial-Scale Recommender Systems: A Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27577)
*Di Bai,Jintao Liu,Zhenwei Tang,Peifan Wu,Nada Al-Thawr,Luoshu Wang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: HA-MoE is a heterogeneity-adaptive mixture-of-experts architecture for unified ranking in heterogeneous content feeds (e.g., Google Discover). It injects explicit heterogeneity context into gating and expert representations, with LENS for expert specialization diagnostics and DL-AUC for evaluation. Both offline and online A/B tests confirm consistent gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unified recommendation feeds like Google Discover aggregate diverse content types (articles, short/long-form videos, UGC) from the open web, each with distinct feature densities and user interaction patterns. Existing unified ranking models suffer from negative transfer, majority bias, and inability to specialize across this heterogeneity without excessive operational overhead.

Method: The authors propose HA-MoE, a multi-gated mixture-of-experts architecture that incorporates explicit heterogeneity context (content type signals) into both the gating networks and expert representations, enabling content-type-aware specialization. They also introduce LENS, a lightweight observability framework for diagnosing and tracking functional heterogeneity of expert specialization during continuous retraining. For evaluation, they propose DL-AUC (Dual-Level AUC), a metric that combines global ranking performance with cross-segment ranking correctness.

Result: Offline evaluations on large-scale industrial data show consistent improvements over baseline models. Online A/B testing demonstrates significant gains in feed activity and exploration metrics, validating the approach in production.

Conclusion: HA-MoE effectively addresses the heterogeneity challenge in industrial-scale unified ranking by enabling content-type-aware expert specialization without significant operational cost. Combined with LENS observability and DL-AUC evaluation, the approach provides a complete framework for deploying and monitoring heterogeneous feed ranking systems.

Abstract: Heterogeneous recommendation feeds present complex challenges that extend beyond those found in highly homogeneous environments (e.g., music-only or video-only closed-ecosystem platforms). In Google Discover, a unified feed integrates diverse content sourced from the decentralized open web, including web articles, long-form and short-form videos, user-generated content (UGC), and beyond. Different content types exhibit distinct feature densities and user interaction patterns. Building a unified ranking model that sustains high performance across such heterogeneity, while avoiding negative transfer or majority bias, remains a significant industrial challenge.
  This paper presents an end-to-end case study on the industrial-scale multi-task ranking of heterogeneous feeds, grounded in real-world deployment. We introduce HA-MoE, a heterogeneity-adaptive multi-gated mixture-of-experts architecture that incorporates explicit heterogeneity context into both gating networks and expert representations. This approach enables effective specialization without significantly increasing operational overhead. To support reliable deployment, we introduce LENS, a lightweight observability framework that provides interpretable diagnostics of expert specialization and tracks this functional heterogeneity across continuous retraining. We evaluate our method using Dual-Level AUC (DL-AUC), a heterogeneity-aware evaluation metric that combines global ranking performance with cross-segment ranking correctness. Offline evaluations on a large-scale industrial dataset demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline models. Furthermore, online A/B testing confirms gains in feed activity and exploration metrics. Together, offline and online results validate the effectiveness of our approach for managing heterogeneity in industrial-scale recommender systems.

</details>


### [173] [An Exploration Graph with Continuous Refinement for Efficient Multimedia Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27623)
*Nico Hezel,Kai Uwe Barthel,Konstantin Schall,Klaus Jung*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper introduces crEG (continuous refining Exploration Graph), a method for fast construction of compact, undirected graphs with guaranteed connectivity for ANNS, plus an optional edge optimization algorithm. It highlights the overlooked problem of "exploratory search" (where the query is part of the database) and shows that high ANNS efficiency does not guarantee good exploratory search performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-based ANNS methods achieve excellent speed-accuracy trade-offs but suffer from slow construction times or high memory usage. Furthermore, most prior work focuses on search with external queries, neglecting "exploratory search" scenarios where the query is drawn from the database itself—a critical use case for recommendation and exploration systems.

Method: The authors propose the "continuous refining Exploration Graph" (crEG), which rapidly constructs a compact exploration graph with even-degree, undirected edges and guaranteed connectivity at all times. An optional edge optimization algorithm further improves search effectiveness. Both algorithms are designed specifically for undirected graphs with structural guarantees.

Result: Experiments show that crEG achieves state-of-the-art search performance with faster construction. Importantly, the paper demonstrates that methods excelling at standard ANNS do not necessarily perform well under exploratory search conditions, validating the need for dedicated design considerations.

Conclusion: crEG provides a fast, memory-efficient graph construction method with strong connectivity guarantees, making it particularly suitable for exploratory search in recommendation and exploration systems—a previously underexplored but important ANNS variant.

Abstract: As datasets and the dimensionality of feature vectors continue to grow, Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) in large multimedia databases becomes increasingly relevant. Graph-based approaches have demonstrated to offer the best trade-off between retrieval precision and search time. Despite their ability to deliver search times several orders of magnitude faster than exact search techniques, existing methods suffer from slow constructions speeds or high memory requirements. This paper presents a "continuous refining Exploration Graph" (crEG), a novel approach for rapidly constructing a compact exploration graph with state-of-the-art search performance. Additionally, it provides the ability to enhance its effectiveness even further through an optional edge optimization algorithm. Both algorithms are specifically designed to produce and operate on undirected graphs with even degrees and guarantee graph connectivity at any time, a property particularly valuable for "exploratory search", where the query is part of the database elements. Although such queries provide an advantageous starting point for graph search algorithms, they have been rarely considered in the context of ANNS, yet are crucial for recommendation and exploration systems. Our experiments demonstrate high efficiency in ANNS does not necessarily translate to a good performance in "exploratory search".

</details>


### [174] [Dynamic Exploration Graph: A Novel Approach for Efficient Nearest Neighbor Search in Evolving Multimedia Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27640)
*Nico Hezel,Kai Uwe Barthel,Bruno Schilling,Konstantin Schall,Klaus Jung*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Dynamic Exploration Graph (DEG), an extension of the Exploration Graph for approximate nearest neighbor search that supports dynamic datasets through a connectivity-preserving vertex deletion algorithm and a distribution-agnostic graph expansion method, achieving superior performance in both streaming and static scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph-based ANNS algorithms perform well on static datasets but struggle with dynamic datasets where points are continuously inserted or deleted. Existing solutions lack robust mechanisms for handling deletions without degrading graph connectivity or search efficiency.

Method: DEG extends the Exploration Graph with two core innovations: (1) a novel vertex deletion algorithm that guarantees graph connectivity is preserved after removal, and (2) a data distribution-agnostic graph expansion method that maintains a balanced, well-connected structure regardless of the underlying data distribution. The approach is evaluated in both streaming and online dynamic scenarios.

Result: Empirical results show DEG surpasses existing dynamic graph algorithms in construction time and search efficiency under both streaming and online settings. On static datasets, DEG matches the performance of current state-of-the-art approaches.

Conclusion: DEG effectively bridges the gap between static and dynamic ANNS, offering a unified solution that handles continuous data alterations without sacrificing performance, thus demonstrating broad applicability across both dynamic and static use cases.

Abstract: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) represents a fundamental problem in various applications (image-search, recommendation systems). While graph-based algorithms have demonstrated a good balance between search accuracy and time, handling dynamic datasets, where data points are continuously added or removed, remains a challenge. This paper introduces the Dynamic Exploration Graph (DEG), an extension of the continuous refining Exploration Graph, which retains high search efficiency for static dataset while adding essential support for dynamic data. At the core of the DEG design are two key innovations: a novel vertex deletion algorithm which guarantees graph connectivity and a data distribution-agnostic method for graph expansion. Through these mechanisms, the DEG maintains a balanced and well-connected structure, even under continuous data alterations. Empirical experiments in both streaming and online scenarios demonstrate the superior performance of the DEG, surpassing existing dynamic graph algorithms in terms of construction time and search efficiency. Although optimized for dynamic datasets, the DEG delivers results as good as current state-of-the-art approaches for static dataset, underscoring its broad applicability.

</details>


### [175] [LoopMemGR: From Behavior Logs to Evolving Memory for Generative Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27647)
*Hui Qian,Changfa Wu,Chang Liu,Binbin Cao,Jian Wu,Yuliang Yan,Han Zhu,Bo Zheng*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: LoopMemGR introduces a closed-loop memory framework for generative recommendation that retains past recommendation-feedback trajectories alongside user behavior, extracting multi-view experience signals (recency, frequency, global) as experience tokens to condition next-item generation, overcoming the asymmetric memory limitation of existing history-as-context approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing generative recommendation methods use a history-as-context paradigm that only retains user behavior history, discarding system-side recommendation decisions and feedback after each request. This creates an asymmetric memory where the system remembers user actions but not its own past recommendations, losing valuable preference-validation signals, negative evidence, and exploration information that could improve future recommendations.

Method: LoopMemGR maintains a recommendation experience log recording recommendation-feedback trajectories in addition to behavior logs. It extracts request-relevant evidence through three complementary views: (1) recency view for short-term interaction dynamics, (2) frequency view for recurring recommendation patterns, and (3) global view for transferable cross-user regularities. These signals are compressed into a fixed number of experience tokens to condition the generative backbone within a bounded input budget.

Result: Extensive experiments on an industrial Taobao dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of closed-loop experience accumulation and multi-view experience extraction, validating the proposed framework's ability to leverage past recommendation-feedback signals for improved generative recommendation.

Conclusion: LoopMemGR effectively addresses the asymmetric memory problem in generative recommendation by enabling closed-loop experience accumulation through a multi-view extraction mechanism, showing that remembering system-side recommendation outcomes alongside user behavior yields meaningful performance gains in industrial-scale settings.

Abstract: Generative recommendation formulates next-item prediction as conditional autoregressive generation over discrete Semantic IDs, enabling end-to-end recommendation over large-scale item spaces. However, most existing methods follow a history-as-context paradigm that repeatedly reconstructs user preference from behavior history while discarding system-side recommendation decisions after each request. This creates an asymmetric memory: the system remembers what the user has done, but not what it has previously recommended or learned from the resulting feedback. Consequently, useful preference-validation signals, potential negative evidence, and historical exploration information cannot be directly reused across requests. To address these limitations, we propose LoopMemGR, a closed-loop recommendation experience memory framework for generative recommendation. In addition to the conventional behavior log, LoopMemGR maintains a recommendation experience log that records past recommendation--feedback trajectories. It extracts request-relevant evidence through three complementary views: the recency view captures short-term interaction dynamics, the frequency view summarizes recurring recommendation patterns, and the global view distills transferable regularities shared across users. These signals are compressed into a fixed number of experience tokens to condition the generative backbone under a bounded input budget. Extensive experiments on an industrial Taobao dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of closed-loop experience accumulation and multi-view experience extraction.

</details>


### [176] [Restoring Collaborative Signals in Semantic-ID Generative Recommendation via Personalized Natural Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27682)
*Changjiang Han,Qingyang Li,Yaqiang Zang,Jikun Kang,Pinghua Gong,Xue Liu,Bowei He*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a framework that injects hierarchical collaborative signals into LLM-based generative recommendation at inference time via personalized natural language, addressing the fundamental problem that semantic-IDs (SIDs) cannot simultaneously encode content and collaborative information, which limits recommendation accuracy and makes explicit reasoning ineffective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
