Motivation: LLM-based generative recommendation models that autoregressively generate item semantic-IDs (SIDs) suffer from a critical bottleneck: a compact SID cannot hold both content and collaborative signal simultaneously — the two compete, collaboration loses, and mis-predicted SIDs directly cap recommendation accuracy. Explicit reasoning fails to translate into correct SIDs because text and SID tokens reside in misaligned embedding spaces. Multi-round training is costly and largely ineffective, and few methods address this signal deficiency at inference time.

Method: The authors propose a framework guided by personalized natural language that adds hierarchical collaborative cues during generation, without modifying the backbone model or retraining SIDs. Instead of mapping language directly onto SIDs, the method uses language to create analyzable links between collaborative patterns and their audiences, thereby restoring the collaborative signal missing from SIDs at inference time.

Result: The framework yields consistent gains in recommendation accuracy by grounding generation in collaborative structure at inference time, outperforming approaches that rely on explicit reasoning or costly retraining.

Conclusion: Restoring collaborative signal into SID generation through personalized natural language-based guidance is an effective alternative to explicit reasoning or retraining for improving LLM-based generative recommendation. The approach addresses the fundamental representation bottleneck where SIDs cannot jointly encode content and collaborative information.

Abstract: Making LLM-based generative recommendation models stronger and more personalized through natural language and explicit reasoning is a widely anticipated yet still unsolved goal. Such models cast recommendation as autoregressively generating an item's semantic-ID (SID), a short tuple of discrete codes, so that recommending well reduces to emitting the right SID. In this setting the model verbalizes its knowledge poorly, and text and SID tokens live in misaligned embedding spaces. Deep reasoning therefore rarely turns into a correct SID, and enabling explicit "thinking" often gives no gain or even hurts. The deeper cause is that a compact SID cannot hold content and collaborative signal at once: the two compete, and collaboration loses. Because a mis-predicted SID is a wrong recommendation, this caps accuracy directly. Costly multi-round training barely helps, and few methods try to supply the missing signal at inference time. What is missing is a reliable channel that carries collaborative signal into SID generation. We therefore propose a framework, guided by personalized natural language, that adds hierarchical collaborative cues as the model generates, without altering the backbone or retraining the SIDs. Rather than mapping language onto SIDs directly, it uses language to attach analyzable links between collaborative patterns and their audiences, restoring the collaborative signal that SIDs miss. The result is consistent gains in recommendation accuracy, grounding generation in collaborative structure at inference time rather than relying on explicit reasoning or retraining.

</details>


### [177] [Measuring Alignment With Reader Highlights Net of Position and Length](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27739)
*Kazuki Nakayashiki,Keisuke Watanabe*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper evaluates context compression for LLMs by measuring how well compressors retain sentences that human readers independently highlight. Using a careful stratification design that controls for position and length confounds, it finds that LM-based importance ranking significantly outperforms naive truncation and classical heuristics, performing comparably to a single human reader.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional evaluation of context compression uses downstream task accuracy, creating circularity (another model judges importance). The authors propose naturalistic social highlighting—crowd-sourced sentence marking—as a non-circular reference. However, naive metrics are confounded by position bias (marks cluster at document start) and length bias (marked sentences tend to be longer), requiring rigorous statistical controls.

Method: The authors collect 120 web documents, each with ≥12 independent reader highlights. They match each marked sentence to unmarked sentences from the same document at equal relative depth and equal within-document length rank. Synthetic null baselines are built from position and length alone to calibrate estimators. An exact randomization test (assumption-free about clustering) compares compressor retention rates. Methods tested include LM importance ranking (GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 5), naive truncation, Luhn's 1958 heuristic, and lexical centrality-based conditioning.

Result: LM importance ranking retains 38.4% of crowd-marked sentences versus 19.9% of matched controls (+0.196 enrichment, p=0.0005). Naive truncation yields near-zero enrichment (+0.003). A single human scores +0.182, indistinguishable from GPT-5.4 (+0.002 difference) and below Claude Opus 5. Luhn's heuristic achieves +0.088. Conditioning on lexical centrality removes only 0.010, indicating agreement is not merely centrality. Depth-only stratification produces false positives on 20-36% of nulls. A prior claim by the authors fails to reproduce on this corpus.

Conclusion: LM-based importance ranking meaningfully captures human reader preferences beyond position and length artifacts. The method rivals single-human performance. Rigorous null calibration is essential—without it, position-length stratification alone inflates false positives. Classical keyword-frequency methods partially recover reader selection, but lexical centrality explains little of the agreement.

Abstract: Context compression discards most of a document before a language model reads it, and is normally evaluated by downstream task accuracy - which makes another model the judge of what mattered. Naturalistic social highlighting offers a non-circular reference: many people independently marking passages on the same page. But the obvious metric, the fraction of crowd-marked sentences a compressor keeps, is confounded twice: crowd marks are front-loaded and crowd-marked sentences are longer, so any method favouring early or long sentences scores well regardless of readers. We remove both by matching each marked sentence against unmarked sentences of the same document at equal relative depth and equal within-document length rank, and we calibrate every estimator on synthetic nulls built from position and length alone - a step that matters, since depth-only stratification returns a false positive on 20-36% of nulls containing no effect. On 120 web documents (at least 12 independent readers each), a language-model importance ranking keeps 38.4% of crowd-marked sentences against 19.9% of their matched neighbours: an enrichment of +0.196 [+0.148, +0.239], at p = 0.0005 under an exact randomization test that assumes nothing about clustering, and replicated cross-vendor. Naive truncation, whose keep rule is position, correctly falls to +0.003. To give the number a scale: scored identically, on the same budget, against a crowd label recomputed to exclude them, a single human reader reaches +0.182 - indistinguishable from GPT-5.4 (+0.002 [-0.081, +0.088]) and below Claude Opus 5. Classical methods are not null - Luhn's 1958 heuristic reaches +0.088 - so reader selection is partly recoverable by counting words; conditioning additionally on lexical centrality removes only 0.010, so the agreement is not centrality. We also report that a claim in our own prior work does not reproduce on this corpus.

</details>


### [178] [A Structured Knowledge Infrastructure for Domain-Specific Data Asset Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27748)
*Mengdi Chen,Yuanxin Huang,Yulin Jiang,Wei Sun*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: A two-layer retrieval system combining a Graph-Guided Retriever and Scene-Aware Ranker, backed by a three-tier dual-purpose knowledge base, improves enterprise data analytics retrieval from 19.1% to 96.6% Hit@10 on commercial advertising data at Xiaohongshu.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise data analytics agents using generic RAG suffer from two structural failures: retrieving the wrong asset (Hit@10=19.1%) and lacking usage knowledge, leading to metric misinterpretation. Four root causes are identified: semantic gap (C1), entity ambiguity (C2), schema drift (C3), and asset-usage gap (C4).

Method: A two-layer solution: (1) A three-tier dual-purpose knowledge base with 179 documents using an eight-section annotation template, maintained by a closed-loop refresh pipeline with day-level freshness (one yes/no approval, 30s hot-reload). (2) Graph-Guided Retriever (GGR) using a 2,859-node knowledge graph as a candidate gate with intent routing, achieving 71.6x token reduction. (3) Scene-Aware Ranker (SAR) employing 19-class entity recognition and explicit scenario annotations, where negative knowledge contributes 25pp of Hit@10 improvement.

Result: On two 100-question benchmarks, Hit@10 improved from 19.1% to 96.6% (+77.5pp), knowledge coverage rose from 56% to 77%, with end-to-end latency of 4.84–5.33 seconds.

Conclusion: The proposed two-layer architecture effectively resolves structural retrieval and knowledge gaps in enterprise analytics, demonstrating that knowledge-graph-guided retrieval with scene-aware ranking and dual-purpose knowledge bases can deliver near-perfect asset identification at acceptable latency in production environments.

Abstract: Enterprise data analytics agents face two structural failures: generic RAG retrieves the wrong asset (Hit@10=19.1%) and delivers no usage knowledge to prevent metric misinterpretation---stemming from four root causes (C1--C4) ranging from semantic gap and entity ambiguity to schema drift and asset-usage gap. We present a two-layer solution deployed in the commercial advertising data warehouse at Xiaohongshu (5,300+ Hive tables, 14 domains). A three-tier dual-purpose knowledge base (179 documents, eight-section annotation template) serves both retrieval and generation, with a closed-loop refresh pipeline maintaining day-level freshness (one yes/no approval, 30s hot-reload). The Graph-Guided Retriever (GGR) uses a 2,859-node knowledge graph as a candidate gate with intent routing to deliver 71.6x token reduction. The Scene-Aware Ranker (SAR) applies 19-class entity recognition and explicit scenario annotations; negative knowledge alone contributes 25 percentage points of Hit@10 gain. On two 100-question benchmarks, Hit@10 rises from 19.1% to 96.6% (+77.5pp) and knowledge coverage from 56% to 77%, at 4.84--5.33s end-to-end latency.

</details>


### [179] [Hierarchical Latent Reasoning for LLM-based Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27760)
*Peiyu Hu,Siying Gu,Weihai Lu,Zhuodong Liu,Yuntian Tang,Jiahao Liang,Yiying Xie,Jiang Rong,Zhaokai Luo,Zhiyong Wang,Jia Wang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: HiLaR proposes a hierarchical latent reasoning framework for LLM-based recommendation that constructs temporal-guided user preference representations aligned with LLM latent states, organized from broad preferences to fine-grained intents, and optimized via layer-aware reinforcement learning combining final recommendation feedback with process rewards derived from marginal likelihood gains. It outperforms strong baselines on four Amazon datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explicit natural-language reasoning in LLM-based recommendation incurs substantial inference overhead, while existing latent reasoning methods inadequately characterize the layer-wise roles and contributions of preference representations during the reasoning process.

Method: HiLaR constructs temporal-guided hierarchical user preference representations and aligns them with multiple LLM latent reasoning states, organizing the process from broad preferences to fine-grained current intents. Optimization uses reinforcement learning with combined final recommendation feedback and layer-aware process rewards, where process rewards are derived from the marginal target-likelihood gain contributed by each latent state.

Result: Experiments on four Amazon benchmark datasets demonstrate that HiLaR generally outperforms strong sequential, generative, and LLM-based recommendation baselines. Ablation and sensitivity analyses verify the contributions of hierarchical representation learning, latent alignment, and process-level optimization.

Conclusion: HiLaR effectively addresses the limitations of both explicit reasoning (inference overhead) and existing latent reasoning (insufficient layer-wise characterization) by introducing a hierarchical latent reasoning framework with layer-aware reinforcement optimization, achieving state-of-the-art performance in LLM-based recommendation.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for recommendation by leveraging their semantic understanding and contextual modeling capabilities. Recent studies further introduce reasoning mechanisms to improve user preference modeling. However, explicit natural-language reasoning incurs substantial inference overhead, whereas existing latent reasoning methods mainly focus on generating or verifying intermediate states, leaving their layer-wise preference roles and contributions insufficiently characterized. We propose HiLaR, a Hierarchical Latent Reasoning framework with layer-aware reinforcement optimization for LLM-based recommendation. HiLaR constructs temporal-guided hierarchical user preference representations, aligns them with multiple LLM latent reasoning states, and organizes the reasoning process from broad preferences to fine-grained current intents. To further optimize the reasoning trajectory, HiLaR combines final recommendation feedback with layer-aware process rewards derived from the marginal target-likelihood gain of each state. Experiments on four Amazon benchmark datasets show that HiLaR generally outperforms strong sequential, generative, and LLM-based recommendation baselines. Ablation and sensitivity analyses further verify the contribution of hierarchical representation learning, latent alignment, and process-level optimization. Our code is available in https://github.com/hupeiyu21/HiLaR.

</details>


### [180] [From Understanding to Action: Feedback-Grounded Policy Discovery for Generative Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27789)
*Zhi Chen,Minmao Wang,Xingchen Liu,Haoqiang Liang,Huihuang Lin,Likang Wu,Hongke Zhao,Yulong Wang,Shijie Yi,Fei Pan,Peng Jiang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Proposes a feedback-driven agent framework that bridges the "Understanding-Action Gap" in LLM-enhanced recommendation by separately learning intent knowledge and policy knowledge, then distilling both into a lightweight Semantic-ID generator for LLM-free inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semantic-ID-based generative recommenders rely on item-level supervision capturing only behavioral co-occurrence, while LLMs can reason over heterogeneous interaction histories to infer user demand but lack recommendation-specific outcome feedback. This creates an "Understanding-Action Gap" where linguistically plausible reasoning does not translate to effective recommendation decisions.

Method: A feedback-driven agent framework that (1) induces task-oriented intent knowledge (capturing user demand) and policy knowledge (specifying recommendation direction/rejection boundaries), (2) evaluates and refines candidate policies using outcome-derived feedback rather than linguistic plausibility, and (3) transfers the learned intent and policy knowledge into two latent tokens of a lightweight Semantic-ID generator via dual-space relational distillation for LLM-free online inference.

Result: Public benchmark experiments show consistent improvements over baselines. Large-scale online A/B tests achieve gains of 4.506% in Revenue and 4.621% in ADVV.

Conclusion: Separating intent knowledge from policy knowledge and optimizing policies via outcome feedback effectively bridges the Understanding-Action Gap. Distilling this knowledge into a lightweight generator enables practical LLM-free deployment with significant real-world performance gains.

Abstract: Semantic-ID-based generative recommenders enable efficient next-item generation, but their item-level supervision mainly captures behavioral co-occurrence and local transitions. Large language models (LLMs) can complement these models by reasoning over heterogeneous interaction histories to understand the user's current demand. However, LLMs are not inherently trained with recommendation-specific outcome feedback, and linguistically plausible reasoning therefore does not necessarily lead to effective recommendation decisions. We term this mismatch the Understanding-Action Gap. Accordingly, we distinguish intent knowledge, which captures the user's current demand, from policy knowledge, which specifies the recommendation direction and rejection boundary under that demand. To bridge this gap, we propose a feedback-driven agent framework that first induces task-oriented intent and then discovers recommendation policies according to their incremental utility over an intent-only baseline. Candidate policies are evaluated and refined using outcome-derived feedback rather than linguistic plausibility. We further transfer the resulting intent and policy knowledge into two latent tokens of a lightweight Semantic-ID generator through dual-space relational distillation, enabling LLM-free online inference. Experiments on public benchmarks show consistent improvements over baselines, while large-scale online A/B tests achieve gains of 4.506% in Revenue and 4.621% in ADVV.

</details>


### [181] [Interpretable Representation via LLM-Driven Generative Disentanglement for Local-Life Service Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27944)
*Long Zhang,Hao Jiang,Sheng Yu,Fei Pan,Peng Jiang,Kun Gai*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: LGRID proposes an interpretable Semantic ID generation framework for local-life service recommendation that disentangles geographic and semantic factors through a generative pipeline, achieving superior AUC, near-perfect attribute decoding, and dramatically reduced SID collisions compared to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Semantic ID (SID) generation for LLM-based recommendation suffers from two critical bottlenecks: (1) semantic entanglement, where heterogeneous attributes like geography, brand, and category are mixed during encoding, leading to information loss in quantization, low-quality SIDs, and severe collisions; and (2) black-box representation learning that provides no explicit attribute semantics or interpretable geographic/semantic meanings for SID positions, weakening retrieval reliability and hindering diagnosis and control of SID generation.

Method: LGRID employs an Encode → Disentangle → Align → Quantize pipeline: (1) Joint LLM encoding preserves cross-attribute geographic-semantic dependencies rather than independent field encoding; (2) A Structured Disentangled Block routes hidden states into attribute-aligned slots for geographic and semantic factors; (3) Synergistic Alignment Learning makes slots both generatively decodable and discriminative for retrieval; (4) Dual-Stream Residual Quantization separately discretizes the two streams into compact SIDs with explicit attribute correspondence, yielding interpretable SIDs grounded in item attributes and local-service semantics.

Result: On Kuaishou and Foursquare datasets, LGRID consistently outperforms strong SID baselines with up to 5.44% relative AUC gain. It achieves over 99% attribute-decoding accuracy for coarse geographic fields and reduces the full-SID collision rate to 39.9%, compared to 97.0% for LGSID.

Conclusion: The generative disentanglement paradigm of LGRID successfully addresses semantic entanglement and interpretability issues in SID generation, providing both superior recommendation performance and explicit, interpretable SID structures grounded in item attributes and local-service semantics.

Abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have advanced ID-based recommendation through Semantic ID (SID) modeling, existing SID generation frameworks largely follow a single-representation-then-quantization paradigm. This design faces two bottlenecks: semantic entanglement mixes heterogeneous attributes, such as geography, brand, and category, causing information loss during quantization, low-quality SIDs, and severe collisions; moreover, black-box representation learning provides neither explicit attribute semantics nor clear geographic or semantic meanings for SID positions. These limitations weaken both retrieval reliability and the ability to diagnose or control SID generation. We propose Interpretable Representation via LLM-Driven Generative Disentanglement for Local-Life Service Recommendation (LGRID). LGRID introduces a generative disentanglement paradigm through an Encode -> Disentangle -> Align -> Quantize pipeline. It first uses joint LLM encoding to preserve cross-attribute geographic-semantic dependencies, rather than encoding fields independently. A Structured Disentangled Block then routes hidden states into attribute-aligned slots for geographic and semantic factors. Synergistic Alignment Learning makes these slots both generatively decodable and discriminative for retrieval, while Dual-Stream Residual Quantization separately discretizes the two streams into compact SIDs with explicit attribute correspondence. This design yields interpretable SIDs with positions grounded in item attributes and local-service semantics. Experiments on Kuaishou and Foursquare show that LGRID consistently outperforms strong SID baselines, achieving up to a 5.44 percent relative AUC gain. It also achieves over 99 percent attribute-decoding accuracy for coarse geographic fields and reduces the full-SID collision rate to 39.9 percent, compared with 97.0 percent for LGSID.

</details>


### [182] [VIG-RL: Learning to Search and Insert for Verified Image Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28055)
*Qinhan Yu,Jun Guang,Chong Chen,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: VIG-RL is a reinforcement learning-based agentic framework that dynamically decides when and where to insert verified images into text responses, outperforming static retrieval-augmented pipelines in knowledge-intensive multimodal tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented frameworks for interleaved text-image generation rely on decoupled, static pipelines that cannot dynamically reason about when external knowledge is needed or where visual assets should be inserted. This gap motivates the need for Verified Image Grounding (VIG) as an active, dynamic decision-making process.

Method: The authors propose VIG-RL, an autonomous agentic framework that formulates the search-selection-insertion workflow within a ReAct-style loop. The agent is optimized via reinforcement learning with a composite reward system that evaluates both step-by-step tool execution and final multimodal alignment holistically.

Result: Extensive evaluations show that VIG-RL establishes a new state-of-the-art, significantly outperforming existing static baselines in producing reliable interleaved text-image responses.

Conclusion: VIG-RL demonstrates that reformulating verified image grounding as an active, RL-optimized decision-making process yields substantial improvements over static retrieval-augmented approaches, enabling more reliable and contextually appropriate multimodal generation in knowledge-intensive scenarios.

Abstract: In knowledge-intensive scenarios, providing reliable interleaved text-image responses requires Verified Image Grounding (VIG): the precise integration of retrieved authentic visual evidence. Existing retrieval-augmented frameworks predominantly rely on decoupled, static pipelines, inherently failing to dynamically reason about when external knowledge is required and where visual assets should be contextually inserted. To bridge this gap, we propose VIG-RL, an autonomous agentic framework that formulates the search-selection-insertion workflow as an active decision-making process. Operating within a dynamic ReAct-style loop, VIG-RL is optimized via reinforcement learning, guided by a composite reward system that holistically evaluates the agent's step-by-step tool execution and final multimodal alignment. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that VIG-RL establishes a new state-of-the-art, significantly outperforming existing static baselines.

</details>


### [183] [CCFormer: Efficient Cross-Field Interaction and Hierarchical Sequence Compression for Industrial Recommendation at Tencent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28070)
*Yunlong Wang,Huizhe Zhang,Haonan Hu,Yudong Li,Bing Wen,Jianchao Tu,Chengxiang Zhuo,Zang Li*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: CCFormer is an efficient Transformer backbone for industrial recommendation that unifies cross-field feature interaction with compressed long-sequence modeling, achieving significant CTR and revenue gains while accelerating training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sequential recommendation models based on self-attention benefit from longer sequences and larger capacity, but practical recommender systems face strict latency and resource constraints. Balancing computational overhead with fine-grained feature interaction remains a key challenge.

Method: CCFormer combines two core components: (1) feature-field separated cross attention for cross-field feature interaction, and (2) long-sequence subspace token mixing for capturing long-term preference signals across heterogeneous feature domains. A hierarchical sequence compression strategy with progressively expanded receptive fields reduces information loss during efficient long-sequence modeling.

Result: CCFormer outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on two public benchmarks and a large-scale industrial dataset. Online A/B tests at Tencent yielded a 3.57% CTR gain in video recommendation and 1.71% advertising revenue lift in ad ranking, while achieving 2.21x training acceleration over the HSTU baseline.

Conclusion: CCFormer effectively bridges the gap between scaling-law benefits and practical deployment constraints in industrial recommendation. It has been fully deployed in Tencent's production system, serving main traffic in both video recommendation and advertising ranking scenarios.

Abstract: Recent studies in industrial recommendation systems have demonstrated that sequential recommendation models built upon self-attention can benefit from predictable scaling laws by increasing sequence length and model capacity. However, practical recommender systems impose strict latency and resource constraints, making it challenging to balance computational overhead with fine-grained feature interaction. In this paper, we propose CCFormer, an efficient Transformer backbone that unifies cross-field feature interaction and compressed long-sequence modeling for industrial recommendation. Specifically, CCFormer combines feature-field separated cross attention with long-sequence subspace token mixing to exploit long-term preference signals across heterogeneous feature domains. A hierarchical sequence compression strategy with progressively expanded receptive fields enables efficient long-sequence modeling with reduced information loss. Extensive experiments on two public benchmarks and a large-scale industrial dataset demonstrate that CCFormer consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Online A/B tests in a video recommendation scenario and an advertising ranking scenario at Tencent further validate its industrial practicality, yielding a 3.57% CTR gain and a 1.71% advertising revenue lift, respectively, while accelerating model training by 2.21x over the strong HSTU baseline. CCFormer has been fully deployed in Tencent's production recommendation system, serving the main traffic of both scenarios.

</details>


### [184] [TCA-SIR: Learning Target-Conditioned Abstractions for Scientific Inspiration Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28498)
*Yuto Suzuki,Farnoush Banaei-Kashani*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper reformulates Scientific Inspiration Retrieval (SIR) as target-conditioned abstraction (TCA), where transferable principles are extracted from candidate papers specifically for a target problem, outperforming prior methods on ResearchBench by over 10 percentage points in HitRate@top4%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SIR methods rely on topical similarity, which fails to capture the value of remote inspirations—papers whose utility lies in reusable problem-solving principles rather than surface-level topical overlap. Humans instead abstract transferable aspects of a source and remap them to a new target; current retrieval systems lack this capability.

Method: The authors propose TCA-SIR, which reformulates SIR as target-conditioned abstraction. Instead of retrieving papers directly, the system learns to generate a transferable abstract principle from each candidate conditioned on the target problem. The representations of these generated abstractions are then used to predict transferability. This is evaluated against prior SIR methods and direct LLM-based retrieval approaches.

Result: TCA-SIR outperforms prior SIR methods and direct LLM retrieval on ResearchBench, improving HitRate@top4% over MOOSE-Chem by more than 10 percentage points. Additionally, learned abstractions recover target-relevant mechanisms more clearly than an untrained TCA prompt, providing both stronger retrieval performance and interpretable rationales.

Conclusion: Target-conditioned abstraction is an effective reformulation of SIR that better captures transferable scientific principles, particularly for remote inspirations. The approach yields both quantitative improvements in retrieval and interpretable outputs, suggesting that explicitly modeling how inspiration transfers is key to scientific hypothesis generation.

Abstract: Scientific hypothesis generation for AI for Science typically involves Scientific Inspiration Retrieval (SIR) followed by hypothesis composition. Existing SIR methods rank papers by topical similarity and do not explicitly represent how a candidate inspiration transfers to a target problem. This is especially limiting for remote inspirations, whose value often lies in reusable problem-solving principles rather than topical overlap. Motivated by how humans abstract transferable aspects of a source and remap them to a new target, we reformulate SIR as target-conditioned abstraction (TCA). The retrieval object is a transferable abstract principle extracted from a candidate specifically for the target. We present TCA-SIR, which learns to generate target-conditioned abstractions and uses their representations to predict transferability. On ResearchBench, TCA-SIR outperforms prior SIR methods and direct LLM retrieval, improving HitRate@top4% over MOOSE-Chem by more than 10 percentage points. Learned abstractions also recover target-relevant mechanisms more clearly than an untrained TCA prompt, yielding both stronger retrieval and an interpretable rationale for scientific inspiration.

</details>


### [185] [MagicSelector: Joint Optimization for Agent Tool Selection via Counterfactual Decomposition and Progressive Reranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17751)
*HONOR Agentic Search Team,Zhengzong Chen,Lei Tang,Lijun Liu,Chuandi Jiang,Fan Yang,Keyun Chu,Chu Zhao,Shihao Liu,Minghang Li,Bo Liang,Can Wen,Hailong Wu,Jingnan Ju,Mian Liu,Nengbin Zhang,Peiqiang Wang,Penghe Nie,Qinhui Gu,Sijia Lv,Siqi Chen,Wei Zhang,Yang Xu,Yuhao Qian,Yuxiang Zhang,Zeng Cheng,Zhen Wang,Zuan Chen,Yuanyuan Zhao,Fei Huang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: MagicSelector is a joint optimization framework for tool retrieval in agents, combining counterfactual task decomposition, progressive reranking with self-distillation hard negative mining, and a dynamic Top-K strategy. It translates ambiguous user instructions into atomic subtasks, improving retrieval precision, OOD generalization, and token efficiency, as validated on the new MTDTool benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool retrieval in LLM-based agents suffers from two core issues: (1) ambiguous user instructions that are hard to map directly to appropriate tools, and (2) redundant noise and context distraction in out-of-domain (OOD) scenarios that degrade retrieval precision. Existing methods lack fine-grained structural supervision for task decomposition and struggle to discriminate between highly similar tools while filtering long-tail noise.

Method: MagicSelector integrates three components: (1) **Preference-guided counterfactual task decomposition** — uses a counterfactual reward to measure the marginal causal gain of decomposition on retrieval ranking, providing fine-grained supervision on logical coherence. (2) **Progressive tool reranking with self-distillation hard negative mining** — optimizes both point-wise and list-wise relevance to enhance discrimination among similar tools. (3) **Dual semantic boundary-aware dynamic Top-K** — monitors reranking score cliffs and inter-tool semantic shifts to adaptively truncate candidate lists, balancing recall and noise filtering.

Result: MagicSelector significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on MTDTool (a newly constructed benchmark for mobile multi-turn interactions with process-level annotations), achieving superior tool retrieval accuracy, OOD generalization, and token efficiency.

Conclusion: The joint optimization of counterfactual task decomposition, progressive reranking, and dynamic Top-K provides an effective solution for tool retrieval in agents, particularly in handling ambiguous instructions and OOD scenarios. The results validate MagicSelector's design and its practical advantages in accuracy, generalization, and efficiency.

Abstract: We present MagicSelector, a joint optimization framework integrating Counterfactual task decomposition, Progressive reranking, and Dynamic Top-K, designed to address the fundamental challenges of tool retrieval in agents. MagicSelector is a specialized framework capable of translating ambiguous user instructions into executable atomic subtasks and guiding high-precision tool retrieval, effectively mitigating redundant noise and severe context distraction in out-of-domain (OOD) scenarios. We empower MagicSelector with these capabilities through three key contributions: (1) a preference-guided counterfactual task decomposition mechanism that utilizes a counterfactual reward to quantify the marginal causal gain of decomposition on retrieval ranking, effectively imposing fine-grained structural supervision on logical coherence; (2) a progressive tool reranking method driven by self-distillation hard negative mining, which optimizes both point-wise and list-wise relevance to enhance fine-grained discrimination among highly similar tools; and (3) a dual semantic boundary-aware dynamic Top-K strategy that adaptively monitors reranking score cliffs and inter-tool semantic shifts to dynamically truncate the candidate list, maximizing relevant tool recall while filtering long-tail noise. Evaluated on MTDTool, the first task decomposition benchmark we constructed tailored for mobile multi-turn interactions with process-level annotations, MagicSelector yields promising performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MagicSelector significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of tool retrieval accuracy, OOD generalization capability, and overall token efficiency, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [186] [Recursive transformers for semiconductor thermo-mechanical reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27251)
*Kart-leong Lim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates three recursive transformer paradigms for surrogate modeling in engineering design, demonstrating that recursive weight-sharing architectures offer an optimal trade-off between predictive accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost on small, low-dimensional datasets typical of thermo-mechanical analysis and PDE solving.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional transformer architectures are over-parameterized for the small, low-dimensional datasets common in engineering design, where generating large simulation data (e.g., finite element analysis) is prohibitively expensive. Excess parameters lead to overfitting and unnecessary computational overhead, motivating a shift toward architectures that prioritize additional compute over additional learnable parameters.

Method: The authors conduct a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms: (a) a Tiny Recursive Model, (b) a proposed Depth Recursive Transformer, and (c) a simple recursive transformer. They systematically compare these on predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, and computational complexity (FLOPs) across two low-dimensional engineering tasks: thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of advanced semiconductor packages and a Laplace PDE iterative numerical solver for capacitance fields.

Result: Recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective, generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small-data engineering surrogate modeling, validated on both thermo-mechanical FEA surrogate prediction and Laplace PDE solving tasks.

Conclusion: For resource-constrained engineering surrogate modeling with small datasets, recursive transformer architectures with weight-sharing offer a superior balance of accuracy and efficiency compared to conventional over-parameterized transformers. The paper provides practical design guidelines for selecting among these recursive paradigms.

Abstract: Transformer-based surrogate models are increasingly used to replace expensive first-principles simulation in engineering design. But conventional transformer architectures are often over parameterized for the small, low-dimensional datasets typical of engineering design spaces, where large simulation data is expensive to generate. Under these conditions, excess parameter capacity leads to overfitting rather than improved accuracy, while also incurring unnecessary memory and compute overhead. This motivates a shift towards architectures that focus on additional compute rather than additional learnable parameters. This paper presents a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms for surrogate thermo-mechanical analysis of advanced packages: a)Tiny Recursive Model, b) our proposed Depth Recursive transformer, c) and a simple recursive transformer. We systematically compare their predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, computational complexity (FLOPs), providing practical design guidelines for selecting recursive transformer architectures under resource-constrained scenarios. We validate this principle on two low-dimensional engineering prediction tasks: 1) thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of advanced semiconductor packages, where stress and warpage from thermal cycling must be evaluated repeatedly across a design-of-experiments sweep under costly finite element analysis (FEA). 2) Laplace PDE iterative numerical solver for capacitance field. Overall, recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective and generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small data engineering surrogate modeling.

</details>


### [187] [Regularizing modality contribution drift in multimodal continual learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27260)
*Zhen Zhang,Jielei Chu,Bin Liu,Tianrui Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) — the instability of individual modalities' relative contributions across incremental tasks — as a key unaddressed cause of forgetting in multimodal continual learning. It proposes CMCDR, a regularization method with both replay-based and replay-free variants that preserves the modality contribution structure of old tasks, validated on class-incremental learning and VQA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MMCL methods focus on cross-modal alignment or semantic similarity but overlook whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across incremental tasks. This "decision-level shift," termed Modality Contribution Drift (MCD), is hypothesized as a critical forgetting mechanism that current methods fail to address.

Method: The authors first formalize MCD and propose an MCD score that quantifies contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes via controlled interventions on modality subsets. They then propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR), which comes in two forms: (1) a replay-based version that uses modality-subset interventions on stored old samples as diagnostic probes, comparing contribution profiles between the current model and a frozen previous model, and constraining changes in modality-specific and interaction contributions; (2) a replay-free version that uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses without requiring exemplars.

Result: Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering demonstrate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR across both replay-based and replay-free settings.

Conclusion: Modality Contribution Drift is a significant yet overlooked cause of forgetting in MMCL. CMCDR, by regularizing the modality contribution structure, effectively mitigates this drift and outperforms existing methods across diverse MMCL settings.

Abstract: Multimodal continual learning (MMCL) aims to learn emerging knowledge from multimodal data while preserving knowledge. To mitigate forgetting, current MMCL methods usually focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity, but they overlook whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across incremental tasks. We term this decision-level shift Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) and quantify it with the MCD score, which combines contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled interventions on modality subsets. Theoretical and empirical analyses further explain why current MMCL methods cannot reliably mitigate this drift. To this end, we propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR), which preserves the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks. Since MMCL settings differ in whether old exemplars are available, CMCDR includes both replay-based and replay-free versions. The replay-based version uses modality-subset interventions as diagnostic probes on stored old samples, compares their contribution profiles between the current model and a frozen previous model, and constrains changes in old-sample modality-specific and interaction contributions. The replay-free version uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses, thereby regularizing the observed contribution profile without exemplars. Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering validate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR.

</details>


### [188] [DoTime: A Synthetic Benchmark Generator for Interventional and Counterfactual Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27263)
*Dennis Thumm,Billy Tim Anthony,Ying Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DoTime is an open-source generator for multivariate temporal structural causal models with interventions, providing four evaluation suites with exact ground truth. It introduces capabilities like continuous-time intervention windows, counterfactual sampling, regime-switching SCMs, and non-stationary dynamics. Experiments show that interventional training yields direction-accuracy gains over purely observational models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for causal inference over time series are predominantly observational, small-scale, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation underserved in critical applications like healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science.

Method: The authors introduce DoTime, a generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions. Key innovations include: (1) continuous-time intervention windows, (2) counterfactual sampling with a positivity guard, (3) regime-switching SCMs generalizing interrupted time series, (4) non-stationary dynamics via switching SCM parameters, and (5) deterministic ramp and sinusoidal intervention profiles. The generator is released as a PyPI package with four frozen evaluation suites spanning 100,000 trajectories and eight identification structures. A causal foundation model reference implementation (prior-fitted network, PFN) is tested against an observational baseline across three seeds.

Result: The interventional prior-fitted network (PFN) outperforms an observational model of identical capacity on held-out episodes, with a positive direction-accuracy gap in every structure, trajectory length, and seed tested.

Conclusion: Interventional training provides a measurable advantage over observational training for causal time-series modeling. DoTime fills a critical gap in benchmarking infrastructure for temporal causal inference and demonstrates utility as a prior for causal foundation models.

Abstract: Most benchmarks for causal inference over time series are observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation under-served exactly where it matters most, such as in healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science. We introduce \textbf{DoTime}, an open, scalable, and theoretically grounded generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions, released as the \code{dotime} PyPI package together with four frozen evaluation suites. Beyond existing work, it adds capabilities absent from prior generators: continuous-time intervention \emph{windows}, counterfactual sampling modes with a positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs as a strict generalization of interrupted time series, non-stationary dynamics by construction with switching SCM parameters, and deterministic ramp and sinusoidal intervention profiles that place trends and structural breaks \emph{inside} the evaluation window. Moreover, it demonstrates the suitability of the generator as a prior for a causal foundation model reference implementation. The released suites span a training-scale snapshot of $100{,}000$ trajectories and eight named identification structures, each with exact ground truth: paired interventional trajectories from the same SCM throughout, and shared-noise counterfactuals in the continuous-time suite. We ship reference baseline implementations with an evaluation harness, and pose a falsifiable claim: interventional training buys a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over an observational model of identical capacity. It is tested across three training seeds per arm. Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional prior-fitted network's (PFN) gap is positive in every structure, trajectory length, and seed tested.

</details>


### [189] [PlatformBid: An Auto-Bidding Benchmark from a Unified Advertising Platform's Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27265)
*Shengtian Yang,Yewen Li,Peng Jiang,Zhiyi Lyu,Bo An,Peng Jiang,Qingpeng Cai,Lei Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PlatformBid proposes the first unified ad-platform-centric benchmark for auto-bidding, covering three competitive settings. It evaluates existing methods (control, RL, generative) and introduces BidFlow, a flow-matching-based auto-bidding approach that achieves +0.68% target cost improvement in Kuaishou online experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional auto-bidding research focuses only on the DSP/advertiser side, maximizing conversions. Large integrated platforms (combining SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange) need algorithms that jointly maximize both advertiser conversions and platform revenue. No existing evaluation framework addresses this platform-centric perspective.

Method: The authors propose PlatformBid, a benchmark with three competitive settings: homogeneous competition (identical algorithms), heterogeneous competition (diverse strategies), and promotional competition (surge budgets). They evaluate classical control, RL-based, and generative auto-bidding methods. They also introduce BidFlow, a novel flow-matching-based auto-bidding method that uses expressive policy representations for dynamic competitive environments.

Result: Systematic evaluation of auto-bidding methods across the three settings. BidFlow demonstrates strong performance. Online A/B testing on Kuaishou shows +0.68% improvement in target cost, validating offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.

Conclusion: PlatformBid fills the gap in platform-centric auto-bidding evaluation and establishes a standardized benchmark. BidFlow, leveraging flow-matching, proves effective in real-world deployment, confirming that the benchmark's offline results translate reliably to online performance.

Abstract: Real-time bidding is central to computational advertising, comprising three elements: Supply Side Platform (SSP) selling ad impressions, Demand Side Platform (DSP) bidding for advertisers, and Ad Exchange conducting auctions between them. Traditional auto-bidding algorithms focus solely on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions by adjusting bids against competitors. However, current big ad platforms, such as social media and e-commerce companies, now integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange functions internally. From such ad platforms' perspective, the goal of the auto-bidding algorithms is not only to maximize the advertisers' conversions, but also the total revenue of the platform. Given the lack of platform-centric evaluation frameworks and the pressing need to advance auto-bidding research, we propose PlatformBid - the first comprehensive benchmark designed from a unified ad platform's perspective. To accurately reflect the real-world auto-bidding scenarios, we define three representative settings: (1) homogeneous competition with identical algorithms across advertisers, (2) heterogeneous competition with diverse algorithmic strategies, and (3) promotional competition where some advertisers surge budgets for boosting sales during promotional events like Black Friday. We systematically evaluate a broad spectrum of existing auto-bidding methods across these settings, encompassing classical control methods, RL-based methods, and recent generative methods. Besides these methods, we further propose a novel auto-bidding method based on flow-matching, termed BidFlow, which leverages the flow-matching method's expressive policy representation to effectively handle dynamic competitive environments. Online experiments on Kuaishou further show a +0.68\% improvement in target cost, providing deployment evidence for the offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.

</details>


### [190] [Beyond KV Reconstruction: Functional Reconstruction for MLA Draft Models in Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27269)
*Weiye Shi,Fanxu Meng,Muhan Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Converting MHA/GQA models to MLA for KV-cache efficiency introduces attention-function errors that harm speculative decoding acceptance rates. The authors propose an end-to-end functional reconstruction method that optimizes converted MLA modules to faithfully reproduce the original model's output response, significantly improving draft-token acceptance without requiring retraining or verifier supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) offers compact KV-cache for long-context LLM inference, but most production checkpoints use MHA/GQA. Direct conversion from MHA/GQA to MLA introduces approximation errors — particularly from low-rank factorization and RoPE handling — that degrade draft-token acceptance in speculative decoding pipelines. The authors aim to close this gap without retraining from scratch.

Method: The authors formulate MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. Their end-to-end (E2E) method optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of the original MHA/GQA counterpart, using calibration hidden states. The procedure is converter-agnostic, preserves the converted cache and inference graph, and requires neither verifier logits nor verifier supervision. Evaluation covers 192 configurations across four Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA converters, HF and vLLM backends, and four 200-prompt tasks.

Result: With a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance, Functional Reconstruction materially improves acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, leaves 26 practically unchanged, and materially decreases only one. The method demonstrates consistent gains in speculative decoding acceptance rates across diverse model pairs and converters.

Conclusion: Functional reconstruction is an effective, lightweight post-conversion procedure that bridges the distributional gap between original MHA/GQA models and their MLA-converted counterparts, enabling more effective speculative decoding without the cost of full retraining. Code is open-sourced.

Abstract: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) is increasingly important for long-context LLM inference because compact latent states replace the growing key-value (KV) cache and reduce decoding memory traffic. Yet most capable open checkpoints use multi-head or grouped-query attention (MHA/GQA), so conversion is needed to obtain MLA's cache efficiency without retraining from scratch. Speculative decoding offers complementary acceleration, but its speedup depends on agreement between draft proposals and target verification. We find that direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion can sharply reduce this agreement: low-rank factorization and RoPE handling introduce attention-function errors that may be tolerable for standalone generation but substantially lower draft-token acceptance. We therefore formulate MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. Our end-to-end (E2E) method optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of its original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states. This converter-agnostic post-conversion procedure preserves the converted cache and inference graph and requires neither verifier logits nor verifier supervision. We evaluate 192 model-converter-backend-method-task configurations spanning four Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA, HF and vLLM, and four 200-prompt tasks. With a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance, Functional Reconstruction materially improves acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, leaves 26 practically unchanged, and materially decreases one. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/swyhahaha/FunctionalMLA.

</details>


### [191] [RLPF: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27271)
*Huihao Jing,Haozhe Cui,Wenbin Hu,Shaojin Chen,Haochen Shi,Changxuan Fan,Yuxuan Liu,Hanyu Yang,Sirui Zhang,Ziyi Chen,Haoran Li,Yangqiu Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RLPF (Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback) is a staged reward framework that trains code models to prefer faster correct implementations by providing useful feedback both before and after correctness, using execution progress for failed programs and relative efficiency improvement for correct ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current code models trained with execution feedback focus only on correctness, ignoring runtime efficiency. Two correct programs can differ greatly in speed, yet training signals don't capture this. Runtime is a fragile reward: it's meaningful only after correctness, varies across tasks, and provides little guidance when most sampled programs fail.

Method: RLPF turns execution outcomes into a two-stage composite reward: (1) For failed programs, ordering by execution progress (e.g., how far they get before failing); (2) For correct programs, ranking by relative improvement from a baseline toward an expert reference. This provides useful gradients both before and after correctness. The approach is applied to fine-tune Qwen3-32B on PerfCodeBench.

Result: Fine-tuning with RLPF raises correct-and-runnable solutions from 11.1% to 54.6% and relative efficiency from 8.1% to 38.6%. The model becomes competitive with stronger open-weight systems and shows modest transfer to EffiBench-X. Model-generated references provide weaker but still useful supervision. The full composite reward is more reliable than correctness-only or runtime-only baselines.

Conclusion: Code agents can be trained not only to pass tests but also to optimize the programs they write. RLPF demonstrates that staged performance feedback enables models to jointly improve correctness and runtime efficiency, with the composite reward proving more reliable than single-objective alternatives.

Abstract: Code models are increasingly trained with execution feedback, but most training signals still stop at correctness. This leaves an important gap for systems code: two programs can pass the same tests while differing greatly in runtime. We study how to train code agents to prefer faster correct implementations, rather than treating efficiency only as an evaluation metric. The key difficulty is that runtime is a fragile reward. It is meaningful only after a program is correct, varies across tasks, and gives little guidance when most sampled programs fail to compile or run. We propose \textbf{RLPF}, reinforcement learning from performance feedback, which turns execution outcomes into a staged reward. Failed programs are ordered by execution progress, while correct programs are ranked by their relative improvement from the baseline toward the expert reference. This gives useful feedback before correctness and performance-sensitive feedback after correctness. Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench raises correct-and-runnable solutions from $11.1\%$ to $54.6\%$ and improves relative efficiency from $8.1\%$ to $38.6\%$. The trained model becomes competitive with stronger open-weight systems, and its optimization behavior transfers modestly to EffiBench-X. Additional studies show that model-generated references provide useful but weaker supervision, and that the full composite reward is more reliable than correctness-only or runtime-only baselines. These results suggest that code agents can be trained not only to pass tests, but also to optimize the programs they write.

</details>


### [192] [SDO: Structure-Aware Data Organization for Efficient LLM Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27273)
*Jinliang Gao,Ning Yang,Hai Wang,Baili Xiao,Pin Lyu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SDO is a plug-and-play data organization framework that dynamically structures mini-batches and sample exposure using embedding-space structure and an exposure-driven feedback mechanism, accelerating LLM post-training convergence without permanently excluding any samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods treat data organization as static preprocessing via embedding-based grouping, which cannot adapt to evolving sample exposure during optimization. This leads to uniform exposure despite differing sample optimization needs, causing redundant updates for some samples and under-optimization for others.

Method: SDO operates epoch-by-epoch on frozen external embeddings, requiring no model warm-up. Within each epoch, locality-aware batching constructs coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal. Across epochs, an exposure-balanced scheduling mechanism tracks per-sample participation and reduces sampling probability for over-exposed samples to ensure long-term coverage.

Result: Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, SDO accelerates convergence—particularly in the early-to-mid training phase—producing more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types.

Conclusion: SDO provides an effective, plug-and-play solution for LLM post-training data organization that adapts to dynamic optimization needs, yielding faster convergence and balanced performance without excluding training samples.

Abstract: Post-training of large language models is expensive, and existing efficiency improvements mainly focus on selecting informative samples or designing training schedules. However, data organization itself is usually treated as a static preprocessing step: embedding-based grouping methods construct fixed partitions before training and cannot adapt to the evolving sample exposure during optimization. As a result, all samples receive similar exposure despite their different optimization needs, leading to redundant updates for some samples while leaving others under-optimized. To address this problem, we propose SDO (Structure-Aware Data Organization), a plug-and-play data organization framework with an exposure-driven feedback mechanism that organizes mini-batch composition and sample exposure according to representation-space structure. SDO operates epoch by epoch on frozen external embeddings, avoiding model warm-up training overhead: within each epoch, locality-aware batching forms coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal; across epochs, exposure-balanced scheduling records per-sample participation and reduces the sampling probability of over-exposed samples to preserve long-term coverage. Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, SDO accelerates convergence, with the largest gains observed in the early-to-mid phase, producing more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding training samples.

</details>


### [193] [Rethinking EEG-Based Disease Diagnosis: Decoupling Instance Representation Learning from Subject-Level Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27274)
*Zhiyuan Ma,Zeyuan Li,Zhiyi Lu,Jiacheng Hao,Youlang Du,Zhen Jiang,Xinche Zhang,Yuhao Sun,Sen Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BridgeMIL is a two-stage framework for EEG-based disease diagnosis that avoids the problematic practice of inheriting subject-level labels to individual EEG instances. Stage 1 learns instance representations via self-supervised contrastive learning without labels, and Stage 2 applies MIL-based subject-level supervision while preserving learned features. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple EEG datasets and backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG disease diagnosis requires one prediction per subject, but standard pipelines segment recordings into instances and naively inherit subject labels to every instance, assuming all instances are equally informative. Existing MIL approaches avoid this issue but suffer from poor representation learning due to the small number of subjects relative to instances. The authors aim to decouple instance representation learning from subject-level supervision to address this fundamental mismatch.

Method: BridgeMIL employs two stages: (1) A self-supervised pretraining stage that learns instance representations by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags, using variance and covariance regularization (inspired by VICReg) to prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. No instance-level labels are used. (2) A supervised stage where the frozen or lightly fine-tuned encoder feeds into an attention-based MIL aggregator, with supervision applied only at the subject (bag) level, using feature retention to limit representation drift.

Result: BridgeMIL achieves the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone combinations, with an overall mean accuracy of 76.57% — 4.28 percentage points above the strongest baseline. Analyses show that inherited-label reliability varies substantially across instances, performance is more sensitive to subject scarcity than instance scarcity, and the learned representation space exhibits distinct subject-wise clusters with improved inter-class separation.

Conclusion: Aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective is critical for EEG diagnosis. Decoupling representation learning from label inheritance — learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances — yields better representations, improved diagnostic accuracy, and a more structured embedding space.

Abstract: EEG-based disease diagnosis requires one prediction per subject, yet common pipelines segment recordings into short instances, inherit the subject label for every instance, and train instance-level classifiers. This assumes that all instances provide equally reliable diagnostic evidence. Multiple instance learning (MIL) avoids inherited labels by treating each subject as a bag. However, EEG datasets contain far fewer subjects than instances, which can limit the quality of the representations learned by end-to-end MIL. We propose BridgeMIL, a two-stage framework that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains the encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags. Variance and covariance regularization prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject predictions, and limits representation drift through feature retention. Across three EEG disease datasets and five representative backbones, BridgeMIL attains the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings and an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, 4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater performance sensitivity to subject scarcity than to instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved separation between diagnostic classes. Together, these findings underscore the importance of aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances.

</details>


### [194] [Flat Score, Amplified Failures: How the Error Budget Masks Damage in Quantized LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27275)
*Jiwon Jang,Kisu Yang,Heuiseok Lim,Hyunwoo Park*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: 4-bit weight quantization appears lossless on standard benchmark metrics, but it silently amplifies existing failure modes (e.g., tool-name hallucinations) by up to 2.5× without creating new ones. The score stays flat because generous error budgets absorb the extra failures; shrinking the budget or using per-channel error rates reveals the hidden degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Challenging the widespread claim that 4-bit post-training quantization is "nearly lossless" by testing it in a high-stakes setting — multi-turn, tool-calling agents — where subtle degradation could have outsized practical consequences.

Method: Evaluated two open-weight model families (dense and MoE variants) across two domains on the τ²-bench, totaling 456 episodes per cell at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit precision. Employed equivalence testing, rank correlation of failure sets, error-budget manipulation (10 → 2), per-channel error rate analysis, and targeted error-repair prompting as diagnostics.

Result: No cell showed statistically significant score change after multiple-comparison correction; the largest damage was bounded within ±7.5 points. However, quantization amplified existing failures (tool-name hallucination, retail entity errors) by up to 2.5× (raw volume +17.6 points/task), with no novel failure modes (rank correlation ≥0.94, only 0.18% novel events). Shrinking the error budget to two re-exposed a 17-point gap in the affected cell. Error-repair prompting eliminated the damage precisely where it occurred.

Conclusion: Standard benchmark metrics mask quantization-induced degradation because generous error budgets absorb amplified failures. The authors recommend reporting per-channel error rates and success under shrinking budgets — diagnostics derivable from existing logs — alongside task reward to surface hidden precision sensitivity.

Abstract: Post-training quantization to 4-bit weights is widely reported to be nearly lossless. We test this claim for multi-turn, tool-calling agents, where it now matters most. On $τ^2$-bench, across two open-weight model families in dense and MoE variants and two domains (eight cells, 456 episodes each, at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weights), quantization indeed looks free on the standard metric. No cell shows a score change that survives multiple-comparison correction, and in the cell that carries the largest process damage, equivalence testing bounds the change within $\pm$7.5 points. The process tells a different story. Quantization amplifies the failure the model already exhibits at full precision (tool-name hallucination in telecom, with the same directional trend in retail entity errors) by up to 2.5$\times$ in volume (+17.6 points per task), while creating essentially no new failures. The failure set is the same at every precision (rank correlation $\geq$ 0.94, 0.18% novel events). The score stays flat because the benchmark's ten-error budget absorbs the extra failures. Shrinking the budget to two errors re-exposes a score gap of 17 points, and it does so only in the one cell where quantization added error volume, exactly as the masking account predicts. A targeted error-repair prompt, run for five telecom models at every precision, removes the damage exactly and only where it lives. Both diagnostics, the per-channel error rate and success under a shrinking budget, come from logs benchmarks already collect; we suggest reporting them alongside task reward.

</details>


### [195] [The Kinetics of Training: A Driven-Nucleation Rate Law for Emergence, Plasticity Loss, and Circuit Control in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27281)
*Lei Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Language model capabilities emerge only when all parts of a circuit align simultaneously — partial credit is worthless. The waiting time until emergence depends solely on the number of missing parts. This rare-event barrier can be manipulated (induced or prevented), and the damage is localized to query-key slices in attention heads, which can be reset to restore learnability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand why capabilities in language models emerge suddenly rather than continuously, and to identify the mechanistic bottleneck that governs capability formation — specifically, the hypothesis that joint alignment of all circuit components (no partial credit) is the rate-limiting step.

Method: The authors use a multi-pronged approach: (1) ablation experiments on Pythia models across seven capabilities and three scales to test partial credit vs. all-or-nothing circuit contributions; (2) a rate equation framework (sites × attempts × drive × exp(-βK) minus destruction) with preregistered frozen constants, tested forward (ignition timing) and backward (withheld capability decay); (3) query-key vs. value slice re-initialization experiments to localize damage; (4) a controlled gated-attention model to prove the deadline mechanism analytically.

Result: Key results: (1) In shortcut-free circuits, wait time depends on number of missing parts, not circuit size (1.19–1.37 ratio). (2) Ablating one part leaves median 17% capability (vs. 50–83% partial-credit prediction, p=2e-10); non-part heads leave 100%. (3) Forward prediction: capability ignites at a concentration floor (10/10 above, 0/12 below); arrival datable to 5% median error on six held-out models. (4) Backward: withheld capabilities past a critical step never ignite, yet validation loss falls smoothly — standard monitors are blind. (5) Re-initializing query-key slices restores learnability (6/6); value slices do nothing (0/6). (6) SGD noise fails fluctuation-dissipation; annealing melts and pins circuits on schedule.

Conclusion: Capability emergence is governed by a rare-event barrier: all circuit parts must jointly align in one stochastic attempt. This "no partial credit" mechanism explains sudden capability onset, enables dating of emergence from precursors, reveals blindness of standard loss monitors, and localizes both damage and cure to query-key attention slices. The findings hold for conjunction circuits in transformers up to 1.4B parameters.

Abstract: A capability appears in a language model when the last parts of its circuit align in one stochastic attempt, and getting all but one right is worth nothing. We show this no-partial-credit joint alignment is the rate-limiting step of capability formation. Two fingerprints: in a shortcut-free apparatus a five-part circuit missing three waits as long as a three-part circuit missing three (1.19-1.37), so the wait counts missing parts, not size; and on Pythia across seven capabilities and three scales, ablating one part leaves a median 17% of the capability in 32 of 32 discriminating cells, where partial credit predicts 50-83% (p = 2e-10), while a random non-part head leaves 100%.
  One rare event whose barrier grows with missing parts yields a rate equation -- sites x attempts x drive x exp(-beta*K), minus destruction -- read three ways, each preregistered with frozen constants. Forward: a capability flat at baseline ignites at a step of our choosing once the mix passes a concentration floor (10/10 above, 0/12 below), and while still flat its arrival is datable from its precursor to 5% median error on six held-out models. Backward: the delay to learn a withheld capability grows with waiting until, past a critical step, it never ignites -- yet validation loss falls smoothly throughout, so standard monitors are blind to it. We locate the damage (heads commit to the base data) and isolate the cure: re-initializing only the query-key slices restores learnability (6/6) while the value slices do nothing (0/6). We prove the mechanism in a controlled gated-attention model: occupation forces a deadline whose consequences need no mixing assumption. Completed: SGD's noise fails the fluctuation-dissipation test, so we install one and anneal, melt and pin circuits on schedule. Scope: conjunction circuits in transformers to 1.4B.

</details>


### [196] [Benchmarking the Residual: What Long-Horizon Evaluations Add Beyond Matched Short-Task Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27283)
*Chao Peng,Zhiheng Lyu,Peijie Dong,Hande Dong,Qiang Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper argues that long-horizon agent failures require rigorous measurement: benchmarks should compare full-task success against a baseline predicted from short individual stages. The log-ratio between these (the "horizon residual") isolates degradation attributable to trajectory length. Targeted experiments must then explain the residual's cause.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current long-horizon benchmarks observe that agents fail more as tasks lengthen, but this observation conflates multiple causes: ordinary error compounding, inherently harder decisions at later stages, and trajectory-induced degradation (where earlier execution makes later work harder, e.g., context rot). Without disentangling these, claims about "long-horizon failure" lack rigor.

Method: The authors propose computing the horizon residual: the log-ratio between a baseline prediction of full-task success (derived from short, individual stage performance) and actual full-task success. This requires using identical agent configurations and pre-specifying how stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets are chosen. The residual quantifies how much the full rollout diverges from the short-stage baseline.

Result: This is a position paper; it presents no empirical results. It offers a conceptual framework and methodology for isolating trajectory-induced degradation in long-horizon agent evaluations.

Conclusion: The horizon residual provides a principled way to claim "long-horizon failure." A non-zero residual shows the full rollout differs from the short-stage baseline, but targeted follow-up experiments are still needed to attribute the residual to specific mechanisms like context rot, error compounding, or changing decision difficulty.

Abstract: Long-horizon benchmarks often show that agents fail more as tasks become longer. This observation is useful for deployment, but it does not by itself explain why failure occurs. More stages create more opportunities for ordinary errors to compound; longer tasks may also contain harder individual decisions or become harder as conversation history, tool outputs, and environment changes accumulate. We use trajectory-induced degradation to mean this last possibility: earlier execution makes later work harder. When the harmful accumulation is specifically the text visible to the model, it is often called context rot. In this position paper, we argue that to claim a "long-horizon failure", benchmarks must compare actual full-task success against a baseline prediction built from short, individual stages. We call the log-ratio between this prediction and actual success the horizon residual. The comparison must use the same agent configuration and specify in advance how stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets will be chosen. The residual shows that the full rollout differs from the chosen baseline; targeted experiments are still needed to explain why.

</details>


### [197] [TIER-MoE: Trust-Informed Expert Routing via Conditional Modality Risk for Multimodal Fusion in Biomedical Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27289)
*Yu Chang,Anzhe Cheng,Chenwei Wu,Zhuoran Wang,Jiahao Chen,Tamoghna Chattopadhyay,Sophia I. Thomopoulos,Paul M. Thompson,Liyue Shen,Paul Bogdan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TIER-MoE introduces a risk-guided mixture-of-experts model that estimates per-sample modality reliability via unimodal prediction loss, enabling sparse modality-expert routing while preserving multimodal complementarity through a shared path. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods on biomedical multimodal tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal fusion methods fail to reveal whether a modality is unreliable, redundant, or mismatched to a specialized expert, even with richer cross-modal interaction and sample-adaptive fusion. More evidence does not always improve predictions.
