We train classifiers on consecutive temporal windows and fit an HMM to the trajectory of their aligned weights, recovering latent states that partition each timeline into coherent phases. On both datasets, classifiers generalize better to data from windows sharing the state of their training window than to windows across state boundaries. This within-state transfer advantage survives a control for temporal proximity and modestly exceeds the advantage recovered by a naive partition into contiguous states of equal size. Although the states are estimated solely from model weights, they correlate more strongly with shifts in the data's class distribution than with the weight-space geometry used to estimate them. After class divergence and lag are residualized out, the within-state advantage exceeds its permutation null on both tasks, indicating that the states recover structure relevant to transfer beyond the data distribution. Every effect replicates on both tasks but is attenuated on Yelp, whose label distribution is more temporally stable.

</details>


### [220] [A Lightweight Foundation Model for Collider Physics with Multi-Domain Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27501)
*Liangyu Wu,Qibin Liu,Alexander Yue,Julia Gonski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NEXUS is a lightweight (~3M parameter) autoencoder-based foundation model pre-trained on unsupervised LHC collision data, demonstrating improved downstream performance on physics tasks with limited labels and transferability to other scientific domains (gravitational waves, flood forecasting, neural activity), while being computationally simpler than transformer-based alternatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation models in science are often large and computationally expensive. The authors aim to show that a lightweight, autoencoder-based model pre-trained on physics data can achieve effective transfer learning across diverse scientific domains while enabling power-efficient inference for real-time and edge applications.

Method: A fully connected autoencoder with ~3M parameters is pre-trained in an unsupervised manner on large-scale LHC charged particle track features. Downstream tasks (kinematic regression, event classification) are then developed by fine-tuning or leveraging the pre-trained weights, compared against equivalent architectures trained from scratch. Latent space interpretation is performed, and cross-domain transfer is evaluated on gravitational wave, flood forecasting, and neural activity datasets.

Result: Pre-trained NEXUS weights yield improved accuracy on collider physics downstream tasks using only small labeled datasets versus training from scratch. The model successfully transfers to out-of-domain scientific tasks. It also demonstrates significantly lower computational cost compared to transformer models at comparable scale.

Conclusion: Lightweight autoencoder-based foundation models can effectively bridge scientific domains through unsupervised pre-training on physics data, offering a practical path to power-efficient, real-time, and edge-deployable foundation models in experimental science.

Abstract: We present a lightweight approach to foundation modeling (\textbf{NEXUS}) that leverages pre-trained learning from collider physics data towards out-of-domain tasks in other scientific datasets, using a fully connected autoencoder model with approximately 3 million parameters. The model pre-trains with no supervision over a large-scale collision dataset from the Large Hadron Collider modeled by charged particle track features. Downstream tasks for collider analyses, such as kinematic regression and event classification, are developed on pre-trained model weights and achieve improved accuracy with only small labeled datasets when compared to equivalent architectures trained from scratch. The benefits of pre-training are additionally investigated through latent space interpretation and application to other domains, including gravitational waves, flood forecasting, and neural activity. Furthermore, the relative computational simplicity of NEXUS is demonstrated compared to transformer approaches at comparable scale, opening the door to power-efficient inference and real-time or edge applications of foundation models in scientific experiments.

</details>


### [221] [Encryption-Compatible Clustered Federated Learning via Distributed Expectation-Maximization over Metadata](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28338)
*Michael Ben Ali,Imen Megdiche,André Péninou,Olivier Teste*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FLAMECHE reformulates metadata-based Clustered Federated Learning as a distributed Expectation-Maximization procedure, enabling compatibility with secure FL encryption while maintaining computational and communication efficiency, thus improving positioning within the CFL trilemma.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) methods face a fundamental trade-off—the "CFL trilemma"—among privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency. Metadata-based CFL approaches achieve efficiency in communication and computation but are incompatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms. The authors aim to bridge this gap by making metadata-based clustering encryption-compatible without sacrificing efficiency.

Method: The authors propose FLAMECHE, which reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure. The key design choice is restricting server-side updates to only additive operations, which preserves efficiency while enabling compatibility with practical secure FL schemes (e.g., homomorphic encryption or secure aggregation). Extensive experiments were conducted across multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios.

Result: FLAMECHE improves the effectiveness of client models compared to baselines and successfully enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering. It achieves a better balance within the CFL trilemma than prior approaches, simultaneously addressing privacy, communication cost, and computational efficiency.

Conclusion: By casting metadata-based CFL as a distributed EM procedure with additive-only server updates, FLAMECHE resolves the incompatibility between efficient metadata-based clustering and privacy-preserving mechanisms, advancing the state of the art in practical, secure clustered federated learning.

Abstract: Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) addresses data heterogeneity in federated settings by grouping clients with similar data distributions to enable effective training. Existing methods face a trade-off between privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency. We formalize this as the CFL trilemma, according to which improving two of these dimensions comes at the expense of the third. A prominent paradigm relies on metadata (i.e., low-dimensional representations of client datasets shared with the server) to enable communication- and computation-efficient clustering. However, such approaches are not compatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms. To address this limitation, we propose FLAMECHE, which reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure, restricting server updates to additive operations while preserving efficiency. This design enables compatibility with practical secure FL schemes. We conducted extensive experiments on multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios. Results show that FLAMECHE improves the effectiveness of client models. It enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering, enhancing its positioning within the CFL trilemma.

</details>


### [222] [Sparsity Induced Identifiability in Matrix Tri-Factorisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27507)
*Tingting Mu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides the first rigorous theoretical analysis of identifiability and recovery guarantees for sparsity-induced general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation, using a novel decomposition strategy that splits the problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems while preserving structural information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While sparsity constraints in two-factor matrix factorisation have been extensively studied with rigorous theoretical guarantees, such guarantees for general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation remain largely unexplored, despite tri-factorisation offering greater modelling flexibility and sparsity improving interpretability and recovery performance.

Method: A novel decomposition strategy transforms the original tri-factorisation problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems, preserving structural information needed for recovering the original factor matrices from observations. Based on this decomposition, the authors derive recovery guarantees and structural consistency results.

Result: The analysis yields recovery guarantees and structural consistency results characterising how coefficient sparsity influences sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Monte Carlo experiments validate the theoretical findings with close agreement between theory and empirical results.

Conclusion: The paper establishes the first rigorous theoretical framework for sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation, filling a significant theoretical gap and providing validated guarantees on recovery and structural consistency.

Abstract: Matrix factorisation is a fundamental tool for exploiting low-dimensional structure in high-dimensional data, with applications such as data compression, denoising, structure discovery, interpretable representation learning, and dimensionality reduction. Compared to conventional two-factor models, matrix tri-factorisation provides greater modelling flexibility, while sparsity constraints often improve both interpretability and recovery performance. Although the role of sparsity has been extensively studied for two-factor matrix factorisation, rigorous theoretical guarantees for general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation remain largely unexplored. To address this gap, we establish, to the best of our knowledge, the first rigorous theoretical study for sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation. Our analysis is enabled by a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the original problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems, while preserving the structural information necessary to the recovery of the original factor matrices from the observations. Building upon this decomposition, we derive recovery guarantees and structural consistency results that characterise how coefficient sparsity influences the sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments validate the proposed theory and demonstrate close agreement between the theoretical results and empirical observations.

</details>


### [223] [Expanding Data-Agnostic Pivotal Instances Selection Models with Proximity Trees and Ensemble Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27522)
*Alessio Cascione,Mattia Setzu,Cristiano Landi,Paolo Maria Mancarella,Riccardo Guidotti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hierarchical pivot selection method is proposed for building interpretable predictive models. By selecting representative examples (pivots) and comparing new instances via similarity, the approach mimics human decision-making. It supports single pivots, pivot pairs (inspired by proximity/oblique trees), and ensembles, is data modality-agnostic via pre-trained networks, and achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art interpretable models with very few pivots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing machine learning methods for complex decision-making often lack interpretability. Since humans naturally make decisions by analogizing to a few representative cases, there is a need for predictive models that select and reason with such exemplars (pivots) in an inherently interpretable, hierarchical manner.

Method: A hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model based on similarity between pivots and input instances. The method extends beyond single pivots to incorporate pivot pairs (drawing on proximity and oblique tree concepts) and ensembles. It is data modality-agnostic, utilizing pre-trained networks for transforming diverse data types (tabular, text, images, time series).

Result: Experiments across tabular, text, image, and time series datasets show the method outperforms alternative instance selection strategies and achieves competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models, all while maintaining a minimal number of pivots.

Conclusion: The proposed hierarchical pivot selection approach successfully bridges interpretability and predictive performance. By using a small number of carefully selected pivots—optionally in pairs or ensembles—it delivers competitive accuracy across diverse data modalities, offering a practical, human-aligned alternative to black-box models.

Abstract: As decision-making processes grow more complex, machine learning tools have become essential for tackling business and societal challenges. However, many existing methods rely on decision-making procedures that are difficult to interpret. Since humans naturally make decisions by comparing new cases with a few representative examples, we aim to design an approach that selects such pivots to construct an interpretable predictive model. Inspired by decision trees, we propose a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model based on the similarity between pivots and input instances. Our method functions both as a pivot selection technique and a standalone predictive model. Extending beyond single pivots, we incorporate pairs of pivots that are used by proximity and oblique trees, as well as ensembles, which enhance the versatility and effectiveness of our proposal. Additionally, our approach is data modality-agnostic, leveraging pre-trained networks for data transformation. Experiments across diverse datasets, including tabular data, text, images, and time series, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming alternative instance selection strategies and achieving competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models while maintaining a minimal number of pivots.

</details>


### [224] [Cybersecurity Detection Classification with Reasoning-enabled Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28460)
*Amol Khanna,Manu Nandan,Cristian Viorel Popa,Joan Pujol-Roig,Diana Bolocan,Laura Vasilie,Alexandru Apostu,Chase Helwig,Mihaela Gaman,Michael Brautbar,Edward Raff,Chase Midler,Sven Krasser*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses SOC alert fatigue by training a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier on Windows endpoint detections. Using prompt optimization, self-training, and RL with verifiable rewards, the system achieves 82.6% accuracy and significantly improves high-confidence recall over direct-label LLMs. A separate calibrator is needed because CoT reasoning degrades label-token probabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Security Operations Centers suffer from alert fatigue — too many detections to triage manually. Prior LLM-based approaches emit triage labels directly without explicit reasoning about threat genuineness. The authors aim to build a system that reasons step-by-step about detections, improving both accuracy and trustworthiness for automated triage.

Method: The authors train a CoT reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections. The training pipeline combines: (1) automated prompt optimization to elicit high-quality reasoning chains, (2) self-training to expand effective training data, and (3) reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards to refine reasoning. Because CoT reasoning degrades raw label-token probabilities, they separately train a calibrator that ingests the full reasoning trace and outputs a calibrated probability of correctness. The system uses a 30B parameter finetuned model.

Result: The system reaches 82.6% test accuracy. At the high-confidence operating point for automated triage, it improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. The trained calibrator is essential — without it, high-confidence recall collapses to zero. A finetuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models, motivating targeted training over simply scaling model size.

Conclusion: CoT reasoning improves triage classification but paradoxically degrades raw confidence scores, necessitating a dedicated calibrator. Targeted finetuning of moderate-scale models with reasoning training yields better results than using larger general-purpose LLMs, providing a practical path to reducing SOC alert fatigue through automated, explainable triage.

Abstract: A major issue in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) is alert fatigue, as the number of detections reported is more than staff can triage in a given day. Prior work prompts or fine-tunes large language models (LLMs) to emit a triage label directly, but does not train them to reason about whether a detection is a genuine threat. We train a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections by combining automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. We find that CoT reasoning also degrades the label-token probabilities that automated triage relies on, so we separately train a calibrator that reads the full reasoning trace and estimates the probability that the verdict is correct. Our system reaches 82.6% test accuracy and, at the high-confidence operating point that governs automated triage, improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. We further show that the trained calibrator is necessary - an untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall to zero - and that a finetuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models, motivating targeted training over scale.

</details>


### [225] [Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps for Few-Step Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27529)
*Mansoor Ahmed,Yue-Tsz Fan,Hemanth Venkateswara,Murray Patterson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LKF introduces a latent-kernel discrete flow map that natively expresses correlated token updates in few-step discrete diffusion/flow-matching for text generation. By mixing M factorized components tied by a shared latent, LKF achieves correlated sequence generation in a single step with the same complexity as factorized models, improving generative perplexity 2.1x–3.3x over baselines and surpassing distilled/rectified few-step samplers at M=8.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing discrete diffusion and flow-matching models use factorized, per-position independent transitions for efficiency, but this fails to capture cross-position dependencies (e.g., subject-verb agreement) in few-step generation. Current solutions distill or rectify slow teacher models, inheriting the teacher's quality ceiling rather than learning correlations natively.

Method: The authors propose Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a flow-map kernel constructed as a mixture of M factorized components conditioned on a single shared latent variable. The latent is drawn once per sequence and reused across all denoising steps. For small M, the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form. The approach retains the same sampling time complexity as factorized models while enabling correlated updates. MDLM is shown to be a special case at M=1.

Result: On LM1B and WikiText-103 unconditional text generation benchmarks, LKF learns strongly heterogeneous components and achieves 2.1x to 3.3x generative perplexity improvement over likelihood baselines without diversity loss. Performance scales with M; at M=8, LKF surpasses both distilled and rectified few-step samplers.

Conclusion: LKF demonstrates that native correlation in discrete flow-map kernels is feasible and effective for few-step text generation, outperforming teacher-dependent methods while maintaining computational efficiency. The approach is trained from scratch and released as open-source.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion and flow-matching models denoise a sequence over many steps, but to keep each step cheap, they factorize the transition across positions and decide every token independently. This makes few-step generation challenging for text when the target couples two positions, such as a subject and a verb that must agree. An independent update commits to them separately, and many function evaluations are spent repairing the mismatch. Existing few-step methods buy back the lost correlation by distilling or rectifying a slow teacher, and so inherit the teacher's quality ceiling. We ask instead whether a model can express correlated steps natively, and answer with Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a from-scratch flow-map kernel that is a mixture of M factorized components tied by a single shared latent. Conditioned on the latent, each component is cheap, and the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M. We show that a single step places mass on correlated completions with the same sampling time complexity as a factorized model, since one latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory. We also show that the Masked Diffusion Language Model (MDLM) is a special case of our LKF model at M=1. The experiments for unconditional text generation on the One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 benchmarks show that our LKF model learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over the likelihood baselines without losing diversity. The gain grows with M, and at M=8, it surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers. The source code is available at: https://github.com/mansoor181/lkf.git

</details>


### [226] [When Does Explicit View Routing Work? A Controlled Study of Multi-View Graph-Text Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27530)
*Xiao Yue,Guangzhi Qu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether multi-head graph-text retrieval models genuinely route queries based on semantic content. Using controlled experiments with deterministic text segments, isolated encoders, and external labels/descriptors, the authors show that correct routing substantially improves retrieval metrics, and that multi-head models can outperform single-head specialists, but the evidence is limited to explicit, externally grounded routing scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-text retrieval models map graphs and descriptions to a single embedding, conflating multiple semantic aspects (e.g., topology, class labels, molecular properties). While multi-head architectures can separate these aspects, changing which head receives a query may alter retrieval even with mismatched content—this reflects architectural channelization rather than true semantic routing. The authors aim to distinguish between these two phenomena and establish conditions under which genuine content-based routing can be empirically demonstrated.

Method: The authors use a controlled version of MV-GTA with: (1) deterministic, verifiable text segments; (2) isolated text encoders per view; (3) view-specific graph heads; and (4) relevance derived from external labels or RDKit descriptors. They perform a causal test using correct routing versus per-sample derangements. Experiments cover BBBP and BACE molecular datasets, comparing correct routing against deranged training, expected head versus best wrong head, joint multi-head models versus separately trained specialists, and property paraphrase augmentation versus matched-exposure controls.

Result: Correct routing improves label and property nDCG by 0.305–0.685 over deranged training. The expected graph head exceeds the best wrong head by 0.303–0.453. Topology does not specialize consistently across both datasets. A joint three-head model achieves mean topology/label/property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877 versus three separate specialists at 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140–0.147. However, consistency and hard-template extensions reduce canonical retrieval in some settings.

Conclusion: The evidence supports explicit, externally grounded label and property routing, and demonstrates observed multi-interface consolidation benefits. However, it does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to specialists, or superior downstream prediction—delineating clear boundaries for the claims that can be made about semantic routing in graph-text retrieval.

Abstract: Graph-text retrieval typically maps a graph and its description to a single embedding, even when a query concerns only one semantic aspect, such as a class label or molecular property. Multiple heads can separate these aspects, but a change in the query head may alter retrieval even when the wrong text is sent to that head. Such behavior demonstrates architectural channelization, not necessarily semantic routing. We examine the conditions under which this distinction can be resolved. Our controlled version of MV-GTA uses deterministic, verifiable text segments; isolated text encoders; view-specific graph heads; and relevance derived from external labels or RDKit descriptors. Correct routing and per-sample derangements form a causal test of whether retrieval depends on content. On BBBP and BACE, correct routing improves label and property nDCG by 0.305 to 0.685 over deranged training. The expected graph head exceeds the best wrong head by 0.303 to 0.453. Topology does not specialize consistently across the two datasets. In a matched three-seed comparison, one joint model obtains mean topology, label, and property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877; three separately trained Single specialists obtain 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation also improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140 and 0.147 over a matched-exposure canonical control. Consistency and hard-template extensions, however, reduce canonical retrieval in some settings. The evidence is therefore limited to explicit, externally grounded label and property routing and observed multi-interface consolidation. It does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to specialists, or superior downstream prediction.

</details>


### [227] [Subtract or Replay? Exact Deletion from Language-Model Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27539)
*Vishwajith Ramesh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Exact deletion from language model memory depends on representation: addressable memories support algebraic decrement, while entangled recurrent writes require checkpointed rewind-and-replay. Experiments on Gemma 3 (1B–12B) with support-vector memory and a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid validate this distinction, achieving bit-identical state recovery and matching never-ingested baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To establish that exact record deletion from language models is fundamentally a property of memory representation — specifically, whether contributions are addressable (allowing simple subtraction) or become entangled through subsequent writes in shared recurrent state (requiring replay from a checkpoint before the write). This addresses the growing need for verifiable machine unlearning in deployed models.

Method: The paper tests the addressable-vs-entangled distinction across two model architectures: (1) Gemma 3 modified with support-vector memory replacing global-attention layers, tested at 1B, 4B, and 12B scales using low-rank recovery, algebraic decrement, and retained-key refit; (2) a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid model where additive writes, diagonal decay, and delta-rule contributions are analyzed for suffix-dependence, with checkpointed rewind-and-replay used for exact deletion of clinical records at contexts up to 18,842 tokens. Evaluation uses KL divergence, perplexity, elicitation, relearning, sampling, and LiRA attacks against never-ingested baselines.

Result: For Gemma 3 at 1B, decrement and retained-key refit agree to median KL of 5.4×10⁻¹⁵ over 31 support-token deletions, with only +2.0% perplexity relative to a matched fine-tune; a masked-refit proxy is indistinguishable from the never-ingested floor. At 4B and 12B, the same certificate ordering holds but utility cost rises to 11.2% and 44.3%. For the 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, additive writes admit a fixed decrement and diagonal decay a corrected one, while delta-rule contributions are 12–49% suffix-dependent. Checkpointed rewind-and-replay yields logits and all recurrent states bit-identical to never-ingested, with replay of a correction providing exact amendment.

Conclusion: Exact deletion is a property of memory representation: addressable records can be subtracted directly, while entangled writes require replaying from a pre-write checkpoint. The work demonstrates that verifiable, bit-identical unlearning is achievable in large-scale models given appropriate architectural choices about how memory is stored and updated.

Abstract: Exact deletion from persistent language-model memory depends on how that memory represents a record. Addressable influence can be removed by algebraic decrement; influence transformed by later writes inside shared recurrent state requires rebuilding from before the write. We test this distinction in two pretrained models against explicit record-omitted references. First, we replace Gemma 3's global-attention layers with support-vector memory. After low-rank recovery at 1B, decrement and retained-key refit agree at the next-token output to median KL $5.4\times10^{-15}$ over 31 support-token deletions, with $+2.0\%$ perplexity relative to a matched fine-tune. A masked-refit proxy is indistinguishable from the never-ingested floor under elicitation, relearning, sampling, and LiRA attacks. At 4B and 12B, certificate ordering persists but utility cost rises to $11.2\%$ and $44.3\%$. Second, in a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, additive writes admit a fixed decrement and diagonal decay a corrected one, whereas the delta rule makes $12$--$49\%$ of a record's contribution suffix-dependent. Checkpointed rewind-and-replay deletes real clinical records at contexts up to 18,842 tokens, matching never-ingested logits and all recurrent states bit for bit within a deterministic MLX implementation; replaying a correction provides exact amendment. Exact deletion is therefore a property of memory representation: subtract addressable records and replay entangled writes.

</details>


### [228] [Memory Efficient Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27546)
*Shuting Luo,Monika Mikhail Kanaan,Cameron Gordon,Anna Leontjeva,Simon Lucey*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates memory compression for Tabular Foundation Models (specifically TabPFN), demonstrating that model compression can reduce memory requirements by up to 7.6× (nearly 87% reduction) while maintaining comparable performance, offering practical deployment guidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While Tabular Foundation Models like TabPFN have shown strong in-context learning performance, prior work has focused on accuracy benchmarks while neglecting practical deployment constraints—particularly memory requirements, which are critical for real-world, resource-limited settings.

Method: The authors apply model compression approaches to TabPFN and systematically evaluate the trade-off between memory reduction and downstream task performance, measuring compression ratios and corresponding accuracy retention.

Result: Memory reductions of up to 7.6× are achievable with similar levels of predictive performance, corresponding to an ~87% decrease in deployment memory requirements.

Conclusion: Model compression is a viable and effective strategy for reducing the memory footprint of Tabular Foundation Models, making them more accessible for practical deployment without sacrificing performance.

Abstract: Tabular Foundation Models, such as TabPFN, have received a large amount of recent attention due to their performance on in-context tabular machine learning tasks, which often exceeds classical baselines. However, practical deployment considerations of these models has received less attention. In this paper we investigate the memory requirements for these models. We demonstrate that employing model compression approaches can enable memory reductions of up to 7.6 with similar levels of performance, reducing deployment requirements by nearly 87%. Our work provides insight to practitioners seeking efficient deployment of these models in practical settings.

</details>


### [229] [Strategies for Milestone-driven Start-ups in Multi-activity Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27563)
*Zhengli Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper solves a continuous-time stochastic control problem for entrepreneurial start-ups navigating milestone-based survival, where the firm's state follows a diffusion process. The authors fully characterize the optimal policy using an "efficient frontier curve" that ranks multiple controls by riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio). A novel finding is that the efficient frontier can take qualitatively different forms depending on parameters, yielding structurally distinct optimal strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: New venture start-ups face a survival problem across multiple milestone stages, but continuous-time stochastic models with three or more controls are notoriously difficult to solve. Existing literature lacks a complete characterization of optimal policies in such settings, and no prior work has analyzed models where the efficient frontier of controls can change type, leading to qualitatively different optimal strategies.

Method: The authors model the start-up's state as a diffusion process with an upper (success) and lower (failure) absorbing boundary. The entrepreneur selects among multiple activities (controls) that differ in drift, volatility, and cost. The problem is formulated as a stochastic control model, which they solve completely. The solution relies on characterizing controls via an efficient frontier curve that orders them by two ratios: riskiness (drift/volatility) and cost-effectiveness (drift/cost).

Result: The authors derive an explicit optimal policy structure: only controls lying on the efficient frontier curve are ever used. Depending on model parameters, the efficient frontier can be of different types, leading to qualitatively distinct optimal policy structures. This is the first study to identify and analyze such type variation in efficient frontier curves within a stochastic control framework.

Conclusion: The paper provides start-up firms with intuitive metrics (riskiness and cost-effectiveness) to evaluate activities and offers insights into how optimal milestone-oriented strategies shift qualitatively across scenarios. The results serve as a foundational contribution to the study of entrepreneurial decision-making under uncertainty.

Abstract: New venture start-ups need to ``survive'' through multiple stages of reaching milestone targets. We investigate the strategies for start-ups in a milestone-oriented setting. We examine a model of an entrepreneurial start-up firm, where its state is captured by a diffusion process. The entrepreneur can choose between multiple activities (or controls), which incur different cost and determine the drift and the variance of the process. Depending on whether the process reaches a fixed upper boundary or a lower one, the start-up firm succeeds or fails. Continuous-time stochastic models with multiple ($\ge 3$) controls are typically very challenging to deal with. In this work, we are able to completely solve for the optimal policy and provide an explicit characterization of its structure. In particular, the optimal policy only uses controls from a set characterized by a so-called efficient frontier curve that orders the controls by two intuitive measures: riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio). A unique feature of our model is that depending on the model parameters, the efficient frontier curves can be of different types, resulting in qualitatively different structures of the optimal policy. As far as we know, this is the first study that analyzes a stochastic control model which admits efficient frontier curves of different types. Our work provides start-up firms with intuitive measures to evaluate their activities and offers valuable insights on how the optimal strategies in a milestone-oriented setting change qualitatively contingent upon the specific scenario. We believe the results provide a foundational block in the study of entrepreneurial decision-making.

</details>


### [230] [MUGEN: A Unified Framework for Efficient Motion Understanding and Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27581)
*Zhankai Ye,Yukai Jin,Bingyang Wei,Bofan Li,Yusen Wu,Fangyi Li,Shangqian Gao,Xin Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MUGEN is a unified motion-language framework that eliminates discrete codebooks and iterative decoding, using a single adaptive-length autoencoder to compress motion into continuous latent slots. It achieves strong text-to-motion generation and motion understanding with minimal decoding cost—just K LM steps, one draw, and one decoder pass—outperforming both language-model baselines and discrete-token state-of-the-art on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing unified motion-language systems rely on discrete motion codebooks for bidirectional generation and understanding, but quantization degrades quality. Stronger generators compensate via stacked residual codebooks, masked decoding, long autoregressive rollouts, multi-step denoising chains, or iterative diffusion heads—all of which inflate inference cost. Critically, this heavy decoding machinery serves only generation, not motion understanding. The authors aim to design a unified framework that achieves high-quality generation and understanding without these costs.

Method: MUGEN employs a single adaptive-length autoencoder that compresses arbitrary-length motion sequences into a small number of continuous latent slots—the sole motion representation for both generation and understanding. A language model generates these latent slots for text-to-motion and reads them back for motion understanding. Key architectural innovations include: (1) depth-routed hidden states allowing each slot to access only the transformer depth it requires, and (2) a calibrated prediction head that outputs a joint distribution over the full latent set, enabling a single draw to capture text-conditional cross-slot variation. The total decoding cost is K LM steps, one draw, and one decoder pass.

Result: On HumanML3D, MUGEN achieves leading FID among language-model baselines and raises retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator. It attains the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores. On SnapMoGen, MUGEN surpasses the discrete-token state of the art on every retrieval and alignment metric.

Conclusion: MUGEN demonstrates that a compact continuous latent representation combined with a single-draw generative process can unify motion generation and understanding without the inference overhead of discrete codebooks, residual quantization, or iterative decoding, advancing the goal of efficient physical AI systems that communicate human behavior bidirectionally.

Abstract: Grounding human motion in language, and language in motion, is a central step toward physical AI systems that can understand, generate, and communicate human behavior. Unified motion--language systems first coupled the two directions through a shared discrete motion codebook, but quantization limits generation quality. The strongest generators buy quality back at growing cost: stacked residual codebooks enlarge the representation; masked decoding stages, long autoregressive rollouts, and denoising chains of tens to hundreds of steps stretch inference; even the continuous-latent designs among them reach their latent only through an iterative diffusion head; and none of this decoding machinery serves understanding. We therefore propose MUGEN, a unified motion--language framework that pays neither cost: no codebook, one draw. A single adaptive-length autoencoder compresses any-length motion into a few continuous latent slots, the system's only motion representation: the language model generates them for text-to-motion and reads them back for motion understanding. Depth-routed hidden states let each slot read from the transformer depth it needs, and a calibrated head predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set, so a single draw carries the text-conditional, cross-slot variation a description permits. At a decoding cost of K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass, MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D while raising retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator, achieves the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses the discrete-token state of the art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen.

</details>


### [231] [Prox: Training-Free FFN Activation Sparsity via Approximate Intermediate-Channel Salience in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27591)
*Jinyi Liu,Wei Chen,Pengyu Chen,Xinyi Yuan,Minghe Bai,Guoquan Wu,Jun Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Prox is a training-free, two-stage framework for sparsifying SwiGLU FFNs in LLMs. It constructs a channel mask from input sparsity and quantized proxy weights (Stage 1), then computes only selected channels exactly (Stage 2), enabling sparse execution of all three projections. It achieves up to 1.99× decoding speedup at 70% sparsity without model-quality degradation typical of prior training-free methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FFNs dominate memory traffic and computation in LLM inference. Existing training-free activation sparsification methods degrade model quality at high sparsity due to poor channel-selection strategies. The SwiGLU intermediate state is an excellent channel-selection signal, but computing it requires the dense FFN computation the authors aim to avoid.

Method: Prox is a two-stage framework: Stage 1 uses input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared channel mask by approximating the magnitude ranking of the SwiGLU intermediate state entries without computing them exactly. Stage 2 computes only the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three FFN projections. The key insight is that sparse execution only needs the mask induced by the intermediate state, not the exact values.

Result: Evaluated across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms all training-free baselines at every sparsity level. It achieves up to 1.99× end-to-end decoding speedup at 70% FFN sparsity and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention techniques.

Conclusion: Approximating the SwiGLU intermediate state's magnitude ranking via input sparsity and quantized proxy weights is a viable and effective strategy for training-free FFN sparsification, enabling practical speedups without sacrificing model quality.

Abstract: Feed-forward networks (FFNs) dominate memory traffic and computation in large language model (LLM) inference, making them a primary target for activation sparsification. However, existing training-free methods suffer substantial model-quality degradation at high sparsity due to limitations in their channel-selection strategies. We observe that the SwiGLU intermediate state provides a highly effective channel-selection signal, but obtaining it requires costly dense computation. To address this, we present \emph{Prox}, a two-stage training-free framework for sparse SwiGLU FFNs. Prox hinges on the key insight: sparse execution requires only the channel mask induced by the intermediate state, which can be constructed from the magnitude ranking of its entries rather than their exact values. Specifically, Stage 1 uses input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared mask; Stage 2 computes the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections. Across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels, achieves up to a $1.99\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup at 70\% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention.

</details>


### [232] [Compliance2LoRA: On-Demand Safety Alignment on Arbitrary Policy Subsets via Hypernetwork-Generated LoRA Adapters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27594)
*Pankayaraj Pathmanathan,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a hypernetwork-based framework that dynamically generates LoRA adapter weights conditioned on specified safety policy subsets, enabling a single large reasoning model to adapt to multiple policy compliance configurations without retraining, avoiding combinatorial overhead and long-context generation costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As large reasoning models (LRMs) are personalized for downstream users, different users require compliance with different subsets of safety policies. Training separate LRMs for each policy subset incurs prohibitive combinatorial overhead, while in-context learning methods introduce computational challenges from long-context generation. A more efficient, unified solution is needed.

Method: The authors propose a unified adaptive hypernetwork-based framework. Safety policy subsets are provided as customizable inputs to a hypernetwork that functions as a LoRA adapter generator. The hypernetwork learns to produce policy-compliant LoRA weights conditioned on the specified policies. These generated weights are then added to the downstream LRM, enabling on-demand generation of responses aligned with the desired policy subset.

Result: The framework enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance. This holds across reasoning models of different sizes and across different evaluation datasets, demonstrating both effectiveness and practicality.

Conclusion: Adaptive hypernetwork-based alignment is an effective and practical approach for multi-policy compliance in LRMs, eliminating the need for training separate models per policy subset while avoiding the computational burdens of in-context learning methods.

Abstract: Post-training alignment in large reasoning models (LRMs) has significantly improved their adaptability to diverse safety compliance settings. However, as LRMs personalization for downstream users takes center stage, the demand for varying levels of policy compliance grows as different user-specific LRMs must adhere to distinct subsets of safety policies. Training a separate LRM for each policy subset introduces severe combinatorial overhead. While in context learning methods overcome this combinatorial overhead, they introduce additional computational challenges associated with long context generation. To address this challenge, we propose \ours, a unified adaptive hypernetwork-based framework for multi-policy compliance. In our framework, safety policies serve as customizable inputs to a LoRA adapter generator, which learns to produce policy compliant LoRA weights for downstream LRM. When added to the LRM these weights enable the generation of responses compliant with the specified policy subsets. In this work, we demonstrate that training such a hypernetwork enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance across reasoning models of different sized and different evaluation datasets. This highlights the effectiveness and practicality of adaptive hypernetwork based alignment in LRMs.

</details>


### [233] [Back from the Future: Key-Value Cache Management by Counter-Causal Surprise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27600)
*Stephen Gould,Anton van den Hengel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A training-free KV cache eviction method that removes past tokens predictable from future context using a counter-causal attention mask, with a fast single-layer approximation variant.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV cache memory grows linearly with context length, consuming GPU memory and limiting long-context generation. Existing compression/eviction methods aim to reduce this footprint while preserving generation quality.

Method: The authors propose scoring KV cache entries by running a counter-causal pass: the model processes tokens in original order but each position attends only to its *future* context (reversed causal mask). Tokens well-predicted from future tokens are deemed redundant and evicted. This reuses cached key/value representations, requires no additional training, and is in-distribution. A fast approximation restricts the counter-causal pass to only the final transformer layer, trading marginal accuracy for significant speedup per refresh cycle.

Result: Competitive or improved performance over existing state-of-the-art KV eviction methods across multiple open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets.

Conclusion: The counter-causal eviction strategy is simple, effective, training-free, and directly leverages the model's own representations to identify redundant cached tokens, with a practical speed-accuracy tradeoff via single-layer approximation.

Abstract: Key-value (KV) cache management through compression and eviction strategies has emerged as an important research direction in recent years. Computational demands of large language models (LLMs) and their multi-modal variants during output generation can be partially alleviated by caching previous key and value calculations needed by subsequent scaled dot-product attention operations. However, this leads to another problem: the size of the resulting KV cache grows linearly with context length and quickly consumes all available GPU memory when either the prompt or the generated output are long. KV cache management periodically prunes entries from the cache thereby reducing its memory footprint while attempting to retain sufficient information for accurate generation. A by-product is faster inference speed. We propose a simple yet effective KV eviction scheme motivated by the insight that past tokens which can be well-predicted from more recent tokens are redundant and their associated keys and values can be removed from the cache. To score entries for eviction we run the model on the tokens in their original order, reusing the key and value representations already stored in the KV cache, and applying a counter-causal attention mask so that each position attends only to its future context. This is in-distribution, tied directly to the actual cache contents, and requires no additional training. To further reduce cost, we additionally propose a fast single-layer approximation that restricts the counter-causal pass to the last transformer layer, achieving a significant speedup per refresh cycle at marginal accuracy cost. We evaluate our strategy on various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets showing competitive or improved performance over other state-of-the-art methods. Reference code is available at https://github.com/metacognitionai/counter_causal.

</details>


### [234] [Kalman Meets Curriculum: Efficient Dynamic Prompt Selection for Adaptive RL Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27610)
*Haodong Zhu,Yangyang Ren,Yanjing Li,Sheng Xu,Haiguang Liu,Linlin Yang,Baochang Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KGPS reformulates prompt selection in RL finetuning of LLMs as a dynamic state estimation problem using a Kalman filter, adaptively selecting prompts of intermediate difficulty while accounting for non-stationary training dynamics, achieving SOTA efficiency and accuracy without extra rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL finetuning of LLMs requires selecting prompts at appropriate difficulty levels, but prompt difficulty evolves non-stationarily as the policy improves. Existing methods face a trade-off: evaluation-based selection is accurate but costly (extra rollouts), while prediction-based selection is efficient but assumes stationary difficulty, failing under RL's dynamic conditions.

Method: KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space using a linear-Gaussian state-space model. Process noise is coupled to the magnitude of policy updates, increasing uncertainty when the policy changes substantially. A Kalman filter maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty. Prompts are selected by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility that favors intermediate-difficulty prompts while naturally revisiting uncertain ones. No additional rollouts beyond standard policy training are required.

Result: KGPS achieves state-of-the-art among online prompt selection methods. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, it uses 83% fewer rollouts than the baseline while improving average performance by 0.12 points across six math reasoning benchmarks. Consistent improvements are demonstrated across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks with multiple RL algorithms.

Conclusion: KGPS effectively addresses the non-stationary prompt selection challenge in RL finetuning by treating it as a dynamic state estimation problem, enabling adaptive, efficient, and accurate prompt selection without extra computational overhead.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning significantly enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet its effectiveness critically depends on selecting prompts of appropriate difficulty for the current policy. This is challenging because prompt difficulty evolves throughout training. Existing online methods therefore face a trade-off: evaluation-based approaches are accurate but expensive, while prediction-based approaches are efficient but typically assume stationary difficulty, making them ill-suited to RL's non-stationary training dynamics. To address these issues, we propose a Kalman-Guided Prompt Selection method (KGPS), which reformulates prompt selection as a dynamic state estimation problem rather than static difficulty prediction. KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space using a linear-Gaussian state-space model, with process noise coupled to the magnitude of policy updates so that uncertainty increases when the policy changes more substantially. A Kalman filter then maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty, and prompts are selected by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility that favors intermediate-difficulty prompts while naturally revisiting uncertain ones. The resulting procedure is adaptive to policy drift and requires no additional rollouts beyond standard policy training. Extensive experiments across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks, as well as multiple RL algorithms, show that KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines, establishing state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods. For example, on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, KGPS uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while even improving the average performance by 0.12 point across six math reasoning benchmarks.

</details>


### [235] [Real-Time Hard Peak Age-of-Information Safety with No-Regret Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27626)
*Wentao Zhang,Wentao Mo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hard real-time scheduling framework (OCO-PAoI-Hard) for safety-critical IoT systems that guarantees zero per-slot peak AoI deadline violations under adversarial conditions by reformulating the fractional peak-AoI deadline as an affine half-space constraint, enabling time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set with O(√T) regret.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety-critical IoT systems (industrial control, V2X, teleoperation) require hard per-slot peak AoI deadlines, not just average bounds. Existing methods fail under adversarial conditions: Whittle-index approaches assume stochastic channels, DRL relies on simulator rollouts, and long-term constrained OCO only achieves sublinear cumulative violation — none guarantee zero per-slot violation.

Method: The authors reformulate the fractional peak-AoI deadline as an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector, converting the problem into time-varying constrained OCO over a polyhedral safe set. A strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop enforces feasibility via one Euclidean projection per slot, while the gradient step preserves no-regret behavior. The virtual queue is reduced to an a-posteriori certificate. They derive closed-form static/dynamic regret bounds, a matching Ω(√T) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant for execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio.

Result: On a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, OCO-PAoI-Hard achieves zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds, while four representative baselines miss between 1.65% and 64.0% of slots. Empirical normalized regret stays below the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.

Conclusion: OCO-PAoI-Hard provides the first framework guaranteeing zero per-slot peak AoI deadline violations under adversarial conditions with provable O(√T) regret, supported by both theoretical bounds (including a matching lower bound) and strong empirical validation against multiple baselines.

Abstract: Safety-critical IoT systems such as industrial closed-loop control, V2X coordination, and remote teleoperation require every sensor's peak Age of Information (peak AoI, also abbreviated PAoI) to stay below a hard per-slot deadline, not merely an average bound. Existing approaches meet this requirement only under restrictive assumptions: stochastic channels for Whittle-index AoI, simulator rollouts for deep reinforcement learning, or sublinear cumulative violation for long-term constrained online convex optimization. Under adversarial coefficients, OCO-PAoI-Hard guarantees zero per-slot violation of the modeled AoI state under one-step viability and O(sqrt(T)) regret against any static safe comparator; packet-level safety requires stronger service assumptions. Our key observation is that the fractional peak-AoI deadline collapses exactly to an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector, turning hard real-time scheduling into time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set. A strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop enforces feasibility through one Euclidean projection per slot, the gradient step preserves no-regret behavior, and the classical virtual queue is reduced to an a-posteriori certificate. We establish closed-form static and dynamic regret bounds, a matching Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant against execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio. On a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, OCO-PAoI-Hard attains zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds, while four representative baselines miss between 1.65 percent and 64.0 percent of slots, and the empirical normalized regret stays below the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.

</details>


### [236] [First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization Over Distributed Networks for Robust Coreset Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27632)
*Yang Jiao,Kaixuan Jiao,Kai Yang,Nadjib Aitsaadi,Ilhem Fajjari,Renwei,Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formulates distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization problem and proposes F²CTO, the first distributed method to solve it, achieving an O(ε^{-3/2}) convergence rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IoT edge networks generate massive data with privacy concerns and robustness requirements. Existing coreset selection methods lack a distributed optimization framework that jointly handles robustness and privacy-aware distributed learning.

Method: The authors formalize the problem as a trilevel optimization with level-wise constraints capturing dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning. They propose F²CTO, combining a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation with a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm.

Result: F²CTO achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(ε^{-3/2}) to an ε-stationary point. Extensive experiments on reliable continual learning validate its effectiveness and efficiency.

Conclusion: F²CTO is the first method for distributed robust coreset selection and the first distributed approach for constrained trilevel optimization, effectively bridging robust optimization and distributed coreset selection for privacy-sensitive edge deployments.

Abstract: With the rapid advancement of the Internet of Things (IoT), massive amounts of data are generated across distributed edge networks. Training models on full data incurs significant computational overhead and storage bottlenecks, rendering coreset selection a critical paradigm. Furthermore, given the privacy-sensitive nature of local data and the escalating demand for model robustness in real-world deployments, developing an effective distributed optimization framework for robust coreset selection is vital, yet remains largely unexplored. To this end, this work first characterizes the hierarchical dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning, and formulates the distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints. Furthermore, to effectively solve the trilevel problem in a distributed manner, the \underline{F}ederated \underline{F}irst-order \underline{C}onstrained \underline{T}rilevel \underline{O}ptimization (F$^2$CTO) is proposed, which synergistically integrates a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation and a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, F$^2$CTO is the first method developed for distributed robust coreset selection, as well as the first distributed optimization approach for trilevel optimization problems with level-wise constraints. Additionally, we prove that the proposed method achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-3/2})$ for finding an $ε$-stationary point. Extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed F$^2$CTO.

</details>


### [237] [Certifying when decision-time information justifies adaptive experimentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27651)
*Jia Bi,Samuel Pinilla,Chenyang Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OPAL is a framework that pre-commits to whether adaptive experimentation should be allowed, using a contract requiring non-trivial adaptation, controlled risk, and positive net value. It establishes impossibility bounds under unrestricted covariate shift, provides a calibrated recovery method, and demonstrates on a large compound screening dataset that only OPAL combined non-zero activation with guaranteed risk control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most adaptive experimentation methods focus on how to adapt during experiments, but none address the foundational question of whether adaptation should be enabled at all. Without such a gate, adaptive procedures may waste resources or produce unreliable results when conditions do not support adaptation.

Method: OPAL uses a precommitted authorization contract with three requirements: non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk, and positive executed value after cost. The framework establishes an impossibility boundary showing source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, then derives a target-calibrated recovery procedure. Evaluation uses a frozen gate on 11,265 compounds from Cell Painting data, with comparison against six baseline methods.

Result: On the Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities, and achieved strictly positive executed value under least-favourable completion, with a 5.18% false-activation upper bound (below the 7.5% limit). Among six compared methods, only OPAL combined non-zero activation with risk control. Pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies further distinguished policy misalignment from non-certifiability.

Conclusion: Authorization constitutes a distinct and necessary layer for safe adaptive science, separate from how adaptation is executed. OPAL provides the first principled framework for deciding whether to adapt, with formal guarantees that prevent unsafe deployment of adaptive methods.

Abstract: Adaptive laboratories choose measurements during experiments, yet most methods begin after adaptation is permitted. We introduce Opportunity-aware Policy Authorization for Laboratories (\OPAL{}), a framework that decides whether adaptation should be enabled at all. \OPAL{} uses a precommitted contract to require non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk and positive executed value after cost. We establish an impossibility boundary: source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, and derive a target-calibrated recovery. Applied to an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities and achieved strictly positive executed value under least-favourable completion; its 5.18\% false-activation upper bound remained below a 7.5\% limit. Among six methods, only \OPAL{} combined non-zero activation with this risk control. Locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies distinguish policy misalignment from non-certifiability, establishing authorization as a distinct layer for safe adaptive science.

</details>


### [238] [Evaluation Protocols and Cross-Subject Generalization in EEG Emotion Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27655)
*Hanting Suo,Yuwen Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper dissects EEG emotion recognition evaluation, revealing that reported accuracy depends on the entire evaluation pipeline—not just the classifier. Using a DGCNN on SEED/SEED-IV, it demonstrates stark performance discrepancies between subject-dependent, cross-session, and subject-disjoint protocols, with held-out participant accuracy dropping to near-chance levels (~53% on SEED, ~40% on SEED-IV) despite near-perfect within-participant trial accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG emotion recognition papers report widely varying accuracies, creating confusion about true progress. The authors argue this variability stems from inconsistent evaluation procedures—differences in target quantities (what is being predicted), development procedures (how models are selected and tuned), and reporting rules (which metrics are reported). A systematic decomposition and empirical demonstration of these factors' impact is needed to improve reproducibility and interpretability.

Method: The authors decompose the evaluation pipeline into three components: target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule. They use a single fixed DGCNN architecture on SEED and SEED-IV datasets to isolate evaluation effects. Three protocols are compared: (1) protocol-matched subject-dependent with session-disjoint splits; (2) five-fold subject-disjoint cross-validation; and (3) fully held-out participant evaluation. They analyze checkpoint selection strategies, compute bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) confidence intervals, and conduct supporting analyses on participant ranking stability and ensemble tail-risk performance.

Result: Key findings: (1) Protocol-matched subject-dependent SEED accuracy was within 1.47 points of the published reference; SEED-IV showed a 3.40-point unresolved gap. (2) Repeated test-set checkpoint selection inflated mean window accuracy from 0.7855 to 0.8892. (3) Under subject-disjoint validation, within-participant trial accuracy reached 0.9990 (SEED) and 0.9920 (SEED-IV), but held-out participant accuracy collapsed to 0.5348 (BCa: [0.4667, 0.5985]) on SEED and 0.3954 ([0.3343, 0.4648]) on SEED-IV. (4) Participant rankings depended on representation and time scale; a tail-risk ensemble showed no positive gain in final evaluation.

Conclusion: Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results answer fundamentally different questions and must be explicitly distinguished in reporting. The large train-to-held-out-subject gap cannot be attributed solely to simple underfitting; instead, subject identity, preprocessing, representation, and distributional factors all contribute. Authors should report all three evaluation paradigms, and the field needs standardized evaluation protocols to enable meaningful comparison.

Abstract: Reported accuracy in electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition depends on the complete evaluation procedure, not only the classifier. We separate the target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule, then use one archived dynamical graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) pathway on SEED and SEED-IV as an illustrative case. In a protocol-matched subject-dependent check, the SEED result was within 1.47 percentage points of the public reference value; the 3.40-point SEED-IV difference remained unresolved. Across 30 matched SEED subject-session trajectories, checkpoint selection based on repeated test-set evaluation increased mean window accuracy from 0.7855 at epoch 80 to 0.8892. Under five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation, validation-selected checkpoints achieved training-participant trial accuracies of 0.9990 on SEED and 0.9920 on SEED-IV. Accuracy for entirely held-out participants was 0.5348 (95% conditional subject-level bias-corrected and accelerated [BCa] interval [0.4667, 0.5985]) on SEED. The SEED-IV estimate was 0.3954 ([0.3343, 0.4648]) and is reported only as secondary sensitivity evidence because its protocol-matched compatibility check remained unresolved. The observed train-to-held-out-subject gaps are inconsistent with simple optimization underfitting, but they do not isolate subject identity from implementation, preprocessing, representation, or distributional factors. Supporting analyses further showed that participant rankings depended on representation and time scale, while a development-selected tail-risk ensemble did not establish a positive gain in a separate final evaluation. Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results should therefore be reported as answers to different questions.

</details>


### [239] [Looped Transformers with Source-Centered State Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27656)
*Bum Jun Kim,Kohei Hayashi,Shunsuke Kamiya,Masanori Koyama,Yusuke Iwasawa,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCSE proposes a novel recurrence mechanism for Looped Transformers that ensures exact invariance at a learned anchor state while allowing nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation, improving quality across language modeling benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In additive-injection looped Transformers, the same shared block must handle varying hidden states across recurrent depth, but reintroducing input-conditioned signals at each step can destabilize the recurrence. The tension between input conditioning and preserving a stable reference state motivates designing a recurrence that reconciles both.

Method: SCSE introduces three key components: (1) a learned anchor representing an input-conditioned reference, (2) an initial deviation from that anchor, and (3) a zero-deviation mask that guarantees exact anchor invariance — mapping zero deviation to zero output. The zero-deviation forcing bias (the deviation produced from the anchor itself) is set to zero by design, making the anchor a one-step fixed point while nonzero deviations remain active for recurrent computation.

Result: SCSE improves the recurrent quality frontier on WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion. Ablations show the learned anchor and anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence are primary contributors. A case study anchors the diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.

Conclusion: SCSE successfully reconciles input conditioning with reference-preserving recurrence in Looped Transformers. Setting the zero-deviation forcing bias to zero (exact anchor invariance) proves beneficial, and the anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence is the key mechanism driving empirical gains.

Abstract: Looped Transformers create a useful train- and test-time compute axis by reusing the same Transformer block over recurrent depth, increasing effective depth at a fixed parameter count. However, that shared block must then govern an entire trajectory of varying hidden states over trained and extrapolated depths. Furthermore, in additive-injection looped Transformers, an input-conditioned signal is reintroduced at every recurrent step, so applying the shared transition at an input-conditioned reference can still move the hidden state. In this paper, we propose Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE), which is designed to reconcile input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence. Specifically, SCSE retains input dependence through its learned anchor and initial deviation, allows nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation while mapping zero deviation to zero, and guarantees exact anchor invariance through its zero-deviation mask. The designated anchor is thereby a one-step fixed point by construction. The zero-deviation forcing bias is the next deviation produced from the anchor itself and vanishes in SCSE, while nonzero deviations remain active and support state-dependent recurrent computation. Our theory shows that the zero-deviation forcing bias is a design degree of freedom whose task effect can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial; SCSE resolves this choice in favor of exact anchor invariance by setting the bias to zero. Across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion, SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier. Ablation studies identify the learned anchor and the anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence as the primary contributors to the gain, and a trained-model case study grounds the anchor-response diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.

</details>


### [240] [Understanding Submodular Information Measure Based Objectives for Representation Learning: A Variance and Separation Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27660)
*Rishabh Iyer,Truong Pham,Anay Majee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides a unified theoretical framework that connects Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) to classical representation learning concepts, characterizing how different Total Information and Mutual Information objectives (Graph Cut, LogDet, Facility Location variants) correspond to specific geometric and statistical properties like within-class variance, covariance volume, class separation, and imbalance handling. The theoretical predictions are validated through controlled synthetic experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the empirical success of SCORE and other SIM-based frameworks for supervised contrastive learning, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood, limiting principled selection and design of these objectives.

Method: The authors develop a unified theoretical framework that analytically connects SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition. They characterize Total Information (TI) objectives for intra-class structure and Mutual Information (MI) objectives for inter-class structure, across three submodular function variants: Graph Cut, LogDet, and Facility Location. Validation uses controlled synthetic experiments that independently manipulate variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap.

Result: Total Information objectives: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation emphasizing rare/confusable classes. Mutual Information objectives: Graph Cut MI relates to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation via Mahalanobis distance, Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap. Synthetic experiments closely match all theoretical predictions across all settings.

Conclusion: The paper presents the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures, providing principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

Abstract: Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for representation learning and multimodal learning. In particular, the SCORE framework~\cite{majee2024score} demonstrated that SIMs can serve as effective objectives for supervised contrastive learning. Despite their empirical success, however, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood.
  In this work, we develop a unified theoretical framework connecting SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition. We show that Total Information (TI) objectives characterize intra-class structure: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, and Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation that emphasizes rare and confusable classes. We further show that Mutual Information (MI) objectives capture complementary notions of inter-class structure: Graph Cut MI is closely related to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation through Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap.
  We validate these theoretical characterizations using controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap. Across all settings, the empirical behavior closely matches the proposed theory.
