Our results provide the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures and offer principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

</details>


### [241] [FedOGL: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Federated Open-World Multimodal Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27665)
*Zekai Chen,Haodong Lu,Shihao Li,Weiwei Ji,Xunkai Li,Xun Wu,Yinlin Zhu,Rong-Hua Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedOGL is a federated graph learning framework for open-world continual learning that mitigates catastrophic forgetting in multimodal graphs through client-side semantic-structural memory preservation (replay, task-start distillation, global structure basis projection) and server-side compact category prototypes, achieving a 42.67% reduction in forgetting compared to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In federated multimodal graph learning, clients face evolving data streams with emerging classes and must retain old knowledge while rejecting unknown samples. Catastrophic forgetting is exacerbated beyond standard classifier drift by three graph-specific mechanisms: modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation.

Method: FedOGL employs a dual client-server framework: (1) Client-side preserves historical decision behavior via replay and task-start distillation, and protects graph-propagation memory by projecting onto a globally shared structure basis. (2) Server-side maintains and transfers compact category prototypes for cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data.

Result: Extensive experiments show FedOGL reduces performance degradation from catastrophic forgetting by 42.67% compared to the best-performing baselines, while maintaining or improving downstream task performance.

Conclusion: FedOGL effectively addresses the unique challenges of catastrophic forgetting in federated multimodal graph learning through its semantic-structural memory preservation framework, demonstrating substantial improvements over existing methods.

Abstract: Federated graph learning enables collaborative training over decentralized graph data without sharing raw graph information. As such risks evolve, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams, retain historical categories, and reject samples outside the known class space. In this setting, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while preserving historical categories and rejecting samples outside the current known class space. The core challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which in federated multimodal graphs is not merely a classifier-level failure: old knowledge can be erased through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{FedOGL}, a semantic-structural memory preservation framework. On the client side, FedOGL preserves historical decision behavior through replay and task-start distillation, while protecting graph-propagation memory via projection onto a globally shared structure basis. On the server side, FedOGL maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to facilitate cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with the best-performing baselines, FedOGL reduces performance degradation caused by catastrophic forgetting by \textbf{42.67\%}, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.

</details>


### [242] [Tight Sample Complexity for Low-Rank Adaptation: Matching Bounds and Rank Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27680)
*Arunan J*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes tight statistical guarantees for Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), proving matching upper and lower bounds of Θ(rd/n) on excess risk. It demonstrates a rank-selection dichotomy: constrained ERM incurs a penalty for over-ranking, while nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators do not. The theory is validated on synthetic and real NLP fine-tuning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on LoRA generalization provided only upper bounds (Õ(√(rd/n)) or Õ(rd/n)) without matching lower bounds, leaving the optimal choice of LoRA rank r formally unanswered. The paper aims to close both gaps by deriving tight minimax rates and characterizing when over-parameterization hurts.

Method: The authors derive an upper bound of Õ(rd/n) on excess risk for the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA using a local Rademacher complexity argument, assuming the target adaptation is at most rank r. A matching minimax lower bound of Ω(rd/n) is proved via a Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace in ℝ^{d×d}, applicable to any estimator within the rank-r LoRA class. These bounds are combined to analyze two estimator classes: constrained ERM and nuclear-norm-then-truncate adaptive estimators. Predictions are tested on synthetic trace regression and real LoRA fine-tuning of DistilBERT/RoBERTa on SST-2 and MRPC.

Result: The upper and lower bounds match at Θ(rd/n), yielding a tight characterization. For constrained ERM, optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r*, and over-ranking strictly hurts (U-shaped risk). For nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators, over-ranking is harmless with rate saturating at Θ̃(r*d/n). Experiments confirm the predicted U-shape in validation loss; two of three (model, task) configurations show statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (paired permutation p = 0.016).

Conclusion: The statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning in the well-specified locally quadratic regime is fully characterized. The empirically observed over-parameterization penalty is a property of unregularized ERM, not of the LoRA class itself. Practitioners can avoid the penalty by using nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators, making rank selection less critical.

Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard mechanism for fine-tuning large pretrained models, yet its statistical properties remain only partially understood. Existing generalization results provide upper bounds of the form O~(sqrt(rd/n)) or O~(rd/n), but a matching lower bound is missing, and the question of how to choose the LoRA rank r has no formal answer. Both gaps are closed here. A local Rademacher argument establishes an upper bound of O~(rd/n) on the excess risk of the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA, whenever the target adaptation has rank at most r. A matching minimax lower bound of Omega(rd/n) is then proved via a Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace of R^{d x d}; the bound applies to any estimator whose output lies in the rank-r LoRA class. Combining the two yields a rank-selection dichotomy. For the constrained empirical risk minimizer, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r*, and over-ranking strictly hurts. For adaptive estimators of the nuclear-norm-then-truncate type, over-ranking is harmless and the rate saturates at Theta~(r* d / n) regardless of r. Taken together, the three results characterize the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning within the well-specified locally quadratic regime, and identify the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty as a property of unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than of the LoRA class itself. Predictions of the theory are verified on a synthetic trace-regression benchmark and on real LoRA fine-tuning across three (model, task) configurations covering DistilBERT and RoBERTa on SST-2 and MRPC. All configurations exhibit the predicted U-shape in validation loss, with two showing statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (paired permutation p = 0.016).

</details>


### [243] [Event-Structured Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Differentiable Critical Clearing Boundaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27681)
*Baoli Hao,Chenxi Hu,Ming Zhong,Ren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes ES-PINN, an event-structured physics-informed neural network for transient stability assessment that aligns with pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing dynamics, enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces, and defines a differentiable stability margin for accurate CCT estimation. Validated on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems with superior accuracy over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transient-stability assessment via critical clearing time (CCT) is essential for preventing cascading outages, but reliable estimation is challenging due to complicated fault-clearing dynamics requiring repeated simulations across many fault severities and clearing times. Existing methods lack physics alignment across distinct event phases.

Method: An event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) that aligns representation with pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics; enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces; uses a smooth trajectory-induced stability margin as a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary for boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and optional direct CCT prediction via distilled readout. A local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate is proved, with exact event chaining eliminating state-interface defect terms.

Result: ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Additional full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses further demonstrate effectiveness and computational efficiency.

Conclusion: The ES-PINN framework provides accurate, efficient CCT estimation with theoretical guarantees, integrating physics structure across fault events to outperform conventional neural surrogates in transient stability assessment.

Abstract: Transient-stability assessment determines whether a power system can recover after a disturbance and is therefore essential to preventing generator trips and cascading outages. A key metric is the critical clearing time (CCT), which specifies the maximum time available to clear a fault before synchronism is lost. Reliable CCT estimation is challenging because complicated fault-clearing dynamics require repeated simulations over many fault severities and clearing times. We propose an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) that aligns its representation with the pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics and enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces. A smooth trajectory-induced stability margin defines a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary, enabling accurate boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and optional direct CCT prediction through a distilled readout. We further prove a local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate, in which exact event chaining eliminates separate state-interface defect terms. Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show that ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Additional full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed framework.

</details>


### [244] [NMINE: Normalized Mutual Information Neural Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27710)
*Petra Eerikinharju,Marko Tuononen,Ville Hautamäki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a fully neural estimator for normalized mutual information (NMI) in continuous multidimensional settings, combining MINE for mutual information and MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators. Experiments on 1–8 dimensional Gaussian data show improved accuracy over KSG-based baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mutual information (MI) is unbounded and not directly comparable across datasets or dimensions. Normalized MI solves this by scaling MI into a dependency score, but existing estimators (e.g., k-NN–based) suffer from sensitivity to dimensionality and numerical instability. A robust, neural alternative for continuous multidimensional NMI estimation is needed.

Method: The estimator combines (1) a MINE-based neural MI estimator using the Donsker–Varadhan dual representation, and (2) MI-NEE–inspired marginal entropy estimators that learn the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference, then recover entropy. Normalization is achieved by dividing estimated MI by the estimated marginal entropies.

Result: On Gaussian data spanning 1 to 8 dimensions, the proposed neural NMI estimator achieves better accuracy than a KSG-based NMI baseline.

Conclusion: Neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings, offering improved accuracy and a viable alternative to nearest-neighbor–based approaches.

Abstract: Mutual information is a general measure of statistical dependence that captures both linear and nonlinear relationships between random variables. For continuous and multidimensional variables For continuous multidimensional variables, mutual information must be estimated from samples. Because mutual information is unbounded, its values are not directly comparable across datasets, dimensions, or applications. Normalized mutual information addresses this limitation by converting mutual information into a normalized dependency score. Recent work has demonstrated the practical value of normalized mutual information in applications such as molecular dynamics {arXiv:2405.04980} and interpretable machine learning {arXiv:2409.16768}, but existing estimators remain sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability {arXiv:2410.07642}.
  In this paper, we propose a fully neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous variables. The proposed approach combines a MINE-based neural mutual information estimator {arXiv:1801.04062} with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators {arXiv:1905.12957}. Mutual information is estimated using the Donsker--Varadhan representation, while marginal entropies are estimated by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference distribution, from which entropy is recovered. The resulting estimator provides a neural alternative to k-nearest-neighbor-based normalized mutual information estimation {arXiv:2405.04980}.
  Experiments on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions show that the proposed estimator improves accuracy over a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline. These results indicate that neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings.

</details>


### [245] [VESTIGE: A Knowledge-Guided Masking Strategy for Corruption-Aware Fine-Tuning of Genomic Transformers, Validated on Ancient DNA Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27712)
*Angshuman Chakravertty,Rahul Maheshwari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VESTIGE replaces the uniform masking distribution in masked language model fine-tuning with an empirically measured, position-dependent corruption profile and shows significant improvement in ancient DNA reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard MLM fine-tuning assumes uniform reconstruction difficulty across token positions, but real-world degradation (e.g., cytosine deamination in ancient DNA) is position-dependent. At peak damage sites, uniform masking causes models to underperform even a frequency-matched random predictor.

Method: VESTIGE is a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that rescales an empirically measured per-position corruption profile (from mapDamage2 for aDNA) so that the mean masking rate matches standard MLM (15%), isolating spatial redistribution as the sole variable. Evaluated on DNABERT-2 with a mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes) across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows.

Result: VESTIGE outperforms standard MLM at every terminal-zone width (Δ = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10⁻⁸), reduces validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold protein reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions even under 10–30× amplified damage. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier achieves AUC = 0.935 with 98.2% of reconstructed windows cleared.

Conclusion: VESTIGE is a domain-agnostic, knowledge-guided training routine that can incorporate any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile (FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, nanopore), significantly improving intelligent systems operating on degraded or noisy sequence inputs.

Abstract: Standard masked-language-model fine-tuning applies a uniform masking probability across every token position, assuming reconstruction difficulty is position-agnostic. When the degradation process is characterised and concentrated at predictable positions, this assumption fails: at peak damage sites the model can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor. We introduce VESTIGE, a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that aligns the masking distribution with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile. We apply it to ancient DNA (aDNA) reconstruction, where cytosine deamination produces a position-dependent C-to-T / G-to-A gradient quantified per-position by mapDamage2. Rescaling so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15% - identical to standard MLM - isolates spatial redistribution as the sole variable, with model, data, seed, and hyperparameters held fixed across both DNABERT-2 runs on a mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes). Across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, VESTIGE leads standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8), cuts validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions (three genes) even under damage amplified 10-30x beyond authentic PMD rates. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier returns AUC = 0.935 and clears 98.2% of reconstructed windows, the 1.76% remainder attributable to reference-genome features, not reconstruction artefacts. The principle is domain-agnostic: any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile - FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore - substitutes directly for the PMD array, making VESTIGE a knowledge-guided training routine for intelligent systems operating on degraded or noisy sequence inputs.

</details>


### [246] [Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27731)
*Jiaxiang Li,Zhiqi Bu,Shiyun Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper derives a joint characterization of training loss in terms of both learning rate and batch size schedules through convex optimization, yielding a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any learning rate schedule, and demonstrates joint scaling laws that outperform static baselines in LLM training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern deep learning practice typically fixes batch size during training, ignoring the coupled effect that learning rate and batch size jointly exert on training dynamics. The authors aim to formalize this relationship and demonstrate that dynamic batch size scheduling can improve training efficiency and performance.

Method: The authors analyze deep learning dynamics through the lens of convex optimization, deriving a joint characterization of the loss function in terms of both learning rate and batch size schedules. This framework is designed to be applicable to general optimizers (e.g., SGD, Adam) and arbitrary model architectures. From this characterization, they derive a closed-form expression for the optimal batch size schedule given any prescribed learning rate schedule, leading to joint scaling laws.

Result: The proposed joint scaling laws and dynamic batch size schedules consistently outperform static batch size baselines. Empirical validation highlights significant gains in large language model training.

Conclusion: Dynamic batch size scheduling, when jointly optimized with the learning rate schedule, provides a principled and practically effective approach to improving deep learning training dynamics, particularly for large-scale models like LLMs.

Abstract: Modern deep learning typically keeps the batch size static throughout training, thus overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on the training dynamics. In this paper, we study the deep learning dynamics through the lens of convex optimization and derive a joint characterization of loss in terms of both schedules, applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. This characterization yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any prescribed learning rate schedule, and further leads to joint scaling laws that consistently outperform static batch size baselines, highlighting the significance of dynamic batch size schedule in large language model training.

</details>


### [247] [Improving the Robustness/Accuracy Tradeoff Against Adversarial Attacks Using Information Bottleneck Distillation Through Dual Teachers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27737)
*Vincent Ryusuke Takahashi,Yoshinari Takeishi,Jun'ichi Takeuchi,Kave Salamatian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper extends the Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) framework by incorporating a dual-teacher distillation approach: a robust teacher (adversarially trained) and a clean teacher (trained on clean inputs only). A cross-layer attention matrix transfers features from both teachers to the student, improving clean accuracy over original IBD while maintaining adversarial robustness, achieving competitive harmonic mean scores against state-of-the-art methods like B-MTARD.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adversarial defense methods like IBD improve robustness but degrade clean-input classification accuracy. The authors aim to bridge this trade-off by leveraging complementary knowledge from both a clean-trained and an adversarially-trained teacher model within a unified distillation framework.

Method: The proposed method extends IBD by introducing a clean teacher model alongside the robust teacher. Feature knowledge from both teachers is transferred to the student via a cross-layer attention matrix mechanism. Experiments are conducted on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, with analysis of how different training settings affect the attention module.

Result: The proposed method improves clean-sample classification accuracy over the original IBD while maintaining similar adversarial accuracy. It is competitive with state-of-the-art dual-teacher methods like B-MTARD, particularly measured by the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy.

Conclusion: A dual-teacher distillation approach combining clean and robust teachers via cross-layer attention effectively mitigates the clean-robust accuracy trade-off inherent in adversarial defense methods like IBD, yielding competitive performance against contemporary dual-teacher frameworks.

Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in classical machine learning problems. However, they are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Countermeasures proposed in the literature, notably Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) introduced by Kuang et al., degrade the classification accuracy on clean inputs while improving the robustness to adversarial inputs. In this work, we extend the IBD framework by introducing an extra teacher model (clean teacher) trained with only clean inputs, into the distillation process from a robust teacher model trained by adversarial training. The features of both clean and robust teachers are transferred to the student through a cross-layer attention matrix. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets show that the proposed method improves classification accuracy on clean samples compared to the original IBD, while maintaining similar accuracy on adversarial samples. Furthermore, our methods are competitive with state-of-the-art approaches, including the recent dual-teacher distillation framework B-MTARD, particularly in terms of the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy. We also analyze the impact of different training settings that have different influences on the attention module.

</details>


### [248] [DAS-PMVC: A Framework for Partial Multi-View Clustering via Dual Alignment and Structure Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27761)
*Shubin Ma,Liang Zhao,Chuanye He,Zhenjiao Liu,Liang Zou,Lin Yuanbo Wu,Yu Shao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DAS-PMVC is a partial multi-view clustering framework that addresses the partial view alignment problem through three components: anchor graph structure alignment for initial cross-view alignment, structure-enhanced feature learning via multi-view GCNs, and a dual alignment strategy combining contrastive learning with the Hungarian algorithm. It achieves SOTA clustering performance on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-view clustering suffers from the partial view alignment problem (PVAP), where data across different views are misaligned due to limitations in data collection devices. Existing methods struggle with view asymmetry and irrelevant samples, motivating a framework that leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance for robust alignment.

Method: DAS-PMVC comprises three parts: (1) Anchor graph structure alignment — derives sample joint embeddings with consistent latent space from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; (2) Structure-enhanced feature learning — pretrains to learn view structure information, then applies multi-view graph convolutional networks to extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure, enhancing discriminative power; (3) Dual alignment strategy — performs initial alignment via the anchor graph during pretraining, then refines latent feature alignment during training using contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm.

Result: Experiments on various datasets show that DAS-PMVC outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance.

Conclusion: The DAS-PMVC framework effectively addresses the partial view alignment problem through dual alignment and structure enhancement, demonstrating superior effectiveness and superiority over existing methods.

Abstract: In recent years, multi-view clustering has attracted widespread research interest. However, due to limitations in data collection devices, data across different views often suffer from misalignment, leading to the partial view alignment problem (PVAP). To mitigate the impact of view asymmetry and irrelevant samples, this paper proposes a framework for partial multi-view clustering via dual alignment and structure enhancement (DAS-PMVC), which leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance. Specifically, DAS-PMVC includes three parts: \textbf{anchor graph structure alignment}, where sample joint embedding representations with consistent latent space are derived from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; \textbf{structure-enhanced feature learning}, where the model learns view structure information through pretraining and combines multi-view graph convolutional networks to further extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure to improve the discriminative power of representations; and \textbf{a dual alignment strategy}, where initial alignment is performed through the anchor graph in the pretraining phase, and contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm are introduced in the training phase to further optimize the alignment of latent features. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the DAS-PMVC framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, showcasing its effectiveness and superiority.

</details>


### [249] [Train Small, Deploy Large: Zero-Shot GNN Transfer Through Geometric Renormalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27767)
*Robert Jankowski,Pedro Almagro-Blanco,Marián Boguñá,Melanie Weber,M. Ángeles Serrano*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Training a GNN on a geometrically renormalized (coarse-grained) replica of a large graph allows zero-shot weight transfer to the original full-scale graph, preserving predictive performance while drastically reducing training costs. Structural similarity, not network size, governs transferability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNNs become infrastructure-sensitive at million-node scales, requiring costly scalable training techniques. The authors investigate whether a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down replica can be deployed on the full-resolution graph without retraining.

Method: A zero-shot transfer protocol: a GNN is trained on a graph coarse-grained via geometric renormalization (GR). The learned weights are then directly transferred to the original, full-resolution graph without any fine-tuning or retraining. The approach is tested on both synthetic and real-world networks, with analysis of learned representations and predictive trajectories across scales.

Result: Training on GR-scaled replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. Learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales.

Conclusion: Structural similarity matters more than network size for GNN transferability. This insight opens a path toward designing scale-equivariant graph architectures that are inherently robust to changes in graph resolution.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) can operate on large graphs but become infrastructure-sensitive at the scale of millions of nodes and typically require scalable training techniques for even larger graphs. This raises a central question: when can a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down replica of a graph be deployed on the full-resolution graph without retraining? We introduce a zero-shot transfer protocol in which a GNN is trained on a graph coarse-grained by geometric renormalization (GR), and the resulting weights are transferred directly to the original network. Across synthetic and real-world networks, training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. We further find that learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales. These findings suggest that structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

</details>


### [250] [Beyond the Best Teacher: Expanding and Compressing the Reasoning Solution Manifold](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27770)
*Songshuo Lu,Zhi Chen,Yaohua Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RL-trained policies amplify only a subset of valid solution modes, making them incomplete teachers. The paper proposes an expand-then-compress framework: RGRPO trains a diverse teacher union covering complementary modes, then TU-OPD with Consensus-Residual Decomposition distills them into a single student that outperforms all individual teachers across math, code, and instruction-following tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A single RL training run often amplifies only a subset of valid solution modes on a multi-basin reasoning manifold, yielding an incomplete teacher. Direct distillation from such a teacher propagates its blind spots. The key insight is that RL-trained policies should be treated as local probes rather than globally reliable supervisors, motivating the construction of a complementary teacher union.

Method: The expand-then-compress framework has two stages. (1) Expansion: Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization, redirecting each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. (2) Compression: Reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes, where only reliable teachers contribute and their losses are weighted by per-example quality. Consensus-Residual Decomposition preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over reliable peers to prevent specialist suppression.

Result: On Qwen3-1.7B, the distilled student outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains: +2.0% on mathematical reasoning, +8.3% on code generation, and +6.9% on instruction following, while maintaining single-model inference cost.

Conclusion: Stronger students arise not from selecting a single better teacher, but from deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union. This principle is simple yet powerful, and the expand-then-compress framework provides a practical instantiation of it.

Abstract: A single reinforcement-learning run can produce a strong reasoner yet an incomplete teacher: it often amplifies only a subset of the valid solution modes. We argue that reinforcement learning (RL)-trained policies should therefore be viewed as local probes of a multi-basin reasoning solution manifold, rather than as globally reliable supervisors. Based on this view, we propose an expand-then-compress framework that couples teacher construction with multi-teacher policy distillation. In the expansion stage, Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization and redirects each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. In the compression stage, reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes. For each example, only reliable teachers contribute, and their sampled-token OPD losses are weighted by their per-example quality. We further introduce Consensus-Residual Decomposition, which preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over its reliable peers, preventing specialist behavior from being suppressed during teacher aggregation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show that the resulting Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains, yielding relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, respectively, while retaining single-model inference. These results establish a simple but powerful principle: stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union.

</details>


### [251] [RIPPLE: Generating Multi-Channel Phase, Not Recovering It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27775)
*Jaehyuk Lee,Yeajin Lee,Dayeon Shin,Donghun Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper argues that for multi-channel signals (spatial audio, seismograms), generating phase is essential rather than recovering it per-channel. They propose RIPPLE, which uses Griffin-Lim as a phase prior initialized from source phase, then refines it via rectified flow with an inter-channel phase loss. Results show dramatic improvements in inter-channel coherence metrics, particularly reducing seismic S-wave polarization error from near-random (57.3°) to 33.8°.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current generative audio/seismic models synthesize high-quality magnitude spectra but delegate phase recovery to channel-independent methods (Griffin-Lim, vocoders, latent decoders). This fails catastrophically for multi-channel data because the physical information — spatial localization in ambisonics, S-wave polarization in seismograms — resides in inter-channel phase relationships. Channel-independent recovery destroys this structure, yet standard magnitude-based metrics fail to detect the loss, creating a blind spot where pipelines score well while discarding physically meaningful information.

Method: RIPPLE reinterprets Griffin-Lim not as a final phase estimator, but as a phase **prior**. The prior is initialized from the source (ground-truth) phase, carrying inter-channel structure. A rectified flow model then refines this prior toward the target distribution under an explicit inter-channel phase coherence loss. The rectified flow provides a straight-line transport path between prior and target, enabling efficient sampling while the phase-aware loss explicitly preserves cross-channel physical relationships.

Result: RIPPLE was tested on two physically unrelated domains: first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation. It outperformed recovery-based pipelines on coherence metrics consumed by downstream analyses. The seismic result is particularly decisive: per-channel recovery yields S-wave polarization error near 57.3° (random baseline), while RIPPLE's learned phase reduces it to 33.8°, demonstrating that explicit phase generation recovers physically meaningful inter-channel structure that channel-independent methods fundamentally cannot.

Conclusion: Phase in multi-channel waveforms should be generated, not recovered independently per channel. RIPPLE demonstrates that treating Griffin-Lim as a phase prior and refining it with a flow model under inter-channel phase loss effectively preserves the physical content encoded in cross-channel phase relationships. This has significant implications for spatial audio, seismology, and any domain where inter-channel phase coherence carries critical information.

Abstract: Generative models synthesize magnitude spectra with high fidelity, while phase is delegated to a recovery module---Griffin--Lim, a vocoder, or a latent decoder---applied independently to each channel. For multi-channel waveforms this delegation is costly: the physical content of spatial audio and three-component seismograms lives in the phase relationships between channels, precisely what channel-independent recovery cannot produce. The cost is also invisible, since the magnitude-based metrics common to both fields barely move when inter-channel phase coherence collapses---so a pipeline can discard the physical information in its output while still scoring well. We argue that phase should be generated, not recovered, and present RIPPLE (Rectified Inter-channel Phase with Prior-based LEarning), which reinterprets Griffin--Lim as a phase **prior** rather than a final estimator: initialized from the source phase, this prior carries the inter-channel structure to be preserved, and a rectified flow refines it toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss. Tested on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation---two physically unrelated domains---RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on the coherence metrics that downstream analyses consume. The seismic case is decisive: across architecturally distinct generators, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the $57.3^\circ$ random expectation, whereas learned phase reduces it to $33.8^\circ$.

</details>


### [252] [LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO): A Sampling-Time Low-Rank Scaffold for Recovering Reinforcement-Learning Gradient on Zero-Reward Cliff Prompts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27787)
*Ken Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GRPO suffers from a "cliff prompt" problem where all rollouts fail, yielding zero gradient. LSPO addresses this by fitting a temporary LoRA adapter on cliff prompts' ground-truth solutions, re-rolling with the augmented model, and splicing successful completions back into the RL batch with importance-sampling correction, then discarding the adapter. On DeepMath-103K, LSPO outperforms DAPO across all 16 benchmark metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In RLVR for mathematical reasoning, GRPO computes group-normalized advantages. When every sampled rollout for a prompt fails (a "cliff prompt"), the advantage is uniformly zero, producing no gradient. These cliff prompts represent the model's capability frontier — precisely where learning signal is most needed — yet GRPO cannot provide it.

Method: LSPO operates per RL step: (1) Detect cliff prompts where all rollouts in a group fail. (2) Fit a small low-rank (LoRA) adapter via a brief supervised step on the cliff prompts' ground-truth solutions. (3) Re-roll the cliff prompts using the base-plus-adapter model. (4) Splice the now-successful completions into the original RL batch with importance-sampling correction to account for the distribution shift. (5) Take a standard GRPO step on the base model only. The adapter receives only the supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpointing, yielding a base-only model.

Result: Evaluated on DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, using n=5 paired seeds per arm over a matched 1000-step horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or surpasses DAPO on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells: 15 strict wins and one tie. Notable gains include +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 on MATH500/pass@1. The average improvement across all 16 cells is +3.8 points.

Conclusion: LSPO effectively recovers learning signal from cliff prompts — the capability frontier — by temporarily augmenting the policy with a LoRA adapter trained on ground-truth solutions. The adapter is discarded at each checkpoint, keeping the final model unchanged in architecture. The method provides consistent and substantial gains over a strong DAPO baseline across diverse math reasoning benchmarks and pass@k settings.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning suffers from a structural blind spot: on "cliff" prompts-those on which every sampled rollout in a group fails-the group-normalized advantage is identically zero, so GRPO produces no gradient on precisely the prompts at the frontier of the model's capability. We introduce LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO), a sampling-time mechanism that recovers this lost gradient. Each RL step, LSPO detects cliff prompts, fits a small low-rank (LoRA) adapter by a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions, re-rolls the cliffs with the base-plus-adapter model, splices the now-successful completions back into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction, and takes a GRPO step on the base alone; the adapter receives only the supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step reporting horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins and one exact tie), with gains of up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1; averaged over the 16 cells the improvement is +3.8 points.

</details>


### [253] [Revisiting Predictive Process Monitoring in the Age of Foundation Models: A Comparative Study of Sequence, Tabular, and LLM Approaches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27797)
*Lennart Fertig,Lukas Kirchdorfer,Tobias Sesterhenn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks three modeling paradigms for predictive process monitoring (PPM)—deep sequence models (LSTMs), tabular foundation models with in-context learning, and large language models (LLMs)—across multiple datasets and tasks. Sequence models excel at next-activity prediction, tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks, and LLMs generally underperform despite higher computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While PPM has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, foundation models (both LLMs and tabular) are emerging as alternatives. However, tabular foundation models with in-context learning have not been systematically benchmarked for PPM, leaving uncertainty about whether classical sequence-based models remain competitive.

Method: The authors conduct a controlled conceptual and empirical comparison of three paradigms: (1) classical deep sequence models (LSTMs trained from scratch), (2) tabular foundation models with in-context learning capabilities, and (3) large language models (LLMs). The benchmark spans multiple datasets and prediction tasks (next activity, remaining time, time to next event).

Result: Sequence models consistently perform best for next-activity prediction. Tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal prediction tasks (remaining time, time to next event). LLMs generally lag behind both alternatives while incurring higher computational cost.

Conclusion: Classical sequence-based models remain the strongest choice for next-activity prediction in PPM. Tabular foundation models represent a viable and competitive alternative for temporal prediction tasks. LLMs, despite their growing popularity, do not yet justify their higher cost for PPM tasks based on current performance.

Abstract: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) leverages event logs to forecast the future of running process instances, for instance, predicting the next activity, the remaining time until case completion, or the time to the next event. While PPM research in recent years has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, foundation-model approaches---particularly large language models (LLMs)---are increasingly explored for PPM. At the same time, tabular foundation models with in-context learning capabilities offer a promising alternative but have not yet been systematically benchmarked for PPM. Thus, it remains unclear whether classical sequence-based models remain competitive in this evolving landscape. This paper compares the three modeling paradigms both conceptually and empirically through a controlled benchmark across multiple datasets and prediction tasks. The results show that sequence models consistently perform best for next activity prediction, whereas tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks, with LLMs usually lagging behind despite higher cost.

</details>


### [254] [Learning-Augmented and Randomized Algorithms for Line Aggregation with Delays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27807)
*Tianhang Lu,Runtian Ren,Shengcai Liu,Ke Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies online aggregation with delays on a line metric, proposing learning-augmented algorithms with robustness-consistency trade-offs, a randomized algorithm achieving (e+1)-competitiveness (beating the deterministic lower bound of 4), and a lower bound of e for randomized algorithms. Randomized learning-augmented variants are also provided, with numerical experiments validating the theoretical results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on online aggregation with delays relied on deterministic algorithms (e.g., the 5-competitive Balance algorithm), with a lower bound of 4 for deterministic approaches. The authors aim to improve competitiveness through randomization (targeting the gap between 4 and existing randomized lower bounds) and to incorporate machine-learned advice (suggested service lengths) to achieve better practical performance while maintaining worst-case robustness guarantees.

Method: The paper proposes three algorithmic contributions: (1) A deterministic learning-augmented Balance algorithm parameterized by λ∈(0,1], achieving (4/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (4+λ)-consistency, using online suggested service lengths as advice. (2) A randomized algorithm for the classical adversarial model achieving (e+1)-competitiveness against an oblivious adversary, improving over the deterministic 5-competitive benchmark. (3) A hybrid randomized learning-augmented algorithm combining both ideas, yielding (e/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (e+λ)-consistency. A lower bound of e is established for randomized online algorithms, tightening the previous e/(e-1) bound. Numerical experiments complement the theoretical analysis.

Result: The deterministic learning-augmented Balance algorithm achieves (4/λ+1/λ²)-robust and (4+λ)-consistent performance. The randomized algorithm attains (e+1)-competitiveness against an oblivious adversary, surpassing the deterministic lower bound of 4 and the prior 5-competitive Balance benchmark. The randomized lower bound is tightened to e (from e/(e-1)). The randomized learning-augmented variant achieves (e/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (e+λ)-consistency. Numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical findings.

Conclusion: Randomization and learning augmentation both yield substantial improvements for online aggregation with delays. The (e+1)-competitive randomized algorithm breaks the deterministic lower bound barrier, and the lower bound of e nearly matches this ratio. Learning-augmented variants provide smooth robustness-consistency trade-offs via the λ parameter, enabling practical deployment where reliable predictions are available while preserving worst-case guarantees when predictions are adversarial.

Abstract: This paper studies learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation with delays on a line metric. We consider advice given as online suggested service lengths, and evaluate the algorithms in terms of robustness and consistency. For each $λ\in (0,1]$, we first propose a deterministic learning-augmented \textsc{Balance} algorithm that is $(4/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(4+λ)$-consistent. We also propose a randomized algorithm for the problem in the classical adversarial model, which is $(e+1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary, improving over the deterministic $5$-competitive \textsc{Balance} benchmark~\cite{bienkowski2013chain}. Notably, this competitive ratio is even lower than the lower bound of $4$ for deterministic online algorithms. Moreover, we establish a lower bound of $e$ on the competitive ratio of randomized online algorithms, improving the previous lower bound of $e/(e-1)$. Besides, we combine the two ideas and obtain a randomized learning-augmented algorithm that is $(e/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(e+λ)$-consistent. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to complement our theoretical analysis and evaluate the empirical performance of our algorithms.

</details>


### [255] [Contrastive Concept Importance: Explaining Pairwise Class Decisions Through Automatically Extracted Concept Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27904)
*Roel Visser,Isaac Roberts,Barbara Hammer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Contrastive Concept Importance (CCI), a method that attributes the logit margin between a target class and a foil class to human-interpretable concepts, producing signed scores that reveal class-pair-specific model behavior not captured by standard non-contrastive concept importance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard concept-based explanations answer "why P?" by attributing contributions to a single output class. However, in misclassification, class confusion, or low-margin predictions, the more natural question is "why P rather than Q?". Existing concept attribution methods lack a contrastive framing, limiting their ability to diagnose fine-grained class distinctions and model errors.

Method: The authors propose CCI, which operates on an automatically extracted visual concept basis (e.g., CRAFT). CCI attributes the logit margin (target minus foil) to individual concepts, yielding signed scores: positive if a concept supports the target over the foil, negative otherwise. These scores decompose into target-logit and foil-logit effects, enabling classification of concept influence as shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive.

Result: Evaluated on ImageNet class pairs using insertion/deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy, CCI reveals class-pair-specific model behavior invisible to ordinary concept importance. Highly contrastive concepts align with semantic superclass structure, indicating they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence.

Conclusion: CCI provides a principled contrastive extension to concept importance, enabling diagnosis of class confusion and fine-grained model behavior. The signed, decomposable attributions offer richer explanatory power than single-class methods, particularly for understanding misclassifications and low-margin decisions.

Abstract: Concept-based explanations are a prevalent way to explain the decisions of complex black-box methods through semantically meaningful, human-interpretable concepts. To attribute the contribution of such concepts to a model's decisions, feature attribution methods are used to quantify how strongly each concept contributes to a model output. These attributions are typically computed for a single output class and therefore answer a non-contrastive "why P?" question. In many situations, however, such as cases of misclassification, class confusion, and low-margin predictions, the more natural question to ask is "why P rather than Q?".
  We introduce contrastive concept importance (CCI), which attributes the logit margin between a target class and a contrast, or foil, class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis. The resulting scores are signed, indicating whether a concept supports the target over the foil or the foil over the target, and can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects. This makes it possible to distinguish globally important concepts from concepts that specifically influence a class-pair distinction, including whether their effect is shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive.
  We evaluate the method on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases, insertion and deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy. The results show that contrastive concept importance reveals class-pair-specific model behavior that is not captured by ordinary concept importance alone, and that highly contrastive concepts can be evaluated against semantic superclass structure to assess whether they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence.

</details>


### [256] [Class-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Counterfactual Explanation Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27905)
*Muhammad Adil Saleem,Syed Ali Raza,Mary-Anne Williams*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Incorporating predicted class information into reinforcement learning state representations significantly improves counterfactual explanation generation, yielding faster convergence, higher validity, and more efficient exploration compared to class-blind approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior RL-based counterfactual explanation methods formulate states using only predictor features, ignoring the instance's predicted class. The authors hypothesize that class-awareness in the state representation can enhance exploration efficiency and policy optimality during CFE generation.

Method: The authors propose a class-aware RL framework where the RL state includes both predictor-derived features and the instance's predicted class. This is compared against a class-blind RL baseline (identical architecture minus class information) across seven diverse datasets. Feature importance is assessed post-hoc using SHAP and LIME to quantify class-awareness contribution to action selection.

Result: Class-aware RL consistently outperforms class-blind RL in convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction during training. It generates significantly more valid counterfactuals. SHAP and LIME analyses confirm that the class-based feature ranks among the most influential predictors in the RL agent's action-selection process.

Conclusion: Class-awareness is a simple yet impactful enhancement to RL-based CFE generation, yielding heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanations (CFEs) enhance the interpretability of black-box models by generating alternative instances with adjusted feature values that achieve a contrastive outcome. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach for CFE generation, enabling efficient exploration of counterfactual instances while ensuring control over key metrics like validity, sparsity, and proximity. Previous studies have formulated RL states exclusively using features derived from the predictors in the supervised dataset. This study explores the impact of including an instance's predicted class, alongside features derived from the predictors, in the RL state representation for generating CFEs. The hypothesis is that class-awareness enhances exploration efficiency and improves policy optimality. We compare the proposed class-aware RL method with the class-blind RL method, which is similar but excludes the instance's class information from the state representation. The comparison was conducted using seven datasets from diverse domains, varying in size. The results show that during training, class-aware RL offers benefits in terms of convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction. Moreover, it generates significantly more valid CFEs compared to class-blind RL. Finally, the instance's class-based feature consistently ranks among the most influential predictors in RL's action-selection, as shown by the SHAP and LIME values, underscoring the significance of class-awareness in RL for CFE generation. The impact is heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets.

</details>


### [257] [S-CEReBrO: Breaking the Memory Barrier in Continuous EEG Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27913)
*Glenn Anta Bucagu,Thorir Mar Ingolfsson,Yawei Li,Luca Benini*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces S-CEReBrO, a streaming EEG foundation model that uses a novel Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism to overcome Transformer memory bottlenecks during continuous monitoring, achieving constant KV cache memory and processing signals significantly longer than prior approaches while maintaining state-of-the-art performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer-based EEG foundation models suffer from global attention mechanisms that couple attention memory to signal duration, causing memory overflow in continuous monitoring scenarios. Existing solutions like low-rank linear attention remain insufficient for very long contexts. The authors aim to enable efficient, generalizable, and truly continuous EEG monitoring without memory constraints scaling with signal length.

Method: The authors propose S-CEReBrO, an evolution of the CEReBrO architecture, featuring a Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism. This factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, ensuring constant KV cache memory since only the active window requires resident attention maps. The model is pre-trained on over 25,000 hours of EEG recordings from more than 12,000 subjects and evaluated across 11 downstream tasks.

Result: Windowed alternating attention processes signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. On long contexts, it uses only 55% of the memory of low-rank linear attention while delivering 2.1× inference throughput. S-CEReBrO achieves state-of-the-art on 7 of 11 downstream tasks with up to 60% fewer parameters compared to baseline models.

Conclusion: S-CEReBrO represents a significant advance toward practical, efficient, and generalizable continuous EEG monitoring by decoupling attention memory from signal duration, enabling indefinite-length streaming inference with strong downstream performance.

Abstract: Foundation models offer a promising paradigm for Electroencephalography (EEG) analysis, leveraging generalizable representations from vast unlabeled datasets. Yet, Transformer-based architectures face a critical bottleneck: global attention mechanisms couple the attention memory state to the signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring. To address this, we introduce S-CEReBrO (Streaming CEReBrO), an evolution of the CEReBrO architecture designed for continuous monitoring. Our novel Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, guaranteeing constant KV cache memory as only the active window requires resident attention maps. Empirical scaling analysis confirms that windowed alternating attention can process signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. Compared to low-rank linear attention on long contexts, windowed alternating attention requires 55% of the memory while increasing inference throughput by 2.1X. Pre-trained on >25,000 hours of recordings from >12,000 subjects, S-CEReBrO achieves state-of-the-art performance on 7 of 11 downstream tasks, with up to 60% fewer parameters. This work represents a significant step toward the realization of efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring. An accompanying code repository is available.

</details>


### [258] [Exact Action Values Are Not Enough: Rollout-Verified Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of a Reasoning Model for Multi-Zone VAV Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27914)
*Takumi Shioda,Kohei Terashima,Tatsuo Nagai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A reasoning LLM (GPT-5) achieves competitive VAV control from text alone without building-specific training, outperforming a TD3-based RL controller. However, attempts to transfer this knowledge via reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) into an open-weight model fail due to unreliable critic rankings and unchanged transition prediction errors, motivating transition-focused supervised fine-tuning as a prerequisite.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying advanced VAV controllers (MPC, RL) is limited by the need for building-specific modeling or training. The authors investigate whether frontier reasoning LLMs can bypass this via zero-shot text-based control, and whether that capability can be distilled into locally deployable open-weight models via RFT, enabling scalable deployment.

Method: Five controllers are evaluated on a physics-based four-zone emulator over three summer days: a Guideline 36 baseline, a trained TD3 agent, zero-shot GPT-5, and an open-weight model before/after RFT. RFT uses deterministic rollouts: restore saved state, apply a candidate action, then follow TD3 to score each action. A learned critic is audited against rollout scores. GPT-5 transition predictions are compared against the open-weight model and persistence.

Result: TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% vs. baseline while improving temperature and CO2 compliance. GPT-5 achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but with reduced ventilation margin. The learned critic showed near-perfect across-time correlation (r=0.9998) yet failed within-state ranking, selecting the rollout-best candidate in only 5/10 states. 200 RFT steps produced no sustained improvement; the open-weight model's electricity use and five-minute predictions remained worse than persistence, while GPT-5 predicted transitions far better.

Conclusion: Rollout scores can rank sampled actions but reveal neither next-state effects nor improvement directions. The unchanged transition prediction errors after RFT indicate that transition-focused supervised fine-tuning should precede value-based RFT to enable effective knowledge transfer from reasoning LLMs to deployable models.

Abstract: Multi-zone variable-air-volume control must balance thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and electricity use across several continuous actuators. Model predictive control and reinforcement learning are widely studied, but deployment typically requires building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. We first test whether a frontier reasoning model (an LLM trained to use additional inference-time computation) can achieve competitive VAV control from text without building-specific training. With that capability established, we then test whether TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) can transfer control knowledge into a locally deployable open-weight model. Five controllers are evaluated over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator. Relative to a Guideline 36-based baseline, TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% while improving temperature and CO$_2$ compliance. Without building-specific training, GPT-5 achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but reduced the ventilation margin. For RFT, deterministic rollouts restore a saved state, apply one candidate, and follow TD3 to score each action. Auditing a learned critic against these rollouts exposed a failure hidden by its near-perfect across-time correlation ($r=0.9998$): within-state ranking was unreliable; the critic selected the rollout-best candidate in only 5 of 10 states. Even with the rollout verifier, 200 RFT steps produced no sustained improvement in sampled-action return; the open-weight controller used more electricity than the baseline before and after training, and its five-minute predictions remained worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better. Exact rollout scores rank sampled actions but reveal neither next-state effects nor an improvement direction. The unchanged transition errors motivate transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.

</details>


### [259] [ODEWorld: A Continuous Predictive Architecture via Physical-Time Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27924)
*Dongxiu Liu,Haoyi Niu,Peng Cheng,Yuan Gao,Xirui Kang,Sangli Teng,Koushil Sreenath,Xianyuan Zhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PT-Flow introduces a continuous-time latent world model (ODEWorld) that uses an ODE-governed latent velocity field to enable efficient, arbitrary-resolution forward/backward prediction, addressing representation collapse and excelling in video generation and robotic control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing world models operate in discrete time, which is inefficient for modeling the fundamentally continuous nature of physical space-time. Discrete-time paradigms also suffer from representation collapse over long horizons and cannot support arbitrary temporal resolution or backward prediction.

Method: PT-Flow learns a continuous latent velocity field parameterized by an ODE in a structured representation space. ODEWorld builds on this by extracting time-variant features and enforcing ODE properties on both the dynamical representation space and the latent velocity field. Future prediction becomes temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space.

Result: ODEWorld resolves representation collapse, enables high-quality image reconstruction after long-horizon prediction, supports arbitrary temporal resolution and backward prediction, and provides planning-oriented information for policy learning. It demonstrates strong performance in both video generation and robotic control tasks.

Conclusion: ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, establishing continuous-time latent world models as a compelling alternative to discrete-time approaches for physical world modeling.

Abstract: In the physical world we inhabit, space and time are fundamentally continuous. However, existing machine learning paradigms for world modeling are largely confined to discrete-time prediction, thereby exhibiting significant inefficiency in capturing the dynamics of physical world. We introduce Physical-Time Flow (\textbf{PT-Flow}), a novel approach that learns a continuous latent velocity field operating in physical time. Crucially, the underlying dynamics of sequential data are parameterized by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) embedded in a well-structured representation space. Under this paradigm, the prediction of future can be recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space. Building upon PT-Flow, we construct \textbf{ODEWorld}, a continuous-time latent world model that is both efficient and versatile. By extracting time-variant features and enforcing ODE properties on both the dynamical representation space and the latent velocity field, ODEWorld effectively addresses the long-standing representation collapse issue in latent world model literature. This also enables high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction. Moreover, its continuous nature allows for arbitrary temporal resolution and even backward prediction, which is impossible for most discrete-time models. Lastly, ODEWorld can provide rich planning-oriented information to facilitate downstream policy learning. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, excelling in both video generation and robotic control. \href{https://dstate.github.io/odeworld_website/}{Project Website}.

</details>


### [260] [Harnessing the Potential of Optimizing Data Mixtures via Bayesian Domain Reweighting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27928)
*Xiang Yuan,Kaiqing Lei,Zhenyu Jin,Jun Shu,Deyu Meng,Zongben Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a Bayesian domain weighting method that infers optimal pre-training data mixture weights from a Dirichlet distribution using Gamma priors learned from observations, achieving stable and efficient optimization with substantially less data consumption than existing search-based function-fitting approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for multi-domain pre-training data weighting either rely on strong structural assumptions (rank invariance, scaling laws) that introduce estimation bias, or suffer from unstable optimization and prohibitive computational overhead when directly optimizing weights. A more robust and efficient approach is needed.

Method: A Bayesian framework that models domain weights via a Dirichlet distribution, incorporating Gamma prior information derived from observed validation loss data. This enables direct, stable optimization of the weighting scheme without relying on restrictive proxy function assumptions.

Result: The method achieves stable and efficient domain weight learning, identifies optimal domain mixtures, and consumes substantially less data compared to search-based function-fitting methods.

Conclusion: The proposed Bayesian approach revitalizes optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale LLM pre-training, offering a practical and theoretically grounded alternative to both heuristic and function-fitting paradigms.

Abstract: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) is fundamentally influenced by the distributional composition of multi-domain pre-training data. While manual heuristics were prevalent in early models, they increasingly fail to capture the intricate synergies between domains as data complexity grows. To overcome the issue, a dominant approach seeks to fit a proxy function mapping between domain weights and their corresponding validation losses, and then find the optimal domain weights to minimize validation losses. These methods rely on strong structural assumptions, such as rank invariance or scaling laws, which are often violated, resulting in non-negligible estimation bias. A promising approach is to directly optimize the weighting scheme from data. However, it suffers from unstable optimization trajectory and prohibitive computational overhead, limiting its potential to search better domain weights configurations. This paper presents a Bayesian domain weighting method to infer the weights from a Dirichlet distribution via introducing Gamma prior information learned from observations. Experimental results demonstrate that proposed method could achieve stable and efficient domain weights learning, and identifies optimal mixtures while consuming substantially less data than search-based function-fitting methods, revitalizing optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale applications.

</details>


### [261] [TriShield: Zero-Utility-Loss Defense Against Privacy Backdoors in Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning via Orthogonal Gradient Projection and Optimizer State Entanglement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27940)
*Cheng Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TriShield is a three-layer deterministic defense against NeuroImprint-style privacy backdoor attacks in federated LLM fine-tuning. It achieves zero reconstruction rate and zero utility loss by combining parameter artifact detection, stateful virtual iteration for gradient entanglement, and zero-utility orthogonal projection via SVD, all with <5% GPU overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The NeuroImprint attack enables a malicious parameter server to reconstruct 59%–79% of client training data from PEFT adapters by implanting memorization neurons. Existing defenses—local differential privacy and gradient clipping—either fail outright or cause unacceptable utility degradation. A defense is needed that completely thwarts this reconstruction without sacrificing model performance or communication efficiency.

Method: TriShield employs three sequential layers: (1) a Parameter Artifact Detector that scans distributed model parameters for memory-neuron signatures before local training; (2) a Stateful Virtual Iteration mechanism that exploits Adam/AdamW momentum to irreversibly entangle gradients across virtual steps, breaking the closed-form inversion; and (3) a Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection operator that uses SVD to project gradient updates onto the main-task semantic subspace, eliminating any gradient components carrying private memorization. A theoretical proof shows that after Layers 2 and 3, mutual information between uploaded gradients and any individual sample is zero.

Result: TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction rate to 0% across all tested attack variants on GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B. Training accuracy is maintained or improved, with less than 5% additional GPU computation overhead.

Conclusion: TriShield provides a complete, provable defense against NeuroImprint-style backdoor reconstruction attacks in federated LLM fine-tuning, achieving zero reconstruction without any utility loss or extra communication rounds, making it practical for real-world deployment.

Abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) enables collaborative training without exposing raw data. However, a recent attack, NeuroImprint [1] (arXiv:2606.20553), demonstrates that a malicious parameter server can corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor: by assigning a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and ensuring each neuron updates at most once, the server can analytically reconstruct 59\%--79\% of client training data with high semantic fidelity. Existing defenses---including local differential privacy (LDP) [8] and gradient clipping---either fail against this attack or impose unacceptable utility degradation. We present \textbf{TriShield}, a three-layer deterministic defense that completely prevents NeuroImprint-style reconstruction with \textbf{zero model utility loss} and \textbf{no additional communication rounds}. TriShield consists of: (1) a \textbf{Parameter Artifact Detector} that identifies memory-neuron signatures in distributed model parameters before local training begins; (2) a \textbf{Stateful Virtual Iteration} mechanism that forces Adam/AdamW's momentum state to irreversibly entangle gradients across virtual steps, invalidating NeuroImprint's closed-form inversion; and (3) a \textbf{Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection} operator that projects all local gradient updates onto the main-task semantic subspace computed via SVD, physically eliminating any gradient components that carry private memorization. We prove theoretically that after Layers 2 and 3, the mutual information between the uploaded gradient and any individual training sample is zero. Experiments on GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B verify that TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction rate to \textbf{0\%} across all tested attack variants, while maintaining or improving training accuracy, with less than 5\% additional GPU computation overhead.

</details>


### [262] [AutoPref: Automatic Discovery of Task-Specific Preference Objectives for Neural Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27953)
*Shengda Gu,Kai Li,Xinyi Ke,Haobo Fu,Yifan Zhang,Jian Cheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AutoPref introduces an LLM-guided framework that automatically discovers preference-based learning objectives for neural combinatorial optimization by factorizing objectives into pairwise loss and set-aware weighting programs, outperforming hand-designed baselines across multiple COPs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing preference-based NCO methods rely on manually specified, one-size-fits-all objective formulations that conflate two design choices: what learning signal to extract from each solution pair and how to weight each pair relative to the sampled set. This limits adaptability and performance across diverse problems.

Method: AutoPref factorizes the preference objective into a pairwise loss program (defining the learning signal) and a set-aware weighting program (determining pair contributions). These compose a unified programmatic objective space. An LLM-driven staged conditional search with behavioral gates filters inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation, making the search tractable.

Result: Across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across various problem scales, demonstrating both the effectiveness and scalability of automated objective discovery for NCO.

Conclusion: Automated preference-objective discovery via LLM-guided program search is a viable and scalable approach for improving NCO, surpassing manually designed objectives and enabling problem-adaptive learning.

Abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) underpin many real-world decisions, but their exponentially large search spaces make high-quality solutions costly to obtain. Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) learns fast construction policies, typically with reinforcement learning (RL), while preference-based NCO improves sample efficiency by learning from relative solution quality. However, existing preference objectives combine two distinct design choices in manually specified, one-size-fits-all formulations: what learning signal to extract from each solution pair and how to weight each pair relative to the sampled set. We present AutoPref, the first LLM-guided framework for automated preference-objective discovery in NCO. AutoPref factorizes the objective into a pairwise loss program, which defines the learning signal, and a set-aware weighting program, which determines each pair's relative contribution.
