Their composition forms a unified programmatic objective space containing existing preference objectives as special cases. To make its search tractable, we introduce a staged conditional search strategy with behavioral gates that filter inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation. Across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across problem scales, demonstrating the benefits and scalability of automated objective discovery for NCO.

</details>


### [263] [What Makes Graph Unified? Principles and Generative Sliding-Window Transformer for Graph Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27966)
*Dongxiao He,Siqi Liu,Jitao Zhao,Yawen Li,Yi Wang,Di Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SliGFM is a Graph Foundation Model that uses topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction to unify heterogeneous node features across graph domains, addressing the gap between dimensional uniformity and meaningful feature unification through four guiding desiderata.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) project heterogeneous node features into a fixed-dimensional space but conflate dimensional uniformity with effective feature unification. Dimensional consistency alone fails to guarantee that unified features preserve informative semantics or capture transferable cross-domain patterns. The paper identifies this as a fundamental conceptual gap.

Method: The authors propose SliGFM, grounded in four desiderata: formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility. SliGFM reorders node feature dimensions by topological smoothness, then applies a shared sliding-window feature encoder to produce ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens. A smoothness-aware transformer captures relational patterns among these tokens, while a generative reconstruction objective preserves original feature information.

Result: The abstract does not provide specific experimental results or quantitative outcomes.

Conclusion: SliGFM bridges the gap between dimensional consistency and meaningful feature unification, enabling effective cross-domain knowledge transfer by ensuring unified features are both dimensionally uniform and semantically informative.

Abstract: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose graph learning, aiming to learn reusable knowledge that generalizes across diverse graph domains and downstream tasks, reducing the need for specific model development. Achieving this goal requires reconciling the substantial heterogeneity in node features, graph structures, and semantic information across domains. Among them, heterogeneous node features constitute a fundamental input-level barrier, as their dimensionality and semantics vary substantially across datasets. Existing studies typically project or map heterogeneous node features into a fixed-dimensional space, often implicitly equating dimensional uniformity with effective feature unification. Yet dimensional consistency alone does not ensure that the unified features preserve informative semantics and capture transferable patterns that can support cross-domain knowledge transfer. To bridge this conceptual gap, we distill four desiderata for cross-domain graph feature unification: formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility. Guided by these principles, we propose SliGFM, a graph foundation model built upon topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction. SliGFM orders feature dimensions by topological smoothness and scans the reordered features with a shared sliding-window feature encoder, transforming heterogeneous features into a common space of ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens. This formulation enables a smoothness-aware transformer to capture transferable relational patterns among feature tokens within each node, while the generative reconstruction objective encourages preservation of the original feature information.

</details>


### [264] [Beyond Binary Rewards: A Comparative Study of Reward Design for Reinforcement Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27968)
*Efstratios Zaradoukas,Davide Gabrielli,Bardh Prenkaj,Gjergji Kasneci*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies reward design in Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) for machine unlearning, proposing a decomposition framework that decouples verifiability from sparsity. Two novel reward functions — exponential (graded penalties by forbidden-concept count) and PageRank-inspired (semantic importance weighting) — achieve up to 3× faster forgetting than binary rewards while preserving model utility on the RWKU benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RLVR-based machine unlearning methods use sparse binary rewards that only indicate whether forbidden content was avoided, providing minimal learning signal and slow convergence. Privacy regulations (GDPR, EU AI Act) create a growing need for efficient, scalable unlearning, motivating better reward design.

Method: The authors introduce a reward decomposition framework that decouples verifiability from sparsity. They propose two reward functions: (1) an exponential reward providing graded penalties proportional to the count of forbidden-concept occurrences, and (2) a PageRank-inspired reward that weights penalties by semantic importance of occurrences. Both are evaluated within the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) framework on the RWKU benchmark.

Result: Both proposed rewards consistently outperform the binary baseline, achieving similar forgetting performance up to 3× faster while preserving general model utility. The exponential and PageRank rewards demonstrate that richer, non-sparse reward signals significantly accelerate convergence in unlearning.

Conclusion: Reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency. Moving beyond sparse binary rewards to graded, semantically-aware reward functions offers a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning for real-world deployment under privacy regulations.

Abstract: Machine unlearning seeks to selectively remove specific knowledge from trained language models without full retraining, a growing necessity under privacy regulations such as GDPR and the EU AI Act. Recent work has reformulated unlearning as a Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) problem, where models are optimized against verifiable rewards computed directly from their outputs. However, existing methods rely on sparse binary rewards that provide minimal learning signal, indicating only whether forbidden content was avoided, and limiting convergence speed. In this paper, we study how reward design affects unlearning efficiency within the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) framework. We introduce a principled reward decomposition framework that decouples verifiability from sparsity, and propose two new reward functions: an exponential reward that provides graded penalties based on the count of forbidden-concept occurrences, and a PageRank inspired reward that weights penalties by semantic importance. We conduct experiments on the Real World Knowledge Unlearning (RWKU) benchmark, demonstrating that both rewards consistently outperform the binary setting, while reaching similar forgetting performance up to $3\times$ faster and preserving general model utility. Our results show that reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency offering a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning.

</details>


### [265] [TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27973)
*Cong Li,Peixi Peng,Yisen Zhao,Xinyu Hu,Shudong Liu,Zhan Su,Zhuojian Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TAPO is a plug-and-play training framework that enhances LLM agent RL by adding transition prediction (action-conditioned next-observation) supervision to standard policy optimization, improving task performance without extra data or inference cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL for LLM agents relies on sparse task rewards, neglecting dense environmental feedback signals. Theoretical work suggests that predictive knowledge of environmental dynamics is critical for generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks. TAPO addresses this gap by explicitly supervising transition dynamics.

Method: TAPO alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision on a shared backbone model. Specifically, it repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction as an auxiliary training objective, making the model sensitive to environmental transition dynamics while simultaneously optimizing the policy. It functions as a lightweight, plug-and-play module compatible with existing agent RL algorithms.

Result: Systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld, using foundation models of various scales with different policy optimization algorithms, show that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.

Conclusion: Leveraging dense transition-level supervision alongside sparse task rewards is an effective and computationally efficient strategy for improving LLM agent post-training, as demonstrated by TAPO's consistent gains across diverse settings.

Abstract: Recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial paradigm for the post-training of Large Language Model (LLM) agents. However, existing methods predominantly rely on sparse task rewards for policy optimization, failing to fully exploit another class of inherently dense supervisory signals naturally present during online interaction: environmental feedback following action execution. Recent theoretical studies suggest that generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks hinges on predictive knowledge of environmental consequences. Inspired by this, we propose TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents, a unified training framework that alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision. Beyond standard RL updates, TAPO repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on a shared backbone model. This approach enhances the model's sensitivity to environmental transition dynamics and action consequences while concurrently optimizing the policy. It serves as a computationally lightweight, plug-and-play enhancement module for existing agent RL algorithms, requiring no additional expert data, extra sampling costs, or inference-time overhead. We conduct systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld, integrating foundation models of various scales with different policy optimization algorithms. Empirical results demonstrate that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.

</details>


### [266] [Generalization Bounds on Optimal Control for Transformer Training and Wasserstein Distributional Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27975)
*Kağan Akman,Naci Saldi,Serdar Yüksel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper derives finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers by viewing training as a Markovian control problem over measure-valued states, quantizing the spaces to obtain concentration-based bounds, and connecting the results to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the empirical success of Transformers, rigorous finite-sample generalization guarantees remain scarce. The authors aim to fill this gap by leveraging a control-theoretic perspective on Transformer dynamics to derive explicit, non-asymptotic generalization bounds.

Method: The paper builds on the doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics, interpreting training as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem over empirical input-output measures. A quantized model is constructed by discretizing the state, action, and measure-state spaces. Finite-sample generalization bounds are then derived using concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces combined with a Lipschitz stability estimate for the value function. These bounds are transferred back to the original (base) model at the cost of an explicit approximation error. The framework is further linked to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

Result: The paper yields explicit finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained via dynamic programming. It also establishes a formal connection between Transformer generalization and Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization, showing that the training problem admits a distributionally robust control formulation.

Conclusion: Viewing Transformers through the lens of measure-valued Markovian control provides a principled pathway to finite-sample generalization guarantees. The quantization approach, combined with concentration and stability arguments, yields explicit bounds, and the distributionally robust interpretation offers new insights into the robustness properties of trained Transformers.

Abstract: We derive finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions. Building on the doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics, we view data sets as probability laws on pairs of empirical input-output measures, allowing us to interpret the training problem as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. We then analyze a quantized model, derived by quantizing the state, action, and measure-state spaces, and derive explicit finite-sample generalization bounds using concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces together with a Lipschitz stability estimate for the value function. These bounds are transferred to the base model at the cost of an explicit approximation error. Finally, we show that the same machinery yields a distributionally robust control formulation of the training problem, connecting Transformer generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

</details>


### [267] [It's All Just Vectorization: einx, a Universal Notation for Tensor Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27987)
*Florian Fervers,Sebastian Bullinger,Christoph Bodensteiner,Michael Arens*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces einx, a universal notation for tensor operations that reduces complex framework APIs to a small set of elementary operations through the unifying concept of vectorization, enabling cleaner, more readable tensor code while preventing shape errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing tensor programming paradigms are problematic: NumPy-like notation is error-prone (especially shape errors) and inconsistent across operations, while alternatives like einsum/einops lack generality and cover only limited operations. A universal, consistent model for tensor programming is needed.

Method: The authors revisit vectorization as a fundamental function for transforming tensor operations. They use vectorization to (1) lift lower-order operations to higher-order ones, and (2) decompose higher-order operations into lower-order ones plus their vectorization. Building on this, they propose einx — a declarative, pointful notation defined by analogy with loop notation that uniformly represents the vectorization of tensor operations.

Result: The einx notation reduces large framework APIs to a small set of elementary operations with consistent rules across all operations. It is implemented as a Python library that integrates seamlessly with existing tensor frameworks, available at github.com/fferflo/einx.

Conclusion: Vectorization serves as a universal foundation for tensor programming. The einx notation, grounded in this principle, provides a clean, readable, writable, and general-purpose alternative to existing tensor operation APIs, overcoming their limitations in consistency and expressiveness.

Abstract: Tensor operations represent a cornerstone of modern scientific computing. However, the Numpy-like notation adopted by predominant tensor frameworks is often difficult to read and write and prone to so-called shape errors, i.a., due to following inconsistent rules across a large, complex collection of operations. Alternatives like einsum and einops have gained popularity, but are inherently restricted to few operations and lack the generality required for a universal model of tensor programming.
  To derive a better paradigm, we revisit vectorization as a function for transforming tensor operations, and use it to both lift lower-order operations to higher-order operations, and conceptually decompose higher-order operations to lower-order operations and their vectorization.
  Building on the universal nature of vectorization, we introduce einx, a universal notation for tensor operations. It uses declarative, pointful expressions that are defined by analogy with loop notation and represent the vectorization of tensor operations. The notation reduces the large APIs of existing frameworks to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and enables a clean, readable and writable representation in code. We provide an implementation of einx that is embedded in Python and integrates seamlessly with existing tensor frameworks: https://github.com/fferflo/einx

</details>


### [268] [Building a User Foundation Model for the Open Web](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28019)
*Solal Vernier,Ivan Can Arisoy,Merwan Barlier,Blaž Škrlj*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a user foundation model for open-web RTB advertising that uses self-supervised learning on fragmented browsing histories, achieving significant gains in production CTR and bid win-rate models, with an LLM-in-the-loop optimization pipeline for pre-training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial user foundation models assume persistent user identity, but open-web RTB has fragmented, non-persistent user identities with short, disjointed browsing sessions. Historical signals are typically reduced to aggregated counters and recency buckets, losing sequential structure. The authors aim to recover this lost signal via self-supervised representation learning.

Method: Pre-train a Transformer encoder on user browsing histories using masked language modeling (MLM) and a sequence-level contrastive objective. Fine-tune on click prediction. Optimize the pre-training pipeline via an LLM-in-the-loop search over a curated catalog of code-level edits (lifters), instantiating the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm. The learned encoder representation is shared across downstream production models.

Result: The shared encoder yields +1.197% RIG on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker. A 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR and -1.13% eCPC (80% CI excludes zero on both).

Conclusion: Self-supervised user foundation models are viable and effective on the open web despite fragmented user identity, and LLM-as-optimizer is practical for industrial-scale pre-training pipeline optimization.

Abstract: User foundation models have demonstrated strong results in e-commerce and social recommendation, but most industrial deployments assume environments where user identity is stable and persistent. Open-web real-time bidding (RTB) operates on a structurally different data distribution: user identity is fragmented and non-persistent across browsing sessions, and the availability of browsing history depends on user privacy choices. Consequently, a significant portion of traffic carries no historical data, and available records often consist of relatively short, disjointed sessions. As a result, historical signals in this domain are typically represented as aggregated counters and recency buckets, leaving the sequential structure unexploited. To address this limitation, we present a user foundation model that applies self-supervised learning on user browsing histories and show that the learned representation improves multiple downstream production tasks, demonstrating the viability of this approach on the open web. We pre-train a Transformer encoder with masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective, then fine-tune it on the click prediction task. We optimize the encoder's pre-training pipeline with an LLM-in-the-loop search over a curated catalog of reviewable, code-level edits (lifters), instantiating the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm in an industrial setting. The same encoder representation yields +1.197% RIG on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker; a 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR, -1.13% eCPC (80% CI excluding zero on both metrics).

</details>


### [269] [Flux-OPD: On-Policy Distillation with Evolving Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28022)
*Yuran Wang,Zekun Wang,Bohan Zeng,Ruixu Zhang,Wenxuan Liu,Liu Yang,Yifan Dai,Yang Shi,Bozhou Li,Chengzhuo Tong,Daili Hua,Yuanxing Zhang,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Flux-OPD introduces an online preference distillation paradigm where evolving contexts serve as in-training supervision. By decomposing the reverse KL objective into a geometric-mean distillation target and a conflict term, the method injects contextual difference signals as corrections into a context-free teacher anchor, weighted by the conflict indicator. It outperforms existing OPD methods on open-ended tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In open-ended LLM training, task preferences are hard to formalize as verifiable rewards. Static contexts provide limited supervision once distilled. Evolving contexts could offer richer signals, but using them directly as in-training targets causes instability due to shifting distillation targets and conflicting teacher distributions. A principled mechanism is needed to stabilize the target and downweight conflicts.

Method: The authors decompose the reverse KL divergence objective, revealing that (1) the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teacher distributions, and (2) the objective contains a conflict term measuring disagreement among teachers. Based on this, Flux-OPD computes contextual difference signals (the divergence between context-conditioned and context-free teachers), injects them as corrections into a stable context-free anchor, and uses the conflict term to adaptively weight correction strength — stabilizing training while leveraging evolving contexts.

Result: Experiments on open-ended tasks demonstrate that Flux-OPD outperforms existing online preference distillation paradigms, validating the effectiveness of combining teacher supervision with evolving contexts through the proposed decomposition-based correction mechanism.

Conclusion: Evolving contexts can be effectively leveraged as in-training supervision for open-ended preference learning when coupled with a principled stabilization mechanism. The reverse KL decomposition provides both theoretical grounding and practical guidance, and Flux-OPD represents a promising direction for online preference distillation in domains lacking verifiable rewards.

Abstract: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences difficult to formalize as effective supervision. Contexts can convey such preferences, yet provide little additional supervision once distilled into the student, motivating contexts that evolve with student performance. However, directly using evolving contexts as in-training supervision results in an unstable distillation target and conflicting distributions, requiring mechanisms to stabilize target and downweight conflicts. In this paper, we analyze the effect of contexts through a decomposition of the reverse KL objective, revealing two findings: the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, and the objective contains a conflict term that measures conflicts among these teachers. Based on this decomposition, we propose Flux-OPD, an OPD paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision to capture task preferences in open-ended domains. Flux-OPD treats the differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, and weights their correction strength using the conflict term as an indicator. Experiments on open-ended tasks show that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, highlighting the potential to combine teacher supervision with evolving contexts.

</details>


### [270] [Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization via Privileged Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28026)
*Xingjian Wu,Junlin Liu,Xingchen Liu,Xuhang Zhu,Jianing Wang,Linsen Guo,Xiaoyu Li,Xuezhi Cao,Xunliang Cai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CRPO reformulates agentic on-policy self-distillation as contrastive learning, using predictive entropy to distinguish reflective exploration from exposure bias, achieving superior stability and generalization in multi-turn LLM reasoning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) for post-training LLMs suffers from exposure bias due to privileged self-teacher information. In multi-turn agentic settings, this causes reasoning route convergence and loss of clear optimization directions. A method is needed that preserves fine-grained optimization signals without succumbing to these failure modes.

Method: CRPO reformulates agentic OPSD through a contrastive learning framework. It uses predictive entropy to partition positions into positive (reflective exploration) and negative (exposure bias) sets, then applies group-wise contrastive learning to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals while suppressing biased ones.

Result: Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks demonstrate that CRPO consistently outperforms existing RL and self-distillation baselines, with significant improvements in training stability and generalization for long-horizon interactions.

Conclusion: CRPO effectively addresses the exposure bias problem in agentic OPSD by leveraging contrastive learning with entropy-based position discrimination, offering a robust post-training paradigm for LLMs in multi-turn agentic scenarios.

Abstract: Recent advances in post-training Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) or On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD). While OPSD provides dense, logit-level supervision, it inherently suffers from exposure bias due to the privileged information of the self-teacher. In multi-turn agentic settings, this leads to reasoning route convergence and the loss of clear optimization directions. To tackle these challenges, we introduce Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization (CRPO), which reformulates agentic OPSD from a contrastive learning perspective. By leveraging predictive entropy to distinguish between positive positions (reflective exploration) and negative positions (exposure bias), CRPO conducts group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals. Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks demonstrate that CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, significantly enhancing training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.

</details>


### [271] [Enhancing Irregular Time Series Forecasting with Continuous-Time Modeling Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28035)
*Tianen Shen,Zhengyu Li,Yutong Li,Xiangfei Qiu,Xingjian Wu,Bin Yang,Jilin Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WrapFlow is a continuous-time forecasting framework for irregular multivariate time series that introduces Continuous-Time Tokenization for raw event encoding and a simulation-free Residual Flow Matching training paradigm, achieving state-of-the-art performance without ODE solver overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Irregular multivariate time series pose challenges due to asynchronous observations and non-uniform sampling. Existing methods either use discretization (interpolation/imputation) which breaks continuous-time semantics, or ODE-based models requiring specialized architectures and expensive numerical solvers. A continuous-time approach that avoids both pitfalls is needed.

Method: WrapFlow has two core components: (1) Continuous-Time Tokenization — directly encodes raw observation events into tokens with explicit gap-aware tokens for modeling long unobserved intervals, processed by a standard Transformer backbone; (2) Simulation-free Residual Flow Matching — learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions, avoiding numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training, requiring only a few fixed rollout steps at inference.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets show that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: WrapFlow successfully bridges the gap between discretization-based and ODE-based approaches by combining continuous-time tokenization with simulation-free flow matching, delivering high-quality continuous forecasting with reduced computational cost.

Abstract: Irregular multivariate time series are widely encountered in applications such as healthcare monitoring, human activity recognition, and environmental sensing. Their core challenges stem from asynchronous observations, non-uniform sampling intervals, and the fact that temporal patterns themselves carry critical dynamic information. Existing approaches either rely on discretization-based preprocessing (e.g., interpolation, imputation, or aggregation), which disrupts the underlying continuous-time semantics, or adopt continuous-time modeling via ODE-based frameworks, which typically require specialized architectures and incur substantial computational overhead due to numerical solvers. To address these limitations, we propose WrapFlow, a continuous-time modeling framework for irregular time series forecasting. On the input side, WrapFlow introduces Continuous-Time Tokenization, which directly encodes raw observation events and explicitly models long unobserved intervals via gap-aware tokens. The resulting continuous-time tokens are then processed by a standard Transformer backbone to capture long-range temporal dependencies. On the output side, we develop a simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching, which learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions while avoiding numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training. This design enables high-quality continuous forecasting using only a small number of fixed rollout steps at inference. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance.

</details>


### [272] [Learning features from Newton's algorithm: a way to accelerate nonlinear parametrized PDE solvers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28036)
*Rémy Vallot,Florian de Vuyst,Thibault Dairay,Mathilde Mougeot*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is proposed, using learned solution features and a GMRES-based residual-minimizing correction to accelerate Newton's method for nonlinear PDE systems. The approach reduces iterations and CPU time with minimal intrusiveness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Newton's method converges faster when initialized close to a root, but good initial guesses are often unavailable for unseen parameters in large-scale nonlinear PDE problems. Existing surrogate-based initializations can be insufficient, motivating a complementary corrective step to further improve the starting point.

Method: The method has two stages: (1) A regression model predicts a surrogate solution approximation using a solution feature space built via discrete Newton trajectories from precomputed solutions. (2) A residual-minimizing correction is computed using a GMRES-based approach that leverages a corrective search direction feature space derived from intermediate Newton increments. This corrective step requires only residual evaluations and a small least-squares solve, making it inexpensive. The corrected state then seeds the high-fidelity Newton solver.

Result: Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems demonstrate quantifiable speedups over standalone surrogate initialization, with significant reductions in both Newton iterations and overall CPU time.

Conclusion: The two-stage strategy is generic, weakly intrusive, and applicable to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems, offering a practical acceleration technique for Newton-based solvers in multi-query settings.

Abstract: It is well known that Newton's method converges faster when the initial guess is closer to a root of a system of nonlinear equations. In this paper, a two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is proposed by learning features from a parameter-space sampling and a database of precomputed solutions. The method uses discrete Newton trajectories to construct two complementary reduced spaces: a solution feature space, built from converged states, and a corrective search direction feature space, built from intermediate Newton increments. For an unseen parameter, a regression model is used to predict a surrogate solution approximation. Then, in a second step, a residual-minimizing correction is computed using a dedicated GMRES-based approach. The resulting state is then used as an initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method, which completes convergence. The corrective step is computationally inexpensive since it only requires residual evaluations and the solution of a small least-squares problem. The methodology is weakly intrusive once the high-fidelity residual fields and a script-based programming interface are available. This strategy reduces the number of Newton iterations and decreases the overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared with standalone surrogate initialization. Significant speedups are observed. This generic approach can be applied to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

</details>


### [273] [ClawTrack: Towards Trace-Level Evaluation and Improvement of Real-World Autonomous Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28037)
*Xingjian Wu,Xuhang Zhu,Xingchen Liu,Junlin Liu,Jianing Wang,Linsen Guo,Xiaoyu Li,Xuezhi Cao,Xunliang Cai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ClawTrack is a benchmark evaluating LLM agents on both final outcomes (Task Score) and reasoning process quality (Process Score) across 320 tasks and 8 domains. It uses 12,541 rubric items across four dimensions to pinpoint where agent reasoning succeeds or fails, demonstrating that process evaluation reveals lucky successes, identifies result verification as a key bottleneck, and enables effective trajectory filtering for post-training improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent benchmarks only evaluate final outcomes, conflating reliable reasoning with lucky guesses and failing to attribute failures to specific process deficiencies — a critical gap as agents are deployed in complex, multi-step workflows requiring long-horizon attribution.

Method: ClawTrack introduces dual assessment: a Task Score (outcome) and a Process Score (reasoning quality). It comprises 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services. A Process Grader scores each reasoning turn on four dimensions — goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, and result verification — anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. 21 models were evaluated over 16,000+ trials.

Result: (1) Process scores attribute success/failure to specific reasoning dimensions, filtering "lucky passes" invisible to outcome-only evaluation. (2) The four dimensions are complementary, with result verification emerging as the systematic bottleneck. (3) The framework is robust to evaluator choice across different judge LLMs. (4) Process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.

Conclusion: Process-aware evaluation is essential for meaningful benchmarking of LLM agents in multi-step tasks. ClawTrack demonstrates that measuring how an agent reasons — not just whether it succeeds — enables precise diagnostics, reveals hidden failure modes, and provides actionable signals for improving agent trajectories through post-training.

Abstract: As LLM-based agents are deployed in complex, multi-step workflows, a critical evaluation gap has emerged: most existing benchmarks judge only final outcomes, unable to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky success or attribute failures to specific process deficiencies, hindering attribution in long-horizon tasks.
  In this work, we present ClawTrack, a dual-assessment benchmark that simultaneously measures what an agent achieves (Task Score) and how it achieves it (Process Score). ClawTrack comprises 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services. A Process Grader scores each reasoning turn along four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, and result verification), anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. Evaluating 21 models over 16,000+ trials, we find that: (1) process scores effectively attribute success and failure to specific reasoning dimensions, filtering lucky passes invisible to outcome-only evaluation; (2) the four dimensions are complementary, with result verification as the systematic bottleneck; (3) the framework is robust to evaluator choice across different judge LLMs; and (4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.

</details>


### [274] [GVR-Coder: A Visual-Feedback Framework for Structured SVG Generation in Complex Document and Meeting Scenarios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28073)
*Yiming Xu,Jihua Kang,Chunsai Du,Qifan Zhang,Wangqiu Zhou,Yiting Wu,Tianqi Li,Qi Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GVR-Coder introduces a framework for generating logically coherent SVG diagrams from lengthy professional texts, addressing data scarcity with DocMeetSVG-100K, layout priors, and a dual-rendering-feedback RL mechanism with a generate-verify-repair agent loop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lengthy professional/meeting texts impose high cognitive load; converting them into SVG diagrams aids comprehension. However, existing Text-to-SVG methods suffer from (1) scarce datasets for complex logic-rich diagrams, (2) missing explicit layout priors causing chaotic spatial arrangements, and (3) no fine-grained visual feedback for validating outputs and fixing aesthetic defects.

Method: (1) DocMeetSVG-100K: a large-scale SVG dataset for document authoring/meeting review. (2) GVR-Coder framework with: curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning for progressive complex structure modeling with explicit layout constraints; reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback (implicit reward signals jointly optimizing structural complexity and visual aesthetics); and a generate-verify-repair agent loop for explicit fine-grained feedback and targeted refinement.

Result: Extensive experiments show GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines, reliably producing logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams.

Conclusion: GVR-Coder effectively addresses key Text-to-SVG challenges through dataset construction, layout-aware training, and dual feedback mechanisms, achieving state-of-the-art performance in generating high-quality logical diagrams from lengthy professional texts. Code and data are publicly available.

Abstract: In demanding professional environments and meeting review scenarios, lengthy text often imposes a high cognitive load. To facilitate efficient information communication, transforming verbose text into logically clear diagrams is essential. Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) provide an effective representation for this purpose due to their editability and resolution independence. However, current research on Text-to-SVG generation remains hindered by three major challenges: (1) the scarcity of datasets for complex, logic-rich diagrams; (2) the absence of explicit layout priors, which leads to chaotic spatial arrangements; and (3) the lack of fine-grained visual feedback to validate rendered outputs and correct aesthetic defects. To address these challenges, at the data level, we introduce DocMeetSVG-100K, a large-scale SVG dataset tailored for document authoring and meeting review scenarios. At the model level, we propose GVR-Coder, a novel framework designed to generate high-quality logical diagrams from lengthy professional texts. Specifically, we adopt a curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning to progressively enhance the model's capability in modeling complex structures, while explicitly incorporating layout constraint knowledge during training. In addition, we introduce reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback, a mechanism that provides implicit feedback through reward signals to jointly optimize structural complexity and visual aesthetics. Furthermore, we design a generate-verify-repair agent loop, which improves generation quality through explicit, fine-grained feedback and targeted refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines and reliably produces logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams. Code and data are available at https://github.com/CurryaNa/GVR-Coder.

</details>


### [275] [Chem World: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Physics-Informed Framework for Trustworthy Chemical Property Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28079)
*Tianyou Bai,Huan Wang,Mingchen Gao,Fangyue Lin,Pinze Ren,Zhenlin Zhao,Siming Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Chem World is a comprehensive benchmark integrating 17 datasets with 800K+ molecules for chemical property prediction. The authors also propose Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network that incorporates chemical prior knowledge, demonstrating improved accuracy and robustness over existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing chemical property prediction benchmarks suffer from limited task diversity, fragmented datasets, and inconsistent evaluation protocols, hindering systematic assessment of AI model reliability and generalization.

Method: The authors introduce (1) Chem World, a unified benchmark comprising 17 diverse chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples spanning properties like density, electrical conductivity, and solubility; and (2) Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network framework that integrates chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning to enhance prediction accuracy and reliability.

Result: Extensive experiments on the Chem World benchmark show that Mixture-PINN outperforms existing methods in chemical property prediction tasks, demonstrating superior accuracy, robustness, and reliability.

Conclusion: Chem World, combined with physics-informed learning, establishes a foundation for building trustworthy AI systems in computational chemistry and advancing AI-driven scientific discovery.

Abstract: Chemical property prediction plays a critical role in accelerating scientific discovery in chemistry, materials science, and drug development. However, existing benchmarks often suffer from limited task diversity, fragmented datasets, and inconsistent evaluation protocols, making it challenging to systematically assess the reliability and generalization of AI models. In this work, we introduce Chem World, a comprehensive benchmark for chemical property prediction that integrates 17 diverse chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples, covering various properties including density, electrical conductivity, solubility, and other molecular characteristics. Chem World provides a unified platform for evaluating AI models across multiple property prediction tasks. Furthermore, we propose Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network based prediction framework that incorporates chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning, improving the accuracy, robustness, and reliability of chemical property prediction. Extensive experiments on Chem World demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared with existing methods. By combining large-scale standardized evaluation with physics-informed learning, Chem World establishes a foundation for developing trustworthy AI systems for computational chemistry and advancing AI-driven scientific discovery.

</details>


### [276] [From Expert Reduction to Behavioral Divergence: Tracing Numerical State through Sparse MoE Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28097)
*Tianyang Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model outputs vary numerically based on mathematically equivalent but computationally different reduction (aggregation) orders. The authors systematically isolate this effect in DeepSeek-V4-Flash, map distinct trajectory basins, and identify "post-mHC" as an intra-token boundary and "full persistent state" as a cross-token continuation boundary, arguing that reduction order and accumulator precision must be part of the numerical compatibility contract for sparse-MoE systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To rigorously demonstrate that mathematically equivalent expert-reduction orders in sparse-MoE models produce observably different execution trajectories, and to identify the precise architectural boundaries where numerical divergence propagates across tokens. This establishes that operand representation, accumulator precision, and reduction order are not implementation details but part of a formal numerical compatibility contract.

Method: The authors freeze local MoE state in DeepSeek-V4-Flash and vary only aggregation semantics across four schemes (P32, A, B, C), differing in operand representation and accumulator precision. They enumerate order variants (720 per mode at one layer-5 fork), classify resulting trajectory basins and structural classes, measure token-level divergence under controlled prompts, and perform bitwise state reconstruction checks (post-mHC, next-router, LM states, persistent states) to pinpoint intra- and cross-token boundaries of divergence.

Result: A-mode: 720 orders → 10 continuation basins. B-mode: 720 orders → 360 exact structural classes, 11 basins; under one Chinese prompt, B-classes split into 202 layoffs, 113 hiring, 45 other continuations. Max-L∞ B-branch selection separates 12/24/36 of 50 prompts by 8/16/32 tokens. Schemes P32, A, and B alter every native-reference trajectory; scheme C preserves routes, token sequences, and texts. A 192-trajectory C check matches native MoE bitwise. For one B branch, exact FP64 reconstruction of full persistent state yields agreement for 301 downstream post-mHC states, checkpoints, routes, predictions, and text over 7 steps. Identical tokens do not guarantee identical autoregressive state; divergence survives token boundaries.

Conclusion: Expert operand conversion, accumulator precision, and reduction order constitute a numerical compatibility contract for sparse-MoE runtimes and hardware backends. Scheme C demonstrates order invariance for the evaluated six-term states and schedules, establishing controlled causal possibility rather than deployment incidence. Post-mHC is an intra-token boundary; full persistent state is a cross-token continuation boundary.

Abstract: Mathematically equivalent expert-reduction orders can produce observably different sparse-MoE executions. We isolate this effect in native DeepSeek-V4-Flash by freezing local MoE state and varying only aggregation semantics. Four schemes separate operand representation from accumulator precision. At one layer-5 fork, 720 A-mode orders yield 10 continuation basins; 720 B-mode orders form 360 exact structural classes and 11 basins. Under one Chinese prompt, the B classes split into 202 layoffs, 113 hiring, and 45 other continuations. Maximum-L-infinity B-branch selection separates 12, 24, and 36 of 50 prompts by 8, 16, and 32 tokens. Across 192 persistent trajectories per scheme, P32, A, and B change every native-reference route trajectory, while C preserves routes, token sequences, and texts. A separate 192-trajectory C check matches native MoE, post-mHC, next-router, and LM states bitwise. For one controlled B branch, exact post-mHC endpoint reconstruction reproduces the measured downstream trajectory. At the next decode boundary, exact FP64 reconstruction of the branch's full persistent state yields agreement for 301 downstream post-mHC states, 301 persistent-state checkpoints, 301 routes, predictions, and text over seven steps, given the same naturally generated next input. These controls identify post-mHC as an intra-token boundary and full persistent state as a cross-token continuation boundary. Identical tokens need not imply identical autoregressive state: divergence can survive a token boundary and become visible later. These results make expert operand conversion, accumulator precision, and reduction order part of a numerical compatibility contract for sparse-MoE runtimes and hardware backends. They establish controlled causal possibility, not deployment incidence; C's order invariance is limited to evaluated six-term states and schedules.

</details>


### [277] [Information Bottleneck Learning for Faithful Time Series Forecasting Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28124)
*Xu Zheng,Wei Cheng,Zhuomin Chen,Mo Sha,Jingchao Ni,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IB-Forecast is an interpretable multivariate time-series forecasting framework that decomposes predictions into learned periodic and masked residual components, using an information bottleneck to control explanation sparsity. It matches black-box accuracy while providing faithful, sparse explanations that consistently outperform post-hoc baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing interpretable forecasters reveal internal structures but lack faithfulness guarantees—their explanations may not reflect the actual evidence driving predictions. Meanwhile, faithfulness-oriented methods exist almost exclusively for post-hoc classification, not for time-series forecasting. There is a critical gap for a forecasting method that is both inherently interpretable and demonstrably faithful.

Method: IB-Forecast decomposes multivariate time-series forecasting into two components: (1) a learned periodic component capturing seasonal patterns, and (2) a residual component computed using explainable masks over input tokens. A budget-constrained information bottleneck enables end-to-end optimization, allowing users to directly control the sparsity of explanations. Faithfulness is evaluated via a rigorous protocol comparing native explanations against gradient-based, occlusion-based, and optimization-based baselines under matched sparsity budgets.

Result: IB-Forecast matches the forecasting error of leading black-box models while providing faithful explanations at no additional inference cost. Under matched sparsity, its native explanations consistently surpass all post-hoc baselines (gradient, occlusion, optimization-based) across all datasets. It requires only 14–20% of observations to achieve low-error predictions, whereas existing interpretable forecasters exhibit poor explanation faithfulness.

Conclusion: IB-Forecast successfully bridges the gap between interpretable-by-design forecasting and faithfulness guarantees, enabling high-fidelity, sparse explanations without sacrificing predictive accuracy. This makes it suitable for high-stakes domains where understanding the evidential basis of forecasts is critical.

Abstract: As forecasts increasingly drive decisions in fields such as energy, transportation, and healthcare, understanding the historical data behind these predictions has become as crucial as the predictions themselves. Although existing interpretable-by-design forecasters reveal their internal structures, they offer no guarantee that these structures faithfully reflect the underlying evidence driving the predictions. In contrast, while faithfulness-oriented methods explicitly verify model behavior, they are almost exclusively designed for post-hoc classification tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose IB-Forecast, an inherently interpretable multivariate time-series forecasting framework. It decomposes forecasting into a learned periodic component and a residual component computed with explainable masks over input tokens. With a budget-constrained information bottleneck, end-to-end optimization enables users to directly control explanation sparsity. With a rigorous faithfulness evaluation protocol, extensive experiments demonstrate that IB-Forecast matches the forecasting error of leading black-box models while providing faithful explanations at no additional inference cost. Furthermore, under a matched sparsity budget, these native explanations consistently surpass gradient-based, occlusion-based, and optimization-based baselines across all evaluated datasets. Ultimately, whereas the native explanations of existing interpretable forecasters exhibit poor faithfulness, IB-Forecast guarantees high explanation fidelity, requiring only 14-20% of the observations to deliver low-error predictions.

</details>


### [278] [LM-GRASP: Instance-Specific Language Models for Combinatorial Construction via Online Imitation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28135)
*Mohand Mezmaz,Grégoire Danoy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LM-GRASP reformulates GRASP's randomized constructive phase as online imitation learning using a decoder-only Transformer trained per-instance, eliminating pretraining and hand-engineered heuristics. It outperforms GPU-GRASP by 28.4 makespan units on the hardest Taillard PFSP benchmark block.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural combinatorial optimization methods rely on expensive offline pretraining on fixed problem classes and generalize poorly. Classical GRASP uses static, myopic heuristic rules requiring problem-specific feature engineering. The authors seek a data-driven alternative that trains online per-instance, leveraging high-quality solutions discovered during search itself.

Method: A hybrid metaheuristic, LM-GRASP, following an iterative learn-infer-improve cycle. A decoder-only Transformer policy is trained from scratch on each instance via behavioral cloning on a dynamic archive of elite trajectories. Local search serves as the expert oracle, and the pipeline interfaces with the domain only through the objective evaluator—no external data, offline pretraining, or hand-crafted features.

Result: Evaluated on Taillard PFSP benchmark instances ta51–ta60 (the most discriminating block where half of optima are unknown), LM-GRASP outperforms GPU-GRASP by an average of 28.4 makespan units, comparable to the gain GPU acceleration provides over sequential execution (27.2 units), though standard deviations overlap.

Conclusion: Instance-specific, online-trained language models are a promising and practical alternative to hand-engineered constructors, especially for optimization landscapes resistant to classical greedy construction.

Abstract: Machine learning for combinatorial optimization typically relies on neural constructors trained via reinforcement learning on large offline datasets for a fixed problem class-incurring high pretraining costs and generalizing poorly outside the training distribution. We propose an alternative: a metaheuristic framework that reformulates the randomized constructive phase of GRASP as an online imitation learning task, trained from scratch on each problem instance. A local search procedure acts as an expert oracle, while a decoder-only Transformer serves as the constructive policy. Unlike classical GRASP, which relies on static, myopic heuristic rules based on localized scalar costs, our approach is fully data-driven: the construction policy emerges from high-quality solutions discovered during the search itself, with no problem-specific feature engineering required.
  We instantiate this as LM-GRASP, a hybrid metaheuristic following an iterative learn-infer-improve cycle, training the policy online via behavioral cloning on a dynamic archive of elite trajectories-no external data or offline pretraining needed. The pipeline interfaces with the domain solely through the objective evaluator used by local search.
  Evaluated on the Taillard PFSP benchmark (ta51-ta60), the most discriminating block due to half its optima being unknown, LM-GRASP outperforms GPU-GRASP by 28.4 makespan units on average-comparable to the gain from GPU acceleration over sequential execution (27.2 units), though with overlapping standard deviations. This suggests instance-specific, online-trained language models are a promising, practical alternative to hand-engineered constructors, especially for landscapes resistant to classical greedy construction.

</details>


### [279] [Search Strategies for Optimal Classification and Regression Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28170)
*Jacobus G. M. van der Linden,Mim van den Bos,Emir Demirović*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a general algorithmic framework for optimal decision trees that unifies existing search strategies and enables new ones. Through empirical evaluation of 18 strategies, the best approach achieves superior anytime performance for classification and over an order of magnitude speedup for regression compared to the state of the art.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Optimal decision trees offer compact, interpretable models with global optimality guarantees, but scalability remains a major challenge. While various search strategies have been proposed to improve scalability, the individual contribution and comparative effectiveness of each strategy remains unclear, making it difficult to advance the field systematically.

Method: The authors propose a general algorithmic framework for optimal decision trees that can instantiate previously proposed search strategies as well as define novel ones. This unified lens enables systematic comparison. They empirically evaluate 18 distinct search strategies derived from the framework to isolate their effects on performance.

Result: The best strategy identified in the evaluation achieves significantly better anytime performance for classification tasks and reduces runtime by more than an order of magnitude for regression tasks compared to the current state of the art.

Conclusion: A unified algorithmic framework for ODTs allows systematic understanding and comparison of search strategies, and the right combination of strategies yields substantial improvements in both anytime classification performance and regression runtime over existing approaches.

Abstract: Optimal decision trees (ODTs) are compact, interpretable machine learning models that globally optimize a given objective, but their scalability remains challenging. While recent work has proposed a variety of search strategies to improve scalability, the precise contribution of each strategy remains unclear. To address this gap, we introduce a general algorithmic framework for ODTs that instantiates previously used search strategies and enables the definition of new ones. This provides a common lens through which to understand and compare different strategies, which we use to empirically investigate the effect of 18 search strategies. Compared to the state of the art, the best strategy in our evaluation achieves significantly better anytime performance for classification, and improves runtime by more than an order of magnitude for regression.

</details>


### [280] [Multi-channel Uplift Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28182)
*Changjian Liu,Tianyu Wang,Xiaoxuan Deng,WenTao Zhu,Yuwei Xu,Jungqi Jin,Yong Gao,Chuan Yu,Jian Xu,Bo Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReAlloc is a causal framework for budget allocation across marketing channels that combines a fast Orthogonal Teacher (extracting unbiased local gradients from short-term data) with a slow Explanation-Guided Student (distilling gradients into long-term marginal fields), enabling conservative, support-aware decisions that capture cross-channel substitution effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard predict-then-optimize (PTO) methods fail in multi-channel marketing budget allocation due to observational confounding and severe extrapolation, necessitating a causal approach that handles simplex constraints and cross-channel interactions.

Method: ReAlloc employs a fast-slow dual architecture: an Orthogonal Teacher leverages short-term experimental logs to derive unbiased local gradient estimates using orthogonalization techniques, while an Explanation-Guided Student distills these gradients into a structured marginal field for long-term decision-making, respecting the simplex constraint and enabling conservative, support-aware allocation that accounts for cross-channel substitutions.

Result: Extensive simulations and large-scale online A/B tests on the Taobao platform show that ReAlloc achieves simultaneous and significant lifts in both pay orders and income.

Conclusion: ReAlloc effectively addresses the compositional budget allocation problem by bridging short-term causal effect estimation with long-term structured decision-making, delivering robust real-world performance gains on a major e-commerce platform.

Abstract: E-commerce platforms must allocate fixed marketing budgets across multiple channels to maximize business utility. However, standard predict-then-optimize (PTO) paradigms fail in this compositional space due to observational confounding and severe extrapolation. We formulate this challenge as a simplex-constrained uplift decision problem and propose ReAlloc, a fast-slow causal framework. Specifically, an agile Orthogonal Teacher extracts unbiased local gradients from short-term logs, while an Explanation-Guided Student distills them into a structured marginal field over long-term horizons. This design enables support-aware, conservative decisions that capture cross-channel substitutions. Extensive simulations and large-scale online A/B tests on Taobao platform demonstrate that ReAlloc achieves simultaneous lifts in both pay order and income.

</details>


### [281] [Persistent Gaussian Perturbations Prevent Oversmoothing in Recurrent Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28185)
*Mostafa Haghir Chehreghani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proves that injecting independent Gaussian noise at each step of a recurrent GNN prevents oversmoothing by establishing a geometrically ergodic Markov chain with a unique invariant measure, yielding a strictly positive lower bound on stationary Dirichlet energy proportional to noise variance and graph spectral gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Oversmoothing fundamentally limits the depth of message-passing GNNs, as node representations collapse toward a low-dimensional subspace with repeated propagation. Existing solutions (residual connections, normalization, rewiring) are deterministic; this work explores whether persistent stochastic perturbations offer a fundamentally different mechanism to preserve representation diversity asymptotically.

Method: The authors model a recurrent GNN with additive Gaussian noise injected after each propagation step and analyze it as a stochastic dynamical system. Under a global contraction assumption on the deterministic update, they prove the hidden representations form a geometrically ergodic Markov chain with a unique invariant probability measure. The key theoretical result lower-bounds the expected stationary Dirichlet energy, explicitly linking it to noise variance and the graph's spectral gap.

Result: The main theorem establishes a positive lower bound on expected stationary Dirichlet energy that scales with noise variance and spectral gap, guaranteeing that asymptotic representations cannot collapse to the constant manifold. Numerical experiments on both linear and nonlinear recurrent GNNs confirm the emergence of a stationary distribution and match the predicted dependence of limiting Dirichlet energy on noise intensity.

Conclusion: Persistent stochastic perturbations constitute a principled, fundamentally distinct approach to preventing oversmoothing in deep GNNs, providing rigorous guarantees of non-vanishing representation diversity at stationarity, complementary to deterministic methods like skip connections and normalization.

Abstract: Oversmoothing is a fundamental limitation of deep graph neural networks (GNNs), where repeated message passing causes node representations to become increasingly similar, eventually collapsing toward a low-dimensional subspace. This phenomenon limits the effective depth of message-passing architectures and motivates the search for mechanisms that preserve representation diversity. In this paper, we study a recurrent graph neural network in which independent Gaussian noise is injected after every propagation step and analyze the resulting architecture as a stochastic dynamical system. Under a standard global contraction assumption on the deterministic update, we prove that the hidden representations form a geometrically ergodic Markov chain admitting a unique invariant probability measure. Our main theoretical result establishes an explicit positive lower bound on the expected stationary Dirichlet energy, proportional to both the noise variance and the spectral gap of the underlying graph. Consequently, the stationary representations cannot collapse onto the constant manifold, providing a rigorous guarantee that asymptotic oversmoothing is prevented in the sense of non-vanishing Dirichlet energy. Our analysis reveals persistent stochastic perturbations as a fundamentally different mechanism for combating oversmoothing, complementing existing deterministic approaches based on residual connections, normalization, and graph rewiring. Finally, numerical experiments on both linear and nonlinear recurrent graph neural networks closely match the theoretical predictions, illustrating the emergence of a stationary distribution and the predicted dependence of the limiting Dirichlet energy on the noise intensity.

</details>


### [282] [TopoFormer: Topology Meets Attention for Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28259)
*Md Joshem Uddin,Astrit Tola,Cuneyt Gurcan Akcora,Baris Coskunuzer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Topoformer introduces Topo-Scan, a module that converts graph topology into ordered token sequences via filtration slicing, enabling Transformer-based graph representation learning that is parallelizable, theoretically stable, and achieves SOTA on graph classification and molecular prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing persistent homology pipelines for graph topology encoding are computationally expensive, not easily parallelizable, and poorly integrated with deep learning architectures. There is a need for a scalable, attention-compatible method that retains topological inductive biases.

Method: Topo-Scan decomposes a graph into a short, ordered sequence of topological tokens by slicing over node or edge filtrations. These tokens capture multi-scale structural patterns (local motifs to global organization) and are fed into a standard Transformer to produce graph-level embeddings.

Result: Topoformer matches or exceeds strong GNN and topology-based baselines on graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks, while providing predictable and efficient compute.

Conclusion: The work establishes a parallelizable, unifying framework that integrates topological structure into attention-based graph representation learning, opening a new paradigm beyond traditional persistent homology and GNN approaches.

Abstract: We introduce Topoformer, a lightweight and scalable framework for graph representation learning that encodes topological structure into attention-friendly sequences. At the core of our method is Topo-Scan, a novel module that decomposes a graph into a short, ordered sequence of topological tokens by slicing over node or edge filtrations. These sequences capture multi-scale structural patterns, from local motifs to global organization, and are processed by a Transformer to produce expressive graph-level embeddings. Unlike traditional persistent homology pipelines, Topo-Scan is parallelizable, avoids costly diagram computations, and integrates seamlessly with standard deep learning architectures. We provide theoretical guarantees on the stability of our topological encodings and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks. Our results show that Topoformer matches or exceeds strong GNN and topology-based baselines while offering predictable and efficient compute. This work opens a new path for parallelizable and unifying approaches to graph representation learning that integrate topological inductive biases into attention frameworks.

</details>


### [283] [HARGO: Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization for RL Post-Training of LLMs on HPC Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28301)
*Tiangang Li,Xiangbo Tian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HARGO is a heterogeneity-aware RL post-training method that uses confidence-modulated advantage weighting to handle extreme task heterogeneity in HPC domains, outperforming uniform-weight methods like GRPO across binary classification, factual QA, and semantic generation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SFT alone gives LLMs domain knowledge but fails to produce task-appropriate behavior. RL post-training can align models to task-specific rewards, but HPC tasks are extremely heterogeneous (58x answer length variation, three distinct reward distributions, widely varying SFT accuracy). Uniform-weight RL methods like GRPO fail under such heterogeneity.

Method: HARGO introduces per-response importance weighting using confidence-modulated advantage. It computes two signals: (1) a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast, and (2) a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities. These signals modulate the advantage before computing per-response weights, without requiring explicit task-type labels.

Result: HARGO achieves best performance across four HPC tasks and nine compared methods on all three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62%, Data Race F1 91.30%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablation confirms both discrimination and confidence signals contribute complementarily.

Conclusion: HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks, demonstrating that heterogeneity-aware reward weighting is crucial for effective RL post-training in multi-task HPC settings.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can equip large language models (LLMs) with domain knowledge for high-performance computing (HPC) tasks such as data race detection and benchmark question answering. However, knowledge alone does not guarantee task-appropriate behavior: the same SFT model that correctly classifies 88.65\% of C/C++ data race samples produces verbose, imprecise answers to factual queries, with 65.9\% of MLPerf responses exceeding 40 characters. Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training addresses this gap by optimizing for task-specific rewards rather than token-level imitation. Yet HPC tasks exhibit extreme heterogeneity, with binary classification, factual QA, and semantic generation differing by 58x in answer length, spanning three distinct reward distributions, and showing widely varying SFT accuracy. This makes uniform-weight RL methods such as GRPO suboptimal. We propose HARGO, Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization, which introduces per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage: computing a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast and a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities, then modulating the advantage before computing per-response weights, without requiring task-type labels. Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves the best performance on all three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62\%, Data Race F1 91.30\%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablation confirms complementary contributions from both signals. HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks.

</details>


### [284] [Semi-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graphs via Ensemble Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28304)
*Rasmus Tirsgaard,Laurits Fredsgaard,Marisa Wodrich,Mikkel Jordahn,Mikkel N. Schmidt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a semi-supervised learning approach using ensemble consensus to improve molecular property prediction. The method avoids the need for label-preserving augmentations (which are hard to design for molecules) by instead enforcing agreement among ensemble members on unlabeled data, yielding superior accuracy, robustness, and better calibration compared to standard supervised ensembles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Labeled molecular data is expensive and scarce, while unlabeled data is abundant. Standard semi-supervised learning relies on label-preserving data augmentations, but in the molecular domain even minor structural changes can drastically alter chemical properties, making such augmentations difficult to design reliably. This motivates an alternative semi-supervised approach that does not depend on hand-crafted augmentations.

Method: The authors employ an ensemble consensus objective for semi-supervised learning. An ensemble of graph neural networks is trained on both labeled and unlabeled molecular data. The key idea is to enforce prediction consistency across ensemble members on unlabeled examples, effectively using the ensemble's agreement as a supervisory signal. This mechanism exhibits an effect analogous to knowledge distillation, where individual models trained under this regime surpass the performance of traditionally trained full ensembles.

Result: The ensemble consensus semi-supervised approach boosts predictive accuracy across diverse molecular datasets, task types, and GNN architectures. Individual ensemble members trained this way outperform fully supervised ensembles in nearly all cases. The method also increases model robustness and reduces calibration error.

Conclusion: Semi-supervised learning via ensemble consensus is an effective, augmentation-free strategy for molecular machine learning. It simultaneously improves accuracy, robustness, and calibration, offering a practical alternative when designing label-preserving augmentations is infeasible.

Abstract: Machine learning is transforming molecular sciences by accelerating property prediction, simulation, and the discovery of new molecules and materials. Acquiring labeled data in these domains is often costly and time-consuming, whereas large collections of unlabeled molecular data are readily available. Standard semi-supervised learning methods often rely on label-preserving augmentations, which are challenging to design in the molecular domain, where minor changes can drastically alter properties. In this work, we show that semi-supervised methods that rely on an ensemble consensus can boost predictive accuracy across a diverse range of molecular datasets, task types, and graph neural network architectures. We find that training with an ensemble consensus objective increases robustness in models and exhibits an effect similar to knowledge distillation; an individual member of an ensemble trained this way outperforms a full ensemble trained in a traditional supervised fashion in almost all cases. In addition, this type of semi-supervised training reduces calibration error.

</details>


### [285] [Beyond Geometric Complementarity: Coherent Overlap in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28308)
*Huiyuan Tian,Bonan Xu,Shijian Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sparse MoE models route tokens to multiple experts, but experts' subspaces overlap substantially. The paper introduces ESSI and controlled interventions to disentangle route coherence from geometric distinctness. Findings show "coherent overlap": experts share geometric neighborhoods yet multi-expert routing still provides functional benefit, meaning geometric similarity does not imply redundancy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing analyses of sparse MoE language models conflate three distinct quantities: route coherence (which experts are chosen together), candidate quality (individual expert capability), and candidate-by-context interaction (how context modulates expert contributions). The paper argues that geometric accounts of MoE benefit — that co-selected experts should contribute distinct representation directions — have not been rigorously tested by separating these factors. The goal is to determine whether the benefit of multi-expert routing truly comes from disjoint geometric coverage or from other mechanisms.

Method: Three tools are introduced: (1) Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI) to measure subspace overlap between experts; (2) matched-route residuals comparing actual routes to counterfactual alternatives; (3) a prefix-controlled 2×2 factorial design crossing selected vs. unselected candidates with contextual prefix presence. Frozen-route interventions and a controlled Top-k training study (Top-1 vs. Top-2, three seeds) assess functional value. Three paired contrasts are conducted across six MoE architectures (including OLMoE, Mixtral, DeepSeek) spanning 39 factorial cells.

Result: (1) Expert subspaces overlap substantially across all six architectures, yet actual routes explain token representations better than matched alternatives. (2) In all 39 factorial cells, the selected candidate explains more residual variance than the strongest unselected rival, but the actual prefix narrows this advantage: all interactions are negative with 95% CIs below zero. (3) This geometric narrowing does not imply functional redundancy: adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24/39 frozen-route comparisons; the controlled Top-2 training beats Top-1 in all three seeds. This pattern is termed "coherent overlap."

Conclusion: MoE routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood, and useful multi-expert computation persists without requiring disjoint linear coverage. Geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning value — separating route coherence from subspace separation is essential for understanding and optimizing MoE architectures.

Abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models route each token to multiple experts, suggesting a geometric account of their benefit: co-selected experts should contribute distinct representation directions. Existing evidence often conflates route coherence, candidate quality, and candidate-by-context interaction.
