We distinguish these quantities using an Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI), matched-route residuals, and a prefix-controlled $2\times2$ factorial; frozen-route interventions and a controlled Top-$k$ study assess functional value. Three paired contrasts organize the findings. First, across six MoE architectures, expert subspaces overlap substantially, yet actual routes explain token representations better than matched alternatives. Second, across the 39 factorial cells in OLMoE, Mixtral, and DeepSeek, the selected candidate explains more of the residual representation than the strongest unselected rival in every cell, yet the actual prefix narrows this advantage throughout: all interactions are negative, and every 95% confidence interval lies below zero. Third, this geometric narrowing does not imply functional redundancy: adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24 of 39 frozen-route comparisons, while the other 15 estimates are inconclusive; a controlled training study also favors Top-2 over Top-1 in all three seeds. We call this joint pattern coherent overlap: routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood, while useful multi-expert computation persists without disjoint linear coverage. Separating these quantities clarifies why geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning value.

</details>


### [286] [Measuring Distortion in the Empty Regions of Dimensionality Reduction Scatterplots with the Gap Index](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28324)
*Jaume Ros,Alessio Arleo,Fernando Paulovich*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The Gap Index (GI) is a new quality metric for 2D dimensionality reduction projections that quantifies spatial distortion in empty areas by comparing low-dimensional empty triangles to their high-dimensional counterparts, capturing visually salient deformations that traditional metrics miss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing projection quality metrics focus on direct point relationships (distances, neighborhoods) while neglecting distortions in empty layout areas, even though these empty spaces often constitute visually relevant features. A metric sensitive to structural deformations in empty regions is needed.

Method: The Gap Index decomposes the 2D projection space into empty triangles (e.g., via Delaunay triangulation of the projected points). Each empty triangle's geometry is compared to the corresponding high-dimensional configuration of the same points to measure deformation. Per-triangle deformations can be aggregated into a global scalar metric or overlaid as a heatmap to reveal regional distortion patterns.

Result: The GI is sensitive to small structural deformations with high visual impact that popular metrics fail to detect. It is computationally fast and interpretable, providing both global and local distortion assessments.

Conclusion: The Gap Index fills a critical gap in projection quality assessment by explicitly modeling empty-space distortion, offering a fast, interpretable metric that aligns better with human visual perception of 2D layouts than existing point-centric alternatives.

Abstract: Quality metrics play a crucial role in the proper use of dimensionality reduction projections for visual analysis of high-dimensional data. They quantify the degree of distortion of a projection compared to the high-dimensional data and provide a reliable indication of how confident users can be in the structures they see in the resulting layouts. However, most popular metrics focus on capturing direct relationships between points (e.g., distances or neighborhoods) while neglecting distortions in empty areas of the layout, even though these often compose visually relevant features of a 2D layout. In this paper, we introduce the Gap Index (GI), a quality metric for 2D projections that captures visual distortion by measuring spatial distortion in empty areas of a projection. It does so by decomposing the space into empty triangles, which are then compared to their high-dimensional counterparts to compute the deformation. This per-triangle deformation can be aggregated into a single scalar value or overlaid on a projection to visualize regional distortion patterns. Results show that, contrary to popular quality metrics, the GI is sensitive to small structural deformations that have high visual impact. It is also fast to compute and interpretable.

</details>


### [287] [Stage-Replay Divergence Follows the KV Cache: Fixed-Prefix Precision Controls and Bidirectional Cache Transplantation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28495)
*Alexander Boesgaard Lorup*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Stage-replay diagnostics in LLM reasoning systems can produce token-exact replay without preserving live-state fidelity. The K/V cache at a reasoning-stage boundary is causally sufficient for carrying divergent trajectories, but numerical precision (BF16 vs. FP32) moderates whether behavioral disagreements manifest.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To audit the assumption underlying stage-replay diagnostics: that reconstructing intermediate token prefixes and continuing from the decoder state that originally reached the prefix faithfully reproduces the original model behavior. The paper tests whether live-cache continuation and fresh-prefill continuation are behaviorally equivalent at reasoning-stage boundaries.

Method: A matched 200-item experiment on a Qwen2.5-derived system compares retained live cache vs. one-shot prefill of identical integer tokens. A fixed-prefix 2×2 design crosses construction method (live-cache vs. prefill) with numerical precision (BF16 vs. FP32). Token-by-token incremental and retained live caches are compared for bit-exactness. Bidirectional transplantation of all 48 K/V layers tests causal sufficiency. An outcome-blind replication at a later checkpoint validates findings.

Result: In BF16, replicas are exact but constructions differ on 166/200 suffixes and 20 correctness labels; accuracy difference is 1 point (paired 95% CI [-3.5, +5.5]). FP32 eliminates all decoded disagreement (95% Wilson upper bound 1.88%). Token-by-token incremental and retained caches are bit-exact on 12/12 rows. Bidirectional K/V transplantation makes every divergent continuation follow its cache donor: 24/24 at primary checkpoint, 43/43 at a later checkpoint.

Conclusion: Exact-token replay is repeatable without live-state fidelity. On the tested states, the boundary K/V cache is a causally sufficient carrier of divergent trajectories, while numerical precision (BF16 vs. FP32) moderates behavioral expression of divergence.

Abstract: Stage-replay diagnostics reconstruct intermediate token prefixes and treat fresh-prefill continuation as continuation from the decoder state that originally reached the prefix. We audit that assumption at a whole reasoning-stage boundary in a Qwen2.5-derived system. A matched 200-item experiment compares retained live cache with one-shot prefill of identical integer tokens and places an exact replica on both sides. In BF16, replicas remain exact while the constructions differ on 166 suffixes and 20 correctness labels; the accuracy difference is only one point (paired 95% CI [-3.5, +5.5]). A fixed-prefix 2x2 holds all 200 token states constant while crossing construction and precision. The BF16 disagreements recur, whereas FP32 produces no decoded disagreement (95% Wilson upper bound 1.88%). A prospective bridge makes token-by-token incremental and retained live caches bit-exact on 12/12 rows; an all-200 saved-ledger audit reproduces every retained trajectory and comparison fingerprint. Bidirectional transplantation of all 48 key/value layers makes every tested divergent continuation follow its cache donor, both on a selected set at the primary checkpoint (24/24) and an outcome-blind replication at a later checkpoint (43/43). Exact-token replay can therefore be repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity. On the tested states, boundary K/V cache is a causally sufficient carrier of the divergent trajectory, while numerical precision moderates its behavioral expression.

</details>


### [288] [LEDGERMIND: Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28374)
*Enjun Du,Hange Zhou,Chenxu Du,Siyi Liu,Zirong Chen,Ziyu Zheng,Yongqi Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LedgerMind introduces a provenance-constrained state machine for multimodal agents, using a Structured Evidence Ledger with formal guarantees to prevent hallucination and unsupported reasoning, improving both answer accuracy and trajectory faithfulness over standard final-answer evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of multimodal agents for VQA reduces to final-answer accuracy, which obscures critical failure patterns: unsupported intermediate reasoning, phantom grounding (citation-backed entity hallucination), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification. There is a need for trajectory-level accountability that distinguishes grounded correct answers from those reached via language priors or error cancellation.

Method: LedgerMind treats agent trajectories as a provenance-constrained state machine. Tool outputs are normalized into a Structured Evidence Ledger that serves as trajectory state. Downstream reasoning can only cite active ledger entries. Grounding is verified at entity and numeric levels. Repair occurs via typed state transitions with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee — no content can be introduced without tool-produced evidence. The system includes a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher matching reasoning depth to question complexity, and an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine.

Result: Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs demonstrate that LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness, targeting the four obscured failure patterns effectively.

Conclusion: Provenance-constrained agent architectures with structured evidence ledgers offer a principled way to ensure grounded, faithful multimodal reasoning, moving beyond aggregate accuracy to fine-grained trajectory accountability.

Abstract: Multimodal agents for visual question answering increasingly operate as multi-step trajectories that interleave perception, retrieval, and reasoning, yet evaluation still largely reduces to final-answer accuracy. This aggregate signal cannot tell whether a correct answer was reached through grounded evidence, language priors, or accidental error cancellation. We propose to treat a multimodal agent trajectory as a provenance-constrained state machine: tool outputs are normalized into a Structured Evidence Ledger that serves as the trajectory state, downstream reasoning and decision claims may cite only active ledger entries, grounding is checked at the entity and numeric level, and repair is realized as typed state transitions that cannot introduce content without tool-produced provenance. We instantiate this design as LedgerMind (Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger), augmented by a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher that matches reasoning depth to question complexity, and an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee. We use LedgerMind to target four recurring failure patterns that final-answer accuracy tends to obscure: unsupported intermediate reasoning, citation-backed entity hallucination (Phantom Grounding), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification. Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs show that LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness.

</details>


### [289] [Hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo for Order-Optimal Neural Actor-Critic in Average-Reward CMDPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28390)
*Ankur Naskar,Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper resolves the open problem of achieving order-optimal convergence in average-reward CMDPs with neural critics by introducing a hierarchical MLMC neural critic that overcomes the bias-cost trade-off, enabling a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm with $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$ optimality gap and constraint violation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In average-reward CMDPs with neural critics, a fundamental bias-cost trade-off exists: reducing critic estimation bias under NTK analysis requires substantially more optimization cost, preventing order-optimal convergence in primal-dual frameworks. This bottleneck has kept the problem open until now.

Method: The authors propose a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that simultaneously debiases across trajectory sampling and critic optimization levels. This estimator achieves the bias of a long optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. This critic is then integrated into a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization.

Result: The proposed algorithm achieves both an optimality gap and constraint violation of order $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$, establishing the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for this setting. Notably, the method does not require knowledge of the underlying mixing time, and the results are novel even in the unconstrained (standard MDP) setting.

Conclusion: The hierarchical MLMC neural critic successfully resolves the bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation, enabling the first order-optimal primal-dual algorithm for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with neural critics and general policy parameterization.

Abstract: Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) provide a natural framework for reinforcement learning in safety-critical applications, where agents maximize long-term reward while satisfying long-term constraints. Although primal-dual actor-critic methods with linear critics are well understood, extending order-optimal convergence guarantees to neural critics in average-reward CMDPs has remained open. The main challenge is a fundamental bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation: under Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) analysis, reducing critic bias substantially increases critic optimization cost, preventing order-optimal convergence in the primal-dual framework. We resolve this bottleneck by introducing a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that performs debiasing simultaneously across trajectory sampling and critic optimization. The resulting estimator attains the bias of a long critic optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. Building on this estimator, we develop a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm that achieves both an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$. This establishes the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, while eliminating the need to know the underlying mixing time. Our results are novel even in the unconstrained setting.

</details>


### [290] [Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late? Decode on the Decision-Time Critical Path, Tested with Pre-Compiled Policy Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28399)
*Zihan Dong,Rui Qian,Qishi Zhan,Dongshen Peng,Kaixin Li,Yu Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Computer-use agents fail on transient GUI events due to slow autoregressive decoding. AAPT solves this by pre-computing a conditional policy tree during idle periods, enabling instant action execution when events occur, dramatically improving success rates without modifying the underlying model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GUI automation agents suffer from a fundamental latency problem: autoregressive decoding of actions takes too long on the critical path, causing agents to miss transient interface events (windows, popups, etc.) that close before the action is generated. The authors aim to eliminate this decoding delay without retraining or fine-tuning the underlying model.

Method: AAPT (Adaptive Anticipatory Policy Trees) operates in two phases. During idle screen periods, the frozen multimodal model constructs a bounded conditional policy tree containing observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines, sized to cover the model's own decoding latency. When a GUI event occurs, a lightweight observer matches change-gated frames to a prepared branch and immediately executes the corresponding action without text generation. This shifts decoding off the critical path entirely.

Result: In paired trials with pre-registered endpoints, AAPT improved success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 within contested decision windows (p=1.8×10⁻³) with zero incorrect actions. Both open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines scored zero. A preparation-time sweep confirmed the latency-based tree-sizing rule. Ablations identified three requirements: fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing. An oracle probe shifted the causal bottleneck hypothesis from planning quality to branch routing. The effect replicated on an independent multimodal model over 126 trials (p=4.9×10⁻¹³). On an external benchmark, AAPT matched reactive baseline performance with complementary strengths.

Conclusion: AAPT performs best when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance, while reactive execution remains stronger when they cannot. Branch routing accuracy, not planning quality, is the primary bottleneck limiting further gains.

Abstract: Computer-use agents often fail on transient GUI events because they produce the correct action only after the relevant window has already closed. We identify the main cause as expensive autoregressive decoding on the decision-time critical path. We propose Adaptive Anticipatory Policy Trees (AAPT), which eliminates this delay without modifying the underlying model. During idle screen periods, the same frozen multimodal model constructs a bounded conditional policy tree with observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines. The tree is sized to cover the model's own decoding latency. When an event occurs, a lightweight observer matches change-gated frames to a prepared branch and immediately executes the corresponding action without generating new text. In paired trials with pre-registered endpoints and exact McNemar tests, AAPT improves the success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 within a contested decision window ($p=1.8\times10^{-3}$), while producing no incorrect actions. Both open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines achieve zero success because they still decode during execution. A preparation-time sweep shows that the gain emerges where the latency-based tree-sizing rule predicts, and ablations reveal three key requirements: fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing. A pre-registered oracle probe rejects our initial hypothesis and instead points to branch routing as the causal bottleneck. We further reproduce the effect on an independent general-purpose multimodal model over 126 paired trials ($p=4.9\times10^{-13}$). On an external benchmark, AAPT matches the overall performance of a reactive baseline, although the two methods exhibit complementary strengths. Together, these results suggest that AAPT performs best when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance, whereas reactive execution remains stronger when they cannot.

</details>


### [291] [On-Policy and Off-Policy Learning for Large Action Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28408)
*Imad Aouali*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This thesis addresses policy learning in contextual bandits with large action spaces, covering both on-policy (regret minimization via structured Bayesian methods like meTS and dTS) and off-policy (variance reduction, optimization, and pessimism via sDM, concave objectives, and PAC-Bayesian smoothing) settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In large action spaces, both on-policy and off-policy contextual bandit learning suffer from inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and challenging optimization landscapes. Existing methods fail to adequately share statistical strength across actions or control the bias–variance trade-off.

Method: The thesis develops: (1) meTS, a mixed-effect Thompson sampling method, and dTS, a diffusion-prior-based Thompson sampling method, both providing regret bounds in terms of an effective number of actions; (2) sDM, a structured direct method using latent variables for off-policy evaluation; (3) concave policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives to mitigate optimization error; and (4) differentiable pessimistic methods combining exponential smoothing with PAC-Bayesian bounds to regularize importance-sampling estimators.

Result: meTS and dTS achieve regret guarantees that scale with an effective (smaller) number of actions. The analysis reveals that optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces. The proposed concave objectives are efficiently optimizable, and the pessimistic PAC-Bayesian methods effectively control the bias–variance trade-off in off-policy evaluation.

Conclusion: Structured Bayesian priors and latent-variable models can effectively share information across actions, reducing the effective action-space complexity. For off-policy learning, addressing optimization error and incorporating principled pessimism via PAC-Bayesian bounds are critical for reliable policy learning in large action spaces.

Abstract: This thesis studies policy learning in interactive systems where an agent observes a context, selects an action from a very large set, and receives partial feedback. The main framework is contextual bandits, with two paradigms: on-policy learning, where the agent interacts sequentially with the environment and minimizes regret, and off-policy learning, where it learns from logged data collected by a logging policy. In large action spaces, both settings face major challenges: inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization landscapes. The first part develops structured Bayesian methods for on-policy learning. We introduce meTS, a mixed-effect extension of Thompson sampling, and dTS, which leverages diffusion-inspired priors to model dependencies between actions. These methods share information across actions and yield regret guarantees depending on an effective number of actions. The second part addresses off-policy learning. We propose sDM, a structured direct method based on latent variables, show that optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces, and introduce concave, efficiently optimizable policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives. Finally, we develop differentiable pessimistic methods based on exponential smoothing and PAC-Bayesian bounds to control the bias-variance trade-off of regularized importance-sampling estimators.

</details>


### [292] [QQWorld: Quantile-Quantile Matching for World Model Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28415)
*Zhoushun Yu,Xiaoyu Hu,Xiangyu Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QQWorld replaces the Epps-Pulley regularization in LeWorld with a quantile-quantile matching objective, which better controls heavy-tailed deviations in latent representations by maintaining effective corrective gradients for tail samples, improving planning success rates across four control environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latent world models like LeWM rely on isotropic Gaussian regularization of latents (via Epps-Pulley), but the corrective gradients of EP rapidly vanish for isolated tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations insufficiently controlled. This motivates a new objective that maintains gradient effectiveness in the tails.

Method: QQWorld introduces a quantile-quantile (QQ) matching objective that directly aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, ensuring effective corrective gradients even in the tails. A cross-batch QQ variant is also proposed, which expands the ranking pool using detached samples from previous batches, with a characterization of the resulting bias-variance trade-off.

Result: QQWorld improves the average planning success rate of LeWM across four control environments, while consistently achieving better Gaussian alignment and producing thinner latent tails.

Conclusion: The QQ matching objective is a more effective regularization approach for latent world models than EP, as it robustly handles tail behavior, leading to better distribution alignment and improved planning performance.

Abstract: Latent world models enable efficient planning by predicting future states in a compact representation space, but their performance depends critically on the quality of the learned latent distribution. LeWorldModel (LeWM) regularizes its latents toward an isotropic Gaussian using the Epps-Pulley (EP) objective. We show that the corrective gradients of EP rapidly vanish for isolated tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations insufficiently controlled. To address this limitation, we propose QQWorld, which replaces EP with a quantile-quantile matching objective that directly aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, thereby maintaining effective corrective gradients in the tails. We further develop cross-batch QQ, which enlarges the effective ranking pool using detached samples from previous batches, and characterize its bias-variance trade-off. Across four control environments, QQWorld effectively improves the average planning success rate of LeWM, while consistently yielding better Gaussian alignment and thinner latent tails.

</details>


### [293] [QAdapt: A Noise-Adaptive Neural Pre-Decoding Framework for Quantum Error Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28422)
*Ran Miao,Rui Luo,Xiaohan Shan,Xiaoming Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QAdapt is a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework that learns spatiotemporal noise correlations from syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving hardware noise without catastrophic forgetting, and feeds residual syndromes to a conventional global decoder, achieving up to 5.79% logical error rate reduction and 9.32% latency reduction on Google's Willow benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FTQC performance is bottlenecked by classical decoder latency and by noise that is strong, heterogeneous, and nonstationary. Fixed neural decoders suffer from simulation-to-hardware distribution shift, motivating an adaptive approach that can track evolving noise conditions in real time.

Method: QAdapt is a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface codes. It captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, uses sequential adaptation to handle evolving noise while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and forwards residual syndrome data to a conventional global decoder rather than replacing it entirely.

Result: Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations on rotated surface-code memory circuits, QAdapt consistently reduced logical error rate vs. the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data (without target-domain fine-tuning), it achieved up to 5.79% reduction in logical error rate and 9.32% reduction in backend decoding latency.

Conclusion: QAdapt offers a practical, decoder-compatible method for improving both the robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise, without requiring replacement of existing global decoders.

Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) relies on quantum error correction to suppress physical errors and preserve logical information at scale. In practice, however, performance is constrained not only by physical noise but also by the latency of classical decoders processing rapidly generated syndrome data. This challenge is exacerbated by hardware noise that is strong, heterogeneous, and nonstationary, as well as by the simulation-to-hardware distribution shift that can substantially degrade fixed neural decoders. We present QAdapt, a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction. QAdapt captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and forwards the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder. Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations for rotated surface-code memory circuits, QAdapt consistently reduces the logical error rate relative to the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data, without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves reductions of up to 5.79 percent in logical error rate and 9.32 percent in backend decoding latency on the residual syndrome. These results demonstrate that QAdapt provides a practical and decoder-compatible approach to improving the robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise.

</details>


### [294] [Kohn-Sham Spectral Embedding on Sparse Graphs at the Nishimori Temperature for Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28428)
*V. S. Usatyuk,D. A. Sapozhnikov,S. I. Egorov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KSSE replaces dense CNN classifiers with a sparse-graph spectral embedding at the Nishimori temperature of a Random-Bond Ising Model. Using FFT on circulant blocks and Rayleigh refinement, it achieves 88.93% Top-1 on ImageNet-1000 with ~21M parameters — outperforming Swin-L and matching ViT-H/14 while using 10–30× fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense classifier layers in vision models incur massive parameter counts. The authors seek a physics-inspired, sparse alternative that preserves or improves accuracy while drastically reducing model footprint, drawing on spectral graph theory and statistical mechanics (the Nishimori temperature and Random-Bond Ising Model) to structure the embedding.

Method: Pre-trained features are mapped onto quasi-cyclic LDPC graphs, with a regularized Laplacian serving as a Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian. D independent channel spectral problems are solved via FFT on circulant blocks (exploiting Pontryagin self-duality of Z/pZ) and low-order Rayleigh refinement in O(N log N + k²_mode N). Graph topology is optimized via star-domain surgery: edge shifts create local convexity around codewords while bounding residual frustration. Six theorems are proved covering Ihara–Bass/BP links, trapping-set eigenvalues, channel separability with exchange-correlation bounds, a surgery theorem, quasi-stationarity perturbation, and fixed-point convergence.

Result: On ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features (D=1792), KSSE attains 88.93% Top-1 accuracy with ~21.24M parameters — surpassing Swin-L (197M, 86.4–87.3%) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0–89.5%), while using ~10× and ~30× fewer parameters respectively. Fractal analysis confirms a landscape transition from rough (D₂>3) to star-domain basins (D₂<1), enabling k_mode=5 Rayleigh refinement.

Conclusion: KSSE demonstrates that a physics-motivated, sparse spectral embedding can match or exceed the accuracy of large dense classifiers and transformers at a fraction of the parameter cost, with rigorous theoretical guarantees spanning spectral graph theory, belief propagation, and optimization landscape analysis.

Abstract: We introduce Kohn--Sham Spectral Embedding (KSSE), a physics-inspired energy-based model replacing dense CNN classifiers with a sparse-graph spectral embedding evaluated at the Nishimori temperature of an associated Random-Bond Ising Model. By mapping pre-trained features onto quasi-cyclic low-density parity-check graphs and constructing a regularized Laplacian acting as a Kohn--Sham Hamiltonian, we solve $D$ independent channel spectral problems in $\mathcal{O}(N\log N + k^2_{\text{mode}} N)$ time via FFT on circulant blocks (leveraging Pontryagin self-duality of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$) and low-order Rayleigh refinement. Graph topology is optimized using \emph{star-domain surgery}: rather than destroying information-carrying codewords by removing frustrated cycles, we construct edge shifts creating local convexity around codewords while bounding residual frustration to $ρ(B_γ)\leq 1+δ$. Multi-scale fractal analysis ($D_2$ spectrum) and fractal learning-rate landscape certifies a landscape transition from rough regimes ($D_2>3$) to star-domain basins ($D_2<1$), enabling Rayleigh refinement with $k_{\text{mode}}=5$ modes. We prove six theoretical results: a generalized Ihara--Bass identity linking belief propagation to the Laplacian; trapping-set eigenvalue correspondence; additive channel separability with an explicit exchange-correlation bound; a surgery theorem bounding frustration with attractor width $Ω(1/\sqrt{d_{\min}})$; a quasi-stationarity perturbation bound; and a fixed-point convergence theorem. In a transductive protocol on ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features ($D=1792$), KSSE achieves \textbf{88.93\%} Top-1 accuracy using $\approx 21.24$M parameters, outperforming Swin-L (197M, 86.4--87.3\%) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0--89.5\%) under standard inductive setups, while reducing model footprint by $10\times$ and $30\times$, respectively.

</details>


### [295] [Oracle-Budgeted Molecular Optimization with Short-Term Graph Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28437)
*Jiannan Yang,Veronika Thost,Xiang Ling,Tengfei Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A plug-in module called short-term graph memory uses an online graph neural surrogate to pre-screen candidate molecules, directing a fixed oracle budget toward higher-utility molecules. It boosts optimization scores across multiple generators at no extra oracle cost, with benefits linked to the generator's search breadth and native exploitation ability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Molecular optimization typically operates under a limited oracle budget, making the selection of which molecules to evaluate as critical as generation. Existing generators often waste oracle calls on low-utility candidates. The authors aim to make oracle spending more selective without altering generator architectures.

Method: The authors propose a plug-in module — short-term graph memory — that maintains an online graph neural network surrogate trained on previously evaluated molecules. Each round, the surrogate pre-screens the candidate pool, ranking molecules by predicted utility so the fixed oracle budget is allocated only to top-ranked candidates. The module preserves the generator's architecture and native update rule.

Result: Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard benchmark, the module improves mean top-10 score with no extra oracle cost and never underperforms the base generator. Gains extend to all four tested generators at a tight 1,000-call budget. At larger budgets, benefit correlates with two backbone properties: search breadth and how effectively native search already exploits oracle feedback.

Conclusion: Short-term graph memory provides a simple, architecture-preserving way to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively. Its effectiveness depends on generator characteristics, offering practical guidance on which generators benefit most from surrogate-guided selection.

Abstract: Molecular optimization is commonly performed under a limited oracle budget, which makes deciding what to evaluate as important as deciding what to generate. We introduce short-term graph memory, a plug-in module that preserves the generator architecture and native update rule while learning from previously evaluated molecules to prioritize subsequent oracle queries. The module maintains an online graph neural surrogate that pre-screens each round's candidate pool, so the fixed oracle budget is spent on molecules with higher predicted utility. Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard molecular optimization benchmark, it improves the mean top-10 score at no extra oracle cost and never falls behind the base on any oracle; the gain extends to all four generators we tested at a tight budget of one thousand calls. We then analyze how surrogate-guided selection interacts with the exploration and exploitation behavior of different generators. Its benefit at larger budgets is consistent with two properties of the backbone: how broadly it searches, and how effectively its native search already exploits oracle feedback. We provide a simple way to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively, and evidence on which generators benefit from it.

</details>


### [296] [The Role of Causality in Algorithmic Recourse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28497)
*Srikanth Avasarala,Varun Gupta,Shahin Jabbari,Saber Salehkaleybar,Juba Ziani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a causal performative framework for algorithmic recourse, showing that recourse recommendations ignoring causal structure can induce strategic gaming and degrade model performance. Causal recourse yields performatively stable equilibria, reducing gaming incentives and the need for repeated retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing algorithmic recourse methods optimize for flipping model predictions without ensuring that recommended changes reflect genuine qualification improvements. This leads to strategic gaming by individuals, degrading classifier accuracy and rendering recourse policies ineffective after retraining—a failure mode not adequately addressed in prior work.

Method: The authors formalize recourse within a causal performative prediction framework. They model how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model (SCM), capturing feature interactions and effects on the true label. This yields a non-convex optimization problem. They characterize conditions for existence of performatively stable solutions and propose efficient iterative dynamics to compute them.

Result: The analysis demonstrates that non-causal recourse policies induce large, misaligned behavioral responses. In contrast, causal recourse converges to stable equilibria that reduce gaming incentives. Experiments on semi-synthetic and real credit datasets show the causal approach consistently outperforms standard empirical risk minimization and reduces the need for repeated model retraining under distribution shifts.

Conclusion: Recourse policies must account for the causal structure underlying features to avoid performative effects and strategic manipulation. Causal recourse provides stable, effective recommendations that align individual incentives with genuine improvement, reducing both gaming behavior and costly model retraining cycles.

Abstract: Algorithmic recourse aims to provide individuals with actionable changes to improve their predicted outcomes in high-stakes classification settings, such as loan and mortgage applications. However, most existing approaches focus only on flipping a model's prediction, without accounting for whether the recommended changes lead to genuine improvement in an individual's true qualifications or merely enable strategic gaming of the classifier. Consequently, deployed recourse policies can induce behavioral responses that degrade predictive accuracy and become ineffective after model retraining.
  In this work, we formalize this failure mode through a causal performative framework for recourse. We model how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model, capturing interactions among features as well as their effect on the true label. These causal responses induce a non-convex optimization problem, even under standard convex losses. We characterize conditions under which performatively stable solutions exist and can be efficiently computed via simple iterative dynamics. Our analysis reveals that recourse policies that ignore causal structure can induce large, misaligned behavioral responses, whereas causal recourse leads to stable equilibria that reduce incentives for gaming. Experiments on both semi-synthetic and real credit datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms standard empirical risk minimization while reducing the need for repeated model retraining to accommodate distribution shifts caused by strategic agent behavior.

</details>


### [297] [Same Graph Cross-Task Transfer in GNNs: Protocols and Predictors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28525)
*Neelam Akula,Surbhi Kumar,Murat Kantarcioglu,Baris Coskunuzer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper formalizes transfer learning between node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP) on the same graph, proposes a leakage-free evaluation protocol, and finds that NC→LP transfer is reliably beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP→NC transfer is fragile and only helps in structure-dominant regimes. A CoTask Score (CTS) is introduced to summarize joint utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of cross-task transfer between NC and LP on the same graph use incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and inconsistent negative sampling, making conclusions unreliable. The authors aim to rigorously characterize when and how supervision can be reused across these two tasks.

Method: A leakage-free protocol is proposed: fixed node and edge splits, a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges, and fixed negatives for LP. Three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS) are evaluated under this protocol. The CoTask Score (CTS) is introduced to measure joint NC+LP utility when sharing one encoder.

Result: NC→LP transfer is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs. LP→NC transfer is fragile and can degrade accuracy with naive representation reuse; it becomes reliably positive only when LP is easy but NC is unsaturated (structure-dominant regime), suggesting LP functions as structural pretraining. Simple dataset statistics like homophily can guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.

Conclusion: Same-graph NC-LP transfer is strongly directional and predictable. The proposed protocol and CTS provide a principled framework for evaluating and designing multi-task graph learning systems, with homophily serving as a practical guide for deployment decisions.

Abstract: Many real-world graphs support multiple predictive tasks over the same underlying structure, creating an opportunity to reuse supervision across node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP). However, existing evaluations often rely on incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and negative sampling rules, making conclusions about same-graph cross-task transfer unreliable. We formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and propose a leakage-free protocol that fixes node and edge splits, uses a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges, and employs fixed negatives for LP. Across three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS), we find that transfer is strongly directional and predictable: NC $\to$ LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP $\to$ NC is fragile and can even degrade accuracy under naive representation reuse. LP $\to$ NC becomes reliably positive mainly in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated, suggesting that LP acts as structural pretraining. Finally, we introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to summarize joint NC+LP utility when a shared encoder must serve both tasks, and show that simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.

</details>


### [298] [$β$-OPSD: Deriving with Policy Optimization, Training with Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28582)
*Jiawei Xu,Minghui Liu,Juzheng Zhang,Tom Goldstein,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Vanilla on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is brittle because it implicitly fixes the KL penalty weight β=1. The authors generalize it to β-OPSD, where β is a tunable regularization parameter that interpolates between a reference policy and a privileged teacher. Instead of costly RL optimization, they use the closed-form solution as a distillation target implemented via token-level logit mixing, achieving efficient and stable policy improvement for reasoning language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vanilla OPSD is promising but empirically brittle, requiring substantial engineering to work reliably. The authors identify that this brittleness stems from a structural limitation: OPSD implicitly fixes the KL divergence weight β at 1, which is suboptimal. By exposing β as a controllable parameter, they aim to improve stability and performance while preserving OPSD's computational efficiency.

Method: The authors frame OPSD as a policy optimization problem with a β-weighted KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy. They derive β-OPSD's optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between the reference and teacher policies. Rather than optimizing via high-variance RL, they convert the closed-form solution into a distillation target by mixing reference and teacher token-level logits according to β. Return-to-go credit assignment is used to align token-level updates with the sequence-level objective.

Result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that β-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, yielding improved optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance.

Conclusion: β-OPSD provides a principled bridge between self-distillation and policy optimization. By tuning β, practitioners can trade off proximity to a reference policy against teacher guidance, achieving more stable and effective training without sacrificing the efficiency that makes OPSD practical.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a promising approach to improve reasoning language models, but it remains brittle in practice: making it work reliably often requires substantial engineering effort. We identify a structural source of this difficulty: vanilla OPSD is precisely the $β=1$ member of a broader policy-optimization family, where $β$ weights the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy. This equivalence turns $β$ from an implicit value fixed at one into a controllable regularization parameter, yielding a more general formulation that trades off proximity to a reference policy against privileged teacher guidance. We introduce $β$-OPSD and derive its optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between the reference policy and the privileged teacher. Directly optimizing this objective with reinforcement learning, however, would be costly and high-variance. Rather than optimize the RL objective directly, we turn its closed-form solution into a distillation target. Each value of $β$ selects a target along the reference-to-teacher path, which we implement efficiently by mixing their token-level logits. In this way, inexpensive distillation approximates the solution of expensive policy optimization. Return-to-go credit assignment further aligns token updates with the sequence-level objective while retaining the simplicity of OPSD. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that $β$-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, improving optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance. Our results provide a principled route from self-distillation to policy optimization and back without sacrificing the efficiency that makes OPSD practical.

</details>


### [299] [KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28608)
*Sparsh Roy,Samuel Girmachew,Nishita Chavan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KAISEN is a five-phase audit pipeline for clinical risk models, stress-tested to failure on synthetic data across 16 diseases and 15 social-determinant axes. Key findings: (1) significance-based disparity detection conflates effect size with statistical power, (2) post-hoc threshold optimization robustly reduces disparity while Platt scaling is unreliable, (3) mechanism diagnostics fail under proxy misspecification without signaling failure, and (4) CUSUM drift monitoring thresholds fail to transfer across cohort realizations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical risk models exhibit disparate error rates across patient subgroups, but existing audit pipelines lack rigorous stress-testing. It is unclear which audit components are trustworthy and under what conditions they break, undermining confidence in fairness assessments and mitigations.

Method: The authors propose KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline: (1) subgroup stratification, (2) disparity measurement, (3) mechanism diagnostics, (4) post-hoc mitigation, and (5) drift monitoring. The pipeline is evaluated on a synthetic benchmark with known ground truth spanning 16 disease prediction tasks, 15 social-determinant-of-health axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. Each component is tested to the point of failure.

Result: Four key findings: (i) Rank correlation between significance count and raw equalized-odds difference (EOD) is ρ=0.56, rising to ρ=0.78 when EOD is standardized by minimum detectable effect, showing significance conflates gap magnitude with statistical power. (ii) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48/48 held-out runs (Δ=-0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]); group-wise Platt scaling improves EOD in only 19/48 runs (95% CI [0.26, 0.55]) with near-zero mean effect. (iii) Mechanism diagnostics classify all 144 controlled cases correctly but recover 0/48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no failure signal. (iv) CUSUM produces 27 false alarms and misses 7/8 shifts across different seeds (χ² p=0.002), showing threshold non-transferability.

Conclusion: Audit pipeline components must be stress-tested to failure before deployment. Significance-based disparity metrics are confounded by statistical power; Platt scaling is unreliable for EOD mitigation; mechanism diagnostics fail silently under proxy misspecification; and CUSUM thresholds do not transfer across cohort realizations. All findings are synthetic and require clinical validation.

Abstract: Clinical risk models routinely achieve strong aggregate performance while producing materially different error rates across patient subgroups. Audit pipelines have been proposed to catch this, but their components are rarely stress-tested, so it is unclear which parts of an audit can be trusted and under what conditions. We present KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline covering subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring, evaluated to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. Four findings follow. (i) Significance tracks each axis's gap against its own minimum detectable effect: rank correlation between significance count and raw equalized-odds difference (EOD) across the 15 axes is rho = 0.56, rising to rho = 0.78 once EOD is standardized by that floor. (ii) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48 of 48 held-out runs (paired delta = -0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]), while group-wise Platt scaling -- the better calibrator -- behaves as a coin flip on EOD (19 of 48 runs improved, 95% CI [0.26, 0.55]) with mean effect near zero, so what an audit should report is the variance, not the average. (iii) The mechanism diagnostic classifies 144 of 144 controlled cases correctly but recovers none of 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no signal that it failed. (iv) CUSUM failures and false alarms track cohort realization far more than disease: at the reference threshold, all 27 false alarms and 7 of 8 missed shifts come from different seeds (chi-squared p = 0.002), so a threshold tuned on one cohort fails to transfer. All results are synthetic with known ground truth and do not establish clinical validity. Code, artifacts, and scripts reproducing every number are released.

</details>
